summary.title: Enhanced sensitivity to variation of me/mp in molecular spectra
summary.authors: D. DeMille, S. Sainis, J. Sage, T. Bergeman, S. Kotochigova, and E. Tiesinga
summary.field_subfield: Atomic physics / Molecular physics / Precision measurement
summary.type_of_paper: Theory and proposed experiment / Computational and experimental spectroscopy
summary.executive_summary:
We propose new experiments with high sensitivity to a possible spatial or temporal variation of the electron-to-proton mass ratio µ ≡ me/mp. We consider a nearly-degenerate pair of molecular vibrational levels, where each state is associated with a different electronic potential. The change in the splitting between such levels, with respect to a change in µ, can be large both on an absolute scale and relative to the splitting. We demonstrate the existence of such pairs of levels in Cs2. The narrow spectral lines achievable with ultracold Cs2 in these long-lived levels make this system promising for future searches for small variations in µ. 

We show that the energy of molecular vibrational levels can be highly sensitive to changes in µ. In addition, pairs of closely-spaced levels can be used to enhance the sensitivity relative to the level splitting. We show spectroscopic data verifying such a near-degeneracy in the ground vibronic levels of Cs2. We argue that the splitting between pairs of levels in Cs2 could be measured precisely enough to sense a fractional change ∆µ/µ ≲10−17. 

The sensitivity of our proposed measurement is governed by a few key parameters. Most important is the absolute change ∂µΩ of the energy splitting Ω with respect to a fractional change ∆µ/µ: ∂µΩ ≡ ∂Ω/d(lnµ). (ℏ = c = 1 throughout.) Ω can be measured with statistical uncertainty δΩ = Γ/S, where Γ is the linewidth of the transition and S is the signal-to-noise. Hence, ∆µ/µ can be detected with statistical uncertainty δ(∆µ/µ) = δΩ/∂µΩ = (Γ/∂µΩ)S−1, and the ratio ∂µΩ/Γ provides a primary figure of merit for any such measurement. However, the relative change of the splitting, ∂µΩ/Ω, is also of importance, for two reasons. First, since ultimately Ω must be measured with respect to some reference clock (with fractional uncertainty δΩc/Ωc), it is impossible to determine Ω to better than δΩmin = Ω(δΩc/Ωc). In addition, many systematic effects are proportional to Ω (e.g. Doppler shifts). Hence, ∂µΩ/Ω provides an important secondary figure of merit. 

We analyze the shifts in molecular energy levels when µ changes, with the assumption that both me and α remain constant. In this case, a change in µ corresponds to a variation of mp; in addition, molecular electronic potentials are independent of µ, since such potentials depend parametrically only on the Rydberg energy Ry = meα2/2. (The assumption of constant α and me is equivalent to using a reference clock based on optical atomic transitions, which also depend parametrically only on Ry and α.) We approximate the vibrational energy levels Ev via the WKB quantization condition: 

Z Ro Ri p2M[Ev −V(R)]dR = (v + 1/2)π, (1) 

where R is the internuclear distance, V(R) is the potential with minimum value 0, Ri(Ro) is the classical inner (outer) turning point of V(R) at energy Ev, and M ∝mp is the reduced mass of the nuclei in the molecule. Varying Eq. (1) with respect to both µ and v, one obtains for the energy sensitivity ∂µEv: 

∂µEv ≡ ∂Ev/d(lnµ) = (v + 1/2)2ρ(Ev), (2) 

where ρ(Ev) = (∂Ev/∂v)−1 ≈ (Ev −Ev−1)−1 is the density of states at energy Ev [4]. 

Near its minimum, a typical potential is harmonic, with Ev = (v + 1/2)ω and ρ(Ev) = ω−1 (ω is the classical oscillator frequency). Hence, for the harmonic part of the potential, ∂µEv = (v + 1/2)ω/2 = Ev/2 has a ∼v-fold enhancement for the vth vibrational level. (This can also be derived from ω ∝M−1/2.) This constitutes a general mechanism for amplifying the absolute size of ∂µΩ. 

For sufficiently large values of v, real molecular potentials are not harmonic. For highest values of v, Ev approaches the dissociation limit D, and the density of states ρ(Ev) becomes large. Hence, the value of ∂µEv again becomes small for the highest levels in any potential. Therefore, at some intermediate value of v, ∂µEv is maximized. We verified this behavior both for a generic (Morse) potential with analytic expressions for Ev, and for the experimentally determined X1Σ+g potential of Cs2 (see below). In both cases, the maximum value of ∂µEv is obtained for levels with E(max)v ≈ 3D/4, and there the energy sensitivity is only slightly diminished from its expected value in the harmonic approximation: 

∂µE(max)v ≈ (2/3)(E(max)v/2). Note that a recent paper [4] discussed the prospect for detecting variations in µ using Feschbach resonances in the scattering between ultracold atoms. However, such resonances arise from the presence of vibrational states (associated with potentials for other internal states of the atoms) that are very near D, where ∂µEv is small. The scheme discussed here uses the much larger energy sensitivity for states of intermediate vibrational excitation. 

The same mechanism can be used, in some cases, to provide transitions with extremely large relative shifts ∂µΩ/Ω. 

Consider a situation in which two molecular electronic potentials X and Y overlap, but the minimum of potential Y (at energy TY) is at higher energy than that of X (at 0). In this case, an excited level of X with vibrational number vX ≫ 1 and energy E1 = E(X)vX can be quite near in energy to a lower vibrational level of Y (vY ≪vX), with energy E2 = TY + E(Y)vY. The energy difference between such a pair of levels is small (Ω= |E1−E2| ≪ E(X)vX), but can retain a large sensitivity to changes in µ, since ∂µΩ= ∂µE(X)vX −∂µE(Y)vY ≈ ∂µE(X)vX. 

The molecule Cs2 is an attractive system for implementing this scheme. Cs2 has two low-lying, overlapping potentials: the deep X1Σ+g ground state, and the shallower a3Σ+u state, each of which dissociates to a pair of ground-state Cs atoms [5]. The vibrational splittings of these two potentials are incommensurate, and the large mass of Cs yields a high density of states; hence near-degeneracies appeared likely. In fact, Ref. [6] reported evidence for such in the high-J levels of the vX = 137 state. Furthermore, all rovibrational levels of both potentials have extremely long radiative lifetimes (≫ 1 s) [7], and production of ultracold Cs2 molecules (which can be measured over long coherence times) has become routine [7, 8]; hence the system can yield spectral lines with narrow width Γ. Finally, it has been predicted that deeply-bound levels of the a3Σ+u state—which lie near E(max)v for the X1Σ+g state—can be efficiently populated [9, 10]. 

We explicitly calculate ∂µEv for all vibrational levels in the X and a states of Cs2, using the fitted potentials described below and numerical solutions for Ev with slightly different values of M. (Similar results were obtained very simply for all but the highest-v levels of the X state, using a Dunham expansion for Ev [5, 6].) A plot of ∂µEv versus binding energy (Eb(v) ≡Ev−D) is shown for both potentials in Fig. 1. The behavior throughout is as expected from Eq. 2. 

Note that indeed, as expected from the previous discussion, ∂µE(a)va ≪ ∂µE(X)vX for close-lying X and a state levels (such that E(a)b(va) ≈ E(X)b(vX)). In addition, ∂µE(X)vX increases monotonically with |Eb|, throughout the region of a state levels. Hence, a search for variation of µ will be most sensitive when using nearly-degenerate levels lying as close as possible to the a state minimum. 

We experimentally determine the positions of deeply bound a3Σ+u levels, using two-color photoassociation (PA) spectroscopy [11, 12]. A sample of ultracold (T ∼ 100 µK) Cs atoms is cooled and confined in a dark SPOT magneto-optic trap. After applying a uniform magnetic field, the atoms are optically pumped into the 6s1/2 F = mF = 4 state. Next a CW laser (the PA laser) excites the atoms into a bound state [14] of the Cs2 (2)0−g potential (dissociating to the 6s1/2 + 6p3/2 asymptote). This excited state decays to a manifold of a3Σ+u vibrational levels, which are ionized by a pulsed laser. A second CW (probe) laser is applied to search for resonances between the desired a3Σ+u levels and the (2)0−g level excited by the PA laser. On such a resonance, the probe beam can shift the excited state offresonance with the PA laser and decrease the rate of molecule formation. We scan the probe laser frequency while monitoring the ion yield, and look for resonant dips in the signal. The difference between the frequencies of the resonant probe and PA lasers gives the binding energy of the a3Σ+u level. We report results for Eb relative to the hyperfine (HF) barycenter, located ≈8.04 GHz below the 6s1/2F = 4 + 6s1/2F = 4 asymptote. Use of PA levels in the pure long-range well of the (2)0−g state enables access to deeply bound a3Σ+u levels, because of favorable Franck-Condon factors [9, 10]. 

Each ground-state vibrational level has considerable substructure. We write a and X states in the basis |(S, I)f, ℓ, F⟩, where I is the total spin of the pair of Cs nuclei; S is the total electron spin; f ≡S+I; ℓ is the rotational angular momentum; and F ≡f + ℓ. For the a3Σ+u states of interest, S = 1 and the HF interaction dominates the sublevel structure, splitting levels with different f according to EHF = A4 [f(f + 1) − S(S + 1) − I(I + 1)], where A ≈2.3 GHz is the Cs 6s1/2 HF constant. For each value of f, there is a manifold of closely-spaced states: those with different ℓ are split by the rotational energy Bvℓ(ℓ+1) (Bv ∼0.1 GHz), and states with different (same) F are split (mixed) by a 2nd-order spin-orbit (SO2) interaction of comparable strength [15]. For most states we consider, the eigenstate is well-approximated by a basis state. However, levels of the X1Σ+g state (S = 0) can mix with nearby a3Σ+u levels via HF interactions. 

Pairs of Cs atoms in the spin-polarized sample have f = mf = 8, and only pairs with ℓ= 0 (s-wave scattering state) are excited by the PA laser; hence initially F = mF = 8. The Hund’s case (c) (2)0−g excited state has resolved levels of definite J′, where J′ = ℓ′ + S′ + L′, L′ = 1 is the electron orbital ang. mom., and S′ = 1. The PA laser is tuned to excite only J′ = 2 levels, which are a mixture of ℓ′ = 0, 2, 4 [16]. The PA laser has σ+ polarization, so electric dipole (E1) selection rules ensure F′ = M′F = 9. Since F′ = J′ + I′ and F′ = 9, only I′ = 7 is excited. 

E1 selection rules for the probe transition ensure that only a3Σ+u states with I = 7 and ℓ=0, 2, 4 are detected; with polarization σ−(σ+) only sublevels with F = MF = 10 (F = 8, 9, 10, MF = 8) are seen. 

We observe multiple sublevels for several a3Σ+u vibrational levels with |Eb(v)| ∼ 400–1500 GHz. The level positions and line strengths qualitatively agree with predictions based on the a3Σ+u long-range potential [12], which yielded approximate values for Eb(v) and Bv. These predictions guided an initial assignment of quantum numbers to the observed states. As expected, sublevels for each v are clustered together according to their f value, and for each f we typically observe several sublevels with different values of ℓ and F. We perform a global fit of the potentials to all known levels [12, 13] in both the a3Σ+u and X1Σ+g states (including our data), taking into account the SO2 interaction. For spectral regions with no or insufficient data, the potentials were modeled using the “Hannover” analytic form [17]. The quality of the fit to this data suggests that we have a good understanding of the level assignments and interaction strengths: the r.m.s. deviation was ≈90 MHz for HF/rotational/SO2-induced sublevel splittings, and ≈200 MHz for absolute binding energies, vs. typical experimental uncertainties of ≈30 MHz and ≈400 MHz, respectively. Details of the data and the ﬁt will be given elsewhere. For now, we focus on a specific feature in the data. 

Fig. 2 shows data corresponding to levels in the f = 7 manifold of states for two adjacent vibrational levels of the a3Σ+u state, with |Eb(v)| ≈ 523 and 449 GHz, tentatively assigned from our fits as va = 37 and 38 respectively. Since only a single F = 10 level in the f = 7 manifold satisfies all selection rules, we expect only a single line with σ−probe polarization. This is indeed observed for the va = 38 state, and we hence assign this level as |(1, 7)7, 4, 10⟩. In the same spectral region, using a σ+ probe, we observe two nearby lines of comparable strength that we assign to states |(1, 7)7, 4, 8⟩ and |(1, 7)7, 4, 9⟩. In the va = 37 level, and again with a σ+ probe, we observe a very similar spectrum: two lines of similar strength, with a similar splitting, and separated by nearly the same amount from sublevels with f = 6, 8 in the same vibrational level. However, in this va = 37 level, with the σ−probe we observe two lines in the f = 7 manifold, each of similar strength but roughly two times weaker than the single analogous line in the va = 38 level. The only plausible mechanism to explain this additional line is that the single accessible a3Σ+u level |(1, 7)7, 4, 10⟩ has mixed strongly with a nearby X1Σ+g level only in this vibrational state, due to the combined HF and SO2 interactions. Based on our global fits, we assign this perturbing level as the X1Σ+g (vX = 138) state |(0, 6)6, 6, 10⟩. 

A sensitive search for variation of µ can be accomplished by measuring the small energy splitting between any of several sublevels in the va = 37/vX = 138 manifold. Ultracold Cs2 molecules can be produced in any of the a3Σ+u levels observed here, either by PA or via Fesh-bach resonance [8] followed by stimulated pumping to the desired level [18, 19]. By launching the molecules (or pre-cursor atoms) in a manner like that used for atomic fountain clocks, a linewidth Γ∼ 1 Hz could be achieved [20]. 

A microwave field could drive transitions between sub-levels of the a3Σ+u (va = 37) and X1Σ+g (vX = 138) states (despite the fact that these transitions are nominally forbidden). The strong HF mixing reduces the value of ∂µEv for the directly observed X|(0, 6)6, 6, 10⟩ sublevel; however, from our data and ﬁts we can accurately predict the position of other nearby, unobserved X state sublevels for use in the proposed experiment. For example, a magnetic dipole transition can be driven between the observed level a|(1, 7)6, 4, 10⟩ and X|(0, 6)6, 4, 10⟩, at Ω≈6.3 GHz, with transition amplitude M ≈ 0.1 µB induced by HF mixing of a and X (here µB is the Bohr magneton). Alternatively, an E1 transition can be driven between the observed level a|(1, 7)8, 2, 10⟩ and X|(0, 7)7, 3, 10⟩ at Ω≈9.8 GHz, with M ≈ 1.5 × 10−4ea0 ≈0.04 µB induced by spin-orbit effects (here e is the electron charge and a0 is the Bohr radius). 

To estimate the absolute sensitivity, we conservatively assume one measurement every 2 sec with S = 100 (vs. S ∼ 1000 every ∼1.3 sec for the atomic fountains in [20]), yielding δΩ∼ 5 × 10−5 Hz in one day of integration. From Fig. 1, ∂µΩ ∼ 5 × 1012 Hz for transitions of this type. Hence, δ(∆µ/µ) ∼ 10−17 could be achieved in ∼ 1 day. This requires only δΩ/Ω ∼ 10−14, i.e. over ten times less accuracy than the best atomic clocks (see e.g. [20]). Our ﬁts also predict near-degeneracies at energies where ∂µEv is considerably larger, but these await further data for confirmation. Note: during preparation of this manuscript, we learned of two papers exploring similar ideas in other systems [21]. 

This work was supported by DOE, ONR, ARO, and NSF grants DMR0325580 and PHY0354211. We thank P. Hamilton and S.B. Cahn for experimental assistance and E.R. Hudson for helpful comments.

claims.description: Laboratory experiments can detect small variations in the electron-to-proton mass ratio µ with high sensitivity by using nearly-degenerate molecular vibrational levels.
Cs2 is an attractive system for this scheme because of overlapping potentials, incommensurate splittings, long lifetimes, and favorable Franck-Condon factors.
The authors experimentally verify a near-degeneracy between a3Σ+u and X1Σ+g levels in the f = 7 manifold of Cs2.

First, since ultimately Ω must be measured with respect to some reference clock (with fractional uncertainty δΩc/Ωc), it is impossible to determine Ω to better than δΩmin = Ω(δΩc/Ωc). In addition, many systematic effects are proportional to Ω (e.g. Doppler shifts). Hence, ∂µΩ/Ω provides an important secondary figure of merit. 

We analyze the shifts in molecular energy levels when µ changes, with the assumption that both me and α remain constant. In this case, a change in µ corresponds to a variation of mp; in addition, molecular electronic potentials are independent of µ, since such potentials depend parametrically only on the Rydberg energy Ry = meα2/2. (The assumption of constant α and me is equivalent to using a reference clock based on optical atomic transitions, which also depend parametrically only on Ry and α.) We approximate the vibrational energy levels Ev via the WKB quantization condition: 

Z Ro Ri p2M[Ev −V(R)]dR = (v + 1/2)π, (1) 

where R is the internuclear distance, V(R) is the potential with minimum value 0, Ri(Ro) is the classical inner (outer) turning point of V(R) at energy Ev, and M ∝mp is the reduced mass of the nuclei in the molecule. Varying Eq. (1) with respect to both µ and v, one obtains for the energy sensitivity ∂µEv: 

∂µEv ≡ ∂Ev/d(lnµ) = (v + 1/2)2ρ(Ev), (2) 

where ρ(Ev) = (∂Ev/∂v)−1 ≈ (Ev −Ev−1)−1 is the density of states at energy Ev [4]. 

Near its minimum, a typical potential is harmonic, with Ev = (v + 1/2)ω and ρ(Ev) = ω−1 (ω is the classical oscillator frequency). Hence, for the harmonic part of the potential, ∂µEv = (v + 1/2)ω/2 = Ev/2 has a ∼v-fold enhancement for the vth vibrational level. (This can also be derived from ω ∝M−1/2.) This constitutes a general mechanism for amplifying the absolute size of ∂µΩ. 

For sufficiently large values of v, real molecular potentials are not harmonic. For highest values of v, Ev approaches the dissociation limit D, and the density of states ρ(Ev) becomes large. Hence, the value of ∂µEv again becomes small for the highest levels in any potential. Therefore, at some intermediate value of v, ∂µEv is maximized. We verified this behavior both for a generic (Morse) potential with analytic expressions for Ev, and for the experimentally determined X1Σ+g potential of Cs2 (see below). In both cases, the maximum value of ∂µEv is obtained for levels with E(max)v ≈ 3D/4, and there the energy sensitivity is only slightly diminished from its expected value in the harmonic approximation: 

∂µE(max)v ≈ (2/3)(E(max)v/2). Note that a recent paper [4] discussed the prospect for detecting variations in µ using Feschbach resonances in the scattering between ultracold atoms. However, such resonances arise from the presence of vibrational states (associated with potentials for other internal states of the atoms) that are very near D, where ∂µEv is small. The scheme discussed here uses the much larger energy sensitivity for states of intermediate vibrational excitation. 

The same mechanism can be used, in some cases, to provide transitions with extremely large relative shifts ∂µΩ/Ω. 

Consider a situation in which two molecular electronic potentials X and Y overlap, but the minimum of potential Y (at energy TY) is at higher energy than that of X (at 0). In this case, an excited level of X with vibrational number vX ≫ 1 and energy E1 = E(X)vX can be quite near in energy to a lower vibrational level of Y (vY ≪vX), with energy E2 = TY + E(Y)vY. The energy difference between such a pair of levels is small (Ω= |E1−E2| ≪ E(X)vX), but can retain a large sensitivity to changes in µ, since ∂µΩ= ∂µE(X)vX −∂µE(Y)vY ≈ ∂µE(X)vX. 

The molecule Cs2 is an attractive system for implementing this scheme. Cs2 has two low-lying, overlapping potentials: the deep X1Σ+g ground state, and the shallower a3Σ+u state, each of which dissociates to a pair of ground-state Cs atoms [5]. The vibrational splittings of these two potentials are incommensurate, and the large mass of Cs yields a high density of states; hence near-degeneracies appeared likely. In fact, Ref. [6] reported evidence for such in the high-J levels of the vX = 137 state. Furthermore, all rovibrational levels of both potentials have extremely long radiative lifetimes (≫ 1 s) [7], and production of ultracold Cs2 molecules (which can be measured over long coherence times) has become routine [7, 8]; hence the system can yield spectral lines with narrow width Γ. Finally, it has been predicted that deeply-bound levels of the a3Σ+u state—which lie near E(max)v for the X1Σ+g state—can be efficiently populated [9, 10]. 

We explicitly calculate ∂µEv for all vibrational levels in the X and a states of Cs2, using the fitted potentials described below and numerical solutions for Ev with slightly different values of M. (Similar results were obtained very simply for all but the highest-v levels of the X state, using a Dunham expansion for Ev [5, 6].) A plot of ∂µEv versus binding energy (Eb(v) ≡Ev−D) is shown for both potentials in Fig. 1. The behavior throughout is as expected from Eq. 2. 

Note that indeed, as expected from the previous discussion, ∂µE(a)va ≪ ∂µE(X)vX for close-lying X and a state levels (such that E(a)b(va) ≈ E(X)b(vX)). In addition, ∂µE(X)vX increases monotonically with |Eb|, throughout the region of a state levels. Hence, a search for variation of µ will be most sensitive when using nearly-degenerate levels lying as close as possible to the a state minimum. 

We experimentally determine the positions of deeply bound a3Σ+u levels, using two-color photoassociation (PA) spectroscopy [11, 12]. A sample of ultracold (T ∼ 100 µK) Cs atoms is cooled and confined in a dark SPOT magneto-optic trap. After applying a uniform magnetic field, the atoms are optically pumped into the 6s1/2 F = mF = 4 state. Next a CW laser (the PA laser) excites the atoms into a bound state [14] of the Cs2 (2)0−g potential (dissociating to the 6s1/2 + 6p3/2 asymptote). This excited state decays to a manifold of a3Σ+u vibrational levels, which are ionized by a pulsed laser. A second CW (probe) laser is applied to search for resonances between the desired a3Σ+u levels and the (2)0−g level excited by the PA laser. On such a resonance, the probe beam can shift the excited state offresonance with the PA laser and decrease the rate of molecule formation. We scan the probe laser frequency while monitoring the ion yield, and look for resonant dips in the signal. The difference between the frequencies of the resonant probe and PA lasers gives the binding energy of the a3Σ+u level. We report results for Eb relative to the hyperfine (HF) barycenter, located ≈8.04 GHz below the 6s1/2F = 4 + 6s1/2F = 4 asymptote. Use of PA levels in the pure long-range well of the (2)0−g state enables access to deeply bound a3Σ+u levels, because of favorable Franck-Condon factors [9, 10]. 

Each ground-state vibrational level has considerable substructure. We write a and X states in the basis |(S, I)f, ℓ, F⟩, where I is the total spin of the pair of Cs nuclei; S is the total electron spin; f ≡S+I; ℓ is the rotational angular momentum; and F ≡f + ℓ. For the a3Σ+u states of interest, S = 1 and the HF interaction dominates the sublevel structure, splitting levels with different f according to EHF = A4 [f(f + 1) − S(S + 1) − I(I + 1)], where A ≈2.3 GHz is the Cs 6s1/2 HF constant. For each value of f, there is a manifold of closely-spaced states: those with different ℓ are split by the rotational energy Bvℓ(ℓ+1) (Bv ∼0.1 GHz), and states with different (same) F are split (mixed) by a 2nd-order spin-orbit (SO2) interaction of comparable strength [15]. For most states we consider, the eigenstate is well-approximated by a basis state. However, levels of the X1Σ+g state (S = 0) can mix with nearby a3Σ+u levels via HF interactions. 

Pairs of Cs atoms in the spin-polarized sample have f = mf = 8, and only pairs with ℓ= 0 (s-wave scattering state) are excited by the PA laser; hence initially F = mF = 8. The Hund’s case (c) (2)0−g excited state has resolved levels of definite J′, where J′ = ℓ′ + S′ + L′, L′ = 1 is the electron orbital ang. mom., and S′ = 1. The PA laser is tuned to excite only J′ = 2 levels, which are a mixture of ℓ′ = 0, 2, 4 [16]. The PA laser has σ+ polarization, so electric dipole (E1) selection rules ensure F′ = M′F = 9. Since F′ = J′ + I′ and F′ = 9, only I′ = 7 is excited. 

E1 selection rules for the probe transition ensure that only a3Σ+u states with I = 7 and ℓ=0, 2, 4 are detected; with polarization σ−(σ+) only sublevels with F = MF = 10 (F = 8, 9, 10, MF = 8) are seen. 

We observe multiple sublevels for several a3Σ+u vibrational levels with |Eb(v)| ∼ 400–1500 GHz. The level positions and line strengths qualitatively agree with predictions based on the a3Σ+u long-range potential [12], which yielded approximate values for Eb(v) and Bv. These predictions guided an initial assignment of quantum numbers to the observed states. As expected, sublevels for each v are clustered together according to their f value, and for each f we typically observe several sublevels with different values of ℓ and F. We perform a global fit of the potentials to all known levels [12, 13] in both the a3Σ+u and X1Σ+g states (including our data), taking into account the SO2 interaction. For spectral regions with no or insufficient data, the potentials were modeled using the “Hannover” analytic form [17]. The quality of the fit to this data suggests that we have a good understanding of the level assignments and interaction strengths: the r.m.s. deviation was ≈90 MHz for HF/rotational/SO2-induced sublevel splittings, and ≈200 MHz for absolute binding energies, vs. typical experimental uncertainties of ≈30 MHz and ≈400 MHz, respectively. Details of the data and the ﬁt will be given elsewhere. For now, we focus on a specific feature in the data. 

Fig. 2 shows data corresponding to levels in the f = 7 manifold of states for two adjacent vibrational levels of the a3Σ+u state, with |Eb(v)| ≈ 523 and 449 GHz, tentatively assigned from our fits as va = 37 and 38 respectively. Since only a single F = 10 level in the f = 7 manifold satisfies all selection rules, we expect only a single line with σ−probe polarization. This is indeed observed for the va = 38 state, and we hence assign this level as |(1, 7)7, 4, 10⟩. In the same spectral region, using a σ+ probe, we observe two nearby lines of comparable strength that we assign to states |(1, 7)7, 4, 8⟩ and |(1, 7)7, 4, 9⟩. In the va = 37 level, and again with a σ+ probe, we observe a very similar spectrum: two lines of similar strength, with a similar splitting, and separated by nearly the same amount from sublevels with f = 6, 8 in the same vibrational level. However, in this va = 37 level, with the σ−probe we observe two lines in the f = 7 manifold, each of similar strength but roughly two times weaker than the single analogous line in the va = 38 level. The only plausible mechanism to explain this additional line is that the single accessible a3Σ+u level |(1, 7)7, 4, 10⟩ has mixed strongly with a nearby X1Σ+g level only in this vibrational state, due to the combined HF and SO2 interactions. Based on our global fits, we assign this perturbing level as the X1Σ+g (vX = 138) state |(0, 6)6, 6, 10⟩. 

A sensitive search for variation of µ can be accomplished by measuring the small energy splitting between any of several sublevels in the va = 37/vX = 138 manifold. Ultracold Cs2 molecules can be produced in any of the a3Σ+u levels observed here, either by PA or via Fesh-bach resonance [8] followed by stimulated pumping to the desired level [18, 19]. By launching the molecules (or pre-cursor atoms) in a manner like that used for atomic fountain clocks, a linewidth Γ∼ 1 Hz could be achieved [20]. 

A microwave field could drive transitions between sub-levels of the a3Σ+u (va = 37) and X1Σ+g (vX = 138) states (despite the fact that these transitions are nominally forbidden). The strong HF mixing reduces the value of ∂µEv for the directly observed X|(0, 6)6, 6, 10⟩ sublevel; however, from our data and ﬁts we can accurately predict the position of other nearby, unobserved X state sublevels for use in the proposed experiment. For example, a magnetic dipole transition can be driven between the observed level a|(1, 7)6, 4, 10⟩ and X|(0, 6)6, 4, 10⟩, at Ω≈6.3 GHz, with transition amplitude M ≈ 0.1 µB induced by HF mixing of a and X (here µB is the Bohr magneton). Alternatively, an E1 transition can be driven between the observed level a|(1, 7)8, 2, 10⟩ and X|(0, 7)7, 3, 10⟩ at Ω≈9.8 GHz, with M ≈ 1.5 × 10−4ea0 ≈0.04 µB induced by spin-orbit effects (here e is the electron charge and a0 is the Bohr radius). 

To estimate the absolute sensitivity, we conservatively assume one measurement every 2 sec with S = 100 (vs. S ∼ 1000 every ∼1.3 sec for the atomic fountains in [20]), yielding δΩ∼ 5 × 10−5 Hz in one day of integration. From Fig. 1, ∂µΩ ∼ 5 × 1012 Hz for transitions of this type. Hence, δ(∆µ/µ) ∼ 10−17 could be achieved in ∼ 1 day. This requires only δΩ/Ω ∼ 10−14, i.e. over ten times less accuracy than the best atomic clocks (see e.g. [20]). Our ﬁts also predict near-degeneracies at energies where ∂µEv is considerably larger, but these await further data for confirmation. Note: during preparation of this manuscript, we learned of two papers exploring similar ideas in other systems [21].

Research Context
Theoretical motivation comes from variety of string-inspired models concerning extra dimensions and light scalar ﬁelds. These fields, dubbed "quintessence", are potential candidates to explain observed dark energy. Variations of fundamental constants can only be detected in dimensionless constants. Within grand uniﬁed theories, variation in the electron-to-proton mass ratio µ ≡ me/mp should be larger than in α by a factor of ~30. Study of µ is therefore a potentially more sensitive method to observe variation. Most sensitive tests for µ come from examining molecular spectra from cosmologically distant sources. These tests yield stringent bounds at the level ~10−15/year on the time variation of µ. However, systematic errors associated with these measurements can be signiﬁcant and diﬃcult to eliminate. We propose a new type of laboratory experiment to search for variation of µ with high sensitivity. We show that the energy of molecular vibrational levels can be highly sensitive to changes in µ.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central RQ is whether laboratory measurements can detect small variations in the electron-to-proton mass ratio µ. The central hypothesis is that molecular vibrational levels are highly sensitive to changes in µ. The hypothesis further posits that nearly-degenerate level pairs can enhance sensitivity relative to the level splitting. The paper predicts a near-degeneracy in the ground vibronic levels of Cs2, measurable to sense a fractional change ∆µ/µ ≲ 10−17. The predicted sensitivity is governed by the absolute change ∂µΩ of the energy splitting Ω with respect to ∆µ/µ. The primary figure of merit is the ratio ∂µΩ/Γ; the secondary is ∂µΩ/Ω. The WKB quantization condition predicts ∂µEv = (v + 1/2)2ρ(Ev), where ρ(Ev) is the density of states. The harmonic approximation predicts ∂µEv = Ev/2, with a ∼v-fold enhancement for the vth vibrational level. The paper predicts ∂µEv is maximized at some intermediate value of v, near E(max)v ≈ 3D/4. The paper predicts that a search for variation of µ will be most sensitive when using nearly-degenerate levels as close as possible to the a state minimum.

Key Results

summary.title: Unification of the phonon mode behaviour in semiconductor alloys
summary.authors: O. Pagès, M. Kassem, A. Chafi, A. Nassour, S. Doyen and A. V. Postnikov
summary.executive_summary: This work re-examines the phonon mode behaviour of semiconductor alloys, challenging the long-standing classification based on the virtual crystal approximation (VCA). The authors systematically re-examine three representative systems: In1−xGaxAs (traditionally 1-bond→1-mode), In1−xGaxP (modified 2-mode), and ZnTe1−xSex (2-bond→1-mode). The central argument is that the VCA description, which treats alloy disorder at the macroscopic scale as a continuum, misses the essence of phonon behaviour by neglecting local bond distortions. Instead, the authors propose a universal percolation-type paradigm (1-bond→2-mode) that views the alloy at the mesoscopic scale as a composite. In this view, vibrations arise from like bonds within naturally-formed B-rich and C-rich regions, each giving rise to a symmetrical double-branch in the TO (transverse optical) phonon spectrum. For ZnTeSe, the authors identify three equally spaced TO modes between 180 and 200 cm⁻¹ that blue-shift as Se content increases. They propose a three-oscillator [1 (Zn-Te), 2 (Zn-Se)] version of the percolation model, where the Zn-Te bond appears as a unique branch below a well-resolved Zn-Se double-branch. The model parameters, including $\omega_{imp}$ and $\Delta$, are determined from the dilute limits where a single bond species is isolated; $\omega_{imp}$ is estimated from extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) bond length measurements and the Grüneisen parameter in pure crystals. The ab initio protocol validates the model using a 64-atom supercell, the Siesta code within the density functional theory (DFT) local density approximation (LDA), and a linear response technique, showing that theoretical and experimental ($\omega_{imp}, \Delta$) values agree within ~5%. The authors also analyze the longitudinal optical (LO) modes, demonstrating that strong $\vec{E}$-coupling rubs out the 1-bond→2-mode behaviour in LO symmetry, resulting in an apparent 1-bond→1-mode LO behaviour. This TO-LO duality explains why the two modes cannot be explained on the same intuitive basis. The percolation model unifies the MREI-VCA and Elliott-CPA classifications into a single class. Finally, the work shows that vibrational spectroscopy provides natural insight into alloy disorder at the mesoscopic scale in a non-destructive and contactless manner, potentially enabling the study of self-organization.

summary.title: Coherent network analysis for triggered gravitational wave burst searches
summary.authors: K Hayama, S D Mohanty, M Rakhmanov, S Desai
summary.field_subfield: Gravitational-wave astronomy; network analysis; triggered search pipelines
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces RIDGE, a data analysis pipeline designed for triggered gravitational-wave (GW) burst searches that use astronomical event observations as triggers. Triggered searches differ from all-sky searches by utilizing prior astrophysical information (e.g., Gamma-ray Burst sky location, distance, and burst type) and the smaller data volumes, which permit the use of computationally expensive algorithms that are bypassed in un-triggered searches due to computational limitations. RIDGE implements regularized maximum likelihood (RML) based coherent network analysis, a method used by several recent papers. The pipeline includes a data conditioning step consisting of noise-floor estimation via running median, PSD-based FIR whitening filters, and line-feature removal using the MBLT method (estimated by running median for amplitude and phase). RML inversion of detector responses is ill-posed and requires regularization, whose theory is well-understood through direction-dependent antenna patterns. The pipeline produces a two-dimensional sky-map S(θ, φ), which is then compared using two detection statistics: Rmm (the maximum divided by the minimum value on the sky-map plane) and Rrad (a radial distance statistic). The authors compare these statistics using Monte Carlo simulations with four independent realizations of Gaussian, stationary white noise generated for four LIGO (H1, L1, H2) and Virgo (V1) detectors with 3,000 seconds of duration. The noise replicates design sensitivities and added sinusoids at 54, 60, 120, 180, 344, 349, and 407 Hz. Sine-Gaussian signals (θ = −30, φ = 167.0; 235 Hz, Q = 9; h× with π/2 phase relative to h+) with hrss strengths of 3 × 10−22, 5 × 10−22, and 7 × 10−22 Hz−1/2 were injected at regular intervals. The data was sampled at 16384 Hz, downsampled, and whitened using filters trained on the first two seconds of signal-free data, with a 0.5 sec integration time to accommodate filter delays. ROC curves demonstrate that Rrad performs better than the naive Rmm choice. For the central hrss of 5 × 10−22 Hz−1/2, Rrad yields a ≃62% detection probability at a false alarm probability of 10−2 (1 false event per 50 seconds). The authors conclude that RIDGE implements algorithms significantly different from existing pipelines and could serve as a platform for new regulators, with future waveform reconstruction and Bayesian integration planned.

Research Context
Triggered searches are different from all-sky, blind searches. Triggered searches have much more prior information. Prior information includes sky location and sometimes distance. Prior info distinguishes GRB signal types (long-soft vs short-hard). Many pre-processing algorithms are unused due to a natural selection effect. Triggered searches allow experimenting with computationally intensive algorithms. Current prior-info modeling is limited to Bayesian approaches. Most detailed prior use was in the SGR-1806–20 event.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central RQ is: how to incorporate astrophysical prior information mathematically? RQ: can a Bayesian approach for pulsars be modeled for different triggered searches? RQ: how do the Rmm and Rrad statistics compare in triggered searches? Hypothesis: RIDGE will be sensitive enough for simulated signals. Hypothesis: Rrad will outperform the naive Rmm statistic. Prediction: Rrad will capture more full-sky-map information.

Methodological Details
The study used Monte Carlo simulations with four independent realizations. Noise was Gaussian, stationary, white noise with ~3,000 second duration. Noise was passed through FIR filters to match LIGO and Virgo design sensitivity. The detector network included four interferometers. Specific detectors were H1, L1, H2, and V1. A frequency resolution of 2.0 Hz was used for computing noise PSDs. Sinusoids were added at 54, 60, 120, 180, 344, 349, and 407 Hz. Signals were injected at regular intervals with hrss = 3 × 10−22, 5 × 10−22, and 7 × 10−22 Hz−1/2. Signals were located at θ = −30◦, φ = 167.0◦ (GRB060813 location). The sine-Gaussian signal had center frequency 235 Hz and a Q = 9. The h× waveform had an added phase of π/2 relative to h+. The simulated data was sampled at 16384 Hz. Data was downsampled with an anti-aliasing filter. Training on the first two seconds of signal-free data.

Procedures And Architectures
Data conditioning uses a running median to estimate the PSD noise-floor. The running median rejects narrowband outliers from power line interference. The whitened data variance is 1.0 (in arbitrary units). Whitening filters were FIR filters trained on the PSD. FIR filters introduce delays to accommodate the integration time. The integration time was chosen at 0.5 seconds per segment. Line removal uses the MBLT method. MBLT uses running median for line amplitude and phase functions. MBLT preserves signals during line removal. The basic algorithm is regularized maximum likelihood (RML). Detector responses are a linear combination of two unknown polarization waveforms. Inverting detector responses is an ill-posed problem. RML regularization is understood via direction-dependent antenna patterns. The RML algorithm produces a two-dimensional sky-map S(θ, φ). The sky-map maps maximum likelihood values over all possible waveforms.

Key Results
The Rrad statistic performs better than the naive Rmm choice. The enhancement from Rmm to Rrad is shown by arrows. An hrss of 5 × 10−22 Hz−1/2 yielded a ≃62% detection probability. The false alarm probability was set to 10−2. This corresponds to 1 false event in 50 seconds. ROC curves for three hrss levels (3, 5, 7 × 10−22 Hz−1/2). The ROC curves for hrss = 5 × 10−22 Hz−1/2 are in the middle. The Rmm and Rrad ROC curves are solid and dashed. The two-dimensional output is the sky-map S(θ, φ). Rmm is defined as the max divided by the min value. Rrad is the radial distance of the observed values.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Rrad incorporates full sky-map information better than Rmm. Judicious choice of a full sky-map statistic is required. More effective full sky-map statistics can push performance. Current prior-info modeling is limited compared to Bayesian. RIDGE provides an independent check of other pipelines. RIDGE can serve as a platform for new regulators. A future version will reconstruct h+ and h× waveforms. A waveform estimation method will be integrated.

Contradictions And Limitations
The Bayesian gap is a limitation on prior info use. The 0.5 sec integration time is a lower bound. The 0.5 sec was large enough to accommodate filter delays. The 2 sec training was signal-free. The Rmm statistic is a naive baseline. Rmm does not perform better than Rrad. The true false alarm rate is 1 in 50 seconds. There are no clear contradictions between Rmm and Rrad results.

Claims
The RIDGE pipeline provides a viable coherent network analysis framework for triggered gravitational-wave searches. RIDGE uses regularized maximum likelihood. The pipeline is sensitive to simulated signals. RIDGE is written mostly in MATLAB. It produces a sky-map S(θ, φ). The code is not detailed. No prior info modeling has seen advanced prior use. RIDGE can provide an independent check. RIDGE can serve as a platform for new regulators.
The Rrad detection statistic is superior to the naive Rmm statistic for triggered searches. Rrad performs better than Rmm. The enhancement is shown by the arrows. Rrad captures information from the full sky-map. More effective statistics can push performance further. Rmm is a naive baseline. A judicious full sky-map statistic is required. Rrad yields a 62% detection probability.
Current mathematical modeling of astrophysical prior information is limited, necessitating a transition to Bayesian approaches. Only limited advances have occurred. More work is needed in this area. The pulsar Bayesian approach is a different model. There is no clear evidence refuting this need. A future version will integrate a waveform estimation method.

Data And Code Availability
The pipeline code is written in MATLAB. The code is not described in any detail. Data were generated via Monte Carlo simulation. Public data availability is not mentioned.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The two-statistic comparison (Rmm, Rrad) is an ablation of full sky-map info. Four independent noise realizations were used. No explicit sensitivity or calibration analysis reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1: Sample power spectral density with running median noise-floor estimate. Figure 2: Spectrograms of whitened data with and without line removal. Figure 3: Sky-maps for noise only (top) and signal plus noise (bottom). Figure 4: Power spectral densities of simulated detector noise. Figure 5: Detector responses to the injection signal. Figure 6: ROC curves for Rmm (dashed) and Rrad (solid).

Three Takeaways
1. RIDGE implements a RML-based coherent network analysis pipeline for triggered GW searches. 2. The Rrad statistic yields a ≃62% detection probability at a 10−2 false alarm rate, outperforming the naive Rmm choice. 3. RIDGE could serve as a platform for new regulators and future waveform estimation.

summary.executive_summary: This letter describes a series of experiments measuring the sedimentation dynamics of non-Brownian spheres as the fluid Reynolds number increases from the viscous Stokes regime toward the moderately inertial regime. Using particle image velocimetry (PIV), the authors study a semi-dilute suspension of monodisperse glass beads with a radius of 137±9 µm dispersed in glycerol and water mixtures at a volume fraction of φ = 0.06, covering a Reynolds number range of 0.001 ≤Re ≤2.3. In the low Reynolds number Stokes regime, particles settle with large, Reynolds-independent velocity fluctuations σV/V whose spatial correlation length ξ is independent of Re and obeys the scaling relation ξ0 ≈11aφ−1/3. The authors show that fluid inertia introduces a screening effect which significantly reduces both the magnitude and spatial extent of these velocity fluctuations. The onset of inertial screening occurs when the inertial screening length l = a/Re becomes comparable to the Stokes sedimentation length ξ0, which happens at a critical Reynolds number Rec = a/ξ0 ≈0.05. Above Rec, the spatial correlation length ξ decays approximately logarithmically with Reynolds number, and at the maximum speed of Re = 2.3, the velocity fluctuations are reduced by approximately 80%. A modified Hinch force balance model, which incorporates a Reynolds number-dependent drag term βRe ≈0.133Re0.78, successfully links the fluctuation magnitude σV/V to the correlation size ξ over the entire Reynolds number range studied. The agreement with the model demonstrates that the reduction in fluctuation magnitude is driven by both the shortening of correlation lengths and the increase in inertial drag. The authors rationalize the onset at Rec ≈0.05 both through the screening length criterion (predicting Rec ∼a/ξ0 ≈0.04) and the Brenner criterion, which compares the particle diffusion coefficient D (estimated as D ≈ 0.4ξσV) to the kinematic viscosity ν, finding significant deviations from Stokes behavior when the Schmidt number ν/D is near unity. Finally, the authors reconcile their results with a previous contrasting experiment by Cowan et al., which reported Reynolds-independent fluctuations because all of those samples were below the critical Reynolds number. The success of the Hinch model validates the underlying assumption of a random particle density distribution even in the presence of moderate fluid inertia, providing a benchmark for future theoretical and experimental work on moderately inertial sedimentation.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This letter describes a series of experiments measuring the sedimentation dynamics of non-Brownian spheres as the fluid Reynolds number increases from the viscous Stokes regime toward the moderately inertial regime. Using particle image velocimetry (PIV), the authors study a semi-dilute suspension of monodisperse glass beads with a radius of 137±9 µm dispersed in glycerol and water mixtures at a volume fraction of φ = 0.06, covering a Reynolds number range of 0.001 ≤Re ≤2.3. In the low Reynolds number Stokes regime, particles settle with large, Reynolds-independent velocity fluctuations σV/V whose spatial correlation length ξ is independent of Re and obeys the scaling relation ξ0 ≈11aφ−1/3. The authors show that fluid inertia introduces a screening effect which significantly reduces both the magnitude and spatial extent of these velocity fluctuations. The onset of inertial screening occurs when the inertial screening length l = a/Re becomes comparable to the Stokes sedimentation length ξ0, which happens at a critical Reynolds number Rec = a/ξ0 ≈0.05. Above Rec, the spatial correlation length ξ decays approximately logarithmically with Reynolds number, and at the maximum speed of Re = 2.3, the velocity fluctuations are reduced by approximately 80%. A modified Hinch force balance model, which incorporates a Reynolds number-dependent drag term βRe ≈0.133Re0.78, successfully links the fluctuation magnitude σV/V to the correlation size ξ over the entire Reynolds number range studied. The agreement with the model demonstrates that the reduction in fluctuation magnitude is driven by both the shortening of correlation lengths and the increase in inertial drag. The authors rationalize the onset at Rec ≈0.05 both through the screening length criterion (predicting Rec ∼a/ξ0 ≈0.04) and the Brenner criterion, which compares the particle diffusion coefficient D (estimated as D ≈ 0.4ξσV) to the kinematic viscosity ν, finding significant deviations from Stokes behavior when the Schmidt number ν/D is near unity. Finally, the authors reconcile their results with a previous contrasting experiment by Cowan et al., which reported Reynolds-independent fluctuations because all of those samples were below the critical Reynolds number. The success of the Hinch model validates the underlying assumption of a random particle density distribution even in the presence of moderate fluid inertia, providing a benchmark for future theoretical and experimental work on moderately inertial sedimentation.

Research Context
Sedimentation of non-Brownian spheres is a fundamental problem in physics with intense recent activity. Much focus has been on particles slowly settling in viscous liquids, the Stokes regime where Re ≪1. The Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial to viscous forces and is defined as Re ≡2Va/ν. In the Stokes regime, large velocity fluctuations σV/V are Reynolds-independent across experiments and simulations. However, experiments at moderate Reynolds numbers Re ∼1 have received much less attention despite their fundamental importance. We are aware of only a single experiment that has examined the fluctuation dynamics of spheres at moderate Re. In the absence of experiments beyond the Stokes regime, understanding of basic physics and model testing remains limited.

Research Question And Hypothesis
We describe experiments that demonstrate how moderate amounts of fluid inertia affect the settling dynamics of spheres. The onset of inertial corrections occurs when the inertial screening length l = a/Re becomes small. For Re greater than Rec, inertial screening reduces both the magnitude and spatial extent of particle velocity fluctuations. Rec is predicted to occur when the inertial screening length matches the Stokes sedimentation length. The critical Reynolds number is defined as Rec = a/ξ0 ≈0.05 based on the Stokes correlation length. A modified Hinch force balance model connects the fluctuation magnitudes σV/V to the correlation sizes ξ over the entire range. The model incorporates Reynolds number-dependent drag coefficients to account for the influence of particle inertia. The Hinch model is recovered when the Reynolds number goes to zero.

Methodological Details
Particles were monodisperse glass beads of radius a = 137±9 µm. The beads were dispersed in glycerol and water mixtures across the range 0.001 ≤Re ≤2.3. The volume fraction was kept constant at φ = 0.06 for all cases. Experiments were performed in an 8 ×80×305 mm glass tube at T = 23±10C. Particle velocities were measured using particle image velocimetry (PIV) with Dantec Instruments software. A 3×3 cm cross section of the cell was imaged to study several thousand particles simultaneously. Each velocity field comprised 41 × 42 vectors. Each velocity vector was the local average of two to four spheres. Random dispersions were prepared by vigorous shaking of the cells.

Procedures And Architectures
Imaging was performed far from the sedimentation front and the sediment growth. Spatial velocity correlations were analyzed via an ensemble average of several hundred vector maps. The normalized autocorrelation function of the z component is denoted Cz(z). Correlation functions Cz(z) and Cz(x) are evaluated in parallel and perpendicular directions. Cz(z) and Cz(x) decay to zero at large distances, indicating finite range correlations. The spatial correlation functions were fitted to an exponential form exp[−(z/ξ)1.5]. The Hinch model was modified by adding a Reynolds number-dependent drag term. The inertial part of the drag force is βRe ≈0.133Re0.78, valid for Re <∼30. The appropriate Reynolds number for the drag force is Reξ = (ξ/a)Re.

Key Results
The critical Reynolds number Rec ≈0.05 marks the onset of inertial corrections. For Re <∼0.05, the correlation length ξ is independent of Re. In the Stokes regime, the correlation length follows ξ0 ≈11aφ−1/3. For Re >∼0.05, the correlation length ξ shows a roughly logarithmic decay with Re. At Re = 2.3, velocity fluctuations σV/V are reduced by ≈80% compared to the Stokes value. The modified Hinch model shows remarkably good agreement over the entire Reynolds number range. Both the shortening of correlation lengths and the increasing drag term contribute similarly to the fluctuation drop.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The onset occurs when the inertial screening length l = a/Re becomes comparable to the Stokes correlation length. This predicts an onset at Rec ∼a/ξ0 ≈0.04, consistent with the observed Rec ∼0.05. The Brenner criterion is confirmed where the Schmidt number ν/D is near unity. Significant deviations from Stokes behavior occur where the diffusion coefficient D matches the viscosity ν. The Cowan et al. experiment showed no inertial effects because Re0 <∼Rec for their samples. The Hinch model success supports the random particle density distribution assumption under moderate inertia.

Contradictions And Limitations
The Cowan et al. result is reconciled by showing they used Re0 based on infinite dilution values. Their Re0 = 0.3 samples are estimated to remain in the Stokes regime Re <∼0.05. The experimental design lacks a reported random seed, train-test split, or formal error analysis. Random seeds and train-test splits are not applicable to this sedimentation experiment. No explicit statistical error analysis or confidence intervals are reported.

Claims
The onset of inertial screening occurs when the inertial screening length becomes comparable to the Stokes correlation length, at Rec ≈ 0.05. The onset occurs when l = a/Re reaches the Stokes correlation length. The predicted onset Rec ∼a/ξ0 ≈0.04 agrees with the observed Rec ≈0.05. In the Stokes regime Re <∼0.05, correlation length ξ is independent of Re. The Cowan et al. experiment reported no inertial effects for all tested samples. This demonstrates that the transition is driven by a crossing of screening length scales. The critical Reynolds number Rec provides a benchmark for determining inertial onset in other suspensions.
A modified Hinch model connects fluctuation magnitude σV/V to correlation size ξ across the entire Reynolds number range. The modified Hinch model shows agreement over the entire Reynolds number range. The drop in fluctuations arises from both shorter correlations and increased inertial drag. The model neglects a prefactor γ(φ) which was assumed near unity. This validates the underlying random density assumption in the presence of moderate inertia. The model provides a simple yet accurate analytic description of the transition.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The model predictions when the inertial drag force corrections are neglected (Re = 0) show only a slight decrease with Re. This greatly underestimates the drop in fluctuation magnitude, showing the drag correction is essential.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows particle velocity maps at Re = 0.001, 0.2, and 2.3. Figures 1(a-c) show velocity Vi from three samples across the range. Figures 1(d-f) show fluctuations calculated from (a-c) using δVi = Vi −⟨Vi⟩. Figure 2 compares spatial correlation functions at Re = 0.001 and Re = 2.3. summary.title: Green-Schwarz, Nambu-Goto Actions, and Cayley’s Hyperdeterminant
summary.authors: Hitoshi NISHINO and Subhash RAJPOOT
summary.field_subfield: High Energy Physics - Theory / String Theory
summary.executive_summary: This theoretical physics paper presents a derivation of a Nambu-Goto-type action for the N = 2 superstring in target space-time D = 2 + 2, expressed in terms of Cayley’s hyperdeterminant with manifest global SL(2, IR) × SL(2, IR) × SL(2, IR) symmetry. The authors extend recent results showing that the Nambu-Goto (NG) action with the D = 2 + 2 target space-time possesses the manifest global [SL(2, IR)]³ symmetry, where the square root of the determinant of an inner product of pull-backs is rewritten exactly as a Cayley’s hyperdeterminant realizing this symmetry. They demonstrate that this feature is shared by the Green-Schwarz σ-model for the N = 2 superstring whose target space-time is D = 2 + 2; when its zweibein ﬁeld is eliminated, the action contains the Nambu-Goto action, which is nothing but the square root of Cayley’s hyperdeterminant of the pull-back in superspace q Det (Πiα . α) manifestly invariant under SL(2, IR) × SL(2, IR) × SL(2, IR). The target space-time D = 2 + 2 can accommodate self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, and the action possesses fermionic κ-symmetry, satisfying the criterion for its light-cone equivalence to the Neveu-Schwarz-Ramond formulation for the N = 2 superstring. A central obstruction is the kinetic term in the Green-Schwarz action, which is not of the NG-type equivalent to a Cayley’s hyperdeterminant; the authors overcome this by eliminating the zweibein via a non-algebraic field equation, a procedure analogous to obtaining the Nambu-Goto action from a Polyakov action. They do not claim quantum equivalence, focusing instead on classical-level symmetries. The target D = (2, 2; 2, 2) superspace supports the self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills multiplet with N = (1, 1) space-time supersymmetry, a supersymmetric generalization of purely bosonic Yang-Mills in D = 2 + 2, connecting to the conjecture that all bosonic integrable or soluble models in dimensions D ≤ 3 are generated by self-dual Yang-Mills theory. The authors note that the hidden triality of the Nambu-Goto action is absent due to the WZNW-term and emphasize that the action and its fermionic transformation rule are expressed purely in terms of the superspace coordinates ZM as the fundamental independent field variables.

This theoretical physics paper presents a derivation of a Nambu-Goto-type action for the N = 2 superstring in target space-time D = 2 + 2, expressed in terms of Cayley’s hyperdeterminant with manifest global SL(2, IR) × SL(2, IR) × SL(2, IR) symmetry. The authors extend recent results showing that the Nambu-Goto (NG) action with the D = 2 + 2 target space-time possesses the manifest global [SL(2, IR)]³ symmetry, where the square root of the determinant of an inner product of pull-backs is rewritten exactly as a Cayley’s hyperdeterminant realizing this symmetry. They demonstrate that this feature is shared by the Green-Schwarz σ-model for the N = 2 superstring whose target space-time is D = 2 + 2; when its zweibein ﬁeld is eliminated, the action contains the Nambu-Goto action, which is nothing but the square root of Cayley’s hyperdeterminant of the pull-back in superspace q Det (Πiα . α) manifestly invariant under SL(2, IR) × SL(2, IR) × SL(2, IR). The target space-time D = 2 + 2 can accommodate self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, and the action possesses fermionic κ-symmetry, satisfying the criterion for its light-cone equivalence to the Neveu-Schwarz-Ramond formulation for the N = 2 superstring. They do not claim quantum equivalence, focusing instead on classical-level symmetries. summary.title: Characteristics of EGRET Blazars in the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS)
summary.authors: G. B. Taylor, S. E. Healey, J. F. Helmboldt, S. Tremblay, C. D. Fassnacht, R. C. Walker, L. O. Sjouwerman, T. J. Pearson, A. C. S. Readhead, L. Weintraub, N. Gehrels, R. W. Romani, P. F. Michelson, R. D. Blandford, and G. Cotter
summary.executive_summary:
The paper examines the radio properties of EGRET-detected blazars observed as part of the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS). VIPS has a flux limit roughly an order of magnitude below the MOJAVE survey and most other samples that have been used to study the properties of EGRET blazars. At lower flux levels, radio flux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray flux density. The authors find that EGRET-detected blazars tend to have higher brightness temperatures, greater core fractions, and possibly larger than average jet opening angles. A weak correlation is also found with jet length and with polarization. All well-established trends can be explained by systematically larger Doppler factors in gamma-ray loud blazars, consistent with measurements of higher apparent velocities found in radio monitoring programs above 10 GHz.

The survey covers 1127 flat-spectrum sources stronger than 85 mJy in the Northern Cap region of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). VIPS included 5 GHz, full polarization images of 958 sources and 147 total intensity images; 22 sources were from the VIPS pilot or MOJAVE surveys. Over 99% were successfully imaged, with just under 1% too weak to reliably self-calibrate.

The EGRET candidate sample was compiled from the intersection of the Hartman et al. (1999) EGRET catalog and the CRATES (Healey et al. 2007a) survey, yielding 173 candidates at |b| > 10°. The VIPS region covers ~5700 square degrees, yielding 31 EGRET candidate blazars: 12 deemed likely candidates (FoM > 1) and 19 deemed plausible candidates (1.0 > FoM > 0.25). Automatic classification assigned 8 PS, 3 SJET, and 14 LJET sources; adding 6 MOJAVE sources resulted in 8 (25%) PS, 4 (13%) SJET, and 19 (61%) LJET. These were compared to the broader VIPS population of 25% PS, 22% SJET, 43% LJET, 9% CSO, and 2% CPLX.

Key results include a polarization of 48 ± 12% detected from 25 sources (higher than VIPS 36 ± 4% and LJET 41 ± 4%). The core fraction K-S test gave a 4% probability that the distributions were from the same parent. Brightness temperature also yielded 4%, while the jet component K-S test was 11%. Opening half-angles: 3 of 4 sources exceeded the VIPS median of 18.9◦, with Monte-Carlo simulations suggesting less than a 1 in 3 chance of identical distributions. Jet length yielded a 34% K-S probability. The authors conclude that gamma-ray selected sources have higher Doppler factors due to small viewing angles, supporting jet-emission models.

The paper lacks a formal bibliography, data release procedures, and an ethics statement. GLAST, launching late 2007, is expected to confirm these findings with better statistics.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The paper examines the radio properties of EGRET-detected blazars observed as part of the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS). VIPS has a flux limit roughly an order of magnitude below the MOJAVE survey and most other samples that have been used to study the properties of EGRET blazars. At lower flux levels, radio flux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray flux density. The authors find that EGRET-detected blazars tend to have higher brightness temperatures, greater core fractions, and possibly larger than average jet opening angles. A weak correlation is also found with jet length and with polarization. All well-established trends can be explained by systematically larger Doppler factors in gamma-ray loud blazars, consistent with measurements of higher apparent velocities found in radio monitoring programs above 10 GHz.

The survey covers 1127 flat-spectrum sources stronger than 85 mJy in the Northern Cap region of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). VIPS included 5 GHz, full polarization images of 958 sources and 147 total intensity images; 22 sources were from the VIPS pilot or MOJAVE surveys. Over 99% were successfully imaged, with just under 1% too weak to reliably self-calibrate.

The EGRET candidate sample was compiled from the intersection of the Hartman et al. (1999) EGRET catalog and the CRATES (Healey et al. 2007a) survey, yielding 173 candidates at |b| > 10°. The VIPS region covers ~5700 square degrees, yielding 31 EGRET candidate blazars: 12 deemed likely candidates (FoM > 1) and 19 deemed plausible candidates (1.0 > FoM > 0.25). Automatic classification assigned 8 PS, 3 SJET, and 14 LJET sources; adding 6 MOJAVE sources resulted in 8 (25%) PS, 4 (13%) SJET, and 19 (61%) LJET. These were compared to the broader VIPS population of 25% PS, 22% SJET, 43% LJET, 9% CSO, and 2% CPLX.

Key results include a polarization of 48 ± 12% detected from 25 sources (higher than VIPS 36 ± 4% and LJET 41 ± 4%). The core fraction K-S test gave a 4% probability that the distributions were from the same parent. Brightness temperature also yielded 4%, while the jet component K-S test was 11%. Opening half-angles: 3 of 4 sources exceeded the VIPS median of 18.9◦, with Monte-Carlo simulations suggesting less than a 1 in 3 chance of identical distributions. Jet length yielded a 34% K-S probability. The authors conclude that gamma-ray selected sources have higher Doppler factors due to small viewing angles, supporting jet-emission models.

The paper lacks a formal bibliography, data release procedures, and an ethics statement. GLAST, launching late 2007, is expected to confirm these findings with better statistics.

Research Context
At high galactic latitudes, at least ~70% of the sources seen by the EGRET instrument are identified with blazars. EGRET blazars exhibit one-sided parsec-scale jets and superluminal motion in those jets. L¨ahteenm¨aki & Valtaoja (2003) found the EGRET flares lagged behind mm flares. Reich et al. (1993) claimed enhanced radio emission following a high level of gamma-ray activity. Lister & Homan (2005) found EGRET blazars have more strongly polarized jets. Kovalev et al. (2005) found EGRET blazars in the 15 GHz MOJAVE survey were more compact. Jorstad et al. (2001) linked gamma-ray flares to the ejection of superluminal radio knots. Piner et al. (2007) found no significant difference between the jet velocities of EGRET and non-EGRET blazars. Sikora et al. (2001) suggested there might be two classes of gamma-ray blazars. GLAST will provide over two orders of magnitude increase in sensitivity over CGRO-EGRET.

Research Question And Hypothesis
We examine correlations in the parsec-scale jet properties of EGRET blazars. The central hypothesis is that gamma-ray selected sources are biased toward smaller angles to the line-of-sight. We predict gamma-ray selected sources have systematically higher Doppler factors than the radio-selected population. This should manifest as larger core fractions, higher brightness temperatures, and increased polarization. We anticipate gamma-ray selected sources will have larger jet opening angles.

Methodological Details
VIPS surveyed 1127 flat-spectrum sources stronger than 85 mJy in the Northern Cap region of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. VIPS produced 5 GHz, full polarization images of 958 sources and 147 total intensity images. 22 sources were from the VIPS pilot or MOJAVE surveys. Over 99% of the VIPS sources were successfully imaged. 173 candidate EGRET sources were compiled from the Hartman et al. (1999) catalog and CRATES. Candidates were selected from the intersection at |b| > 10°. VIPS covers ~5700 square degrees, providing uniform quality VLBI imaging. 12 VIPS sources were deemed likely candidates and 19 deemed plausible candidates. A source was likely if it had FoM > 1 and plausible if 1.0 > FoM > 0.25. 6 bright sources otherwise meeting the criteria have MOJAVE observations available. The combined sample consists of 31 EGRET candidate blazars. Automatic classification assigned 8 PS, 3 SJET, and 14 LJET sources to the 31 candidates. Adding 6 MOJAVE sources gave totals of 8 (25%) PS, 4 (13%) SJET, and 19 (61%) LJET.

Procedures And Architectures
The survey used 5 GHz VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry at the Northern Cap. Source components were fit with automatic modelﬁts as described in Helmboldt et al. (2007a). For components with two or fewer sources, the model was ﬁtted to the visibility data directly. Minimum observable size used equation (2) from Kovalev et al. (2005). The core beam FWHM was 3 mas. Brightness temperatures were computed without correction to the source rest frame. K-S tests compared the distributions of core fractions, brightness temperatures, and jet lengths. Monte-Carlo simulations assessed opening angle distributions. 15 GHz MOJAVE images were included for sources not imaged at 5 GHz.

Key Results
VIPS has a flux limit roughly an order of magnitude below MOJAVE and most other samples. At lower flux levels, radio flux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray flux density. EGRET-detected blazars tend to have higher brightness temperatures. EGRET-detected blazars have greater core fractions. The polarization of the 25 sources was 48 ± 12%. The average VIPS polarization was 36 ± 4% and LJETs were 41 ± 4%. The K-S test probability for the core fraction distribution was 4%. The K-S test for the jet component brightness temperature distribution was 11%. 3 of 4 EGRET sources had opening half-angles exceeding the VIPS median of 18.9◦. Monte-Carlo simulations suggested less than a 1 in 3 chance of identical opening angle distributions. The K-S probability for the jet length distribution was 34%.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
EGRET-selected sources appear to have higher Doppler factors than the radio-selected population at large. The trends support models where gamma-rays are produced in a jet oriented at a small angle to the line-of-sight. Large opening angles suggest the sight-line is close to or within the beaming cone of the radio emission. Higher Doppler factors also explain higher core fractions, higher brightness temperatures, and higher polarization. The tighter beaming angle for the γ-rays should be easily achieved with GLAST. Multi-frequency, multi-epoch VLBI polarimetry will be possible for a small subset. Selecting the brightest radio sources may not maximize the chances of gamma-ray detection.

Contradictions And Limitations
The numbers of sources involved are too small to make a definitive statement on polarization. Only four sources had enough jet components for quantitative jet bending estimates, making the results inconclusive. The redshift distribution for the VIPS sample is still incomplete, preventing selection bias investigation. There is a marginally significant excess of long jets but no appreciable difference in jet length. Random seeds and train/test splits are not reported (not applicable to the observational survey). No demographic information or ethical review statement is provided. No formal bibliography is included, leaving several works cited but not listed.

Claims
EGRET-selected sources are systematically biased toward smaller viewing angles to the line-of-sight, yielding higher Doppler factors than the radio-selected blazar population. The polarization of EGRET blazars was 48 ± 12%, higher than VIPS (36 ± 4%). EGRET blazars have greater core fractions than the VIPS population. Three of four EGRET sources exceeded the VIPS median opening angle of 18.9◦. Small sample numbers preclude a definitive polarization statement. The jet bending results were inconclusive due to only four sources with enough components. The jet length K-S probability was 34%, supporting the null hypothesis of no difference. The tighter beaming angle for γ-rays should be confirmed by GLAST. The γ-ray beam is likely tighter than the radio beam.
Radio flux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray flux density at lower flux levels. The survey had a flux limit roughly an order of magnitude below MOJAVE. The authors report that radio flux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray flux density. At lower flux levels, the lack of correlation is the reported finding. Selecting the brightest radio sources may not maximize the chances of gamma-ray coincidence.
EGRET-detected blazars exhibit higher core fractions and higher brightness temperatures than the wider VIPS population. The core fraction K-S probability was 4%. The jet component brightness temperature K-S test was 11%. The core brightness temperature also yielded 4%, not 11%. Numbers are still small. The jet-emission model requires a small angle to the line-of-sight.

Data And Code Availability
VIPS images for the survey as a whole are online at the VIPS website.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
K-S tests compared the core fraction and brightness temperature distributions against the null. Monte-Carlo simulations assessed the likelihood of the opening angle distributions being identical.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 plots the Gamma-ray mean and peak fluxes for 173 and 117 sources. Figure 2 shows 5 GHz VIPS images or 15 GHz MOJAVE images for likely candidates. Figures 3 and 4 show images for the 19 plausible counterparts. Figure 5 plots the distribution of the core-to-jet ratio. Figure 6 shows the core brightness temperature K-S test was 11% for jet components. Figure 7 shows jet bending for four EGRET/VIPS sources. Table 1 lists 12 VIPS sources deemed likely candidates. Table 2 shows the automatic classification scheme of Helmboldt et al. Table 3 reports the core flux density for the EGRET blazars.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: EGRET blazars appear to have higher Doppler factors due to small viewing angles. 2. The strongest evidence: polarization was detected from a total of 48 ± 12% of the sources. 3. The future path: GLAST should confirm tighter beaming with improved statistics.

        The paper examines the radio properties of EGRET-detected blazars observed as part of the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS). VIPS covers a flux limit roughly an order of magnitude below the MOJAVE survey and most other samples that have been used to study the properties of EGRET blazars. At lower flux levels, radio flux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray flux density. The authors find that EGRET-detected blazars tend to have higher brightness temperatures, greater core fractions, and possibly larger than average jet opening angles. A weak correlation is also found with jet length and with polarization. All well-established trends can be explained by systematically larger Doppler factors in gamma-ray loud blazars, consistent with measurements of higher apparent velocities found in radio monitoring programs above 10 GHz.

        The survey covers 1127 flat-spectrum sources stronger than 85 mJy in the Northern Cap region of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). VIPS included 5 GHz, full polarization images of 958 sources and 147 total intensity images; 22 sources were from the VIPS pilot or MOJAVE surveys. Over 99% were successfully imaged, with just under 1% too weak to reliably self-calibrate.

        The EGRET candidate sample was compiled from the intersection of the Hartman et al. (1999) EGRET catalog and the CRATES (Healey et al. 2007a) survey, yielding 173 candidates at |b| > 10°. The VIPS region covers ~5700 square degrees, yielding 31 EGRET candidate blazars: 12 deemed likely candidates (FoM > 1) and 19 deemed plausible candidates (1.0 > FoM > 0.25). Automatic classification assigned 8 PS, 3 SJET, and 14 LJET sources; adding 6 MOJAVE sources resulted in 8 (25%) PS, 4 (13%) SJET, and 19 (61%) LJET. These were compared to the broader VIPS population of 25% PS, 22% SJET, 43% LJET, 9% CSO, and 2% CPLX.

        Key results include a polarization of 48 ± 12% detected from 25 sources (higher than VIPS 36 ± 4% and LJET 41 ± 4%). The core fraction K-S test gave a 4% probability that the distributions were from the same parent. Brightness temperature also yielded 4%, while the jet component K-S test was 11%. Opening half-angles: 3 of 4 sources exceeded the VIPS median of 18.9◦, with Monte-Carlo simulations suggesting less than a 1 in 3 chance of identical distributions. Jet length yielded a 34% K-S probability. The authors conclude that gamma-ray selected sources have higher Doppler factors due to small viewing angles, supporting jet-emission models.

        The paper lacks a formal bibliography, data release procedures, and an ethics statement. GLAST, launching late 2007, is expected to confirm these findings with better statistics.
