judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates whether giant planets can form by the gravitational fragmentation of circumstellar discs in the inner region (R < 40 AU) of solar-type stars. The authors conduct radiative hydrodynamic simulations using Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) to test the thermodynamics and cooling requirements for fragmentation. The study adopts a newly developed method for the energy equation and equation of state that accounts for radiative transfer effects, including the different chemical and internal states of hydrogen and dust properties across densities and temperatures. They examine two cases: a disc heated by a 10 K ambient radiation field and a disc with additional heating from the central star. In both cases, the disc does not fragment. In the first case, the disc is Toomre unstable at 30–35 AU but cannot cool fast enough, with cooling times generally >2 tORB. In the second case, the disc is not gravitationally unstable (Q > 1.5). The results corroborate previous works by Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007) and support the conclusion that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~50 AU. The paper links these findings to theoretical cooling conditions (tCOOL < C(gamma) tORB) and the impact of adiabatic index changes near the central star.

Research Context
The discovery of ~250 exoplanets around nearby stars has highlighted that giant planets exist very close to central stars on orbits of apparently random eccentricity. Two main theories have been proposed for the formation of giant planets: (i) core accretion and (ii) gravitational fragmentation. Core accretion predicts planets form within a few million years, but circumstellar discs may not be that long-lived. Gravitational fragmentation predicts planets form on a dynamical timescale, i.e. within a few hundred years, but requires massive discs. Two conditions must be fulfilled for discs to fragment: (i) the disc must be gravitationally unstable (Toomre Q < 1) and (ii) the disc must be able to cool fast enough. The required cooling condition is tCOOL < C(gamma) tORB, with 0.5 < C(gamma) < 2.0. It is uncertain whether real discs actually satisfy these conditions, with conflicting views on the sufficiency of convective cooling. Analytic studies suggest convection cannot provide required cooling and that discs cannot cool fast enough close (R < ~50 AU) to the central star. Hydrodynamic simulations have produced contradictory results due to different treatments of radiative transfer in discs.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether disc fragmentation can produce giant planets close to the central star in the inner region of real discs. The paper tests whether discs satisfy the fragmentation conditions: being gravitationally unstable (Q < 1) and cooling on a dynamical timescale. The researchers hypothesize that discs in the inner region will fail to fragment because they cannot cool fast enough or are not gravitationally unstable. Specifically, the hypothesis is that even if Toomre unstable, the cooling time throughout the disc will exceed the dynamical threshold. The study also tests whether stellar irradiation stabilizes the disc, making it even less prone to fragmentation. The null hypothesis is that fragmentation produces giant planets close to solar-type stars; the expected result is a refutation of this. A predicted outcome is that at R <~50 AU, the cooling times remain >~2 tORB, preventing fragmentation despite instability.

Methodological Details
The study uses the SPH code dragon, which invokes an octal tree for gravity and neighbors, adaptive smoothing lengths, and multiple particle timesteps. Artificial viscosity is set to alpha = 0.1, beta = 0.2 with the Balsara switch, using a second-order Runge-Kutta integration scheme. The energy equation is treated with the method of Stamatellos et al. (2007), accounting for compressional, viscous, and radiation heating/cooling. The gas is assumed to be a mixture of hydrogen and helium with an equation of state from Black & Bodenheimer 1975, Masunaga et al. 1998, and Boley et al. 2007. The equation of state accounts for the rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom of molecular hydrogen and different chemical states. Variations in the equation of state are included, including H2 dissociation and the first and second ionisation of He. However, temperatures are not high enough for molecular hydrogen to dissociate, and contributions from metals are ignored. The gas composition remains the same (mean molecular weight mu is constant), and metal contributions are omitted. Dust and gas opacity is parameterized by Bell & Lin 1994, kappa(rho, T) = kappa0 rho^a T^b. Opacity changes due to ice mantle melting, dust sublimation, molecular and H- contributions are included. The code has been extensively tested, reproducing the detailed 3D results of Masunaga & Inutsuka 2000 and the analytic test of Spiegel 1957.

Procedures And Architectures
The simulation models a 0.07 M⊙ disc around a 0.5 M⊙ star, representing a relatively massive disc. The disc initially extends from 2 to 40 AU and is assumed to be confined to R < 40 AU. Initial surface density is sigma(R) ~ R^-1/2 with sigma0 = 1.6 x 10^3 g cm^-2. The initial temperature profile is Td(R) = (T0^2 (R/AU)^-2 + Tinf^2)^1/2 with T0 = 1200 K and Tinf = 10 K. Initial thickness z0(R) is calculated by balancing star gravity, disc gravity, and pressure force. Two disc simulations are performed: (i) one without stellar irradiation with a constant background field of TBGR = 10 K. The second simulation includes radiation from the central star with a radially varying background temperature TBGR(R) ~ R^-1. Both cases use 2x10^5 SPH particles to represent the disc. In both cases, the disc relaxes from initial conditions to a quasi-steady state within ~250 yr. The cooling time is measured in units of the local orbital period tORB.

Key Results
In the disc with TBGR = 10 K, the disc is Toomre unstable at 30–35 AU, but does not fragment. Weak spiral arms form but do not show any tendency to fragment despite the instability. The cooling time throughout the disc is generally >~2 tORB, preventing fragmentation. The disc relaxes to a lower-temperature quasi-steady state when stellar heating is ignored compared to when irradiation is included. The temperatures calculated are estimated to be ~15% higher than those of Boley et al. (2006) at large radii. The temperatures calculated are less than 3% higher than those reported by Cai et al. (2007) across the disc. In the disc with stellar heating, the disc appears axisymmetric with no signs of spiral arms. The disc is overall hotter due to stellar heating and the temperature remains almost constant. With stellar heating, the disc cools fast enough to fragment at radii >~20 AU but does not fragment because Q > 1.5. The Toomre parameter reaches Q >~1.5, preventing fragmentation in the stellar heating case. Both simulations show no sign or even any tendency to fragment.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The cooling time constraint tCOOL < C(gamma) tORB (0.5 < C(gamma) < 2.0) is the central criterion. The adiabatic index gamma = 5/3 outside ~10 AU where T < ~80 K, and gamma = 7/5 closer to the central star. The increase from gamma = 5/3 to 7/5 increases the maximum allowed cooling time from 0.5 to 2 tORB. The cooling time is always >~2 tORB within ~30 AU, so discs are not expected to fragment and they do not fragment. Discs heated by the central star are even less prone to fragment because the disc is not gravitationally unstable. Fragmentation at large radii (>~100 AU) might produce brown dwarfs but they are unlikely to migrate inwards as hot Jupiters. Most planetary-mass objects formed at large radii would be ejected into the field though 3-body interactions. The primary conclusion is that gas giant planets probably cannot form close to the central star by gravitational fragmentation of discs. The results corroborate Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007), who use a different radiative transfer treatment.

Contradictions And Limitations
The spiral arms in the TBGR = 10 K simulation are weaker than those reported by Boley et al. (2006). The temperatures calculated are generally larger than those of Boley et al. (2006) at large radii (>~30 AU). Differences at large radii are attributable to a different background radiation field (10 K vs. 3 K). At small radii, discrepancies could be due to higher viscous heating in the authors' simulations. The Toomre parameter is generally higher than that of Boley et al. (2006) but the cooling times are lower. The adiabatic index gamma = 7/5 is due to the excitation of rotational degrees of freedom, but it is not fully resolved. The simulation assumes an axisymmetric disc in equilibrium for comparison with Hubeny (1990). External disc irradiation and self-gravity are included but convection and external irradiation are neglected in the analytic model. The authors admit metal contributions are ignored and the gas composition remains constant throughout. The simulation does not cover the formation of planets at radii >~50 AU where fragmentation may occur.

Claims
Disc fragmentation cannot produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <~50 AU because discs cannot cool fast enough. The disc is Toomre unstable at 30–35 AU but does not fragment. The cooling time throughout the disc is generally >~2 tORB. The adiabatic index gamma = 7/5 increases the fragmentation cooling threshold to 2 tORB. Even at radii >~20 AU with stellar heating, the disc is not gravitationally unstable (Q > 1.5). Some studies (Boss 2004, Mayer et al. 2007) suggest convection could provide sufficiently fast cooling. Analytic studies suggesting fragmentation could occur at larger distances (>~100 AU) are not addressed here. The simulation ignores metal contributions and assumes constant mean molecular weight. Gas giant planets cannot form by gravitational fragmentation of discs close to solar-type stars. This favors core accretion or other non-fragmentation formation mechanisms.

Data And Code Availability
The simulations were performed using the UK Astrophysical Fluids Facility (UKAFF). The code is an SPH code called dragon, developed by Goodwin et al. (2004). The energy equation treatment is from Stamatellos et al. (2007). The paper does not specify a publicly available repository for the code or data.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The simulation was repeated with a smaller number of 5x10^4 SPH particles, yielding essentially the same thermal energy, density, and Toomre results. The results are consistent with both the Indiana University Hydrodynamics Group and the SPH-RT code despite different treatments. Ablation of stellar heating shows that heating stabilizes the disc and removes spiral arms. Ablation of the RT scheme shows the results are similar to grid-based treatments by Cai et al. (2007).

Ethical Considerations
No human participants were involved; the study is entirely computational and theoretical. No ethical approvals or conflicts of interest were reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 plots internal energy evolution, showing a lower-temperature quasi-steady state without stellar heating. Figure 2 shows logarithmic column density and x-z cross-sections for the 10 K background case. Figure 3 shows logarithmic temperature in the x-y and x-z planes for the 10 K case. Figure 4 shows the Toomre parameter in the x-y and x-z planes for the 10 K case. Figure 5 shows the cooling time in units of tORB in the x-y and x-z planes for the 10 K case. Figures 6 and 7 show azimuthally averaged surface density, temperature, Toomre parameter, and cooling time at 5 instances. Figure 8 shows the vertical temperature structure compared to the Hubeny (1990) analytic model. Figure 14 shows azimuthally averaged Toomre parameter and cooling time for the stellar heating case, with Q > 1.5.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: The study uses a new SPH-RT method to prove that discs in the inner region cannot cool fast enough to fragment into giant planets. 2. The strongest evidence: For the 10 K case, the disc is Toomre unstable at 30–35 AU, yet the cooling time throughout is >~2 tORB. 3. The future path: Further study is needed at larger radii (>~100 AU) where the cooling threshold might be met, potentially producing brown dwarfs.

summary.title: On the Anomalous Gyromagnetic Ratio
summary.authors: G. G. Nyambuya
summary.executive_summary: The author proposes a curved spacetime version of the Dirac equation developed mainly to account naturally for the observed anomalous gyromagnetic ratio of Fermions. The Dirac equation, originally designed to overcome the Klein-Gordon equation's negative probabilities, accounts well for the electron's gyromagnetic ratio (g = 2) but fails for the proton (g_p = 5.58) and neutron (g_n = -3.83). The author argues that while the prevailing wisdom attributes these discrepancies to the non-fundamental nature of the proton and neutron, this theory claims the deviation arises because particles have a finite spatial size and spacetime is curved. The derived equation suggests the electron and muon possess finite spatial sizes rather than being point particles. A serendipitous result is that the equation exhibits an asymmetry in positive and negative energy solutions, suggesting the problem of why we do not observe negative energy and mass particles may be solved. The theory predicts four particle solutions, each with the same electric charge and gyromagnetic ratio, suggesting a particle will have a heavier or lighter partner, potentially explaining the electron-muon relationship. The muon's instability is heuristically attributed to vacuum energy being less than the particle's total energy. The author explicitly notes that the original paper contained a slight error regarding positive/negative solutions and was corrected in this version.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The author proposes a curved spacetime version of the Dirac equation developed mainly to account naturally for the observed anomalous gyromagnetic ratio of Fermions. The Dirac equation, originally designed to overcome the Klein-Gordon equation's negative probabilities, accounts well for the electron's gyromagnetic ratio (g = 2) but fails for the proton (g_p = 5.58) and neutron (g_n = -3.83). The author argues that while the prevailing wisdom attributes these discrepancies to the non-fundamental nature of the proton and neutron, this theory claims the deviation arises because particles have a finite spatial size and spacetime is curved. The derived equation suggests the electron and muon possess finite spatial sizes rather than being point particles. A serendipitous result is that the equation exhibits an asymmetry in positive and negative energy solutions, suggesting the problem of why we do not observe negative energy and mass particles may be solved. The theory predicts four particle solutions, each with the same electric charge and gyromagnetic ratio, suggesting a particle will have a heavier or lighter partner, potentially explaining the electron-muon relationship. The muon's instability is heuristically attributed to vacuum energy being less than the particle's total energy. The author explicitly notes that the original paper contained a slight error regarding positive/negative solutions and was corrected in this version.

Research Context
The Dirac equation was invented in 1928 to overcome the Klein-Gordon equation's negative probabilities. The Klein-Gordon equation was physically meaningless but accounted well for spin-zero bosons. The Dirac equation successfully predicted anti-particles and accounts well for the electron. The first success was the electron's gyromagnetic ratio g = 2, which non-relativistic QM could not explain. Stern and Frisch experiments in 1933 showed the proton's g_p = 5.58 and the neutron's g_n = -3.83. Prevailing wisdom attributes these discrepancies to the particles not being fundamental. Brodsky and Drell proposed a sub-structure giving rise to a gyromagnetic ratio varying with size. The author argues that anomalous gyromagnetic ratios arise from spin-Lorentz interaction in curved spacetime for finite-size particles.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the electron and muon are point particles or have finite size. The central hypothesis is that the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio results from finite particle size and curved spacetime. The theory predicts that particles have a finite spatial size. A predicted asymmetry between positive and negative energy solutions exists. The author hypothesizes that negative energy mass particles are not observed because the Universe is filled with positive energy. The theory predicts four particle solutions with the same charge and gyromagnetic ratio.

Methodological Details
The paper is a theoretical derivation without an experimental dataset or sample. It derives the equation starting from Einstein's 1905 special relativity paper. It uses the Klein-Gordon equation as a foundation. The Dirac equation is expressed as a four-component wave-function. Greek indices denote µ, ν, ... = 0, 1, 2, 3 and lower-case indices i, j, k... = 1, 2, 3. The Dirac gamma matrices are 4x4 matrices defined by γ0 and γi. The paper makes no new experiments or uses an empirical dataset. The paper references Zee (2003) for the gyromagnetic ratio discussion.

Procedures And Architectures
The paper derives a curved spacetime Dirac equation by modifying the flat spacetime equation. It defines a bar-gamma matrix set ¯γ0 and ¯γi satisfying {¯γµ, ¯γν} = 2Iµν. The curved spacetime Klein-Gordon equation is ¯□Ψ = (m0c/ℏ)Ψ. The Dirac bar matrices satisfy the anti-commutation relation {¯γµ, ¯γν} = 2Iµν. The curved spacetime Dirac equation is h(iℏ¯γµ∂µ - m0c/i)ψ = 0. For a point particle in an ambient magnetic field, the author uses a non-relativistic limit. The orbital angular momentum is defined via the Bohr condition pnrn = nℏ with n = 1. The resulting equation is the modified curved spacetime equation.

Key Results
The Dirac equation predicts g = 2 for the electron. The curved spacetime Dirac equation admits two energy solutions, E+ and E−. The energy solutions are E = Pc ± sqrt(P2c2 + m0c2). The asymmetry implies |E+| and |E-| are positive for all pi and m0 > 0. The derived anomalous gyromagnetic ratio is a = sqrt(2) [1 ± λc/Rp]^-1. A similar relation |g - 2| = Rp/λc was proposed by Brodsky & Drell (1980). The theory predicts four particle solutions, each with the same charge and gyromagnetic ratio. The first pair has energy E+ and opposite spins; the second has energy E− and opposite spins.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The author claims the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio arise from spin-Lorentz interaction in curved spacetime. Finite particle size explains the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio. The theory predicts the existence of anti-particles with positive mass and energy. The electron and muon are interpreted as a heavy-partner pair. The muon's instability is heuristically attributed to vacuum energy less than its total energy. The theory suggests the electron's partner exists as a heavier or lighter partner.

Contradictions And Limitations
The theory does not explain why the charge-conjugated partner of the electron is unstable. The theory does not explain why anti-particles are not naturally observed in the accessible Universe. The asymmetry solution is yet to be fully developed and will be in Paper II. The paper admits that it is an original, self-contained theoretical derivation without empirical proof. The paper notes a previous slit error was corrected. The theory remains largely heuristic and speculative in its vacuum energy interpretation.

Claims
The anomalous gyromagnetic ratio arise because particles have finite size and spacetime is curved. The derived relation is similar to Brodsky and Drell's. The anomalous gyromagnetic ratio arises from spin-Lorentz interaction in curved spacetime. Particles do have a finite spatial size. QED is currently the best-supported theory of the phenomena. QED renormalisation yields the right numbers but is questioned for naturalness. The electron and muon have finite spatial sizes. The electron and muon are a heavy-partner pair.
Negative energy and mass particles are not observed because of an asymmetry in the energy solutions. For all pi and m0 > 0, energy |E+| and |E-| are positive. The theory predicts anti-particles with positive mass. Anti-particles have not been confirmed to have negative mass. The solution will be presented in Paper II. Anti-particles may have positive mass and energy. The Universe appears filled with positive energy and mass.

Data And Code Availability
The paper is a theoretical derivation; no raw data or code is released.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The paper does not perform numerical ablations or robustness tests.

Ethical Considerations
The paper does not contain human or animal subjects.

Key Figures Tables
No figures or tables are provided.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the derivation of a curved spacetime Dirac equation where anomalous gyromagnetic ratios arise from finite spatial size. 2. The strongest evidence is the mathematical reproduction of the electron's g = 2 and the finite-size scaling |g-2| = Rp/λc. 3. The future path is Paper II, which will resolve the negative energy problem and the instability of the heavy-partner.

summary.title: Frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions in TbB4
summary.authors: T. Inami, K. Ohwada, Y. H. Matsuda, Z. W. Ouyang, H. Nojiri, D. Okuyama, T. Matsumura, and Y. Murakami
summary.executive_summary:
This work investigates the anomalous multi-step magnetization curve of TbB4, a frustrated Shastry-Sutherland lattice, using resonant magnetic x-ray diffraction (RMXD) in strong pulsed magnetic fields. Conventional magnetization plateaus are typically ascribed to Ising-type anisotropy where Sz is a good quantum number; the 1/3 and 1/2 plateaus in CoCl2·2H2O, PrCo2Si2, CeSb, Cs3Cr2Cl9, Ba3Mn2O8, and SrCu2(BO3)2 all exhibit collinear magnetic structures with no ordered perpendicular components. However, TbB4 exhibits an XY-type ground state and a multi-step magnetization process above 16 T, which the authors argue belongs to a rare class of magnets like CsFeCl3 characterized by ordered perpendicular components in the plateau phase.

The authors conducted RMXD at the Tb LIII absorption edge (7.514 keV) at SPring-8 using undulator beamline BL22XU, with fields up to 29 T generated by a 20 mm × 24 mm pulsed magnet with a 0.6 ms pulse duration. Magnetic moments were observed in the basal ab-plane between TN1=44 K and TN2=22 K, with the nearest-neighbor interaction J1 antiferromagnetic and a probable antiferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor J2, forming a frustrated SS lattice. Below TN2, moments rotate in the ab-plane toward a collinear-like structure accompanied by a structural change.

Applying a field along the c-axis, they observed that the 100 magnetic reﬂection intensity remains significant in the magnetization plateau phases above 16 T and stays constant between 20 and 24 T, where the 1/2 plateau resides. Using the characteristic RMXD polarization dependence, they conclude that the observed large (1,0,0) component consists of ab-plane components, which is surprising because all plateau moments are expected to be parallel or antiparallel to the field. A simple spin model with a hard XY ground state and excited Ising states (E → ∞, J1=2, J2=1, J3=2, D=1) reproduced the 1/2 plateau; frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields, creating the multi-step metamagnetic behavior. They conclude that frustration is not only an origin of degenerate states but also breaks degeneracy, and that RMXD coupled with pulsed fields enables studying magnetic structures near 30 T.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work investigates the anomalous multi-step magnetization curve of TbB4, a frustrated Shastry-Sutherland lattice, using resonant magnetic x-ray diffraction (RMXD) in strong pulsed magnetic fields. Conventional magnetization plateaus are typically ascribed to Ising-type anisotropy where Sz is a good quantum number; the 1/3 and 1/2 plateaus in CoCl2·2H2O, PrCo2Si2, CeSb, Cs3Cr2Cl9, Ba3Mn2O8, and SrCu2(BO3)2 all exhibit collinear magnetic structures with no ordered perpendicular components. However, TbB4 exhibits an XY-type ground state and a multi-step magnetization process above 16 T, which the authors argue belongs to a rare class of magnets like CsFeCl3 characterized by ordered perpendicular components in the plateau phase.

The authors conducted RMXD at the Tb LIII absorption edge (7.514 keV) at SPring-8 using undulator beamline BL22XU, with fields up to 29 T generated by a 20 mm × 24 mm pulsed magnet with a 0.6 ms pulse duration. Magnetic moments were observed in the basal ab-plane between TN1=44 K and TN2=22 K, with the nearest-neighbor interaction J1 antiferromagnetic and a probable antiferromagnetic next-nearest-neighbor J2, forming a frustrated SS lattice. Below TN2, moments rotate in the ab-plane toward a collinear-like structure accompanied by a structural change.

Applying a field along the c-axis, they observed that the 100 magnetic reﬂection intensity remains significant in the magnetization plateau phases above 16 T and stays constant between 20 and 24 T, where the 1/2 plateau resides. Using the characteristic RMXD polarization dependence, they conclude that the observed large (1,0,0) component consists of ab-plane components, which is surprising because all plateau moments are expected to be parallel or antiparallel to the field. A simple spin model with a hard XY ground state and excited Ising states (E → ∞, J1=2, J2=1, J3=2, D=1) reproduced the 1/2 plateau; frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields, creating the multi-step metamagnetic behavior. They conclude that frustration is not only an origin of degenerate states but also breaks degeneracy, and that RMXD coupled with pulsed fields enables studying magnetic structures near 30 T.

Research Context
Magnetization plateaus keep a constant value at a ﬁnite range of magnetic ﬁelds. This 'zero compressibility' is simply ascribed to the fact that Sz is a good quantum number. The easy-axis magnetization of an Ising antiferromagnet is most comprehensible. A combination of a ﬁnite number of Ising spins produces step-like magnetization. The plateau phases are described by a complex seaquence of up- and down-spins. Isolated (or weakly interacting) dimers are a trivial case. Cs3Cr2Cl9 (S= 3/2 dimers) and Ba3Mn2O8 (S=1 dimers) exhibit three-step and two-step magnetization curves, respectively. In the orthogonally connected S=1/2 dimers SrCu2(BO3)2, superstructures of excited triplet dimers are stabilized and one-eighth, one-fourth, and one-third magnetization plateaus are observed. Geometrically frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnets also frequently exhibit a magnetization plateau. All plateau phases have a collinear magnetic structure. No ordered magnetic moment perpendicular to the magnetic ﬁeld exists in the plateau phases. TbB4 resembles none of the above-mentioned magnets. CsFeCl3 is considered to be the only example. The net-work of the rare-earth ions is equivalent to the frustrated Shastry-Sutherland (SS) lattice. Classical continuous spins on the SS lattice are not frustrated. Each spin is not satisﬁed and still feels 'frustration'.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is why an XY-type magnet exhibits a multi-step magnetization process above 16 T. The hypothesis is that TbB4 belongs to a rare class characterized by ordered perpendicular components. They predict that the magnetization curve parallel to the c-axis exhibits multi-step metamagnetic behavior. The hypothesis is that there are low-lying Ising excited states just above the XY ground state. Frustration is predicted to be the key to understanding the observed multi-step magnetization. The model predicts the plateau phase includes the (1,0,0) component in its magnetic structure.

Methodological Details
Experiments were carried out at undulator beamline BL22XU at SPring-8. The x-ray energy was tuned to the Tb LIII absorption edge at 7.514 keV. Magnetic ﬁelds up to 29 T were generated using a small pulsed magnet. The magnet has a 20 mm outer diameter and 24 mm in length. The magnet is a split-pair, and two windows are prepared for incoming and outgoing x-rays. The pulse duration is about 0.6 ms. The magnet and a sample were attached to the cold head of a conventional closed cycle refrigerator. Single crystals of TbB4 were grown by the ﬂoating zone method. The scattering plane was horizontal, and the a*axis was in the plane. Magnetic ﬁelds were vertical and parallel to the c-axis. A high-counting-rate detector, an avalanche photodiode, was used. Diffraction intensity was measured with a typical resolution of 10 µs. The sample surface was locally heated by irradiation of synchrotron x-rays. The true sample temperature was estimated by the temperature dependence of the magnetic peak intensity.

Procedures And Architectures
The magnetic structure between TN1 and TN2 revealed by neutron powder diﬀraction is shown. The magnetic moments are conﬁned in the basal ab-plane. Additional in-plane anisotropy orients the moments parallel to the diagonal line. The nearest-neighbor interaction J1 is antiferromagnetic. The next-nearest-neighbor interaction J2 is probably antiferromagnetic, forming a frustrated SS lattice. The total angular momentum of the Tb ion is large (J=6). The Tb spin is approximated by a classical spin. The ground state is the XY-spin S with in-plane anisotropy E. The excited state is the Ising spin s with energy gap D. The spin Hamiltonian has no cross-term between the XY and Ising spins. Magnetization curves were calculated for ﬁnite-size cells with periodic boundary conditions. We consider 4 spins in the crystallographic unit cell (1x1 cell). Allowed states for spins 1 and 3 are listed. We initially consider the limit E → ∞, such that each spin has only 4 states. We took J1 = 2, J2 = 1, J3 = 2, D = 1. Similar results were obtained with other cell sizes (2x2 and 1x3 cells).

Key Results
The magnetic diﬀraction was observed below TN2 and above TN1. The intensity away from the resonant energy is background. The net diﬀraction intensity is about 2×105 counts/s. The intensity appears below TN1 and is constant below TN2. The 100 reﬂection intensity decreases with increasing magnetic ﬁelds above 16 T. The intensity keeps a constant value between 20 and 24 T, where the one-half plateau is observed. The one-half magnetization plateau phase is visible between 20 and 24 T. The data are an average of 30 ﬁeld-scans. The diﬀracted intensity of this structure is about one-quarter of the ground state. This is about 30∼50% of the intensity at 0 T.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The plateau phases include the (1,0,0) component in their magnetic structures. The π-π′ channel is proportional to sin 2θ. Since θ for the 100 reﬂection is only 6.6◦, the scattering amplitude for the c-axis component is very small. The observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consists of the ab-plane components. A canted magnetic structure results in a continuous magnetization curve. In TbB4 the magnetic structures in the plateau phases consist of very hard XY-type magnetic moments and Ising-like magnetic moments. Many states are degenerate at the critical ﬁelds Hc1/2 and Hc1. When E is ﬁnite, the one-third plateau phase reduces its energy, while the one-half plateau phase does not. Hence, when a defect is introduced, the magnetic struc-ture around the defect relaxes. This does not happen in magnetic lattices without frus-tration. Frustration is not only an origin of degen-erate states, but also breaks degeneracy. The basic scenario that frustration lifts the degeneracy at a metamagnetic transition is common for both magnets. We can state that frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions are a general mechanism.

Contradictions And Limitations
The proposed spin model is very much simpliﬁed. The spin models for TbB4 and CsFeCl3 are quite diﬀerent. We assume that the ground state is the XY-spin S with the in-plane anisotropy E. This is in fact a normal phe-nomenon observed in metamagnetic transitions. Interactions further than J3 must be included to account for the splitting at Hc1. We initially consider the limit E → ∞. The spin Hamiltonian has no cross-term between the XY and Ising spins. We assume the ground state is the XY-spin S and the excited state is the Ising spin s. The total angular momentum of the Tb ion is large (J=6).

Claims
The magnetization plateau phases include the (1,0,0) component in their magnetic structures, but the observed large (1,0,0) component consists of ab-plane components. The 100 reﬂection intensity remains in the magnetization plateau phases above 16 T. The intensity keeps a constant value between 20 and 24 T, where the one-half magnetization plateau is observed. The π-π′ channel is proportional to sin 2θ, and since θ for the 100 reﬂection is only 6.6◦, the scattering amplitude for the c-axis component is very small. All plateau phases have a collinear magnetic structure, and no ordered magnetic moment perpendicular to the magnetic ﬁeld exists. In TbB4 the magnetic structures in the plateau phases consist of very hard XY-type magnetic moments and Ising-like magnetic moments.
Frustration lifts the degeneracy at the critical fields and creates the observed multi-step metamagnetic behavior. Frustration is predicted to be the key to understanding the observed multi-step magnetization. Many states are degenerate at the critical ﬁelds Hc1/2 and Hc1. When E is ﬁnite, the one-third plateau phase reduces its energy, while the one-half plateau phase does not. Hence, when a defect is introduced, the magnetic struc-ture around the defect relaxes and gains exchange energy. The proposed spin model is very much simpliﬁed, and the spin models for TbB4 and CsFeCl3 are quite diﬀerent. We can state that frustration-driven successive metamagnetic transitions are a general mechanism.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The magnetization curves were calculated for ﬁnite-size cells with periodic boundary conditions. We initially consider the limit E → ∞. The magnetization curve for E → ∞ is clearly reproduced. Similar results were obtained with other cell sizes (2x2 and 1x3 cells).

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows examples of magnetization plateaus, the ground states (left) and magnetization plateau phases (right). Figure 1(a) shows an Ising antiferromagnet with competing J1 and J2 interactions. Figure 2(a) shows the magnetic structure of TbB4 between TN1 and TN2, with a large square as the unit cell. Figure 2(b) shows the magnetization process of TbB4 taken from Ref. [17]. Figure 3(a) shows the incident energy dependence of the 100 reﬂection below TN2 and above TN1. Figure 3(b) shows the intensity of the 100 reﬂection as a function of temperature. Figure 3(c) shows the field dependence of the 100 reﬂection. Figure 4(a) shows the calculated magnetization curve for E → ∞. The inset of Figure 4(a) shows the magnetic structure of the one-half plateau phase. Figure 4(b) shows a possible magnetic structure of the one-third plateau phase. Figure 4(c) shows the schematic energy diagram as a function of magnetic ﬁeld.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the discovery that the 1/2 magnetization plateau in TbB4 is composed of hard XY-type moments and Ising-like components, making it a rare magnet where ordered perpendicular components coexist with aligned components. 2. The strongest evidence is the RMXD intensity, which persists in the plateau phases (especially between 20 and 24 T) and is about 30∼50% of the 0 T intensity, with polarization evidence placing the large (1,0,0) component in the ab-plane. 3. The future path is the wide application of integrated RMXD and excellent pulsed-field techniques to study magnetic structures near 30 T in other high-field phases of many interesting magnets.

summary.executive_summary: This paper describes a novel immobilization strategy for carbon nanotubes (CNTs) that enables the direct, energy-resolved mapping of sidewall functionalization using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM). Sidewall functionalization, achievable through chemical processing like acid oxidation, drastically alters the electronic properties (band structure, topography, doping) of CNTs, making them useful for sensors, medical applications, and composite materials. However, STM imaging is typically impeded by mechanical instability; functional groups reduce the van der Waals anchors between nanotubes and the substrate, and the electrostatic force of the STM tip can 'sweep' or 'brush' the tubes out of the scan area, as illustrated by AFM imaging of an area after STM scanning. The authors present a simple solution: incorporating functionalized multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) into a few-layer graphene – nanotube composite (buckypaper). The nanotubes stick out from beneath the graphene layer, and the movement of the protruding tubes is restricted by the clamping graphene support, creating a stable sample for Current Imaging Tunneling Spectroscopy (CITS). CITS allows the simultaneous measurement of tunneling current vs. voltage at each pixel, generating local tunneling conductance maps qualitatively proportional to the local density of states (LDOS). The MWCNTs were prepared by chemical vapor deposition of acetylene over an alumina-supported Co/Fe catalyst and functionalized in a three-step process involving acid treatment, SOCl2 reaction, and diaminopropane cross-linking. Raman spectroscopy confirmed increased defect density (ID/IG), and ATR-IR identified amine and hydroxyl groups. STM imaging on the composite revealed several distinct regions: graphitic-like regions with high, symmetrical conductance (p-doped, showing a global Fermi level shift of around 0.25 eV); low-conductance, amorphous regions where atomic resolution is lost; and asymmetrical regions whose origin may be impurity states. Crucially, the functionalized regions follow the zigzag direction on the atomic lattice, suggesting that acid-oxidation preferentially advances along the zigzag crystallographic orientation. This is the first atomic-resolution report of crystallographic directionality in CNT functionalization and demonstrates the power of energy-resolved maps to spot sample features hidden from topography.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper describes a novel immobilization strategy for carbon nanotubes (CNTs) that enables the direct, energy-resolved mapping of sidewall functionalization using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM). Sidewall functionalization, achievable through chemical processing like acid oxidation, drastically alters the electronic properties (band structure, topography, doping) of CNTs, making them useful for sensors, medical applications, and composite materials. However, STM imaging is typically impeded by mechanical instability; functional groups reduce the van der Waals anchors between nanotubes and the substrate, and the electrostatic force of the STM tip can 'sweep' or 'brush' the tubes out of the scan area, as illustrated by AFM imaging of an area after STM scanning. The authors present a simple solution: incorporating functionalized multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) into a few-layer graphene – nanotube composite (buckypaper). The nanotubes stick out from beneath the graphene layer, and the movement of the protruding tubes is restricted by the clamping graphene support, creating a stable sample for Current Imaging Tunneling Spectroscopy (CITS). CITS allows the simultaneous measurement of tunneling current vs. voltage at each pixel, generating local tunneling conductance maps qualitatively proportional to the local density of states (LDOS). The MWCNTs were prepared by chemical vapor deposition of acetylene over an alumina-supported Co/Fe catalyst and functionalized in a three-step process involving acid treatment, SOCl2 reaction, and diaminopropane cross-linking. Raman spectroscopy confirmed increased defect density (ID/IG), and ATR-IR identified amine and hydroxyl groups. STM imaging on the composite revealed several distinct regions: graphitic-like regions with high, symmetrical conductance (p-doped, showing a global Fermi level shift of around 0.25 eV); low-conductance, amorphous regions where atomic resolution is lost; and asymmetrical regions whose origin may be impurity states. Crucially, the functionalized regions follow the zigzag direction on the atomic lattice, suggesting that acid-oxidation preferentially advances along the zigzag crystallographic orientation. This is the first atomic-resolution report of crystallographic directionality in CNT functionalization and demonstrates the power of energy-resolved maps to spot sample features hidden from topography.

Research Context
Sidewall functionalization of CNTs is a versatile tool to change their electronic properties. Changes to the nanotube electronic structure are usually investigated via spectroscopic methods. Complementary to these methods are scanning probe methods that provide spatially resolved information. STM gave a first account of the relation between CNT wrapping direction and band structure. Another STM work was able to map individual wavefunctions of CNTs. CITS allows acquiring a tunneling current vs. voltage at each pixel. CITS has been applied in mapping the local photovoltaic performance of organic solar cells. CITS also mapped the charge inhomogeneity of SiO2 supported graphene. Sample stability is the key bottleneck in achieving full STM potential on functionalized CNTs. The contact area decreases because of functional groups weakening the van der Waals anchors.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can STM be used to map energy-resolved functionalization at the atomic scale? The authors hypothesize that clamping the nanotubes against a graphene layer provides stability. They predict that acid treatment will promote functionalization along a specific crystallographic direction.

Methodological Details
Multiwalled CNTs were prepared by CVD of acetylene over an alumina-supported Co/Fe catalyst. Functionalization was carried out in a three step process. Step 1 treated pristine CNTs in H2SO4/HNO3 (3:1) mixture for 24 h. Step 2 involved overnight stirring in SOCl2. Step 3 involved stirring in diaminopropane for 24 h. Raman spectra used ID/IG to quantify functionalization. ATR-IR spectra identified amine, carboxyl, and hydroxyl groups. The final buckypaper was prepared by mixing with exfoliated graphite in isopropyl alcohol. A polycarbonate membrane filter with a 200 nm pore size was used for filtration. Electrical contact was made with carbon colloid paste. STM was performed using a Veeco Multimode III SPM in CITS mode. Data was processed separately using Scilab for STS extraction. The STM probe was a Pt/Ir wire cut from 80:20 Pt/Ir. Atomic resolution images were taken at 500 pA tunneling current and 100 mV bias. STM topography and CITS images used 300 pA current and 300 mV bias. TEM was performed on a Philips CM20 microscope at 200 keV.

Procedures And Architectures
CITS mode allows acquiring tunneling conductance maps. The STM probe was mechanically cut from the Pt/Ir wire and tested for reproducibility. CITS conductance maps were taken at -160 mV bias voltage. The fast scan direction was defined as horizontal. Red lines mark the zigzag direction on the atomic resolution image. The dI/dV maps were 75x75 nm in size.

Key Results
The functionalized sample showed an increase in the ID/IG Raman peak. ATR-IR spectra contained amine peaks in the functionalized sample. The nanotubes were immobilized by the graphene clamping layer. Most CNT regions were graphitic with symmetrical conductance. Global doping caused a Fermi level shift of around 0.25 eV. Functionalized regions appeared as protrusions on the surface. Functionalized regions corresponded to low-conductance areas. Functionalized bands followed the zigzag direction on the lattice. Atomic resolution was lost on the low-conductance regions. The p-doping minimum was shifted towards positive tip-sample bias.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Functionalization converts sp2 carbon to sp3. This reduces the number of delocalized pi electrons. Monovalent functional groups theoretically predict impurity states near the Fermi level. The expected signature was contrary to other systems we have studied. The graphitic layers of the tubes were damaged. Oxidation reactions can prefer a specific crystallographic direction. The zigzag orientation suggests nitric-sulfuric acid oxidation is directed.

Contradictions And Limitations
The electronic structure of the surface is unknown in damaged regions. The origin of the asymmetric dI/dV curves is not clear. The acid treatment was much milder than prior CNT oxidation. The global doping source may be acid adsorbents or ambient oxygen. No bibliography was provided to verify specific reference numbers.

Claims
Graphene clamping immobilizes functionalized nanotubes, enabling stable atomic-resolution CITS mapping. The nanotubes were restricted by the clamping FLG layer. Low-conductance areas corresponded to functionalized protrusions. The dI/dV maps were qualitatively proportional to the local DOS. The origin of some dI/dV asymmetries is not clear. The interpretation in heavily damaged regions is unknown. The technique is applicable to any type of functionalized nanotube. It allows local functionalization and doping state identification.
Acid-oxidation functionalization preferentially advances along the zigzag crystallographic direction. Functionalized regions followed the zigzag direction. Lattice superstructure patterns marked defect scattering. Only a few such STM studies exist. The acid treatment was much milder than prior oxidation. Oxidation reactions can prefer a specific crystallographic direction. This supports the idea that nanotubes can unzip into nanoribbons.

Data And Code Availability
STS data was processed separately using Scilab. No raw CITS data or source code was deposited.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Tips were tested for reproducible STS and atomic resolution. Atomic resolution was confirmed on graphite. Imaging was done at different current/bias setpoints.

Ethical Considerations
No explicit ethical considerations are reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows CNTs swept away by the STM tip. Figure 2b shows increased D peak intensity (ID/IG). Figure 3a illustrates the CNT – FLG composite. Figure 4b shows tunneling conductance maps at -160 mV. Figure 5 shows functionalized regions follow the zigzag direction. Figure 6 shows the dI/dV minimum color map.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is an immobilization technique enabling CITS mapping of functionalized CNTs. 2. The strongest evidence is that functionalized bands follow the zigzag direction. 3. The future path involves using CITS for gas sensing and environmental studies.

summary.executive_summary:
The paper investigates the Cauchy problem for a two-dimensional nonlocal nonlinear wave equation that governs anti-plane shear motions in a nonlocally elastic medium. The governing equation is a nonlocal wave equation where the nonlocal nature is represented by a convolution integral with a kernel β. The nonlinearity arises from a strain energy density function F, modeled as F(|∇w|2) with F(0) = 0, where the spatial gradient of the out-of-plane displacement w is involved. The kernel β is assumed to be an integrable function whose Fourier transform bβ is nonnegative and satisfies a specific growth condition at infinity (1.3). The primary analytical goal is to establish the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem, as well as the conditions for global existence versus finite-time blow-up of the solutions for initial data in L2 Sobolev spaces.

The local well-posedness is established in C2 spaces over a small time interval by converting the initial value problem into a system of Banach space-valued ordinary differential equations and proving the operator K—representing the nonlocal stresses—is locally Lipschitz. The regularizing effect of the kernel is parameterized by a growth constant r, and a comparison of Theorem 3.7 and Theorem 3.8 illustrates that a larger r increases the regularizing effect. Theorem 3.7 establishes local well-posedness for Sobolev index s > 2 and kernel regularity r ≥2, while Theorem 3.8 improves this to s ≥1 when the kernel is highly regularizing (r > 3). Global existence is proven in Theorem 4.3 for r > 4, requiring an energy functional to be bounded below and the initial configuration energy to be integrable. A conservation of energy argument is key to the global existence proof. Finite-time blow-up is established in Theorem 5.2, requiring a sublinear growth condition on the nonlinearity and negative initial energy E(0) < 0. The energy E(t) is shown to be constant, and the blow-up is characterized by the L∞-norm of the spatial gradient exploding in finite time.

Research Context

summary.title: Blow-up and global existence for a general class of nonlocal nonlinear coupled wave equations
summary.authors: N. Duruk, H. A. Erbay, A. Erkip
summary.executive_summary: This mathematical research paper investigates the initial-value problem for a general class of nonlinear nonlocal coupled wave equations. The study focuses on a coupled system of two equations where the nonlinearity is nonlocal, implemented via convolution operators with kernel functions whose Fourier transforms are nonnegative. The authors generalize a known single-equation model for one-dimensional nonlocal elasticity to a coupled system of two nonlocal nonlinear equations. This framework encompasses several important coupled systems: as a special case, a suitable choice of nonlinearity gives the system governing one-dimensional pure transverse nonlinear waves in a nonlocal elastic isotropic homogeneous medium. Furthermore, for specific kernel functions, the system reduces to well-known coupled models: the exponential kernel leads to the coupled improved Boussinesq equations, which model bi-directional wave propagation in Toda lattice, two-layered lattice, and diatomic lattice models. Kernels corresponding to the Green's function for a fourth-order operator lead to the coupled higher-order Boussinesq system. This higher-order system arises in models of a dense chain of particles with elastic couplings, for water waves with surface tension, and for longitudinal waves in a nonlocal nonlinear elastic medium. The authors prove that while the single-component form of the coupled higher-order Boussinesq system is globally well-posed, the questions of global well-posedness and finite-time blow-up for the coupled system are open problems. The paper addresses these questions by considering a closely related, slightly more general Cauchy problem. The authors establish a local existence theory for kernels with $r_1, r_2 \geq 2$ and initial data in Sobolev spaces. They establish that the problem is well-posed in the Sobolev space $H_s$ for $s > 1/2$ and kernels with the Fourier transform bound $0 \leq \hat{\beta}_i(\xi) \leq C_i(1 + \xi^2)^{-r_i/2}$. They further establish an energy conservation result, showing that the energy $E(t)$ remains constant under the exactness condition $\partial g_1 / \partial u_2 = \partial g_2 / \partial u_1$ and the integrability of the potential $G$. The paper proves a finite-time blow-up theorem, showing that solutions blow up in finite time when the initial energy is negative and a growth inequality holds. They establish two global existence theorems: one for smooth kernels ($r_1, r_2 > 3$) under an energy-bound condition on the nonlinearity, and another for mildly singular kernels with a jump in the first derivative and a Dirac measure term in the distributional second derivative. They show that the blow-up can even occur for positive initial energy under certain initial data conditions. The results extend existing global existence theory from the single-component case to the coupled system.

Executive Summary
This mathematical research paper investigates the initial-value problem for a general class of nonlinear nonlocal coupled wave equations. The study focuses on a coupled system of two equations where the nonlinearity is nonlocal, implemented via convolution operators with kernel functions whose Fourier transforms are nonnegative. The authors generalize a known single-equation model for one-dimensional nonlocal elasticity to a coupled system of two nonlocal nonlinear equations. This framework encompasses several important coupled systems: as a special case, a suitable choice of nonlinearity gives the system governing one-dimensional pure transverse nonlinear waves in a nonlocal elastic isotropic homogeneous medium. Furthermore, for specific kernel functions, the system reduces to well-known coupled models: the exponential kernel leads to the coupled improved Boussinesq equations, which model bi-directional wave propagation in Toda lattice, two-layered lattice, and diatomic lattice models. Kernels corresponding to the Green's function for a fourth-order operator lead to the coupled higher-order Boussinesq system. This higher-order system arises in models of a dense chain of particles with elastic couplings, for water waves with surface tension, and for longitudinal waves in a nonlocal nonlinear elastic medium. The authors prove that while the single-component form of the coupled higher-order Boussinesq system is globally well-posed, the questions of global well-posedness and finite-time blow-up for the coupled system are open problems. The paper addresses these questions by considering a closely related, slightly more general Cauchy problem. The authors establish a local existence theory for kernels with $r_1, r_2 \geq 2$ and initial data in Sobolev spaces. They establish that the problem is well-posed in the Sobolev space $H_s$ for $s > 1/2$ and kernels with the Fourier transform bound $0 \leq \hat{\beta}_i(\xi) \leq C_i(1 + \xi^2)^{-r_i/2}$. They further establish an energy conservation result, showing that the energy $E(t)$ remains constant under the exactness condition $\partial g_1 / \partial u_2 = \partial g_2 / \partial u_1$ and the integrability of the potential $G$. The paper proves a finite-time blow-up theorem, showing that solutions blow up in finite time when the initial energy is negative and a growth inequality holds. They establish two global existence theorems: one for smooth kernels ($r_1, r_2 > 3$) under an energy-bound condition on the nonlinearity, and another for mildly singular kernels with a jump in the first derivative and a Dirac measure term in the distributional second derivative. They show that the blow-up can even occur for positive initial energy under certain initial data conditions. The results extend existing global existence theory from the single-component case to the coupled system.

Research Context
The study examines a general class of nonlocal nonlinear coupled wave equations. The nonlocal Cauchy problem generalizes a single-equation model of nonlocal elasticity. The convolution operators are nonlocal with nonnegative Fourier transforms. As a special case, the system describes pure transverse nonlinear waves. The improved Boussinesq equations are a motivating coupled wave system. Dense particle chains and water waves motivate the higher-order Boussinesq system.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Global well-posedness and blow-up of coupled higher-order Boussinesq are open. The question concerns the coupled higher-order Boussinesq system (1.10)-(1.11). The paper addresses this via a general Cauchy problem (1.1)-(1.4). The central hypothesis is global existence for certain kernels and nonlinearities.

Methodological Details
The nonlocal Cauchy problem is posed in $H_s$ Sobolev spaces. Initial data is required in $\phi_i, \psi_i \in H_s$. Kernel functions $\beta_i$ have Fourier transforms $\leq C_i(1 + \xi^2)^{-r_i/2}$. The exactness condition $\partial g_1 / \partial u_2 = \partial g_2 / \partial u_1$ is assumed. The Sobolev embedding $H_s \subset L^\infty$ requires $s > 1/2$. The Sobolev space is $H_s = H_s(\mathbb{R})$ on the real line. The norms are defined via the Fourier transform representation. The Fourier transform preserves the Sobolev space $H_s$.

Procedures And Architectures
The Cauchy problem is reduced to an $H_s$-valued system of ODEs. Standard ODE well-posedness [16] is applied to the system. The nonlinear functions are rewritten as $f_i = u_i + g_i$. Lipschitz continuity is shown by Corollary 2.3. The blow-up is detected by a divergent $H_s$ norm and derivative. The energy $E(t)$ is constant under exactness and integrability. The energy identity requires $G(u_1, u_2) \in L^1$.

Key Results
Theorem 2.4: Local well-posedness for $s > 1/2$ and $r_1, r_2 \geq 2$. Theorem 4.2: Negative initial energy and growth bound imply blow-up. Theorem 5.1: Smooth kernels $r_1, r_2 > 3$ guarantee global solution. Theorem 5.2: Mildly singular kernels yield a global solution. The energy is constant under the exactness condition.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Exactness is necessary for the conservation law of Lemma 3.2. Mildly singular kernels have jumps in the first derivative. The jump gives a Dirac measure term in $\beta''$. The singularity is quantified by $\lambda = -2\gamma'(0) > 0$. Blow-up can occur for $E(0) > 0$ under weak initial data.

Contradictions And Limitations
$L^\infty$ bounds in Lemma 2.2 are unnecessary for $s > 1/2$. Exactness and nonnegativity are not needed for local existence. The global existence theorems require energy integrability. There is no discussion of physical parameters or random seeds. No analysis on $L^2$ alone ($s \leq 1/2$).

Claims
Local existence holds in $H_s$ for $s > 1/2$ and $r_1, r_2 \geq 2$. Theorem 2.4 proves well-posedness in $C^2([0, T], H_s)$. The kernels satisfy $r_1, r_2 \geq 2$. The problem is reduced to an ODE system. The local regularity is $s > 1/2$. It provides a foundation for further analysis.
Solutions blow up in finite time under negative initial energy and a growth inequality. Theorem 4.2 yields finite-time blow-up. The energy condition is $E(0) < 0$. The growth inequality involves $\nu > 0$. Blow-up may occur even if $E(0) > 0$. The blow-up condition is $A^2 < E(0)B$. Remark 4.3 nuances the energy-negative case. Finite-time blow-up contradicts global existence. Global solutions exist only under certain conditions. The criterion is initial-data-dependent.
Smooth kernels with $r_1, r_2 > 3$ guarantee a global solution under a nonlinearity bound. Theorem 5.1 establishes global existence. The kernel regularity is $r_1, r_2 > 3$. A quadratic growth bound on $G$ is required. Blow-up may still occur under other data. The bound is $2k - 1$ on the energy norm. It contrasts with the $E(0) < 0$ blow-up case. Smooth kernels provide a global existence regime. Energy remains bounded in $H_s$. The growth bound ensures regularity persists.
Mildly singular kernels yield a global solution. Theorem 5.2 proves global existence for mild kernels. The kernels have a jump in $\beta'$. The jump gives a Dirac measure in $\beta''$. None reported explicitly for mild kernels. The condition involves $q_i > 1$ exponents. It extends [14] to the coupled system. Mild singularity allows a global existence result. It extends a single-component result. The result relies on a $C^2$ kernel bound.

Data And Code Availability
Data and code availability are not reported.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The blow-up uses $\Phi(0) > 0$ and $\Phi'(0) > 0$. The blow-up functional is $\Phi(t) = \|P1u1\|_2 + \|P2u2\|_2 + b(t + t_0)^2$. Blow-up data conditions: $A -E(0)t_0 > 0$ and $B -E(0)t_0^2 > 0$. Blow-up exists if $A^2 < E(0)B$. Gronwall's lemma provides the energy bound.

Ethical Considerations
No ethical considerations are reported.

No figures or tables are included in the text.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is global well-posedness and blow-up of nonlocal coupled wave equations. 2. The strongest evidence is the conservation law and blow-up thresholds. 3. The future path lies in lower regularity and more general nonlinearies.

summary.title: SEARCH FOR HIGH-ENERGY GAMMA-RAY EMISSION FROM ANOMALOUS X-RAY PULSAR, 4U 0142+61
summary.authors: Sinem S¸as¸maz Mus¸1, Ersin G¨o˘g¨us¸1
summary.type_of_paper: observational; observational study of a single source with upper limits
summary.executive_summary: Anomalous X-ray Pulsars (AXPs) are young isolated neutron stars powered by extremely strong magnetic fields, exhibiting high X-ray luminosities and slow spin periods. A major development was the discovery of hard X-ray components from AXPs like 4U 0142+61, but the emission mechanism remains unresolved. This study utilizes Large Area Telescope (LAT) data on board Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope to probe the persistent and pulsed high-energy gamma-ray emission of the brightest AXP, 4U 0142+61, over a broad energy range. Contemporaneous Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) data were used to obtain the spin ephemeris. The persistent emission was searched within 15 and 2 degree extraction regions, yielding no detection and resulting in 3sigma upper limits: 2.32 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 (0.2−1.0 GeV band) and 1.28 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 (1.0−10.0 GeV band) for the 15 degree region, and 5.72 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 and 1.29 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 respectively for the 2 degree region. The pulsed emission was searched using a Fourier-based epoch folding technique, yielding 3sigma upper limits to the RMS pulsed fraction: 1.5% (0.2−1.0 GeV band), 2.3% (1.0−10.0 GeV band), and 1.6% (30−200 MeV band). None of the objectives reached significant detection. Constructing a combined nuFnu spectrum from 15 keV to 10 GeV using the hard X-ray spectrum from den Hartog et al. (2008) (index 0.93 ± 0.06) and the new upper limits, they place a power-law upper-limit curve (index −0.76) intersecting the hard X-ray fit at ~1.1 MeV, establishing an upper limit to the spectral break energy. This is consistent with the Beloborodov & Thompson coronal model (photons > ~1 MeV trapped or split) and the Heyl & Hernquist QED model (lower limit ~1 MeV). While the optical excess in 4U 0142+61 complicates the QED model interpretation, the overall lack of increase in the 10−200 MeV range constrains the QED model if the emission is from the compact object.

Contemporaneous Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) data were used to obtain the spin ephemeris. The persistent emission was searched within 15 and 2 degree extraction regions, yielding no detection and resulting in 3sigma upper limits: 2.32 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 (0.2−1.0 GeV band) and 1.28 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 (1.0−10.0 GeV band) for the 15 degree region, and 5.72 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 and 1.29 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1 respectively for the 2 degree region. The pulsed emission was searched using a Fourier-based epoch folding technique, yielding 3sigma upper limits to the RMS pulsed fraction: 1.5% (0.2−1.0 GeV band), 2.3% (1.0−10.0 GeV band), and 1.6% (30−200 MeV band). None of the objectives reached significant detection. Constructing a combined nuFnu spectrum from 15 keV to 10 GeV using the hard X-ray spectrum from den Hartog et al. (2008) (index 0.93 ± 0.06) and the new upper limits, they place a power-law upper-limit curve (index −0.76) intersecting the hard X-ray fit at ~1.1 MeV, establishing an upper limit to the spectral break energy. This is consistent with the Beloborodov & Thompson coronal model (photons > ~1 MeV trapped or split) and the Heyl & Hernquist QED model (lower limit ~1 MeV). While the optical excess in 4U 0142+61 complicates the QED model interpretation, the overall lack of increase in the 10−200 MeV range constrains the QED model if the emission is from the compact object.



Research Context
AXPs were known as strong emitters of soft X-rays only (< 10 keV until 2004. The discovery of hard X-ray component from AXPs provided important insight while posing a serious challenge. The physical mechanism of the hard emission component has still not been fully resolved. AXPs are bright X-ray sources with X-ray luminosities in the range of 10^33−10^36 erg s^-1. They possess spin periods clustered in a narrow range of 2−12 s. The lack of binary evidence eliminates the possibility they accrete matter from a donor. Their spin-down rates are relatively large, ranging between 10^-10−10^-12 s s^-1. Rotational energy loss is insufficient by orders of magnitudes to provide observed X-ray luminosities. AXPs are commonly regarded as young isolated neutron stars powered by extremely strong magnetic fields, B>10^14 G. Such fields can efficiently slow systems via magnetic braking and provide X-ray energy via field diffusion. The hard X-ray emission from 1RXS J170849.0-400910 was discovered in the Galactic Plane Survey. The hard emission from 4U 0142+61 was discovered during INTEGRAL observations of the Cassiopeia region. The hard X-ray emission nature is still not well understood. The authors note the lack of a broad-energy spectral shape for AXPs.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The research question is to investigate the persistent and pulsed high-energy gamma-ray emission of 4U 0142+61. The objective is to establish the spectral behavior over a broad energy span. The hypothesis is that the source may show persistent or pulsed emission, detectable by Fermi/LAT. The researchers expect to find upper limits that constrain existing physical models. They hypothesize that a non-detection will constrain the coronal and QED models.

Methodological Details
Fermi/LAT operates in the energy band of 20 MeV−300 GeV. The LAT has operated as an all-sky monitor since 2008 August 4, covering the sky every ~3 hours. Data were collected from 2008 August 4 to 2010 April 29 with an exposure time of ~31.7 Ms. The data were selected within a 15-degree radius centered at 4U 0142+61. A 2-degree radius region was used for spectral analysis to avoid nearby bright source contamination. Unbinned likelihood analysis was performed using ScienceTools v9r15p2 with P6 V3 DIFFUSE. The maximum zenith angle was set to 105-degrees to eliminate background from the Earth limb. All time intervals where the zenith cut intersected the region were excluded. The diffuse gamma-ray emission from the Milky Way was modeled with glliem v02.fit. The isotropic iem v02.txt model accounted for extragalactic diffuse emission and residual background. Spectral fits and flux calculations used the python version of gtlike, pyLikelihood. Photon arrival times were converted to the solar system barycenter using gtbary of ScienceTools. Contemporaneous RXTE PCA observations were used for the spin ephemeris. RXTE PCA is sensitive to photon energies between 2−60 keV. 53 RXTE observations between 2008 August 4 and 2010 April 30 were selected. RXTE pointings are typically 3 and 4 ks long, with a total exposure of about 196 ks. For each RXTE observation, events were extracted in the 2−10 keV range. RXTE arrival times were converted to the solar system barycenter using faxbary of HEASoft 6.8.

Procedures And Architectures
The Fermi/LAT instrument is a pair conversion telescope with a silicon tracker and calorimeter. For pulsed emission, a Fourier-based epoch folding technique was employed to obtain the spin ephemeris. Three consecutive PCA observations around MJD 54713.5 generated the initial pulse profile. Observations were grouped to be spaced at least 0.2 days apart. Each group pointing's pulse profile was cross-correlated with the template profile for phase shifts. Phase shifts were fit with a 3rd-order polynomial, yielding chi-squared/DoF of 59.6/42. The spin ephemeris for 4U 0142+61 is tabulated in Table 1. LAT pulse profiles were generated in the 0.2−1.0 GeV and 1.0−10.0 GeV energy ranges. For persistent emission, a point source search used the filtered event list with gtfindsrc. The 15-degree region fit included all bright cataloged sources and a recently discovered blazar. The blazar was included based on the Vandenbroucke et al. 2010 reference. Galactic and extragalactic diffuse emission models were added with free parameters. The 3-sigma flux upper limits assumed a power-law index of 2.5. For the 2-degree region, a power-law model of index 3 was used. A Fourier-based epoch folding technique cross-correlated each group's profile with the template. The spin ephemeris period ν was calculated as 0.1150900026(9) Hz. The period derivative ˙ν was measured at −2.745(8) × 10^-14 Hz s^-1. The second derivative ¨ν was measured at 3.6(3) × 10^-23 Hz s^-2.

Key Results
4U 0142+61 was clearly not detected in the LAT energy passband. A point source search resulted in a potential source whose coordinates were inconsistent with 4U 0142+61. The 15-degree region fit yielded a Test Statistics (TS) value of ~0.23. This TS implies a detection significance less than 1-sigma. The 3-sigma flux upper limit in the 0.2−1.0 GeV band was 2.32 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1. The 3-sigma flux upper limit in the 1.0−10.0 GeV band was 1.28 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1. The 2-degree region fit yielded a TS value of ~3. This TS implies a detection significance less than 4-sigma. The 3-sigma upper limit in the 0.2−1.0 GeV band was 5.72 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1. The 3-sigma upper limit in the 1.0−10.0 GeV band was 1.29 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1. The 3-sigma upper limit to the RMS pulsed fraction in the 0.2−1.0 GeV band was 1.5%. The 3-sigma upper limit to the RMS pulsed fraction in the 1.0−10.0 GeV band was 2.3%. The 3-sigma upper limit to the RMS pulsed fraction in the 30−200 MeV band was 1.6%. The LAT upper limits are much lower than the high pulsed fractions seen in hard X-rays. The hard X-ray spectrum from den Hartog et al. (2008) has an index of 0.93 ± 0.06. The upper limit curve has a power-law index of −0.76. The two curves intersect at ~1.1 MeV, setting an upper limit to the spectral break energy. The spectral break upper limit of ~1.1 MeV is consistent with den Hartog et al. (2008).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results constrain existing physical models of AXPs. The estimated spectral break energy upper limit is ~1.1 MeV. This is in accordance with the coronal emission model by Beloborodov & Thompson (2007). Beloborodov & Thompson suggest photons above ~1 MeV are trapped in ultrastrong magnetic fields (B>10^14 G). Photons > ~1 MeV would split into two photons or create an electron-positron pair. The spectral break upper limit also agrees with the Heyl & Hernquist (2005a,b) QED model. They expect the lower limit to the break energy to be around 1 MeV. However, they claim sources with optical excess should continuously increase in the 10−200 MeV range. Optical emission originates from the neutron star itself and from a disk. The origin of the excess optical emission in 4U 0142+61 is not clear. If from the compact object, results constrain the QED model due to lack of increase in the 10−200 MeV range. If the disk provides a significant contribution, the QED model remains feasible.

Contradictions And Limitations
The 4U 0142+61 source was not detected in the LAT passband. The point source search coordinates were inconsistent with 4U 0142+61. The detection significance was less than 1-sigma and 4-sigma respectively. The upper limits are much lower than hard X-ray pulsed fractions seen by INTEGRAL. The spectral break upper limit of ~1.1 MeV is an upper limit, not a measurement. The coronal and QED models agree on the break energy but differ on the 10−200 MeV range. The interpretation hinges on whether the optical excess is from the star or the disk. The upper limit curve assumes a power-law index of −0.76 between the LAT measurements. The hard X-ray spectrum was adopted from den Hartog et al. (2008) without new measurements.

Claims
The hard X-ray emission from 4U 0142+61 does not extend significantly into the Fermi/LAT gamma-ray band, placing a low upper limit on the spectral break energy. 4U 0142+61 was clearly not detected in the LAT energy passband. The 3-sigma flux upper limits in the 0.2−10.0 GeV band are ~1.28-1.29 × 10^-6 MeV cm^-2 s^-1. The 3-sigma upper limit to the RMS pulsed fraction is 1.5% to 2.3%. The LAT upper limits are much lower than high pulsed fractions seen in hard X-rays. The spectral break upper limit was calculated to be ~1.1 MeV. The 2-degree region fit yielded a TS value of ~3, implying <4-sigma significance. The point source search coordinates were inconsistent with 4U 0142+61. The upper limit curve has an index of −0.76, not a measured value. The result is consistent with the coronal emission model by Beloborodov & Thompson (2007). The result also agrees with the Heyl & Hernquist (2005a,b) QED model. The interpretation hinges on the unknown origin of the excess optical emission.

Data And Code Availability
The authors did not explicitly state where the processed data or analysis code is available.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The spectral parameters and fluxes of cataloged sources were consistent with catalog values, showing the analysis is robust. The zenith cut excluded all time intervals where it intersected the region. The 2-degree region was used to avoid contamination from nearby bright sources.

Ethical Considerations
The paper does not mention ethical considerations or human participants.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the smoothed Fermi-LAT count map with 15-degree and 2-degree extraction regions. Figure 2 shows the spin phase shifts and the best-fitting 3rd-order polynomial model. Figure 3 presents the gamma-ray flux upper limits and the combined nuFnu spectrum. Table 1 tabulates the spin ephemeris parameters of 4U 0142+61. The νFν spectrum is constructed from 15 keV to 10 GeV using the hard X-ray spectrum from den Hartog et al. (2008).

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the establishment of 3sigma upper limits on the persistent and pulsed gamma-ray emission of 4U 0142+61. 2. The strongest evidence is the null detection in both the 15-degree and 2-degree extraction regions across the LAT passband. 3. The future path involves resolving the unknown origin of the optical excess to constrain the QED and coronal models.

summary.title: Can we predict the failure point of a loaded composite material ?
summary.authors: Srutarshi Pradhan
summary.executive_summary:
This paper investigates whether the failure point of a loaded composite material can be predicted from observable precursors within the framework of the fiber bundle model (FBM). The FBM describes a collection of fibers with statistically distributed strength thresholds subjected to external load, where load is shared among intact fibers following a rule. The study adopts an equal-load-sharing model where a failed fiber's load is shared equally by all remaining intact fibers. The authors use a bundle of N elastic fibers obeying Hooke's law with unity force constants and independent uniform strength thresholds P(x) = x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. Three loading scenarios are analyzed: quasi-static (strain-controlled), equal-step load increments (force-controlled), and the over-loaded case. 

In the quasi-static case, the expected force F(x) reaches a maximum at critical elongation x_c; the burst size distribution follows a power law D(∆) ∝ ∆^{-5/2} globally, but shows a crossover to -3/2 near the breakdown point. Predictability arises as the average burst size ∆_av behaves as (x_c - x)^0.9, so plotting ∆_av^{-1/0.9} against x yields a straight line touching the axis at x_c. For load increment by equal steps, a recursion relation U_{t+1} = 1 - P(σ/U_t) governs the surviving fraction; susceptibility χ and relaxation time τ diverge as (σ_c - σ)^{-1/2}, allowing extrapolation of χ^{-2} and τ^{-2} to predict σ_c. In the over-loaded case (σ = σ_c + ε), the breaking rate R(t) reaches a minimum at t_f/2, halfway to collapse. Finally, the paper explores energy emission bursts (acoustic emissions), showing that below-critical stresses produce many small bursts with a -1 exponent, while over-critical stresses produce a -1.5 exponent, with a crossover in behavior. The core conclusion is that FBM provides multiple measurable precursors allowing prediction of the critical failure point before complete collapse occurs.
