The throughput could be increased by setting up multiple cuvettes in parallel. Setting up more than 5-10 cuvettes in the same freezer system resulted in non-uniform results. In setting up 10 cuvettes at the same time, a difference of a few degrees' between cuvettes was observed. High throughput screening (HTS) in multi-well plates miniaturization and automation is a well-established method. Polydispersity is detrimental in icenucleation studies because freezing temperature is proportional to the logarithm of droplets diameter. This approximation will lead to a 2.3 °C difference of mean freezing temperature between 1 mm and 0.1 mm diameter droplets.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to expand the system to higher throughput and accuracy. The goal was to add three functional advantages: increased efficiency, increased accuracy due to increased sample size, and increased uniformity of temperature. The authors describe steps for automated droplets generations, freeze-float system adaptations using controlled and uniform temperature cooling, and semi-automated detection. The hypothesis is that droplet freezing is a random nucleation process which can be accelerated by ice nucleators. Due to stochastic freezing behavior, the freezing spectra usually shows inherent distributions, making it difficult to determine temperature from a small number of samples. The authors hypothesized that expanding the assay vessel would increase throughput and that a constant rate freezer would improve uniformity. The prediction was that controlled-rate cooling would provide better detection of INA compared to commodity freezer systems.

Methodological Details
The study employed a 96 deep well plate compatible with the Biomek 3000 robotic liquid handling machine. They used the same silicone oil buoyant layer with a 1% silicone surfactant system and HFE-7500 cushion layer as the previous publication. 30 1 μL droplets were dispensed into the silicone oil layer of the 96 deep well plate. At a standard dispensing rate of 1 droplet per 2 seconds, 40 uniform droplets were generated in each of the 96 wells. The system could generate up to ~3800 droplets at once in ~15 minutes. 60 1 μL droplets with fluorescein dye were prepared in a 12 well plate for dispersion assessment. Fluorescent images were acquired by a ChemiDoc MP (Bio-Rad, CA). The droplet diameters were measured by a Matlab automated circle detection program Droplet_Dispersion.m. The polydispersity of the 60 droplets was 9.2%. The standard deviation of the radii was 2.86 × 10^-5 divided by the mean radius 3.10 × 10^-4 m. To remove contact with the plastic wall, HFE-7500 was always placed at the bottom as a cushion layer. Static electricity from the Biomek 3000 was removed using an Auto-set Ion Pump (#19500). When moving the droplet system, wet filter paper was placed below the plastic plate to minimize static electricity accumulation. The freeze-float validation used 30 aqueous droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax colored with yellow fluorescein dye. A Python script KStest.ipynb compared the freezing temperature distribution using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Confidence interval of the freezing temperature required more than 30 droplets sample to observe reliable temperature. The required sample number was calculated as n ≈ (2 k CI / s^2). k was set to 1.96 for a 95% confidence level.

Procedures And Architectures
A Biomek® 3000 robotic liquid transfer system was introduced to enable automated parallel droplet generation. Biomek 3000 replaced manual generation by repeat pipetting employed in the previous report. The robotic system provides spatial positioning compatible with many multi-well plate geometries. Modification to the Biomek program allowed changing droplet number or size. The cooling setup employed a metal cooling plate and sample holder to achieve homogeneous cooling. An Asymptote VIA freezer was used to achieve constant rate cooling with high precision down to -0.5 °C/min. A custom-made glass lid enabled automated image recording by a generic digital camera. Each cryovial contained 50 μL of HFE-7500, 1 mL silicone oil, and 40 total droplets. The 48 cryovials each contained 20 aqueous droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax and 20 droplets of INA-free water. Snomax was marked with fluorescein and INA-free water with Coomassie Brilliant Blue dye. The Asymptote freezer accommodated up to 48 1 mL cryovials in an instrument-specific metal holder. Droplets with INA froze at -7.1 ±0.59 °C and without INA did not freeze until -12.3 °C in the Asymptote freezer. Compared to the previous publication mean temperature of -7.5 ±0.97 °C.

Key Results
The robotic system successfully generated 40 uniform droplets in 96 wells in ~15 minutes. The polydispersity of the 60 droplets was 9.2%, indicating sufficiently uniform volume. Expected no more than ±0.09 °C dispersion based on the standard deviation of the radii. The INA droplets froze and floated with good agreement with the previous report. The freezing temperature in cells in the same 96 deep well plate showed p-value of 4.4 × 10^-7 at constant temperature -28 °C. The thermal gradient decreased (p = 0.31) with linear cooling (-0.25 °C/min) compared to constant temperature cooling. Linear cooling increased the range of freezing time, with mean times of 47.4 and 50.6 min. The Asymptote freezer provided better detection of INA than a commodity freezer system. 96 deep well system showed well-to-well variability with p = 0.31 and standard deviation 1.6 in freezing time. The Asymptote freezer showed less freezing temperature difference with p = 0.83 and standard deviation 0.73. The Asymptote freezer showed an overall 36% lower dispersion than the 96 deep well system.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results support the theory that droplet freezing is a stochastic random nucleation process. The 2.3 °C difference for droplet size implies that monodispersity is crucial for accuracy. The transition to an Asymptote freezer proved that linear cooling reduces thermal gradients and improves uniformity. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test showed that linear cooling made distributions statistically indistinguishable (p = 0.31). The controlled-rate cooling system provided better differentiation of INA concentrations.

Contradictions And Limitations
The droplet stability was not sufficient to move the system between laboratories. Static electricity from friction caused droplet coalescence during transport. This prevented combining the droplets generation system and the freezer system into a single unit. The thermal gradient in the 96 deep well plate was a limitation that linear cooling mitigated. The paper admits the drawback that droplet systems cannot easily measure droplets of arbitrary compositions.

Claims
The robotic system successfully automates droplet generation with high uniformity and throughput. The Biomek 3000 dispensed 30 droplets into each of the 96 wells. 40 uniform droplets were generated in each well in ~15 minutes. The polydispersity of the 60 droplets was 9.2%. The standard deviation of the radii was 2.86 × 10^-5. Static electricity caused droplets to coalesce during movement. The droplet stability was not sufficient to move the system between laboratories. The system is reliable for single-lab HTS but cannot yet be a portable unit. The automated generation is consistent with previous reports.
Controlled-rate cooling with an Asymptote freezer improves temperature uniformity and INA detection accuracy over a commodity freezer. The Asymptote freezer gave -7.1 ±0.59 °C for INA droplets vs -12.3 °C without INA. The thermal gradient in the 96 deep well plate showed p-value of 4.4 × 10^-7 at -28 °C. The freezer showed 36% lower dispersion with p = 0.83. Linear cooling increased the range of freezing time between cells. The mean freezing times were different, 47.4 and 50.6 min. Linear cooling is statistically indistinguishable from constant cooling (p = 0.31). The controlled-rate cooling provided better differentiation accuracies.

Data And Code Availability
The droplet diameter detection software Droplet_Dispersion.m is available as Source Code S1. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test script KStest.ipynb is available as Source Code S3.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The thermal gradient was compared between constant-temperature and linear cooling. The Asymptote freezer was compared against a 96 deep well system. The p-value improved from 4.4 × 10^-7 to 0.31 under linear cooling.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 A-B shows the 96 deep well plate compatible with the Biomek 3000. Figure 1C shows 60 1 μL droplets with fluorescein dye. Figure 1D-E show the droplet diameter measurement results. Figure 2 shows the freeze-float validation of 30 aqueous droplets. Figure 3 shows the p-value of 4.4 × 10^-7 at constant temperature -28 °C. Figure 4 shows droplets freezing at -7.1 ±0.59 °C in the Asymptote freezer. Figure 5 shows the distribution of freezing in the Asymptote freezer with p = 0.83. Figure 6 shows 36% lower dispersion in the Asymptote freezer.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a robotic, controlled-rate freeze-float platform for high-throughput ice nucleation measurement. 2. The strongest evidence is that the Asymptote freezer achieved 36% lower dispersion and better INA differentiation. 3. The future path is to solve the static electricity coalescence problem to create a mobile, integrated unit.

summary.title: Dimeric cyclobutane formation under continuous flow conditions using organophotoredox catalysed [2+2]-cycloaddition
summary.authors: Helena F Grantham; Marc C Kimber; M F C Grantham; Kimber
summary.executive_summary: The authors report a protocol for the organophotoredox catalyzed dimerization of vinylcarbazoles and styrenes under continuous flow conditions, aimed at synthesizing cyclobutane functional materials and lignan natural products. By merging homogenous small molecule sustainable organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow technology, they deliver a general robust and scalable route to carbazole host materials, notably the carbazole cyclobutane material dimer t-DCzCB. A batch versus continuous flow study demonstrates that continuous flow delivers higher chemical yields and significantly reduced reaction times compared to traditional batch chemistry. The radical cation-initiated dimerization of electron rich alkenes serves as an expedient method for cyclobutane synthesis; by merging organophotoredox catalysis and continuous flow technology a batch versus continuous flow study has been performed providing a convenient synthetic route to an important carbazole cyclobutane material dimer t-DCzCB using less only 0.1 mol% of an organophotoredox catalyst. The scope was explored giving a new class of functional materials as well as an improved synthetic route to styrene based lignan dimeric natural products. The carbazole cyclobutane dimer t-DCzCB is used as a host material for blue electrophosphorescence and PhOLEDs; its synthesis was initially achieved via chemical oxidation or TiO2 photodimerization or Ru-and Ir complexes. The organophotoredox catalyzed dimerizations were noted to have excessive reaction times, cryogenic conditions, and catalysis loadings typically 3 mol%, contrasting with Ru-based systems using 0.025% loadings. Continuous flow was expected to offer more efficient irradiation of starting substrates and higher conversions. The commercial off-the-shelf continuous flow platform was employed for optimization of the VCZ dimerization; in batch the organophotoredox catalyst 10 (3 mol%) provided t-DCzCB in 82% isolated yield, requiring deoxygenated acetone, cryogenic temperatures, and extended reaction times. Flow optimization used HPLC-analysis with p-terphenyl as internal standard; optimal synthesis was realized at a flow rate of 0.5 mL.min -1 (tau = 20 min) with 2 mol% catalyst loading at 450 nm. A flow rate of 0.1 mL.min -1 (tau = 100 min) resulted in a 53% yield and carbazole formation attributed to background oxidation by adventitious oxygen. Flow conditions allowed t-DCzCB at a 10 mmol scale using 0.1 mol% of catalyst providing 79% isolated yield, nearing Ru-based efficiencies. The brominated carbazole scope included 12a which flowed to 64% isolated yield while batch yielded 48%; 13a flowed to 71% while batch yielded 31%; 16a flowed to 65%; 17a showed batch slightly outperforming. Several mono- and disubstituted carbazoles flowed cleanly; the styrenes were dimerized using anthracene as an electron relay. E-aserone flowed to the lignan magnosalin in 40% isolated yield under flow without cryogenic temperatures. The flow protocol was validated against traditional batch conditions, demonstrating scalability and robustness, with the lignan synthesis highlighting the methodology's applicability.

summary.title: A New Organocatalytic Desymmetrization Reaction Enables the Enantioselective Total Synthesis of Madangamine E
summary.authors: Shinya Shiomi; Benjamin D A Shennan; Ken Yamazaki; Ángel L Fuentes De Arriba; Dhananjayan Vasu; Trevor A Hamlin; Darren J Dixon
summary.executive_summary:
The enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E was achieved in 30 steps via a new organocatalytic desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition of a prochiral ketone to a tethered nitroolefin. This key carbon-carbon bond forming reaction efficiently constructed a chiral bicyclic core in nearperfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity, establishing three stereogenic centers including a quaternary carbon stereocenter, and was highly scalable. The pathway and origins of enantioselectivity were probed using density functional theory (DFT) calculations, revealing the crucial substrate/catalyst interactions in the enantio-determining step. The core construction was followed by a mild one-pot oxidation-lactamization, a two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone, and ring-closing metatheses to install the two macrocyclic rings.

The madangamine natural product family, isolated from marine sea sponges of the Xestospongia genus, features a complex pentacyclic fused-ring system with two nitrogen atoms. Three rings form a diazatricyclic core common to all members (madangamines A–F), while the D ring differs in each. Prior reports include Amat's asymmetric total synthesis of madangamine D (2014) and Chida and Sato's unified total synthesis of madangamines A, C, and E (2017). The authors recognized that the AC bicyclic motif would be well-suited to construction from a catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization reaction as a rigid scaffold.

The retrosynthetic plan relied on functionalizing tetracyclic ketone 3, mirroring Amat's stereoselective Wittig approach or introducing alkyl chains for ring-closing metathesis. The key disconnection was an unprecedented enantioselective desymmetrizing Michael addition of a 4-aminocyclohexanone derivative with a tethered nitroolefin 6. Inspiration came from the group's previous work on α,β-unsaturated esters using bifunctional primary amine thiourea catalysts, though expanding this to nitroolefins while maintaining selectivity was challenging. An oxidative radical nitration constructed model nitroolefin 7 in 3 steps from 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal.

With 7, a range of amine catalysts was tested; most failed, but Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f gave the bicyclic Michael adduct 8 in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee, while catalyst 9e gave 51% yield in 96% ee. DFT calculations mapped the reaction pathway: hemiaminal (Int1), then imine (Int2), and enamine (Int3). TS1 was the most energetically favorable by 3.0 kcal mol -1 versus the second-lowest, amounting to 99% ee. The Michael addition is highly exergonic (-19.4 kcal mol -1) and proceeds via a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism.

Nitroolefin 17 was accessed via reductive amination of 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal with allylamine, N-tosylation, oxidative cleavage, Henry reaction, dehydration to β-substituted nitroolefin 13, and then installation of the butenyl chain via organo-zinc-copper complex (Denmark) in 90% yield. Selenoxide elimination proceeded in 52% yield over 3 steps with an E:Z ratio of 3.8:1. Treatment of 17E with 9f gave bicyclic nitroalkane 18 in 95% yield and nearperfect selectivity on a >5g scale. Ketone 20 was obtained via a 70% yield, 4-step sequence. Dehydrogenation used Nicolaou's IBX-NMO-mediated oxidation to enone 21, followed by H2O2/NaOH epoxidation, and Wittig homologation with TMMCl/NaHMDS. The diol 24 was accessed in 77% yield, aminodiol 4 in 79% yield, and the B ring closed via oxidative lactamization with AZADO/CuCl/2,2'-bipyridine/DMAP. RCM closed the D ring in 82% yield using Grubbs 1st generation, and saturated ketone 3 followed. Amat's Wittig failed on ketone 3; thus, Ishihara's triorganozincate reagents gave tertiary alcohol 27 in high yields. Early elimination gave Z-configured diene 28 in 90% yield (4.3:1), and Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation closed the macrocyclic E ring in 71% yield. Final reduction with excess LiAlH4 in Et2O gave synthetic madangamine E.

Density functional theory calculations rationalized the near-perfect enantioselectivity through a cooperative push-pull mechanism.

Final reduction with excess LiAlH4 in Et2O gave synthetic madangamine E.

Research Context
The madangamine natural product family was isolated from marine sea sponges of the Xestospongia genus. These products are characterized by a complex pentacyclic fused-ring system with two nitrogen atoms. Three of the rings constitute a diazatricyclic core common to all family members (madangamines A-F). Amat reported the first asymmetric total synthesis of madangamine D in 2014. Chida and Sato's unified total synthesis of madangamines A, C and E was reported in 2017. There exist only two reports of total syntheses and one formal synthesis of madangamine A. The study aims to develop an organocatalytic desymmetrization reaction to convert achiral starting materials to stereochemically-rich products. A gap exists in the number of total syntheses despite significant synthetic community attention.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization reaction can install all stereochemical information from a single chirality-inducing step. The authors hypothesize that an enantioselective desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition of a prochiral ketone to a tethered nitroolefin will efficiently construct a chiral bicyclic core. The authors predict the reaction will concurrently establish three stereogenic centers, including a quaternary carbon stereocenter. The reaction is predicted to proceed with near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity. The pathway and origins of enantioselectivity were probed using density functional theory (DFT) calculations. It is predicted that the transformation will be highly scalable for application in natural product synthesis.

Methodological Details
The study utilizes nitroolefin 7 as a model substrate to develop the enantioselective intramolecular Michael addition reaction. Nitroolefin 7 was constructed from commercially available 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal via oxidative radical nitration. A range of chiral single enantiomer primary and secondary amine organocatalysts was tested. Catalysts included trans-cyclohexanediamine and proline-derived scaffolds. The reaction was conducted in dichloromethane at 20 mol% catalyst loading with benzoic acid as a co-catalyst. The substrate was converted to a β-butenyl nitroolefin via a three-step sequence from 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal. Nitroolefin 17 was accessed via reductive amination of 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal with allylamine and subsequent N-tosylation to give tosyl amide 11. Oxidative cleavage of the terminal alkene and Henry reaction led to β-substituted nitroolefin 13 in 72% yield. The butenyl chain was installed via Michael addition of an organo-zinc-copper complex. Selenoxide elimination proceeded in 52% yield over 3 steps with an E:Z ratio of 3.8:1. The optimal solvent mixture for selenoxide elimination was Et2O:CH2Cl2 in a 2:1 ratio. The bicyclic nitroalkane 18 was obtained in 95% yield and near-perfect selectivity on a >5g scale. The stereochemistry of 18 was determined by X-ray diffraction analysis of the oxidized enone S10.

Procedures And Architectures
The catalytic cycle begins with the primary amine of the catalyst adding to the ketone substrate to form a hemiaminal intermediate Int1. Elimination of water forms an imine Int2, which tautomerizes to enamine Int3. The key C-C bond forming step is an irreversible intramolecular Michael addition through TS1. A conformational search identified 16 possible transition structures for the key stereoselectivity-determining C-C bond forming intramolecular Michael addition. TS1 emerged as the most energetically favorable by 3.0 kcal/mol versus the second-lowest energy transition structure. The Michael addition is highly exergonic with a computed value of -19.4 kcal/mol. The reaction proceeds via a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism stabilized by hydrogen bonding. A secondary pathway involving the formation of dihydrooxazine oxide intermediate IV is energetically unfavorable. The nitroalkane 18 was converted to ketone 20 through reduction and conversion with a 70% yield over 4 steps. Dehydrogenation used Nicolaou's IBX-NMO-mediated oxidation to afford enone 21. Epoxidation was carried out with hydrogen peroxide and aqueous NaOH in MeOH. Wittig homologation used (methoxymethyl)triphenylphosphonium chloride and NaHMDS as base. A rigorous reaction mixture quench at 60 °C for 3 hours improved the yield of aldehyde 23 to 86%. Sequential aldehyde reduction used sodium borohydride and ceric ammonium nitrate (CAN). Closure of the B ring was enabled by an oxidative lactamization with AZADO, copper chloride, 2,2'-bipyridine, and DMAP. The D ring was closed by a RCM reaction using Grubbs 1st generation at 40 °C in CH2Cl2. Reduction gave saturated ketone 3, and the overreduction product S6 was converted back to ketone 3. The macrocyclic E ring was closed via RCM using Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation at 110 °C in PhMe. The final double amide reduction used excess LiAlH4 in Et2O to give synthetic madangamine E.

Key Results
The model bicyclic Michael adduct 8 was obtained in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee. The catalyst 9f provided an almost uniquely efficient reaction profile compared to other tested catalysts. A simpler bifunctional primary amine catalyst 9e yielded 8 in 51% yield and 96% ee. The experimental enantioselectivity of 99% ee agreed with the computed value. Nitroolefin 13 was accessed in 72% yield over 3 steps. The butenyl chain was installed in 90% yield and proved scalable up to 17 g. Bicyclic nitroalkane 18 was obtained in 95% yield and near-perfect selectivity on a >5g scale. Aldehyde 23 was obtained in 86% yield with a 99% b.r.s.m. The diol 24 was accessed in 77% yield over 2 steps. Aminodiol 4 was obtained in 79% yield over 2 steps. The tricyclic enone 25 was obtained in good yield. Tetracyclic enone 26 was obtained in 82% yield. The RCM product 30 was obtained in 71% yield. The final reduction gave synthetic madangamine E. All analytical data were consistent with Chida and Sato.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The reaction is governed by a cooperative push/pull-type mechanism where hydrogen bonding stabilizes the preferred transition structure. The deprotonation of the thiourea by the enolate is favorable, whereas deprotonation by the nitronate is unfavorable. This preference reflects the pKa difference between the nitronate and enolate [pKa = 17 (nitro) < 20 (thiourea) < 30 (ester)]. The irreversible and stereoselectivity-determining step is the C-C bond formation through TS1. The results demonstrate the utility of catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization for the synthesis of highvalue saturated molecular scaffolds.

Contradictions And Limitations
The reaction profile of Jacobsen's catalyst 9f was almost uniquely efficient compared to other tested catalysts. Most catalysts 9a-9d and 9g-9k produced complex product mixtures instead of the cyclised product 8. The selenoxide elimination efficiency depended strongly on the solvent mixture. Amat's Wittig reaction failed due to the ketone's different bond geometries and flexibility compared to the original substrate. The organocerium reaction was highly capricious and sensitive to reagent quality. All attempts to form the macrocyclic E ring via RCM resulted in no desired cyclisation. The yield of aldehyde 23 was low (26%) under standard reaction conditions. The overreduction product S6 could be converted back to ketone 3. The paper reports no random seed, train/test split, or demographic data, consistent with a synthetic chemistry publication.

Claims
The early application of an organocatalytic enantioselective desymmetrization reaction enabled the construction of the bicyclic madangamine core with exquisite enantio- and diastereo-selectivity. The model bicyclic Michael adduct 8 was obtained in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee. The catalyst 9f provided an almost uniquely efficient reaction profile compared to other catalysts. Bicyclic nitroalkane 18 was obtained in 95% yield and near-perfect selectivity on a >5g scale. Most catalysts 9a-9d and 9g-9k produced complex mixtures instead of the cyclised product 8. The catalyst 9f provided an almost uniquely efficient reaction profile compared to other tested catalysts. A simpler catalyst 9e gave 51% yield and lower enantioselectivity than 9f. This enables the rapid and atomeconomical generation of stereochemical complexity in target molecule synthesis. The irreversible and stereoselectivity-determining step is the C-C bond formation through TS1.
The new synthetic route for the β,β'-disubstituted nitroolefin 17 was scalable, yielding multigram quantities. The butenyl chain was installed in 90% yield and proved scalable up to 17 g. Bicyclic nitroalkane 18 was obtained in 95% yield and near-perfect selectivity on a >5g scale. The route provided both scalable and efficient access to multigram quantities of the desired nitroolefin. The selenoxide elimination efficiency depended strongly on the solvent mixture. The organocerium reaction was capricious and sensitive to reagent quality. The scalability supports the generation of highvalue saturated molecular scaffolds on laboratory scale.
Density functional theory calculations rationalized the near-perfect enantioselectivity through a cooperative push-pull mechanism. TS1 emerged as the most energetically favorable by 3.0 kcal/mol versus the second-lowest-energy transition structure. The Michael addition is highly exergonic with a computed value of -19.4 kcal/mol. The preferred TS benefits from hydrogen bonding with the thiourea, nitro group, and enamine moieties. The pathway involving the dihydrooxazine oxide intermediate IV is energetically unfavorable. The aci-nitro species VII is less electronegative at the α-position and does not undergo protonation. The mechanistic understanding confirms the cooperative push/pull-type mechanism is the origin of selectivity.
The spatial arrangement of alkenes was crucial for the macrocyclic E ring closure, as initial ring-closing metathesis failed. All attempts to form the macrocyclic E ring via RCM resulted in no desired cyclisation. The spatial organisation of reacting alkenes had a profound effect on the outcome of the RCM reaction. Changing the order of events gave the desired Z-configured skipped diene. Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation gave the desired diamide in 71% yield. The RCM of 25 with Grubbs 1st generation closed the D ring in 82% yield. The outcome should guide future macrocyclization campaigns employing this strategy.

Data And Code Availability
The experimental yields and spectra are available in Supporting Information; no code is reported.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A range of amine organocatalysts was tested, with most yielding complex product mixtures instead of the cyclised product 8.

Ethical Considerations
No ethical considerations are stated in the paper.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the pentacyclic fused-ring system with two nitrogen atoms. Figure 2B summarizes the catalytic cycle. Figure 3 shows the computed reaction pathway. Figure 4B shows the route to nitroolefin 17.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a new organocatalytic desymmetrization reaction that constructs a chiral bicyclic core with near-perfect selectivity. 2. The strongest evidence is that DFT calculations rationalize the near-perfect enantioselectivity through TS1 and a cooperative push-pull mechanism. 3. The future path is the application of catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization for the rapid and atomeconomical generation of stereochemical complexity in target molecule synthesis.

    *   *Executive Summary (~400 words):*
        "The enantioselective total synthesis of madangamine E was achieved in 30 steps, enabled by a new organocatalytic desymmetrizing intramolecular Michael addition of a prochiral ketone to a tethered nitroolefin. This key carbon-carbon bond forming reaction efficiently constructed a chiral bicyclic core in near-perfect enantio- and diastereo-selectivity, concurrently establishing three stereogenic centers including a quaternary carbon stereocenter, and proved highly scalable. The pathway and origins of enantioselectivity were probed using density functional theory (DFT) calculations, revealing the crucial substrate/catalyst interactions in the enantio-determining step. Following core construction, the synthesis was completed via a mild one-pot oxidation-lactamization, a two-step Z-selective olefination of a sterically hindered ketone, and ring-closing metatheses to install the two macrocyclic rings.
        The madangamine natural product family, isolated from marine sea sponges of the Xestospongia genus, is characterized by a complex pentacyclic fused-ring system with two nitrogen atoms. Three rings form a diazatricyclic core common to all members (madangamines A–F), while the D ring differs in each. Prior reports include Amat's asymmetric total synthesis of madangamine D (2014), which used a phenylglycinol cyclocondensation, and Chida and Sato's unified total synthesis of madangamines A, C, and E (2017), which used an N-acyl-iminium cyclization and allene hydroboration. In contrast, the authors recognized that the AC bicyclic motif would be well-suited to construction from a catalytic enantioselective desymmetrization reaction as a rigid scaffold.
        The core retrosynthetic plan relied on the functionalization of tetracyclic ketone 3, with strategies mirroring Amat's stereoselective Wittig approach or introducing two alkyl chains for ring-closing metathesis. The key disconnection was an unprecedented enantioselective desymmetrizing Michael addition of a 4-aminocyclohexanone derivative possessing a tethered nitroolefin 6. Inspiration came from the group's previous work on α,β-unsaturated esters using bifunctional primary amine thiourea catalysts, though expanding this to nitroolefins while maintaining selectivity was challenging. An oxidative radical nitration constructed model nitroolefin 7 in 3 steps from 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal.
        With 7, a range of chiral single enantiomer amine catalysts was investigated; most failed, but Jacobsen's thiourea catalyst 9f gave the bicyclic Michael adduct 8 in 70% yield as a single diastereomer in 99% ee, with a simpler catalyst 9e giving 51% yield in 96% ee. DFT calculations identified the computed reaction pathway beginning with hemiaminal formation (Int1), then imine (Int2), and enamine (Int3). TS1 emerged as the most energetically favorable, with $\Delta\Delta$G$\ddagger = 3.0$ kcal/mol versus the second-lowest, amounting to 99% ee. The Michael addition is highly exergonic ($\Delta$G$_{rxn} = -19.4$ kcal/mol) and proceeds via a cooperative push-pull-type mechanism.
        The nitroolefin 17 was accessed via reductive amination of 1,4-cyclohexanedione monoethylene acetal with allylamine, N-tosylation, oxidative cleavage, Henry reaction, dehydration to β-substituted nitroolefin 13, and then installation of the butenyl chain via organo-zinc-copper complex (Denmark) in 90% yield. Selenoxide elimination (52%, E:Z 3.8:1) then gave precursor 17, with Et2O:CH2Cl2 (2:1) optimal. Treatment of 17E with catalyst 9f gave bicyclic nitroalkane 18 in 95% yield and near-perfect selectivity on a >5g scale. Ketone 20 was obtained via a 70% yield, 4-step sequence employing a methyl enol ether protecting group. Dehydrogenation used Nicolaou's IBX-NMO-mediated oxidation to enone 21, followed by H2O2/NaOH epoxidation, and Wittig homologation with TMMCl/NaHMDS, which needed a rigorous NH4Cl quench at 60 °C for 3 hours to improve the yield of aldehyde 23 to 86%. The diol 24 was accessed in 77% yield, aminodiol 4 in 79% yield, and the B ring closed via oxidative lactamization with AZADO/CuCl/2,2'-bipyridine/DMAP. RCM closed the D ring (82%) using Grubbs 1st generation, and saturated ketone 3 followed. Amat's Wittig failed on ketone 3; thus, Ishihara's triorganozincate reagents gave tertiary alcohol 27 in high yields. Early elimination gave Z-configured diene 28 (90%, 4.3:1), and Hoveyda-Grubbs 2nd generation closed the macrocyclic E ring (71%). Final double amide reduction with excess LiAlH4 in Et2O gave synthetic madangamine E."

summary.title: Tuning the Dielectric Response in a NC Material through Nanoparticle Morphology
summary.authors: Archita Adluri; Brett Henderson; Irina Paci
summary.executive_summary: This computational study explores how molecular-scale silver nanoparticles (mNPs) included within a magnesium oxide (MgO) matrix affect the overall dielectric response of a nanocomposite (NC) material. The researchers aim to expand the range of available high-κ dielectric materials for devices like transistors, high-density charge storage super-capacitors, and quantum computing by selectively modifying permittivity. The authors use the Modern Theory of Polarization and Car-Parinello Molecular Dynamics (CPMD) implemented in the Quantum Espresso (QE) code to model the polarization of silver inclusions in MgO. MgO is chosen because it is a well-researched high-κ metal-oxide gate dielectric with a cubic crystal structure and isotropic polarization, which simplifies computational costs compared to materials like HfO₂. The study compares three rod-like and five disk-like inclusions built on an ideal Ag fcc lattice, ranging in size from 8 to 32 atoms. Results show that dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30-100% were observed with inclusion sizes varying from 8 to 32 atoms, considering both rod-like and disk-like inclusions, with alignment either parallel or perpendicular to the external field. Specifically, asymmetric inclusions (rods and disks) bring about dielectric enhancements larger than expected based on volume ratios; for example, multi-layer disks (disks 332, 432, and 442) exhibit more than 70% enhancement in εᵣ over the matrix permittivity at similar volume loading. The study attributes these effects to local field enhancements at the nanoparticle-matrix interface, where the induced field is strongly localized to two layers of matrix ions. The authors also examine Born effective charge (BEC) maps to visualize the forces contributing to the increased or decreased dielectric response and observe that the induced field reach is further physically and also stronger when a nanoparticle is oriented parallel to the applied field. A key limitation noted is that the reported polarization values are volume averages that do not account for surface charge and edge effects, and that computational constraints limit the study to mNPs of <30 atoms, below the metallic threshold. The paper concludes that increasing the atoms aligned to the applied field increases the charge density in the interface, and that disk-shaped mNPs suffer from severe screening rings that interact with neighboring inclusions. Future work is proposed to include other matrix materials (SiO₂, HfO₂) and transition metal inclusions (Cu, Co, Fe).

Research Context
The demand for new high-κ dielectric materials is increasing as energy storage and processing power demands reach the limit of traditional single-phase materials. Nanocomposite materials combining a standard dielectric matrix with high and mid-κ inclusions have been advanced as a possible avenue to expand the range of materials for device engineering. One area in need of innovation is materials with tunable dielectric constant (κ) for electrical and computational devices that rely on metal-oxide semiconductors like transistors and super-capacitors. Traditional Si/SiO₂ gate manufacturing gave way to higher-permittivity materials such as silicon-germanium and hafnium oxides to address current leakage and tunnelling effects at few-nanometer sizes. Molecular nanoparticles (mNPs) bridge the gap between single-atom dopants in classical semiconductors and traditional nanoparticles with metallic properties, providing a range of unique features. mNPs are insulating, do not present a band structure and their high-electron density leads to low percolation thresholds and tunnelling. Theoretical approaches for macroscale mixtures like effective medium approximations are suitable where experimental data is broadly available. Classical atomistic approaches work at the nanoscale for certain optical responses but do not encompass quantum response and local field effects that dominate dielectric response in complex solid-state materials. A previous publication from our group used the modern theory of polarization to develop a model for describing the polarization of mNP NCs.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study asks how the distribution and shape of mNP inclusions affect the dielectric capacity of a metal-oxide material. The authors hypothesize that at mNP scales of <30 atoms, the size, shape, and orientation of the inclusion greatly alter how inclusion electrons behave and affect atomic-scale polarization. They predicted that asymmetric inclusions would bring on a dielectric enhancement larger than expected based on volume ratios. The authors expected rod-like and disk-like inclusions to further enhance the dielectric response through both volume increases and specific local field enhancements. The hypothesis is that the nature of the induced field depends on electron dynamics as the metal atom polarizes.

Methodological Details
The NC systems use a magnesium oxide (MgO) matrix with an array of silver mNP inclusions. MgO is chosen as a high-κ metal-oxide gate dielectric with a cubic crystal structure and isotropic polarization. MgO has a bulk dielectric constant of 8-9.8 and a bandgap of 7.8 eV. Models were built using the Avogadro software. Three rod-like inclusions and five disk-like inclusions were considered. Inclusions were built on an ideal Ag fcc lattice but allowed to optimize in the CPMD simulation. The matrix extended 2 Mg-O layers beyond the edge of the inclusion in each direction to keep the cell from conducting into its periodic image. Inclusions were kept between 3-5% loading by volume, reported in numbers of atoms. In the Ag 8 inclusion, the volume occupied by an inclusion atom is on average the same as the volume occupied by individual matrix ions. All calculations used periodic boundary conditions, and the Brillouin zone was sampled at the Γ point. A wavefunction cutoff (wfcut) of 50-60Ry and charge density (rhocut) cutoff of 560Ry were used. The total energy convergence criteria was increased to 10^-8 and a force threshold of 10^-4 was used. Electron masses were kept at 300 a.u then increased to 450 after initial damped minimizations. Mg atoms used Bachelet-Hamann-Schluter norm-conserving pseudopotentials; O and Ag used Rappe-Rabe-Kaxiras-Joannopoulos ultra-soft pseudopotentials. The CPMD methodology was implemented in Quantum Espresso code version 6.0 and 6.6.

Procedures And Architectures
The process for calculating low-frequency polarization using the modern theory of polarization and partitioning is described in Ref 1. The CPMD method is used in the Quantum Espresso code with two major stages: structural relaxation and polarization. Initial electron minimization was calculated with Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization followed by damped dynamics steps. An additional step relaxed lattice vectors to remove stress from the cell due to the inclusion. A static field (ε_field) of 0.001 a.u was applied along the z-axis. The reference polarization is that of the cell without an applied field. Electronic and ionic polarization is calculated using damped dynamics (P_ε_damped) showing mainly ionic polarization. After fully relaxing electronic structure in the field, P_ε_relax describes electronic polarization. The fully-relaxed static polarization was calculated by releasing ionic clamps and allowing full relaxation under the field. Born effective charge tensors were calculated by taking the difference in force experienced by each atom under zero-field and static polarization. Forces were normalized to the bulk matrix to highlight the effect of the NP. A thermostat was not applied and temperatures were not controlled. Test runs using thermostats between 200 and 600K showed temperature effects on geometry were negligible. The polarization-quantum-of-polarization jumps were processed during post-processing with mathematical corrections. Quantum of polarization effects were described as shifting charge distributions relative to the reference coordinate system.

Key Results
Dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30-100% were observed with inclusion sizes varying from 8 to 32 atoms. An ≈ 30% increase in εᵣ was observed with an ≈ 4% mNP volume ratio in the Ag 8 case. Multi-layer disks (disks 332, 432, and 442) exhibit more than 70% enhancement in εᵣ over the matrix permittivity at similar volume loading. The distortion of the crystal structure only extended in general to the nearest neighbors, up to around 3 angstroms from the edge. For the Rod224 inclusion, polarization along the z-axis (ε_||) resulted in a greater increase in polarization than the perpendicular. Disk nanoparticles showed an exponential increase in ε compared to their rod counterparts. Disk442 had twice the x,y dimensions of Rod223 yet had a polarization increase of more than twice. Disk-like nanoparticles showed higher polarization than similarly sized rods. 2-Dimensional nanoparticles (421 and 441) showed a decrease in polarization compared to the bulk in both directions. The induced field reach is further physically and also stronger when a nanoparticle is oriented parallel to the applied field. Perpendicular polarization shows a much larger depolarization field that never decays to the normal bulk values.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The distortion of the MgO matrix was sufficient to prevent NP-induced stress from extending to neighboring cells. Born effective charges reflect the influence of the NP polarization on the charge distribution in the matrix ions. Enhanced polarization is seen in the matrix in regions adjacent to the NP poles in the direction of the applied field. A depolarization arises in the equatorial region where the effective ionic charge is less than in the absence of the external field. The weaker depolarization field is often extended over large regions of the cell. The induced field is strongest in the ions close to the mNP-matrix interface. The shape of the nanoparticle influences the shape and reach of the induced polarization. Increased silver d-electron polarization occurs as they couple to the oxygen p-band. Wannier functions for nanoparticles larger than 8 atoms were unable to converge due to delocalization and movement of centers. The induced fields are always perpendicular to the direction of polarization due to distortion of the internal field on the mNP. The perpendicular response in the matrix sometimes dominates the overall polarization and the dielectric constant is lower than for pure matrix.

Contradictions And Limitations
The reported values are volume averages and do not take into account surface charge and edge effects. The values calculated for εᵣ are not 'true' dielectric constants for a real material. The paper notes that the calculated bandgap is generally expected to be significantly lower than the experimental bandgap due to DFT and LDA. Computational constraints limit the study to mNPs of <30 atoms, below the metallic threshold. The study notes a possible threshold at which the exponential growth changes as the inclusion behaves more metallic. The authors state that the dielectric response is significantly more complex than a simple correlation to the mNP length. The study lacks a full treatment of the quantum polarization of the mixed material. The paper notes that there may be a threshold at which this exponential growth changes. The study lacks information on random seed or specific train/test split. The paper is missing a bibliography, preventing the identification of specific citations.

Claims
The inclusion of silver nanoparticles in an MgO matrix enhances the dielectric response through shape-dependent local field effects. Dielectric permittivity enhancements of 30-100% were observed. Asymmetric inclusions bring on a dielectric enhancement even larger than expected based on volume ratios. The induced field reach is further physically and also stronger when a nanoparticle is oriented parallel to the applied field. Disk-like nanoparticles showed higher polarization than similarly sized rods. Dielectric enhancement is significantly more complex than a simple correlation to the mNP length. The perpendicular depolarization area only affects the interfacial atoms whereas the enhancement is localized to two layers. The dielectric constant calculated is sometimes lower than for pure matrix when the perpendicular response dominates. The nature of the induced field depends on the electron dynamics as the metal atom polarizes. Increasing the atoms aligned to the applied field increases the charge density in the interface. Disk shaped mNPs suffer from severe screening rings that interact with neighboring inclusions.
The Born effective charge tensor captures the force distribution at the interface. The Born effective charges reflect the influence of the NP polarization on the charge distribution in the matrix ions. The forces felt by atoms at the matrix-nanoparticle interface are what drive the increased or decreased dielectric response. The BEC plots resemble an induced field on the nanoparticle with moving electrons throughout the simulation creating areas of higher and lower force. Wannier functions for nanoparticles larger than 8 atoms were unable to converge due to delocalization. The BEC converges to +2, -2 values of matrix in a very short distance for perpendicular polarization. The BEC plots are a useful tool for mapping the local charge density and spatial manipulation of induced fields.

Data And Code Availability
The CPMD methodology was implemented in Quantum Espresso version 6.0 and 6.6. There is no explicit statement on the availability of the data or code.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Test runs using thermostats between 200 and 600K showed temperature effects on geometry were negligible. The inclusion of silver atoms only distorted the local structure to around 3 angstroms from the edge.

Ethical Considerations
The paper is missing an explicit ethical considerations statement.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows an example of a NC with a Ag 8 inclusion. Figures 2 and 3 show three rod-like inclusions and five disk-like inclusions. Figure 4 shows the six steps of the electronic structure calculation. Figure 5 illustrates the polarization steps using Quantum Espresso. Figure 6 shows the mathematical corrections for polarization jumps during post-processing. Table 1 presents the dielectric response for Ag/MgO NCs with rod-like and disk-like inclusions. Figure 7 and 8 show densities of states and the bandgap. Figure 9 shows a smeared BEC plot of normalized born charges for a 224 rodlike inclusion. The equation for the low-frequency dielectric constant is labeled as Equation 1.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the systematic study of shape-dependent dielectric enhancements in Ag-MgO nanocomposites using the Modern Theory of Polarization and CPMD. 2. The strongest evidence is that asymmetric multi-layer disks exhibit more than 70% dielectric enhancement at similar volume loadings compared to the matrix. 3. The future path involves extending the study to other matrix materials like SiO₂ and HfO₂ and transition metal inclusions like Cu, Co, and Fe.

summary.title: Low density interior in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets expels ions to the subsurface
summary.authors: Shahrazad M A Malek (Memorial University of Newfoundland); Ivan Saika-Voivod (Memorial University of Newfoundland); Styliani Consta (The University of Western Ontario)
summary.field_subfield: Atmospheric Chemistry / Soft Condensed Matter Physics
summary.type_of_paper: Computational research article / Molecular dynamics study
summary.executive_summary:
The interaction between water and ions within droplets plays a key role in the chemical reactivity of atmospheric and man-made aerosols. The study reports direct computational evidence that in supercooled aqueous nanodroplets a lower density core of tetrahedrally coordinated water expels the Na+ ions to a denser and more disordered subsurface. In contrast, at room temperature, the radial distribution of a single Na+ ion in the droplet core is nearly uniform. To investigate this, the authors analyze the spatial distribution of a single ion in terms of a reference electrostatic model where the energy of the system is expressed as the sum of the electrostatic and surface energy of a deformable droplet. The model predicts that the ion is subject to a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass, an effect termed "electrostatic confinement" (EC). The model's predictions are consistent with the simulation findings for a single Na+ ion at room temperature but not at supercooling. The authors anticipate the study will be a starting point for investigating the structure of supercooled electrosprayed droplets used to preserve the conformations of macromolecules originating from the bulk solution. 

The computational study investigates supercooled aqueous mesoscopic clusters charged with a single and multiple ions, referring to these as nanodroplets. Previous atomistic simulations of multiple ions in aqueous nanodroplets with diameters 2 nm to 16 nm at 300 K to 450 K found that in droplets with ≈ 1000 water molecules, the radial ion distribution is almost uniform, decaying toward the droplet's center of mass by a slow almost exponential decay. The solution of the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation for a spherical geometry is used as a reference model. Here the authors study clusters with sizes 100 to 1100 water molecules (diameters ≈ 1.8 nm to ≈ 4.0 nm). Previous simulations for pristine supercooled water clusters showed an anomalous, inverted radial density profile emerging for N ≥ 200 molecules at low temperature, in which a low density core with relatively good tetrahedral ordering is surrounded by a high density subsurface. These observations have some commonalities with studies of nucleation within droplets and thin films. The authors hypothesize that the low density water core in supercooled droplets will differentiate the ion distribution from that at room temperature. To obtain insight into the forces determining a single ion's location in a fluctuating droplet, they introduce a reference analytical model, which they claim is still missing from the literature. The model treats the charged droplet as a deformable charged dielectric droplet where the charge carrier is a single (macro)ion with bound charge. In the model, the energy is the sum of electrostatic and surface energy, and the ion is subject to a harmonic potential centered at the droplet's center of mass. The theory predicts the effect is more pronounced at low temperature, high charge, small radius and intermediate values of the dielectric constant. For high charges, the authors model charged cyclic peptides, noting that DNA and RNA strands are other examples where the effect should be observed. The theory predicts the minimal excursions of an ion are r^2 < 12 Å. The electrostatic confinement effect is more pronounced for an ion with a charge of at least +/- 3e found in a droplet with a small radius. The model can be extended to include ion size and hydrophobic effects. 

The simulation methods use molecular dynamics as implemented in GROMACS v4.6.1, modeling water with TIP4P/2005 and Na+ with OPLS-AA parameters. Nanodroplets are placed in periodic cubic boxes of length L with a Coulomb and Lennard-Jones cutoff at L/2. Simulations are carried out in the canonical ensemble using the Nosé-Hoover thermostat with time constant 0.1 ps and integrated with the leap-frog algorithm with a time step of 2 fs. Simulations are initiated with a pure water nanodroplet where the Na+ ion is placed at the surface for most single Na+ runs, and in the center for two runs at N = 360 and 776 at T = 200 K. All multiple Na+ ion runs start near the droplet center of mass. For equilibration, the authors run two simulations for each of N = 360 and N = 776 nanodroplets; at N = 776, ion densities converge after 400 ns. For N = 1100, equilibration time is assumed longer by a factor of tau1100 / tau776 ≈ 2. The authors report water density rho(r), Voronoi-based density rho_v(r), tetrahedral order parameter q_T(r), and distance to the fifth neighbor d_5(r). 

At high temperature, rho(r) is that of a typical liquid droplet, characterized by a flat curve in the interior that decays sigmoidally to zero over approximately an intermolecular distance at the liquid-vapor interface. At low temperature, there is significant layering and an increase in density towards the surface. rho_v(r) is significantly smoother than rho(r) and decays to zero approximately 0.3 nm before rho(r). Surface molecules are where rho_v(r) is small, and subsurface molecules are at an intermolecular distance below where rho_v(r) has decayed to near zero. At high T, rho_Na(r) is approximately constant in the interior and decays within the subsurface. At T = 300 K the Na+ radial distribution is consistent with the EC effect, but geometric confinement dominates because of low charge, so the distribution appears almost uniform. At low T, rho_Na(r) is located within 0.1 nm of the peak in rho_v(r). Thus the Na+ ion tends to reside in the highest density environment. For N = 776, the ion density when five Na+ ions are present shifts at low T to peak at approximately the same position as the single ion case. At T = 200 K, the multiple ions are expelled from the droplet core and show a maximum at the same location as the single ion. For N = 1100, two peaks are observed at distance 0.52 nm and at 1.5 nm, where the outer peak is not a metastable state. At 300 K, multiple-ion distributions decay toward the center as an exponential function; at 200 K, they cannot be analyzed using the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation. 

At low temperature, the water molecules around the center are adjacent to the first solvation shell of Na+, so their organization is affected by the ion. The N = 100 cluster does not show a tetrahedrally organized core and is subject to larger relative shape fluctuations. The study finds that in supercooled aqueous droplets, a heterogeneous solvent structure leads to a different ion distribution relative to room temperature: at supercooling a tetrahedral interior network can form that expels single and multiple Na+ ions to the subsurface. The structure of the solvent has not been studied previously. The droplet of 100 H2O molecules does not form a tetrahedral network in the center because the central molecules participate in the immediate solvation of the Na+ and the system is subject to large relative shape fluctuations. Our results are in agreement with those of Voth et al. for the Na+ location in a cluster of 100 H2O molecules. The multiple ion distribution cannot be explained by the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation. The electrostatic confinement model serves as a reference model, but may deviate when the low density core affects ion location, and can be extended with hydrophobic effects. A conical deformation in the droplet is key to the mechanism of ion emission, and whether this is hindered by the low density core remains an intriguing question. A future study of the low temperature droplets containing unstructured peptides will assist in interpreting ion mobility mass spectrometry data on the conformations of macromolecules in the bulk solution.

Research Context
The spatial distribution of ions in droplets plays a decisive role in chemical reactivity in atmospheric and man-made aerosols. Applications of the man-made aerosols relevant to this study include spray-based ionization methods used in native mass spectrometry analysis 1 Aerosol droplets in the lower atmosphere carry a small charge determined by at most a few excess ions Experiments have detected abundance of certain "magic" cluster sizes associated with clathrate structures 5 and have studied their reactivity relevant to atmospheric chemistry. 6 In certain FT-ICR experiments the temperature of clusters composed of 50-70H2O molecules is estimated to be 130 K-150 K. Voth and co-workers 14 have investigated the location of a single Na+, Cl- and H+ in the temperature range of 100 K-450 K. Voth et al. found that below the freezing temperature in clusters of 100 H2O molecules H3O+ and Na+ were excluded from the cluster interior and tend to reside within a few monolayers of the surface. Above the cluster melting point, both the Na+ and Cl- ions tend to be found nearer to the center. The solution of the non-linear Poisson-Boltzmann equation for a spherical geometry 29 is used as a reference model to compare with the atomistic simulations. The distribution of multiple ions and biological molecules such as peptides at supercooling is still completely unknown.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study examines the location of a single ion and multiple ions in relation to the solvent organization in supercooled aqueous clusters with sizes 100 to 1100 water molecules. The nanodroplet sizes vary from corresponding to a diameter of ≈ 1.8 nm to diameter ≈ 4.0 nm. Previous computer simulations for pristine supercooled water clusters revealed an anomalous, inverted radial density profile emerging for N ≥ 200 molecules at low temperature. In this profile, a low density core with relatively good tetrahedral ordering 31 is surrounded by a high density subsurface. These observations have some commonalities with studies of nucleation within droplets and thin films. [32] [33] [34] [35] [36] We hypothesize that the low density water core in supercooled droplets will differentiate the ion distribution from that at room temperature. The hypothesis could not be explored in earlier research 14 because the small cluster sizes (number of water molecules ≤ 100) precluded the formation of the low density core. To obtain insight into the forces determining a single ion's location in a fluctuating droplet, we introduce a reference analytical model, which is still missing from the literature.

Methodological Details
The study simulates Na+ ions in aqueous nanodroplets at temperatures 200 K, 260 K, and 300 K. The system sizes and length of simulations are shown in Table 1. Simulations are performed by molecular dynamics (MD) as implemented in GROMACS v4.6.1. Water molecules are modeled with the TIP4P/2005 transferable intermolecular potential with four points model. For Na+, OPLS-AA parameters are taken from Ref. 48. Each nanodroplet is placed in a periodic cubic box of length L. The box length avoids interaction between the water droplet and its periodic images. The length of cutoff for interactions (Coulomb and Lennard-Jones) is at L/2. Simulations are carried out in the canonical ensemble with a constant number of molecules N. Temperature is controlled by the Nosé-Hoover thermostat with time constant 0.1 ps. The equations of motion are integrated with the leap-frog algorithm with a time step of 2 fs. Simulations are initiated with a condensed pure water nanodroplet where the Na+ ion is placed at the surface for the majority of the single Na+ runs. The ion is placed in the center for two runs at N = 360 and 776 at T = 200 K. All runs with multiple Na+ ions start with the ions near the droplet center of mass. Table 1 reports the mean number of molecule, Nd, forming the connected cluster. The relaxation time tau is determined from the neighbor correlation function. To ensure sufficient sampling after addition of a single Na+ ion at 200 K, two simulations are run for each of N = 360 and N = 776 nanodroplets. For N = 776 after 400 ns, the ion densities converge for the two simulations. For N = 1100, the equilibration time is assumed longer by a factor of tau1100 / tau776 ≈ 2. For multiple ions, the relaxation time is presumed shorter, with single ion simulations providing upper bounds on the relaxation times. The Voronoi cells for all O sites are computed, while the H sites are ignored. The average density as determined by the Voronoi cell volumes is defined as rho_v(r). The tetrahedral order parameter q_i is defined at the level of a single particle. The radial function q_T(r) is the average q_i for molecules within r ± Delta r/2. The distance to the fifth O neighbor, d5(r), is reported for atoms in the same spherical shell. Data for both q_T(r) and d5(r) are taken from Ref. 31.

Procedures And Architectures
The reference analytical model treats a charged dielectric droplet that may undergo shape fluctuations. The charge carrier is a single (macro)ion with bound charge that cannot ionize. The energy of the charged droplet is the sum of electrostatic energy and surface energy. The energy related to the distance of the ion from the droplet's COM (Delta E1) is given by EQUATION. The energy has the functional form of a harmonic potential. From this point the effect is named electrostatic confinement (EC). The spring constant K(epsilon) depends on the dielectric constant. Fig. 1 plots the value of the spring constant as a function of the relative dielectric constant for a droplet with 1000 water molecules and an ion. The electrostatic energy has limiting cases epsilon = 1 and epsilon = infinity. In the former case the droplet does not perturb the electric field of the ion. In the latter case the electrostatic field is localized in the vicinity of the ion. The maximum of the coefficient K(epsilon) is attained at epsilon = 1 + sqrt 3 ≈ 2.73. If the ion is localized in the center, the Gibbs-Boltzmann distribution of ion positions is given by EQUATION. The expectation value of the square of the distance of the ion from the center of mass is given by EQUATION. The EC is more pronounced when r^2 / R^2 < 1. The effect will be more pronounced at low temperature, high charge, small radius and intermediate values of the dielectric constant. Small droplets with high charge may undergo Rayleigh instability leading to star-shaped droplets. If this is an issue, the droplet radius must be increased keeping the Rayleigh parameter X ~ Q^2 / R^3 constant. High charges are modeled by creating models of charged cyclic peptides. DNA and RNA strands are other examples where the effect of EC will be clearly observed. summary.executive_summary: The design of heterogeneous catalysts is challenged by the complexity of materials and processes that govern reactivity and the fact that the number of good catalysts is very small compared to the number of possible materials. Here, we show how the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach can be applied to an experimental plus theoretical data set to identify constraints on key physicochemical parameters, the so-called SG rules, which exclusively describe materials and reaction conditions with outstanding catalytic performance. By using high-throughput experimentation, 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten and phosphorus were synthesized and tested in the catalytic oxidation of propylene. As candidate descriptive parameters, the temperature and ten parameters related to the composition and chemical nature of the catalyst materials, derived from calculated freeatom properties, were offered. The temperature, the phosphorus content, and the composition-weighted electronegativity are identified as key parameters describing high yields towards the value-added oxygenate products acrolein and acrylic acid. The SG rules not only reflect the underlying processes associated to high performance but also guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements in their composition. The study addresses the difficulty of heterogeneous catalysis where explicit atomistic modelling of the full catalytic progression by first-principles methods is impractical. While high-throughput experimentation (HTE) tests large amounts of materials, deciding on next promising materials is not straightforward because the number of possible materials is practically infinite and the number of good catalysts is very small. Global models are trained to minimize the expected average prediction error over all samples, which provides an accurate prediction on average but does not necessarily allow for focused modelling of the most interesting materials and mechanisms. Alternative approaches for catalyst design are therefore required. The authors apply the SGD artificial-intelligence local approach to a hybrid data set obtained from HTE & theory to identify key physicochemical descriptive parameters and rules associated with high performance. The reactivity measured by HTE is used as target, and temperature plus composition-dependent physicochemical properties evaluated with density-functional-theory (DFT) are used as candidate descriptive parameters. The SGD approach identifies selectors, i.e., statements formed by propositions and the AND connector that select subgroups of materials and conditions with the most outstanding distributions of the target values with respect to the whole data set. The propositions are rules describing exceptional SG behavior, while the parameters are the key descriptive parameters associated with the desired reactivity. Because the SG search maximizes a quality function measuring how outstanding specific subselections of data points are, the approach identifies local behavior, reflecting specific underlying processes resulting in outstanding performance. The authors apply the SGD-HTE-&-theory approach to the selective oxidation of propylene on SiO2-supported catalysts based on ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus. By using the product yield measured by HTE as target, they circumvent the need for the explicit modelling of the full catalytic progression. Additionally, because candidate descriptive materials parameters can be calculated by first-principles methods, extensive experimental characterization is not required, and the resulting SG rules can identify promising catalyst candidates not yet synthesized by experiment.

Alternative approaches for catalyst design are therefore required. The reactivity measured by HTE is used as target, and temperature plus composition-dependent physicochemical properties evaluated with density-functional-theory (DFT) are used as candidate descriptive parameters. The SGD approach identifies selectors, i.e., statements formed by propositions and the AND connector that select subgroups of materials and conditions with the most outstanding distributions of the target values with respect to the whole data set. The authors apply the SGD-HTE-&-theory approach to the selective oxidation of propylene on SiO2-supported catalysts based on ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus. By using the product yield measured by HTE as target, they circumvent the need for the explicit modelling of the full catalytic progression. Additionally, because candidate descriptive materials parameters can be calculated by first-principles methods, extensive experimental characterization is not required, and the resulting SG rules can identify promising catalyst candidates not yet synthesized by experiment.

Research Context
Catalyst design is challenged by the complexity of materials and processes. Explicit atomistic modelling of the full catalytic progression by first-principles methods is impractical. The number of good catalysts is very small compared to the number of possible materials. Global models are trained to minimize the expected average prediction error over all samples. Detailed characterization of each material in the large testing library is typically not feasible. Only little information on the structure and physicochemical properties of each compound might be available. Distinct catalytic mechanisms might operate depending on materials and reaction conditions.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The authors apply the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach to a hybrid dataset. The goal is to identify key physicochemical descriptive parameters and rules associated with high performance. The target is the yield of the value-added oxygenate products measured by HTE. The SGD approach identifies selectors as AND-connected statements of propositions. The propositions enter the selectors as rules describing exceptional SG behavior. The identified rules reflect specific underlying processes resulting in outstanding performance.

Methodological Details
120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus were tested. The three-component catalysts are based on ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus. The study focuses on the selective oxidation of propylene on SiO2 support. Candidate parameters include temperature and ten freeatom-derived properties. The target is the yield of the value-added oxygenate products. DFT-PBEsol and the FHI-aims code were used for elemental properties. The elemental properties were calculated for isolated atoms. L PQR is the radius of the highest-occupied state. Reaction temperatures ranged from 200ºC to 400ºC. The gas feed included five molar rates for the reactants. All reactions used the same mass of catalyst. Contact time was kept fixed across all experiments.

Procedures And Architectures
Catalyst properties were averaged by composition-weighted means. J ` is the molar content of element b in the composition. The candidate parameters are inequality constraints on continuous values. Selectors are AND-connected statements formed by propositions. The AND connector is denoted by the symbol ∧. Ru content was fixed to ensure combustion is not significant. The phosphorus content was fixed according to the rule. V Ç elements showed octahedral coordination and small radius difference. Molar contents 0.05, 0.175, 0.30, and 0.35 were evaluated. The highest yield was achieved with a tellurium V Ç element. The five-component highest yield material contains tantalum as V ^. The electronegativity and electron affinity are related by VY =.

Key Results
The vast majority of observations correspond to low performance, with 50% of measurements having less than 2% oxygenate yield. Out of 1220 measurements, only 41 are associated with oxygenate yields above 20%. The average oxygenate yield over the whole dataset is equal to 4.83%. The maximum oxygenate yield value is 26.85 %. The selected subgroup contains 15 data points and presents an average oxygenate yield of 24.15%. This subgroup average is five times higher than the average oxygenate yield on the whole dataset. The rule on temperature highlights that the highest yields are observed for intermediate temperatures within the 200-400ºC range. The phosphorus content rule indicates that a relatively high phosphorus content is needed to achieve outstanding catalytic performance. The electronegativity rule limits the range of ruthenium contents and links to active site dilution. The reaction temperature rule is not transferable from the three-component dataset to the four-component dataset. The highest-yielding four-component catalyst (60.19 % at 400ºC) contains tellurium as the additional element. The highest-yielding five-component catalyst contains tantalum as the additional element and achieves a yield of 59.60 % at 400ºC. The four-and five-component outstanding catalysts achieve oxygenate yields twice as large as any training observation.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The reaction temperature rule is not transferable to the four-component catalysts. The rule on temperature highlights that the highest yields occur at intermediate temperatures. The phosphorus rule highlights that a relatively high phosphorus content is needed. The electronegativity rule effectively limits the range of ruthenium contents. The identified rules detect interpretable, chemically meaningful, and complex patterns. The rules guide the design of more complex catalysts beyond the training data. The identified rules identify a local behavior reflecting specific underlying processes. The approach circumvents explicit modelling of the full catalytic progression. The rules reflect the specific underlying processes resulting in outstanding performance.

Contradictions And Limitations
The dataset is unbalanced between high-and lowperformance scenarios. Only little information on the structure of each compound is available. Detailed characterization of each material in the large testing library is typically not feasible. The number of good catalysts is very small compared to the number of possible materials. The reaction temperature rule is not transferable to four-component catalysts. The atomic structures of all the tested catalysts are not known in detail. The oxygen content was not known nor measured for all materials. The SG analysis may need to include new data points covering unexplored materials space. The number of possible materials is practically infinite.

Claims
The SGD rules for three-component catalysts generalize to four-and five-component systems, predicting oxygenate yields over twice as high as any training observation. The selected subgroup contains 15 data points. The average oxygenate yield in the subgroup is 24.15%. This yield is five times the whole-dataset average. The phosphorus rule is Jₖ > 0.55. The electronegativity rule is 3.910–4.002 eV. The four-component highest yield is 60.19%. The five-component highest yield is 59.60%. The temperature rule is not transferable. The training was only 90% of the data. Oxygen content is not known. SGD rules capture exceptional performance. The rules guide the design of complex catalysts. The five-component catalyst exceeds training.
The subgroup-discovery approach identifies a local behavior that isolates a high-performance subgroup representing ~1.2% of the data. The subgroup represents 1.2% of the dataset. The average whole-dataset oxygenate yield is 4.83%. The maximum whole-dataset oxygenate yield is 26.85%. Fifty percent of observations have low yield. The selected SG yield is five times higher. The dataset is unbalanced between high and low performance. Detailed characterization of each material is not feasible. Only little information on the structure is available. The number of good catalysts is very small. Local modeling targets exceptional materials. The SGD approach detects complex patterns. This circumvents explicit modelling of the catalytic progression.

Data And Code Availability
Further calculation details and elemental properties are available in the electronic supporting information, ESI. The FHI-aims code was used for the DFT calculations. The DFT calculations were performed using DFT-PBEsol.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The training was performed with randomly-selected 90% of the data points. Yields lower than 3% were excluded from training. The SG rules are not strongly affected by variations on the data. The ranges of minimum and maximum thresholds were reported.

Ethical Considerations
The study does not report ethics, IRB, or safety protocols.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the SG propositions and selectors. Figure 1B shows the three-component Ru-W-P catalyst space. Figure 2A shows the propylene conversion and oxygenate selectivity. Figure 2B shows the distribution of oxygenate yield. Figure 2C shows the temperature, phosphorus, and electronegativity rules. Figure 2D shows the phosphorus rule. Figure 2F shows the composition-averaged electronegativity rule. Figure 3B shows the ternary diagram of ruthenium contents. Figure 4A shows the four-component catalyst map. Figure 4B shows the five-component catalyst map. Figure 5A shows the four- and five-component HTE data. Figure 5B shows the corresponding conversion and selectivity. Figure 5C shows the rules for the five-component SG.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is using SGD to extract rules for oxygenates. 2. The strongest evidence is the ~60% yield exceeding training. 3. The future path is to enlarge the materials space.
