    *Expanded Executive Summary (~400 words):*
    "The design of heterogeneous catalysts is challenged by the complexity of materials and processes that govern reactivity and by the fact that the number of good catalysts is very small compared to the number of possible materials. Here, we show how the subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence approach can be applied to an experimental plus theoretical data set to identify constraints on key physicochemical parameters, the so-called SG rules, which exclusively describe materials and reaction conditions with outstanding catalytic performance. By using high-throughput experimentation, 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten and phosphorus were synthesized and tested in the catalytic oxidation of propylene. As candidate descriptive parameters, the temperature and ten parameters related to the composition and chemical nature of the catalyst materials, derived from calculated freeatom properties, were offered. The temperature, the phosphorus content, and the composition-weighted electronegativity are identified as key parameters describing high yields towards the value-added oxygenate products acrolein and acrylic acid. The SG rules not only reflect the underlying processes particularly associated to high performance but also guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements in their composition. The study addresses the difficulty of heterogeneous catalysis where explicit atomistic modelling of the full catalytic progression by first-principles methods is impractical. While high-throughput experimentation (HTE) tests large amounts of materials, deciding on next promising materials is not straightforward because the number of possible materials is practically infinite and the number of good catalysts is very small. Global models are trained to minimize the expected average prediction error over all samples, which may provide an accurate prediction on average but does not necessarily allow for a focused modelling of the most interesting materials and mechanisms. Alternative approaches for catalyst design are therefore required. The authors apply the SGD artificial-intelligence local approach to a hybrid data set obtained from HTE & theory to identify key physicochemical descriptive parameters and constraints on their values, i.e., rules, which are particularly associated with high performance. summary.title: Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4
summary.authors: Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych; Caue Ribeiro
summary.executive_summary:
The present article describes an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method of producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) aimed for soil conditioning by a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4. The methodology is based on reverse logistics, which enables the collection and restitution of solid waste to the business sector for reuse in a productive cycle.

Normally, solid-state mechanochemical activation consists in applying mechanical energy—mainly friction and impact forces—to promote chemical reactions from solid reagents. In this study, mechanical energy breaks the reagent bonds to promote solid phase ion migration to form a new structure. The process mainly produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4, along with CO2 resulting from CaCO3 decomposition. Compared to KH2PO4, these phosphates exhibit very different solubility depending on cation size and charge, influencing the reticular energy of the structure. The experimental release essays reveal that KH2PO4 exhibits much faster solubilization than calcium or calcium and potassium phosphates. The produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, providing a delay in the bioavailability of P and K and improving the bioavailability of Ca, making them an excellent alternative in nutrient management.

The solid-state mechanochemical activation allows reactions in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste, thus ensuring huge savings during production. The authors argue that no mechanochemical process has been reported for the production of calcium and potassium hydrogen phosphate (K3CaH(PO4)2) and potassium calcium phosphate (CaKPO4) from calcite provided by eggshell and KH2PO4, producing different structures from hydroxyapatite. In conclusion, the study proposes using eggshell (a food industry residue) and KH2PO4 to design an eco-friendly fertilizer that guarantees better nutrient management by playing on the solubility of calcium, potassium and phosphorus via a solvent-free mechanochemical process that presents no unwanted subproduct.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The present article describes an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method of producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) aimed for soil conditioning by a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4. The methodology is based on reverse logistics, which enables the collection and restitution of solid waste to the business sector for reuse in a productive cycle.

Normally, solid-state mechanochemical activation consists in applying mechanical energy—mainly friction and impact forces—to promote chemical reactions from solid reagents. In this study, mechanical energy breaks the reagent bonds to promote solid phase ion migration to form a new structure. The process mainly produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4, along with CO2 resulting from CaCO3 decomposition. Compared to KH2PO4, these phosphates exhibit very different solubility depending on cation size and charge, influencing the reticular energy of the structure. The experimental release essays reveal that KH2PO4 exhibits much faster solubilization than calcium or calcium and potassium phosphates. The produced potassium calcium phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, providing a delay in the bioavailability of P and K and improving the bioavailability of Ca, making them an excellent alternative in nutrient management.

The solid-state mechanochemical activation allows reactions in a solvent-free environment, producing no liquid or solid waste, thus ensuring huge savings during production. The authors argue that no mechanochemical process has been reported for the production of calcium and potassium hydrogen phosphate (K3CaH(PO4)2) and potassium calcium phosphate (CaKPO4) from calcite provided by eggshell and KH2PO4, producing different structures from hydroxyapatite. In conclusion, the study proposes using eggshell (a food industry residue) and KH2PO4 to design an eco-friendly fertilizer that guarantees better nutrient management by playing on the solubility of calcium, potassium and phosphorus via a solvent-free mechanochemical process that presents no unwanted subproduct.

Research Context
The production of new materials is now closely related to reverse logistics, which enables solid waste reuse. Solid-state mechanochemical activation applies friction and impact forces to promote chemical reactions. Solid-state mechanochemical activation requires enough energy to break bonds and promote ion migration. The process mainly produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4 with CO2 from CaCO3 decomposition. Potassium dihydrogen phosphate exhibits much faster solubilization than calcium or potassium phosphates. The produced phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers, delaying bioavailability of P and K. Solid-state mechanochemical activation allows for a solvent-free environment with huge production savings. Mechanochemical synthesis of hydroxyapatite exists, but uses phosphoric acid instead of phosphate salts. No reported mechanochemical process produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 from calcite and KH2PO4. Eco-friendly fertilizer production now prioritizes using industrial wastes in new products.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 be formed from calcite and KH2PO4 by mechanochemical activation? The mechanochemical reaction will form new phosphate phases through solid-phase ion migration. The produced K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 will release nutrients more slowly than the KH2PO4 precursor. The milled phosphates will release calcium more readily than the eggshell precursor CaCO3. Milled samples will release K and P at similar rates in both citric acid and soil. The products will form hydroxyapatite under soil conditions for slow long-term release.

Methodological Details
Eggshells were collected at home, washed with water, and dried at room temperature. Eggshells had a diameter between 1 and 10 mm before grinding. KH2PO4 PA was supplied from Vetec. The Fritsch Pulverisette 7 mill had a 250 ml zirconia bowl. Five zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter were used for milling. The weight ratio of eggshell and KH2PO4 was 1:1 (w/w). Essays were performed at 600 rpm for 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h and 24 h. Secondary speed essays were at 100, 200, 400 and 600 rpm for 2 h. The mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. Samples were characterized by XRD, NMR MAS, TGA, and DSC. Nutrient content used acid digestion in H2SO4/H2O2 (8:1 v/v by 24 h at 250 °C). K and Ca were determined by atomic absorption and P by colorimetric methods. The material was pelletized at 5 bar to 100 mg/L of P. Pellets were placed in 10 mL beakers immersed into 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution. The system was kept at 25 °C under constant temperature and magnetic stirring. Aliquots of 1.2 mL were collected from 15 min to 30 days. Phosphorus diffusion was tested in Petri dishes of 8.6 cm diameter. 78 g of 2.0 mm mesh dry soil were added to a 1.2 g.cm -3 density. 15 mL deionized water was added to reach 70% water retention. Images were processed with GNU Image Manipulation Program, v. 2.6.11. Soil release was at 75% water saturation in 50 g of sandy soil. Experiments were at 3, 7, 15 and 30 days at 300 mg of P per kg of soil. Potassium was extracted by HCl and calcium by KCl methods. Phosphorus was extracted using the Mehlich 1 method. Molybdenum blue was used to quantify phosphorus. Potassium and calcium were quantified by FAAS using a PerkinElmer PinAAcle 900T.

Procedures And Architectures
A high-energy ball mill performed the grinding. Milling parameters were time (15 min–24 h) and speed (100–600 rpm). The mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol KH2PO4 and 1 mmol CaCO3. The TGA analyzer operated between 25°C and 600°C. Synthetic air at 60 mL.min -1 and 10°C/min heating rate was used. TGA employed platinum crucibles and air atmosphere at 20 to 900 °C. XRD patterns were registered from 3-40° using a Cu Kα incident beam. The XRD used 30 kV voltage and 40 mA current at 2° min -1. 31P NMR MAS used an Avance III HD at 10KHz with the HPDEC sequence. The chemical shift reference was ADP (Adenosine diphosphate) at 0.8 ppm. The sample was rotated at 10KHz with HPDEC decoupling. Citric acid solution was 2% by wt. The beaker was immersed in 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution. A 600 mL beaker held the citric acid solution. Alloquots of 1.2 mL were collected.

Key Results
XRD of milled powders showed 98% of CaCO3. The 2 h and 400 rpm milling produced K3CaH(PO4)2. A second phosphate phase was possibly CaKPO4. Below these parameters only the reactants diffraction patterns appeared. A minimal energy was required to initiate mechanochemical reaction. High energy changes were attributed to polymorphic potassium calcium phosphates. When time increases, secondary mechanochemical dehydroxylation occurred. CaKPO4 was more evident after 24 h of milling. KH2PO4 TGA showed 89% residual mass, consistent to 87% theoretical. Eggshell TGA showed moisture loss below 300 °C. Eggshell calcite decomposition occurred below 700 °C. Eggshell XRD confirmed CaCO3 composition. The eggshells were mainly composed by CaCO3. Experimental residue was 56% vs theoretical 59%. Milled samples TGA showed mass loss centered at 280°C, 420°C, and 710°C. Milled samples at 600 rpm lacked calcite decomposition. Calcined fractions revealed K3CaH(PO4)2. Thermal treatment at 280°C left the K3CaH(PO4)2 phase unchanged. Thermal treatment at 420°C converted the samples to KCaPO4. Treatment at 710°C achieved complete KCaPO4 conversion. 31P NMR showed a single intense signal at δ = 3.74 ppm. Two signals were at δ = 3.28 ppm and δ = 2.82 ppm. Calcium phosphate signals appeared at δ = 3.28 ppm and δ = 2.82 ppm. A signal at δ = 0.74 ppm suggested H(PO4)2 5-. A shift at δ = -5 ppm appeared in the 2 h at 600 rpm sample. Pyrophosphate formed by phosphate dimerization at δ = -5 ppm. Phosphorus release was slower for the milled samples. The new phosphates delayed nutrient bioavailability. Calcium release was faster than from eggshell. New phosphates made calcium readily available. KH2PO4 P release rose from 0 mg/kg to 107 mg/kg in 3 days. KH2PO4 P release accounted for 40% of total precursor P. Sample 2 h/600 rpm P release rose to 45 mg/kg at 30 days. Sample 2 h/600 rpm recovered 15% of total P. Sample 2 h/600 rpm had a longer phosphorus delay. Struvite had no phosphorus release at day 2. Sample 2 h/600 rpm P diffusion reached 1.99 cm. KH2PO4 P diffusion reached 2.62 cm. Struvite has ideal formula NH4MgPO4•6H2O. Sample 2 h/600 rpm P diffusion was intermediate. Sample 2 h/600 rpm diffusion was 22% slower than KH2PO4. Soil Ca release for eggshell showed no increase. Ca rose to 30.97 mg/kg in the 2 h/600 rpm sample. The 2 h/600 rpm sample recovered around 8% of calcium. The 2 h/600 rpm sample was an efficient calcium source. The slower release in soil related to hydroxyapatite formation. Hydroxyapatite formed from 3 until 30 days. Hydroxyapatite was observed when milled samples were suspended and dried.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The novel phosphates were classified as smart release fertilizers. Delayed bioavailability of P and K improved nutrient management. Solubility depends on cation size and charge influencing reticular energy. Hydroxyapatite is a long-term calcium and phosphorus slow release fertilizer. Hydroxyapatite releases slowly under natural soil pH acidification. The materials turn soluble especially under pH 5. Fast release requires nanocomposites. Hydroxyapatite nanocomposites improve solubilization of P and Ca.

Contradictions And Limitations
The process mechanism involved is still quite complex to evaluate. Low rotation speeds do not provide enough energy to degrade all calcite. The milling 2 h at 600 rpm produced an unclear phosphate phase. The release kinetic constants for calcium could not be compared. Each release essay used only one pellet in triplicate. K release in soil showed a slight decrease at 3 days.

Claims
The mechanochemical synthesis successfully produces K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 from calcite and KH2PO4. The milling 2 h and 400 rpm produced K3CaH(PO4)2. A second phosphate phase was possibly CaKPO4. The eggshell was mainly composed of CaCO3. The milling 2 h at 600 rpm gave an unclear phosphate phase. The process mechanism remains complex to evaluate. The authors claim no reported mechanochemical production of these phases. The novel phosphates create different structures from hydroxyapatite.
The milled phosphates delayed P and K release while increasing calcium availability relative to the precursor. The phosphates obtained by milling improved nutrient management. The milled phosphates released P and K more slowly. The calcium release showed an opposite effect to P and K. The new phosphate phases made calcium readily available. K release in soil showed a slight decrease at 3 days. The phosphates may be classified as smart release fertilizers. Smart release fertilizers improve calcium bioavailability.
Hydroxyapatite forms under soil conditions and enables long-term calcium and phosphorus release. The phase transition to Hydroxyapatite was observed. The hydrolytic phase formed from 3 until 30 days. Hydroxyapatite is a long-term slow release fertilizer. The milling 2 h at 600 rpm had an unclear phosphate phase. Low rotation speeds do not provide enough energy. Slow release is viable under soil pH acidification. Fast release requires nanocomposites for P and Ca.

Data And Code Availability
Scanned images were processed with GNU Image Manipulation Program, v. 2.6.11. Supplementary Material contains characterization details.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The milling time was varied from 15 min to 24 h. The milling speed was varied from 100 to 600 rpm. The calcined fractions were examined at 280, 420 and 710 °C. The samples were milled at 600 rpm and compared to 2 h at 400 rpm.

Ethical Considerations
The study used eggshell food industry residue. The method is environmentally beneficial and cost-effective. The process produces no unwanted subproducts. The solid-state activation is solvent-free.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the XRD patterns of the powders. Figure 2 shows the TGA curves of the precursor and samples. Figure 3 shows the calcined solid fractions after main loss mechanisms. Figure 4 shows the 31P NMR MAS spectra. Figure 5 shows the phosphorus and potassium release behavior. Figure 6 shows the soil release essays. Figure 7 shows hydroxyapatite formation in soil. Table S1 lists the nutrient content of the samples and precursors. Table S2 shows the chemical and physical soil properties. Table 1 shows the pseudo-second order model correlation. Figure S3 and S4 show the P radial diffusion in soil.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the mechanochemical synthesis of K3CaH(PO4)2 and CaKPO4 from eggshell waste and KH2PO4 via reverse logistics. 2. The strongest evidence is the delayed P and K release in citric acid and soil and faster Ca release compared to the eggshell precursor. 3. The future path is the use of hydroxyapatite nanocomposites to promote faster release of P and Ca.

summary.title: Environmentally friendly and roll-processed flexible organic solar cells based on PM6:Y6
summary.authors: Marcial Fernández Castro (Technical University of Denmark); Jean Truer (Technical University of Denmark); Espíndola Rodríguez (Technical University of Denmark); Jens Wenzel (Technical University of Denmark)
summary.field_subfield: Organic photovoltaics (OSCs); renewable energy materials; roll-to-roll processing
summary.executive_summary:
Organic solar cells (OSCs) have achieved high efficiencies using lab-scale device manufacturing on active areas far below 0.1 cm2, but this tends to widen the "lab-to-fab gap," posing a major hurdle to competitiveness.

Standard spin-coating has poor potential for upscaling and substantial material waste; thus, roll-to-roll compatible techniques like blade or slot-die coating are preferred. This work implements open-air slot-die coating on flexible lightweight substrates using a PM6:Y6 active layer in o-xylene, a green solvent, without additives, to promote environmentally friendly upscaling. The optimal coating process was defined through fine-tuning parameters like drying temperature and solution concentration, complemented by ternary devices with PCBM and fully printed variants.

Power conversion efficiencies (PCE) of 6.3% and 7.2% were achieved for binary PM6:Y6 and ternary PM6:Y6:PCBM, respectively. The authors report that matching the flexible substrate temperature with the hot slot-die head at 100 °C maximizes PCE by reducing bimolecular recombination, which boosts the short-circuit current; the optimal active layer thickness was found to be around 200 nm. The ternary strategy added a small amount of fullerene acceptor, improving both current and fill factor by enhancing dissociation and collection probabilities. After more than 1000 h of dark storage, devices retained over 99% of their initial efficiency, showing promising stability.

The demonstration proves that open-air slot-die processing on flexible substrates is feasible and that results can be easily transferred to a roll-to-roll platform. Limitations include high trap-assisted recombination due to the lack of cleanroom processing, a key trade-off of the open-air setup. Also, the average binary PCE of 5.8% in the conclusion is lower than the 6.3% reported in the abstract, a nuanced discrepancy the authors qualify as averages versus champion values. Overall, this study paves the way for industrializing OSCs based on the outstanding PM6:Y6 system using roll-to-roll compatible manufacturing.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
Organic solar cells (OSCs) have achieved high efficiencies using lab-scale device manufacturing on active areas far below 0.1 cm2, but this tends to widen the "lab-to-fab gap," posing a major hurdle to competitiveness.\n\nStandard spin-coating has poor potential for upscaling and substantial material waste; thus, roll-to-roll compatible techniques like blade or slot-die coating are preferred. This work implements open-air slot-die coating on flexible lightweight substrates using a PM6:Y6 active layer in o-xylene, a green solvent, without additives, to promote environmentally friendly upscaling. The optimal coating process was defined through fine-tuning parameters like drying temperature and solution concentration, complemented by ternary devices with PCBM and fully printed variants.\n\nPower conversion efficiencies (PCE) of 6.3% and 7.2% were achieved for binary PM6:Y6 and ternary PM6:Y6:PCBM, respectively. The authors report that matching the flexible substrate temperature with the hot slot-die head at 100 °C maximizes PCE by reducing bimolecular recombination, which boosts the short-circuit current; the optimal active layer thickness was found to be around 200 nm. The ternary strategy added a small amount of fullerene acceptor, improving both current and fill factor by enhancing dissociation and collection probabilities. After more than 1000 h of dark storage, devices retained over 99% of their initial efficiency, showing promising stability.\n\nThe demonstration proves that open-air slot-die processing on flexible substrates is feasible and that results can be easily transferred to a roll-to-roll platform. Limitations include high trap-assisted recombination due to the lack of cleanroom processing, a key trade-off of the open-air setup. Also, the average binary PCE of 5.8% in the conclusion is lower than the 6.3% reported in the abstract, a nuanced discrepancy the authors qualify as averages versus champion values. Overall, this study paves the way for industrializing OSCs based on the outstanding PM6:Y6 system using roll-to-roll compatible manufacturing.

Research Context
Lab-scale OSCs reach high efficiencies on active areas below 0.1 cm2. This widens the lab-to-fab gap, hindering commercial competitiveness. Spin-coating has poor potential for upscaling and material waste. Blade or slot-die coating is suitable for roll-to-roll manufacturing. Slot-die coating is preferred for low waste and one-dimensional patterns. PM6 donor and Y6 acceptor showed over 15% on rigid substrates. Inks based on green solvents without additives are needed for eco-friendly upscaling. The PM6:Y6 combination matches the solar spectrum peaks. But PM6 exhibits temperature-dependent aggregation and needs heating. There was a need to transfer devices to roll-processing on flexible substrates.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can PM6:Y6 be fabricated via open-air slot-die on flexible substrates with green solvents and no additives? Hypothesis: Higher coating temperature improves PCE via drying kinetics. Hypothesis: Ternary devices with fullerene improve dissociation and collection. Hypothesis: Active layer thickness influences absorption and recombination. Hypothesis: Reduced bimolecular recombination boosts the short-circuit current.

Methodological Details
The devices follow an inverted geometry: ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag. Materials were used directly without purification from commercial suppliers. Active layer PM6 was purchased from 1-Material Inc. Y6 was also purchased from 1-Material Inc. PB61BM was purchased from Ossila. ZnO nanoparticle ink came from Sigma-Aldrich. MoO3 pellets came from Kurt J. Lesker Co. Substrate was pre-patterned ITO-coated PET from FOM Technologies. Pure silver for evaporation came from Sigma-Aldrich. Silver paste for flexographic printing came from DuPont. The solvent was o-xylene with ≥ 98% purity from Sigma-Aldrich. ZnO was coated at a substrate temperature of 75 °C. The flow rate was 0.06 mL/min. The drum speed was 1.08 m/min. ZnO was annealed at 100 °C for 10 min in air. The AL PM6:Y6 ratio was fixed at 1:1. Coating temperatures screened from 60 °C to 120 °C. Concentrations screened from 12 to 28 mg/mL. The drum speed was kept at 1.5 m/min. The flow rate was 0.12 mL/min. 10 nm of MoO3 was deposited as the HTL. 150 nm of Ag was evaporated. Evaporation occurred at a base pressure of 2 x 10 -5 mbar. Up to 24 solar cells were fabricated per evaporation. An active area of about 0.8 cm2 was used. Activation used a reverse bias current. Encapsulation used epoxy-based glue, EPXR. Curing occurred under UV light for about 5 min at 66 ± 0.5 °C. Curves were measured with a Keithley source meter. A Fraunhofer monocrystalline reference cell calibrated the simulator. A shadow mask defined an aperture area of 0.3996 cm2. EQE and absorbance used a QEX10 system. Light intensity ranged from 62.14 to 147.33 mW/cm2. Thickness was measured with a DS95-50 AFM.

Procedures And Architectures
The device has an inverted geometry of ITO/ZnO/PM6:Y6/MoO3/Ag. The ZnO and AL were coated on a homemade roll-coater. A syringe pump controlled the flow rate. A hot tube carried the AL from the syringe to the head. ZnO was coated at 75 °C with a 0.06 mL/min rate. ZnO was annealed at 100 °C for 10 min in air. The AL was coated at 60 to 120 °C. All heads, syringes, drums, and tubes shared a temperature. The AL drum speed was 1.5 m/min. The AL flow rate was 0.12 mL/min. 10 nm of MoO3 and 150 nm of Ag were thermal evaporated. Deposition was monitored by an INFICON XTM/2 system. A shadow mask defined the active aperture. Activation required a reverse bias current. Encapsulation used epoxy and two glass slides. J-V curves were measured with a 50 mV step. The simulator was calibrated at 1000 W/m2. EQE/absorbance covered 300 to 1100 nm. Afm scans were 5 × 5 ²m surface scans.

Key Results
6.3% and 7.2% PCE were achieved for binary and ternary devices. PCE averaged 5.8% for binary and 6.7% for ternary. The champion efficiency was 7.2%. Short-circuit current was boosted by reducing bimolecular recombination. Coating at 100 °C was optimal for PCE. The S factor at 100 °C was 0.978. Trap-assisted recombination dominated the devices. PCE improved with temperature but saturated. The average FF dropped at 120 °C. The average FF at 120 °C was 42.2%. The average FF at 100 °C was 47.10%. AL thickness screened from 101 to 217 nm. Jsc peaked at 154 nm with 17.3 mA/cm2. Maximum PCE of 6.3% occurred at 24 mg/mL. The FF was 49.0% at 24 mg/mL. Average PCE at 217 nm was 5.8%. The 217 nm device had S = 0.987. The ternary blend [1:1:0.2] reached up to 20 mA/cm2. Ternary blend gave a 12% higher JSC. Ternary devices averaged PCE of 6.6% and 6.7%. FF was 49.1% compared to 47.3%. Dissociation probability was 93.7% for the binary device. Ternary dissociation was 96.3% and 95.7%. Collection for the binary was 69.6%. Ternary collection reached 77.7% and 73.2%. Ternary retained 99.4% after 1050 hours. Binary retained more than 97% after 1500 hours.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Drying kinetics and solvent aggregation control AL morphology. Drying much faster above 100 °C induces aggregation. Morphology and efficiency are closely related. Trap-assisted recombination dominates in open-air devices. Fullerenes enable better electron mobility. Energy cascade effects from PC61BM increase JSC and VOC. PCBM adds donor/acceptor interfaces to boost dissociation. Better charge extraction was achieved with small PCBM.

Contradictions And Limitations
The abstract reports 6.3% but conclusion gives 5.8% average. Trap recombination is high because devices were not in a cleanroom. The study was performed without a glovebox or cleanroom. Open-air processing was a deliberate but limiting choice. The dataset lacks an actual bibliography for references. No random seed or specific train/test split reported.

Claims
Feasibility of open-air slot-die coated flexible PM6:Y6 devices without additives. Slot-die coated flexible devices were fabricated in open-air. PCE averaged 6.7% for the ternary device. Retained 99.4% after dark storage exceeding 1000 hours. Trap-assisted recombination was high due to open-air processing. The device was not made in a cleanroom. This paves the way for industrializing OSC production. Results can be easily transferred to a roll-to-roll platform.
Ternary fullerene addition boosts both short-circuit current and fill factor. A 12% higher JSC was obtained. Short-circuit current values reached up to 20 mA/cm2. FF was 49.1% compared to 47.3%. Binary collection probability was 69.6%. EQEs did not show a specific photocurrent maximum. Improved dissociation and collection confirm fullerene benefit.
Hot slot-die coating at 100 °C maximizes PCE by reducing bimolecular recombination. PCE is maximized at the 100 °C substrate temperature. The S factor was closest to unity at 100 °C (0.978). Short-circuit current was higher at higher temperatures. FF value dropped at 120 °C to 42.2%. Coating at 120 °C did not improve the device. Optimal thickness was found to be around 200 nm.

Data And Code Availability
Data and code availability are not reported in the paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The coating temperature was screened from 60 to 120 °C. Active layer concentration was screened from 12 to 28 mg/mL. The D/A ratio was fixed at 1:1. Ternary fullerene content was reduced from 0.2 to 0.1. Thickness was screened across 101 to 217 nm.

Ethical Considerations
No formal ethical statement or cleanroom-free qualification is reported.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the device geometry and PM6/Y6 absorption. Table 1 presents PV parameters at different coating temperatures. Figure 2 shows J-V curves and EQEs across temperatures. Figure 3 shows PCE and FF box plots. Figure 4 shows dried active layer aggregation. Figure 5 shows thickness PV parameter box plots. Figure 6 shows ternary J-V curves and EQEs. Figure 7 shows binary vs ternary parameter box plots. Figure 8 shows pristine vs aged device PCE plots. Figure 10 shows dark storage stability under ISOS-D-1. Table 2 summarizes thickness-related PV parameters.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first slot-die coated flexible PM6:Y6 device. 2. The strongest evidence is the 12% higher JSC and higher FF. 3. The future path is transfer to a roll-to-roll platform.

summary.title: Stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals: accessing highly efficient photothermal conversion with restricted radiative decay
summary.authors: Zejun Wang; Jiawen Zhou; Yiheng Zhang; Weiya Zhu; Yuan Li
summary.field_subfield: Materials Chemistry; Organic Photothermal Materials; Radical Chemistry
summary.executive_summary: The study develops a series of stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) as high-performance organic photothermal materials for solar-driven water evaporation and desalination. Most open-shell radicals are thermodynamically or kinetically unstable in air due to incompletely satisfied valency, but ANARs maintain high electrochemical and thermal stability because of rich resonance structures including closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide structures with unpaired electrons delocalized in conjugated backbones. Compared to inorganic materials (containing precious, nondegradable metals and causing potential in vivo safety issues), 2D framework and conjugated polymers (suffering from poor synthesis reproducibility, high cost, poor solubility, and performance decay), and previous organic small molecules (cumbersome synthesis, poor photothermal stability), these radicals offer excellent structural definiteness, convenient preparation without heavy metal poisoning, and air stability. Four star-shaped ANARs—TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8—were prepared via facile demethylation and consequent oxidation of their phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air by introducing triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, and spiro fluorene cores. Characterized by cyclic voltammetry (CV), UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, and electron spin resonance (ESR), the radicals showed highly reversible CV curves (15 cycles with negligible change), low photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQY < 1% demethylated), and a high concentration of radical spin with strong donor-acceptor conjugation reducing the optical bandgap. The TPA-TPA-O6 powder was totally black with absorption extending from 305 to 2000 nm. Under 808 nm laser irradiation (0.8 W cm⁻²), TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 heated from 25 °C to about 40 °C in 60 s, while TPA-TPA-O6 heated rapidly to 210 °C in 60 s, and to about 250 °C within 60 s at 1.0 W cm⁻² with excellent stability over ten laser cycles. For seawater desalination, TPA-TPA-O6 loaded in white polyurethane (PU) porous foam (30 mg loading) achieved a water evaporation efficiency of 89.41% and a rate of 1.293 kg m⁻²h⁻¹ under 1 sun, reaching an equilibrium temperature of 81.2 °C after 600 s continuous irradiation and 45 °C after 1 h of continuous illumination (1 kW m⁻²). The foam was about 10 °C hotter than pure PU foam (36 °C) and achieved the 1.293 kg m⁻²h⁻¹ evaporation rate, while the desalination process reduced all four primary ions (Na+, Mg2+, Ca2+, K+) to values below typical membrane-based methods. TPA-TPA-O6 is cheap and easy to synthesize in 2 steps with high yield and convenient purification, offering comparable performance to previous pure organic photothermal materials while preserving scalability. The study provides a novel strategy for stable high spin radical materials, opening future paths to ANARs with enhanced planarity for photothermal conversion, organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices.

Four star-shaped ANARs—TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8—were prepared via facile demethylation and consequent oxidation of their phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air by introducing triphenylamine, triazine, pyrene, and spiro fluorene cores. Characterized by cyclic voltammetry (CV), UV-vis-NIR spectroscopy, and electron spin resonance (ESR), the radicals showed highly reversible CV curves (15 cycles with negligible change), low photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQY < 1% demethylated), and a high concentration of radical spin with strong donor-acceptor conjugation reducing the optical bandgap. The TPA-TPA-O6 powder was totally black with absorption extending from 305 to 2000 nm. Under 808 nm laser irradiation (0.8 W cm⁻²), TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 heated from 25 °C to about 40 °C in 60 s, while TPA-TPA-O6 heated rapidly to 210 °C in 60 s, and to about 250 °C within 60 s at 1.0 W cm⁻² with excellent stability over ten laser cycles. For seawater desalination, TPA-TPA-O6 loaded in white polyurethane (PU) porous foam (30 mg loading) achieved a water evaporation efficiency of 89.41% and a rate of 1.293 kg m⁻²h⁻¹ under 1 sun, reaching an equilibrium temperature of 81.2 °C after 600 s continuous irradiation and 45 °C after 1 h of continuous illumination (1 kW m⁻²). The foam was about 10 °C hotter than pure PU foam (36 °C) and achieved the 1.293 kg m⁻²h⁻¹ evaporation rate, while the desalination process reduced all four primary ions (Na+, Mg2+, Ca2+, K+) to values below typical membrane-based methods. TPA-TPA-O6 is cheap and easy to synthesize in 2 steps with high yield and convenient purification, offering comparable performance to previous pure organic photothermal materials while preserving scalability. The study provides a novel strategy for stable high spin radical materials, opening future paths to ANARs with enhanced planarity for photothermal conversion, organic electronics, spintronics, and magnetic devices.

        The study explores the synthesis and application of stable open-shell aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) as organic photothermal materials. While most radicals are unstable in air, ANARs exhibit high thermal/electrochemical stability due to rich resonance structures including closed-shell nitro-like and open-shell nitroxide structures with unpaired electrons delocalized in conjugated backbones. Compared to inorganic materials (precious metals), 2D frameworks (poor reproducibility), and prior organic small molecules (cumbersome synthesis), these radicals offer structural definiteness and convenient preparation without heavy metal poisoning. Four star-shaped ANARs (TPA-TPA-O6, TPA-TPZ-O6, TPA-PY-O8, and Spiro-O8) were prepared via facile demethylation and oxidation of phenolic hydroxyl precursors in air. Characterized by CV (15 cycles), UV-Vis, and ESR (0.02 mmol), the radicals showed highly reversible CV, low PLQY (< 1% after demethylation), and high radical spin concentration. The TPA-TPA-O6 powder was totally black with wide absorption (305-2000 nm). Under 808 nm laser irradiation (0.8 W cm⁻²), TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 rose from 25°C to ~40°C, while TPA-TPA-O6 rose rapidly to 210°C in 60 s. At 1.0 W cm⁻², TPA-TPA-O6 reached ~250°C within 60 s and showed stability over ten laser cycles. For seawater desalination, TPA-TPA-O6 loaded in white PU foam (30 mg loading) achieved a water evaporation efficiency of 89.41% and a rate of 1.293 kg m⁻²h⁻¹ under 1 sun, with an equilibrium temperature of 81.2°C after 600s and 45°C after 1h. The surface temperature of the foam was 10°C hotter than pure PU foam (36°C) and showed a 1.293 kg m⁻²h⁻¹ rate. The desalination reduced primary ions Na+, Mg2+, Ca2+, K+, outperforming typical membranes. ANARs are cheap and easy to synthesize in 2 steps with high yield. This study provides a novel strategy for stable high spin radical materials, opening paths for enhanced planarity in photothermal, organic electronic, spintronics, and magnetic devices.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports a sustainable metal-free photocatalytic oxidative coupling (POC) methodology that synthesizes azoaromatics from arylamines in an aqueous medium under ambient conditions. The authors utilize the charged aqueous interfaces (CAIs) of micelles to host both the photocatalyst, Eosin Y (EY), and the arylamine substrates. This specific microenvironment enables a non-diffusive photoinduced electron transfer (PET) with an ultrafast time constant of 0.3 ps, significantly accelerating reaction kinetics to 4 hours with high selectivity and yields up to 100%. The approach uses only 0.6 mole% of the photocatalyst, outperforming previously reported catalytic methodologies that required higher catalyst doses and organic solvents. Mechanisms elucidated include micellar association of EY and CTAB at the critical micellar concentration (CMC), PET occurring before proton abstraction, and O2 acting as a sacrificial oxidant producing H2O2. The methodology shows broad substrate scope, yielding 100% conversion for electron-rich amines and 98/95% for haloanilines. The work is positioned as the first report on aqueous phase synthesis of azo compounds using this interface-mediated photocatalysis. 

Research Context
Synthesis of azoaromatics is highly desirable in aqueous media under ambient conditions for green and sustainable chemistry. Azoaromatics are important organic molecules with potential in optical storage and molecular switches. The traditional method produces unstable diazonium intermediates and unwanted waste. Metal nanoparticle-catalyzed synthesis of azo compounds has been reported but suffers from slow kinetics. Photocatalytic reductive coupling of nitrobenzenes suffers from poor product selectivity and requires inert atmosphere. Photocatalytic oxidative coupling (POC) of arylamines with Ir-based photocatalysts has been demonstrated but has slow kinetics. Earlier reports utilized organic solvents because of low solubility of amine substrates in aqueous medium. CAIs can dramatically modulate chemical reactions which are otherwise inefficient in bulk medium.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how to design an efficient green catalytic route for azo synthesis in aqueous media. The hypothesis is that micellar CAIs provide a unique microenvironment to bring PC and substrates in close proximity. The authors hypothesize that interfacial surface charges dictate the interaction with the charged molecules. It was hypothesized that EY and CTAB would associate electrostatically at the micellar Stern layer. The predicted outcome is that the reaction would proceed via a non-diffusive PET with ultrafast kinetics. The authors predict that atmospheric O2 would act as a sacrificial oxidant regenerating the photocatalyst.

Methodological Details
Photophysical behavior of EY was studied with CTAB, SDS, and TX-100 to probe micellar interaction. The absorption peak of EY in water is 516 nm. EY shows a bathochromic shift of 9 nm with CTAB and 16 nm with TX-100. EY exhibits fluorescence quenching with premicellar CTAB and TX-100. EY shows enhanced fluorescence (2.4-fold) only in the presence of CTAB near the CMC. The CMC of CTAB was noted as 0.75-1.0 mM. The fluorescence lifetime of EY was measured from 1.17 ns in water to 2.74 ns upon micellization. K3PO4 and KOH were used as inorganic bases, and DABCO as an organic base. Optimized conditions for p-anisidine: green light at 525 nm, 0.6 mol% EY, 2 equiv. K3PO4, and 40 mM CTAB. CTAB forms spherical micelles at 40 mM per HR-TEM. The reaction was monitored by GC-MS and NMR measurements. Radical trap experiments used 2,6-di-tert-buty-4-methylphenol (BHT). The reaction mixture was irradiated with green light for 5 minutes before adding BHT. BHT addition was followed by 4 hours of irradiation.

Procedures And Architectures
The photocatalyst used is the organic dye Eosin Y (EY). The base used is K3PO4 to promote proton abstraction. The surfactant used to form micelles is cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB). The reaction was triggered by a green light at λ = 525 nm. The reaction was carried out under ambient air atmosphere. The product for p-anisidine is 1,2bis(4-methoxyphenyl)diazene. GC-MS measurements determined 100% conversion in 4 hours. HR-TEM confirmed the spherical geometry of CTAB micelles. A linear Stern-Volmer plot with a rate constant of 6.3 × 10^12 M⁻¹s⁻¹ was used. PET precedes the proton abstraction step by base. Fluorescence up-conversion determined a time constant of 0.3 ps. A characteristic HR-MS peak at 342.2399 g/mol appeared with the BHT adduct.

Key Results
The optimized reaction of p-anisidine achieved 100% conversion in 4 hours with 0.6 mol% EY. CTAB forms spherical micelles at 40 mM according to HR-TEM. The fluorescence lifetime rose from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns upon micellization. A 2.4-fold enhanced fluorescence was observed only with CTAB near the CMC. The fluorescence intensity of EY@CTAB decreased gradually with p-anisidine. The quenching rate constant was 6.3 × 10^12 M⁻¹s⁻¹. The PET time constant was 0.3 ps with p-anisidine. p-chloroaniline and p-bromoaniline gave conversion yields of 98% and 95%. With BHT, conversion fell to negligible (~5.0%) after 4 hours. EY@TX-100 suffered disassembly in the presence of K3PO4. EY@CTAB was stable in the presence of K3PO4.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The micellar surface acts as a scaffold to host both EY and substrates. The non-diffusive PET with 0.3 ps time constant explains the fast kinetics. The binding of EY to CTAB is electrostatic due to two negative charges at pH 7. Arylamines solubilize at the less polar hydrocarbon/aqueous interface of the Stern layer. The reaction is feasible only with a base because proton abstraction is critical. O2 acts as a sacrificial oxidant generating H2O2 via reduction. PET precedes the proton abstraction step by base.

Contradictions And Limitations
EY@TX-100 suffered disassembly in the presence of base, limiting its use. The conversion yields were slightly less with the organic base DABCO. Conversion for p-chloroaniline (98%) and p-bromoaniline (95%) was lower than electron-rich amines. The fluorescence quenching of p-nitroaniline was absent, indicating no electron transfer. The paper is a ChemRxiv preprint and has not been peer-reviewed.

Claims
The micellar CAI environment enables non-diffusive PET and high efficacy at low catalyst dose. A 2.4-fold fluorescence enhancement only with CTAB occurred. The fluorescence lifetime rose from 1.17 ns to 2.74 ns upon micellization. The reaction reached 100% conversion in 4 hours with 0.6 mol% EY. The PET time constant was ultrafast at 0.3 ps. EY@TX-100 suffered disassembly in the presence of base. Conversion for haloanilines was slightly lower than electron-rich amines. This methodology out-performs all previously reported catalytic methodologies. The work is the first aqueous phase synthesis of azo compounds.
O2 acts as the terminal oxidant and is reduced to H2O2 to regenerate the catalyst. The strip color change indicated H2O2 formation. O2 is involved in the regeneration of the PC via formation of H2O2. BHT addition reduced conversion to negligible (~5.0%). No counter-evidence reported; this is the primary mechanism for catalyst regeneration. The reaction proceeds without requiring high oxidant doses. The methodology is sustainable by using ambient O2.

Data And Code Availability
The paper is hosted on ChemRxiv under a CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 license. Data were analyzed by GC-MS and NMR measurements.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
EY@TX-100 disassembly in K3PO4 showed the requirement of the CTAB composite. Radical trapping with BHT reduced azo conversion to ~5.0%. The PET preceding proton abstraction was confirmed by SV plots.

Ethical Considerations
The content has not been peer-reviewed as a preprint.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows the EY absorption peak at 516 nm and micellar association. Figure 1b shows fluorescence quenching with premicellar CTAB and TX-100. Figure 1c shows EY undergoing aggregation and then dissociation near the CMC. Figure 1d shows the fluorescence lifetime increase. Figure 2b shows the linear Stern-Volmer quenching plot. Figure 2d shows the 0.3 ps PET time constant. Table 1 details the optimized conditions and 100% conversion. Figure S4 shows the spherical CTAB micelles. Figure S15 shows the HR-MS BHT adduct peak.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a metal-free aqueous POC synthesis of azoaromatics using micellar CAIs and EY. 2. The strongest evidence is the non-diffusive PET with a 0.3 ps time constant and 100% conversion in 4 hours. 3. The future path is opening new aqueous-phase azoaromatic synthesis opportunities.

summary.title: Spontaneous crystal fluctuation in hydrocarbon polymer-coated monolayer MoS2, MoSe2, WS2, and WSe2 with strong photoluminescence enhancement
summary.authors: Takahiro Nakahara, Takashi Kobayashi, Tetsuji Dohi, Takeshi Yoshimura, Norifumi Fujimura, Daisuke Kiriya
summary.field_subfield: Materials Science; Condensed Matter Physics; Two-dimensional Materials
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the disparate strategies for enhancing photoluminescence (PL) intensity in different monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs). While p-type dopants and superacids effectively enhance sulfur-based MoS2 and WS2, few universal methods exist for selenium-based MoSe2 and WSe2. The authors propose a universal postpreparation method: coating monolayers with paraffin, a simple hydrocarbon. Leveraging paraffin's large thermal expansion coefficient and high melting point (42-45 °C), they apply paraffin via hot-plate melting at 80 °C and spin coating with a heat blower. The paraffin penetrates the monolayer-substrate interface, causing spontaneous fluctuation, deformation into wrinkles or bundles, and desorption from the substrate. This removes the substrate effect—the primary PL dampener—and induces strain. Quantitative results show remarkable PL enhancements: 215-fold for MoS2, 55-fold for WS2, 9-fold for WSe2, and 50-fold for MoSe2 relative to as-exfoliated flakes. Raman spectroscopy tracks the in-plane Eʹ peak shifting negative by 0.72 cm⁻¹ (strain) and the out-of-plane Aʹ peak shifting positive by 1.03 cm⁻¹ (reduced carrier concentration). The mechanism combines strain from volume shrinkage and desorption. The method is applicable to any 2D material and creates transparent, flexible materials suitable for optoelectronics.

claims.description: The paraffin coating is a universal method to enhance PL in both sulfur and selenium TMDCs.
The PL enhancement mechanism is a combination of strain and desorption.

These citations cite prior methods for WSe2 involving substrate removal via floating or ion insertion.
These citations describe defects, strain, and chemical treatments like hydrohalic acid for MoSe2.
These works discuss strain modulation of electronic states and the funnel effect in wrinkles.

Executive Summary
This study addresses the disparate strategies for enhancing photoluminescence (PL) intensity in different monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs). While p-type dopants and superacids effectively enhance sulfur-based MoS2 and WS2, few universal methods exist for selenium-based MoSe2 and WSe2. The authors propose a universal postpreparation method: coating monolayers with paraffin, a simple hydrocarbon. Leveraging paraffin's large thermal expansion coefficient and high melting point (42-45 °C), they apply paraffin via hot-plate melting at 80 °C and spin coating with a heat blower. The paraffin penetrates the monolayer-substrate interface, causing spontaneous fluctuation, deformation into wrinkles or bundles, and desorption from the substrate. This removes the substrate effect—the primary PL dampener—and induces strain. Quantitative results show remarkable PL enhancements: 215-fold for MoS2, 55-fold for WS2, 9-fold for WSe2, and 50-fold for MoSe2 relative to as-exfoliated flakes. Raman spectroscopy tracks the in-plane Eʹ peak shifting negative by 0.72 cm⁻¹ (strain) and the out-of-plane Aʹ peak shifting positive by 1.03 cm⁻¹ (reduced carrier concentration). The mechanism combines strain from volume shrinkage and desorption. The method is applicable to any 2D material and creates transparent, flexible materials suitable for optoelectronics.

Research Context
Monolayer TMDCs are attracting attention due to their thin crystal structure and excellent mechanical robustness. They exhibit a direct band gap at the K and K' points in the Brillouin zone. A drawback is their poor optical property, such as poor photoluminescence (PL) intensity. Over-carrier concentrations, strains, and defects in the crystalline lattice cause poor PL. P-type doping enhances PL in n-type MoS2 and WS2 but is not effective for selenium-based TMDCs. Oleic acid and hydrohalic acid treatments have been reported for MoSe2 but lack a universal strategy. There is no universal strategy for improving the optical behavior of a large variety of two-dimensional semiconductor materials.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether a universal strategy can enhance PL in all TMDC types. The hypothesis is that removing the substrate effect via mechanical floating or coating would improve PL intensity. The authors hypothesize that spontaneous fluctuation via paraffin coating will cause desorption and enhance PL. They predict that paraffin's large thermal coefficient will apply the strain effectively during coating. The expected outcome is a remarkable PL enhancement across all compounds due to substrate removal.

Methodological Details
The study applies the coating to four compounds: WS2, MoS2, WSe2, and MoSe2. The paraffin used has a melting point of 42-45 °C. The paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C in advance. The melted paraffin was dropped onto a sample placed on a spin coater. A heat blower (hair dryer) kept the paraffin in a melted state during application. PL spectra were recorded for monolayer WS2 on a Si/SiO2 substrate. PL was also measured on monolayer WS2 on a quartz substrate. PL mapping images confirmed enhancement in the whole plane with partial area greater enhancement. The samples were monitored via optical microscopy. Raman spectra tracked 30 samples of monolayer MoS2 before and after coating.

Procedures And Architectures
Paraffin was melted on a hot plate at 80 °C before drop application. The coating was applied by dropping melted paraffin onto a spin-coated sample. A heat blower was used to prevent the paraffin from solidifying during casting. A thick film obtained by simple casting resulted in a non-transparent glassy appearance. PL enhancement was measured relative to the as-exfoliated flakes. Raman shifts tracked the Eʹ peak (in-plane) and Aʹ peak (out-of-plane). Monolayer MoS2 was monitored over 3 hours at room temperature (Figures 3a-d). The deformation was identified using white circles in optical images. Figure S1 shows the WS2 PL on quartz; Figure S5 shows a deformation situation. The data is reported for 30 samples in the Raman statistical analysis.

Key Results
MoS2 showed a PL enhancement of over 200 times. WS2 showed PL enhancement of about 36 times. WSe2 showed a factor of enhancement of 9. MoSe2 showed a factor of enhancement of 50. The Eʹ peak shifted in the negative direction by -0.72 cm⁻¹ on average. The Aʹ peak shifted in the positive direction by 1.03 cm⁻¹. The center PL intensity was 2.3 times greater than the rim. The peak position shifted 5-10 meV lower in energy around the center. The paraffin coating removed the substrate effect. PL enhancement occurred both on Si/SiO2 and quartz substrates.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Paraffin penetration at the interface removes the substrate effect by decreasing electron concentration. The mechanism combines strain from thermal expansion and desorption. Strain induces the fluctuation that causes the monolayer to desorb. Wrinkles and folding edges produce PL enhancement and peak shifts. The paraffin is insulative, flexible, and transparent for optoelectronics. This method extends the design of applying TMDCs as optoelectronics material. The underlining science is applicable to other 2D layered materials. Paraffin enables packaging flexible light-emitting displays and solar cells.

Contradictions And Limitations
A thick film achieved by simple casting was not transparent. Enhancement was nonuniform and dependent on the fluctuation state. The interpretation of the peak shift is especially applicable for sulfur-based TMDCs. The exact random seed for spin coating and temperature profiles are not reported. Statistical Raman data covers 30 samples of MoS2 but not all TMDCs. The specific volume shrinkage value for paraffin is not quantified. Sample demographics or flake sizes are not reported.

Claims
The paraffin coating is a universal method to enhance PL in both sulfur and selenium TMDCs. MoS2, WS2, WSe2, and MoSe2 all showed PL enhancement. Enhancement occurred on both Si/SiO2 and quartz substrates. The Eʹ and Aʹ Raman shifts indicate a general mechanism. Enhancement factor varied widely between 9 and 215-fold. The thick film obtained by casting was not transparent. The method can be used for generic 2D materials. It supports flexible and transparent optoelectronics.
The PL enhancement mechanism is a combination of strain and desorption. Eʹ shifted -0.72 cm⁻¹ (strain) and Aʹ shifted 1.03 cm⁻¹ (carrier reduction). The center was 2.3 times brighter than the rim. Wrinkles and folding edges show PL enhancement. The exciton explanation is noted as especially applicable to sulfur-based compounds. The mechanism is tied to paraffin's thermal expansion.

Data And Code Availability
The authors did not state where data or code are available.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A thick film was compared to a spin-coated thin film. A sample surrounded by bulk flakes prevented bundling.

Ethical Considerations
No specific ethical approval or considerations are mentioned.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows paraffin applied via spin coater. Figure 1b shows WS2 PL with 36x enhancement. Figure 1c and 1d show optical and PL mapping of WS2. Figure 2a shows as-exfoliated flake band gaps. Figure 2b shows enhancement factors for each flake. Figure 3 shows time-resolved MoS2 deformation. Figure 3e shows PL spectra of the deformed sample. Figure 4 shows statistical Raman shifts of 30 samples. Figure 5 shows a monolayer surrounded by bulk flakes.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a universal paraffin coating method to enhance PL across all TMDCs. 2. The strongest evidence is the consistent substrate removal and dramatic PL enhancements across compounds. 3. The future path is using paraffin for transparent and flexible optoelectronic devices.

summary.authors: Anuradha V Jagtap A †$ (CSIR-National Chemical Laboratory); Pawan Kumar A †$ (CSIR-National Chemical Laboratory); Sharad Gupta (CSIR-National Chemical Laboratory); N Abharana (Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)); S N Jha (Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)); D Bhattacharyya (Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC)); T G Ajithkumar (CSIR-National Chemical Laboratory); C P Vinod (CSIR-National Chemical Laboratory)
summary.executive_summary: This research tackles the "holy grail" challenge of the partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol, a transformation traditionally hampered by harsh conditions and a propensity for complete oxidation to CO2. The authors develop an Au-Fe bimetallic catalyst supported on hydrophobic silica (HS) to enable methanol production at atmospheric pressure in a continuous flow reactor using H2O2 as a green oxidant. The catalyst, AuFeHS, features an optimum composition of 0.23 wt % Au and 0.46 wt % Fe, as determined by ICP-OES. Fe speciation by XPS and XANES reveals low-valent Fe3-δ+ species stabilized by Au, which act as active sites for hydrogen peroxide activation and methane C-H bond cleavage. The hydrophobic support is critical; contact angle analysis yields 118°, and a specific surface area of 392 m2/g is achieved. Key performance results: in batch, AuFeHS produced a methanol yield of 1666 mmol per gFe+Au with 95% selectivity; in continuous flow at atmospheric pressure, it achieved 224 mmol per gFe+Au methanol yield over 4 hours. Co-feeding CO induces a selectivity switch, forming acetic acid with an overall methanol-to-acetic acid yield of 92 mmol per gFe+Au and 648 µmol per gcat of acetic acid formed within 4 hours. The study establishes that the synergy between Fe and Au, combined with acidic sites and hydrophobicity, allows methane activation at benign conditions. Control experiments and isotope labeling (CD4) rule out support-derived products. Compared to SBA-15, which yielded 111 mmol per gFe+Au, the hydrophobic support markedly enhances activity. The catalytic cycle is attributed to the formation of a C-H sigma complex on acid sites, followed by conversion to CH3 radicals on low-valent Fe3-δ+ sites. While the role of sodium and Lewis acid sites was noted as beyond scope, the work provides a promising pathway toward commercial low-pressure methane-to-oxygenate (M2O) technologies. The work surpasses the best reported atmospheric flow values, including a previously cited 0.081 molProduct kgcatalyst-1h-1 under 20 bar using H2O2. This catalysis enables the transformation of natural gas and waste-derived methane into value-added chemicals under commercially favorable, continuous flow conditions.

Executive Summary
This research tackles the "holy grail" challenge of the partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol, a transformation traditionally hampered by harsh conditions and a propensity for complete oxidation to CO2. The authors develop an Au-Fe bimetallic catalyst supported on hydrophobic silica (HS) to enable methanol production at atmospheric pressure in a continuous flow reactor using H2O2 as a green oxidant. The catalyst, AuFeHS, features an optimum composition of 0.23 wt % Au and 0.46 wt % Fe, as determined by ICP-OES. Fe speciation by XPS and XANES reveals low-valent Fe3-δ+ species stabilized by Au, which act as active sites for hydrogen peroxide activation and methane C-H bond cleavage. The hydrophobic support is critical; contact angle analysis yields 118°, and a specific surface area of 392 m2/g is achieved. Key performance results: in batch, AuFeHS produced a methanol yield of 1666 mmol per gFe+Au with 95% selectivity; in continuous flow at atmospheric pressure, it achieved 224 mmol per gFe+Au methanol yield over 4 hours. Co-feeding CO induces a selectivity switch, forming acetic acid with an overall methanol-to-acetic acid yield of 92 mmol per gFe+Au and 648 µmol per gcat of acetic acid formed within 4 hours. The study establishes that the synergy between Fe and Au, combined with acidic sites and hydrophobicity, allows methane activation at benign conditions. Control experiments and isotope labeling (CD4) rule out support-derived products. Compared to SBA-15, which yielded 111 mmol per gFe+Au, the hydrophobic support markedly enhances activity. The catalytic cycle is attributed to the formation of a C-H sigma complex on acid sites, followed by conversion to CH3 radicals on low-valent Fe3-δ+ sites. While the role of sodium and Lewis acid sites was noted as beyond scope, the work provides a promising pathway toward commercial low-pressure methane-to-oxygenate (M2O) technologies. The work surpasses the best reported atmospheric flow values, including a previously cited 0.081 molProduct kgcatalyst-1h-1 under 20 bar using H2O2. This catalysis enables the transformation of natural gas and waste-derived methane into value-added chemicals under commercially favorable, continuous flow conditions.

Research Context
Methane is a major constituent of natural gas, but its storage and transportation require compression to high pressures:  The direct partial oxidation of methane to methanol is a long-standing catalysis holy grail problem:  Thermodynamics favors the complete oxidation of activated C-H bonds to CO2:  Molecular oxygen and H2O2 are the primary green oxidants for commercial catalysis:  Most previous reports on methane partial oxidation suffer from high-pressure reaction conditions:  A reported benchmark for H2O2 oxidation at 20 bar yielded 0.081 molProduct kgcatalyst-1h-1:  Prior methanol reports over O2 at 210 °C yielded only 1.81 µmolh−1gcat−1:  A continuous flow reactor was desired to replace the dominant high-pressure batch approach:  Prior reports of POM to methanol in continuous flow remain limited and rely on O2:  A gap exists for a catalyst that activates methane at mild conditions with high selectivity: 

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether an Au-Fe catalyst can achieve methanol POM at atmospheric pressure:  The authors hypothesize that an Au-Fe bimetallic system will activate methane at benign conditions:  Au is expected to generate and stabilize low-valent Fe3-δ+ active sites:  The hydrophobic silica support is predicted to enhance peroxide proximity and reduce poisoning:  Synergistic Au-Fe interactions are expected to activate H2O2 and CH4:  CO co-feeding is predicted to switch selectivity to acetic acid:  Acidic sites are predicted to promote methane C-H sigma complex formation:  The predicted outcome is a methanol yield surpassing previous atmospheric flow benchmarks:  Methanol production is expected to be the main product under methane feed:  Acetic acid formation is expected when CO is co-fed: 

Methodological Details
Catalysts were prepared by a modified deposition precipitation method:  A hydrophobic silica (HS) support was employed:  The optimum Fe concentration was confirmed as 0.46 wt % by ICP-OES:  The optimum Au concentration was confirmed as 0.23 wt % by ICP-OES:  H2O2 (15% w/v) was used as the green oxidant:  The hydrophobicity was confirmed by a contact angle of 118°:  Powder XRD confirmed a fine dispersion with no characteristic Au or Fe reflections:  HRTEM revealed Au nanoparticles with a range of 1.3-3.0 nm:  Au was estimated to have a specific surface area of 392 m2/g:  Fe 2p XPS showed a peak at 710.3 eV for FeHS and 709.5 eV for AuFeHS:  Fe 2p XPS at 710.6 eV corresponded to Fe3+ species:  The spin-orbit splitting of Au 4f was 3.7 eV:  Atomic percentages of Au were estimated as 85% Au0 and 15% Auδ+:  XANES showed Fe is in the +3 oxidation state for FeHS:  Linear combination fitting gave 72% Fe3O4 and 28% FeO for AuFeHS:  Fe K-edge EXAFS first peak appeared at ~1.5 Å:  The Au L3-edge peak lies above 2 Å, indicating elemental Au:  In-situ IR CO adsorption yielded signals at 2105 and 2175 cm−1:  23 Na NMR and Na 1s XPS characterized the Na framework:  CD4 labelling and N2 gas feed experiments ruled out support-derived methanol:  The optimal continuous flow temperature was 80 °C:  ICP-OES quantified metal loads; XRD and HRTEM confirmed dispersion:  XPS and XANES confirmed oxidation states; ex-situ HRTEM imaged nanoparticles:  Solid-state NMR and FT-IR analyzed the support and adsorbed species: 

Procedures And Architectures
The continuous flow process operated at atmospheric pressure:  Reaction proceeded for up to 7 h in a continuous flow fixed-bed reactor:  The batch reactor operated at 10 bar methane and 20 bar total pressure:  The oxidant was H2O2 at 15% w/v:  CO was co-fed with methane at a 15 bar CH4:5 bar CO ratio:  The Fe loading was fixed at 0.5 wt %:  The optimum Au loading was found at 0.23 wt %:  The AuFeHS catalyst used a modified deposition precipitation method:  A comparison was made with Au and Fe on SBA-15:  The temperature for continuous flow was optimized to 80 °C:  Product formation was confirmed by gas chromatography and NMR:  Yields were quantified by GC using standard calibrations:  Batch and flow yields were quantified in mmol per gFe+Au:

Claims
AuFeHS achieves the highest reported methanol yield at atmospheric pressure in a continuous flow reactor Flow yield of 224 mmol per gFe+Au surpasses benchmarks:  The overall conversion is the best reported:  Previous H2O2 benchmark was 0.081 molProduct kgcatalyst-1h-1:  Continuous flow at atmospheric pressure surpasses high pressure:  The high-pressure batch yield is still absolute highest:  This opens the doors for M2O technologies:  Methanol is the main product under methane feed: 
Co-feeding CO switches selectivity from methanol to acetic acid CO co-feeding forms acetic acid as the main product:  Acetic acid formed within 4 h yields 648 µmol per gcat:  The overall methanol-to-acetic acid yield is 92 mmol per gFe+Au:  The CO-induced selectivity switch was demonstrated:  Methanol remains a side product with CO co-feed:  CO2 selectivity is higher than without CO:  Demonstrates a switchable platform for acetic acid:  The reaction converts lower alkanes to oxygenates: 
The hydrophobic silica support is essential for high methanol productivity AuFeHS (224 mmol) yields over SBA-15 (111 mmol):  Hydrophobicity enhances methane activation:  Hydrophobic silica promotes peroxide proximity:  The hydrophobic support is key for activity:  Nearest neighbor of Au is Au, not Fe:  Au remains in an elemental state:  The Fe K-edge first peak is lower than Fe foil:  Care must be taken in support preparation:  Hydrophobicity prevents moisture poisoning: 

Data And Code Availability
HS, FeHS, and AuFeHS characterization and synthesis data in supplementary information:  No code availability is reported: 

Robustness And Ablation Notes
CD4 labelling confirmed the methyl group originated from CD4:  Nitrogen gas feed produced no products:  Control experiments showed no product without flow, oxidant, or catalyst:  Support-derived products were ruled out by isotope labeling:  SBA-15 was used as a hydrophilic support control: 

Ethical Considerations

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows catalyst dispersion, TEM Au particles, and mapping:  Figure 2 shows XPS and XANES confirming Fe oxidation states:  Figure 4 shows steady methanol production in continuous flow:  Figure 5 shows solid-state NMR of the silica matrix:

1. The core contribution is continuous flow methane oxidation to methanol at atmospheric pressure:  2. The strongest evidence is the 1666 mmol per gFe+Au methanol yield with 95% selectivity:  3. The future path lies in low-pressure methane-to-oxygenate technologies:

    This research addresses the challenge of the partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol, a "holy grail" reaction that typically requires harsh conditions and often leads to over-oxidation to CO2. The authors develop an AuFeHS catalyst—an Au-Fe bimetallic system supported on hydrophobic silica—to enable methanol production at atmospheric pressure in a continuous flow reactor using H2O2 as a green oxidant. The Fe sites, identified as low-valent Fe³⁻δ⁺ via XPS and XANES, are generated and stabilized by Au, which promotes H2O2 activation. Hydrophobic silica is used to maintain peroxide activity and prevent moisture-induced poisoning or Au particle growth. Key performance metrics include a batch yield of 1666 mmol per gFe+Au with 95% methanol selectivity, and a continuous flow methanol yield of 224 mmol per gFe+Au under atmospheric pressure. Co-feeding CO switches selectivity to acetic acid with a yield of 648 µmol per gcat. The study supports the hypothesis that the synergistic Au-Fe interaction and acidic sites promote the C-H sigma complex activation, converting CH3 radicals to methanol. Control experiments and isotope labeling (CD4) rule out support-derived methanol. This work surpasses previous reported atmospheric flow yields, demonstrating a promising path toward low-pressure methane-to-oxygenate (M2O) technologies.

summary.title: A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12
summary.authors: Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris
summary.field_subfield: Materials science / solid-state electrolytes / crystal structure prediction
summary.executive_summary: Solid-state electrolytes, specifically cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), are promising materials for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries because they offer improved safety, longer cycle lives, and potentially reduced production costs compared to liquid electrolytes. However, experimental and theoretical efforts have been unable to identify the ground state configuration of c-LLZO, leading to a lack of consensus on its Li site occupancy and resulting in disagreement about the ground state in the literature. This study addresses the problem by developing a workflow to produce all possible structures of a c-LLZO unit cell and rank them energetically. The workflow begins by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance cutoff of 1.7 Å, which eliminates physically impossible configurations with overlapping atoms. The configuration space is further reduced by removing symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH) to perform fast approximate similarity searches.
