judge_context:
Executive Summary
Solid-state electrolytes, specifically cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), are promising materials for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries because they offer improved safety, longer cycle lives, and potentially reduced production costs compared to liquid electrolytes. However, experimental and theoretical efforts have been unable to identify the ground state configuration of c-LLZO, leading to a lack of consensus on its Li site occupancy and resulting in disagreement about the ground state in the literature. This study addresses the problem by developing a workflow to produce all possible structures of a c-LLZO unit cell and rank them energetically. The workflow begins by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance cutoff of 1.7 Å, which eliminates physically impossible configurations with overlapping atoms. This geometric constraint reduces the configuration space and limits the physically allowable 24d:96h ratios. The configuration space is further reduced by removing symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH) to perform fast approximate similarity searches. LSH reduces the complexity of symmetry checks from O(N^2) to O(N), allowing the processing of over 100 million structures in a reasonable time frame and attainable memory requirements. The remaining ~2 × 10^6 unique structures are then energetically ordered by fitting a multiple linear regression model to DFT energies. The training data came from 1235 single-point DFT calculations performed with the ONETEP code using the PBE functional and a kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV. The MLR model achieved a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. Key results include: all structures occur within 5.8 eV of the lowest energy structure; 19 of the 20 lowest energy structures have an 8:48 ratio; the average energy for all structures is 1.47 eV higher than the ground state; and the 8:48 ratio dominates the lowest-energy structures. Geometry relaxation of 20 structures was tested and showed that movement from crystallographic sites is preferable to attain lower energies but movement to another site is not necessary. The workflow also highlights that many published literature structures are not reflective of a real system. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals. A database of all generated structures is made freely accessible to improve reproducibility in future c-LLZO research. This research provides a complete, systematically ranked population of crystallographically predicted structures for c-LLZO, replacing arbitrary starting points with a full ranked population.

Research Context
Solid electrolytes promise higher energy density, improved safety, longer lifetimes, and reduced production costs. Dendrite formation through the electrolyte causing the batteries to short-circuit has been reported. LLZO has the best interfacial stability of all popular fast ion conducting solid electrolytes against metallic Li. LLZO has two primary polymorphs: disordered cubic LLZO and ordered tetragonal LLZO with a diffusivity over two orders of magnitude smaller than the cubic phase. c-LLZO is not stable at room temperature but has been stabilised with substitutional dopants on 24d sites. The 24d site is tetrahedral and the 96h site occurs at a tetrahedral/octahedral interface. Despite the material's technological relevance and intensive study, there is no consensus of c-LLZO's Li occupancy. The range of predicted structures in the literature indicates some disagreement about the ground state. Without knowing if the structures used are close to the ground state, more complicated properties may not be well described.

Research Question And Hypothesis
We intend to produce all possible structures of a c-LLZO unit cell and order them energetically to find the most stable structures. We hope to elicit whether structural properties, such as the 24d:96h ratio, are indicative of a structure's energy. We neglect to include the 48g site between the 96h sites as it is not reported in most refinements. We expect to find a significant energy difference in choice of structure and that 24d occupancy is energetically discouraged. The structures produced in this work are be published alongside our results to provide further clarity and improve reproducibility. The method developed here could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals. We assume the base LaZrO structure remains relatively unchanged and the majority of energetic changes are due to Li placement. The structures will be used as a baseline to assess existing literature structures and improve future computational research.

Methodological Details
The number of ways to populate 120 sites with 56 Li is 120_56 ≈ 7.4 × 10^34. To reduce the configuration space, we begin by eliminating all overlapping Li atoms by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance. We use 1.7 Å, which is less than 2 times the ionic radius of a Li atom. The cutoff is smaller than the minimum distance in t-LLZO (2.56 Å). In practice, any minimal distance between 1.67 Å and 2.3 Å would be suitable for a numerical implementation. A maximum of 48 out of 96h sites can be occupied at anyone time. Each 96h site exists as a pair within 0.68 Å of each other, at most one site can contain a Li atom. Each of the 24d occupation eliminates 4 out of 96h sites within 1.67 Å of this site. The number of structures for each 24d:96h ratio, for one unit cell, are given in Table 1. We use the crystal structure sites reported by Buschmann et al. [19] as our framework. This method generates all possible structures, approximately 2.3 × 10^8, including symmetry-equivalent duplicates. We define a connectivity matrix as the distances between each Li atom to every other Li atom. The matrix is flattened and sorted to ensure uniformity in all matrices. We use local sensitive hashing (LSH) to perform fast approximate similarity searches. LSH optimises the pairwise comparison from scaling at O(N^2) to O(N). We performed symmetry checks on over 100 million structures in a reasonable time frame. We validated this method for both 13:43 and 12:44 ratios. We find that only approximately 1% of our structures are symmetrically unique. We can reduce the configuration space by a further factor of approximately 100. We reduced the configuration space to around 2 × 10^6 structures for energetic ordering.

Procedures And Architectures
To achieve this, we perform DFT calculations on small subsets of the total number of structures. The first subset was the 200 energetically lowest structures according to the COMPASSIII forcefield. The second subset was a random selection of approximately 1000 structures across the entire configuration space. In total 1235 single point DFT calculations were performed. All DFT calculations were performed with the ONETEP code. The computational cost scales linearly with the number of atoms. We use the PBE GGA exchange correlation functional and a kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV. The DFT energies were paired with a numerical representation and fit using a multiple linear regression model. The structures were represented by a frequency occurrence list of all possible Li-Li interactions. The data were split into test and training sets with a 1:3 ratio. We found a correlation of 0.9996 on our test set. We tested the effect of geometry relaxation on a small dataset of 20 structures. Geometry optimisation used the Broyder-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) algorithm. None of these site changes correlated significantly with the geometry optimised energy.

Key Results
All structures are found to occur within a range of 5.8 eV of our lowest energy structure. 19 out of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48. The 19th lowest was 9:47. The average energy for all structures occurs at 1.47 eV higher than the ground state. The average energy for each ratio increases with increasing 24d occupancy, showing energetic preference to avoid 24d. There are four structures, all 8:48, within 0.026 eV of the lowest energy structure we find. The four lowest energy have very similar atomic coordinates. The four lowest have the same 24d configuration with slight variations in the 96h configuration. We perform geometry optimisation and find the energy gap between them narrows further. Our energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions and assumes reasonable ordering retention. We create a fast evaluation procedure to generate and energetically order all crystallographically predicted structures. A large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature are predicting or working with non-reflective structures. Movement from original crystallographic sites is preferable to attain lower energies. Movement to another site is not necessary in order to attain a lower energy structure.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
There appears to be a slight correlation between lower energy and higher symmetry. The mean distance moved of Li atoms correlates negatively with the final optimised energy. Movement from crystallographic sites is preferable to attain lower energies. Movement to another site is not necessary in order to attain a lower energy structure. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.

Contradictions And Limitations
Our energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions. We assume a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation, which are both approximations. This method is limited to comparison of monoatomic sub-lattices with predefined positions. The trade-off for increased speed and lower memory costs is the high specificity of the method. The coulombic forces alone is not sufficient to energetically order c-LLZO structures.

Claims

All structures are found to occur within a range of 5.8 eV of our lowest energy structure. None of these site changes correlated significantly with the geometry optimised energy. We could bring further accuracy and reproducibility to future computational LLZO research. We could provide further clarity and improve reproducibility in this field of research.
A large proportion of previously reported experimental and theoretical c-LLZO structures are geometrically infeasible. We begin by eliminating all overlapping Li atoms by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance. A large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature are predicting or working with non-reflective structures. The 24d site is tetrahedral and the 96h site occurs at a tetrahedral/octahedral interface. Only approximately 1% of our structures are symmetrically unique. The structures produced in this work are be published alongside our results in the hope that we can provide further clarity. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals.
The MLR model shows high correlation but may be limited by excluded entropy and the choice of descriptor. We found through applying this model to our test set a correlation of 0.9996. We assume a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation, which are both approximations. We note that our energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions. The coulombic forces alone is not sufficient to energetically order c-LLZO structures. A large-scale energy prediction of the geometry optimised structures falls outside the scope of this communication. We note that our energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions.

Data And Code Availability
We provide all structures generated in a freely accessible database to improve accuracy and reproducibility. The structures produced in this work are be published alongside our results. The data for this image is provided in the supporting information (Tables S1 and S2).

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The COMPASSIII forcefield was able to order the 13:43 with a correlation coefficient of 0.991. COMPASSIII predicts a more pronounced separation of energies depending on the 24d:96h ratio. This issue was considered too large to surmount in this paper. We have tested the effect of geometry relaxation on a small dataset of 20 structures. A large-scale energy prediction of the geometry optimised structures falls outside the scope.

Key Figures Tables
c-LLZO has a Hermann-Maguin space group of Ia3d with Li atoms partially occupying the 24d and 96h sites (c.f. Figure 1b). We begin by eliminating all overlapping Li atoms based on nearest neighbour counts (c.f. Figure 1a). The number of structures for each 24d:96h ratio, for one unit cell, are given in Table 1. A comparison of 1235 relative DFT energies to that of COMPASSIII. Figure S3 shows that COMPASSIII predicts a more pronounced separation of energies. Figure 3: The workflow we employ to find our 4 final structures from given occupancies. The four lowest energy have very similar atomic coordinates, all have the same 24d configuration. Figure S4: The energy of a Li Dimer with changing inter-atomic distance. The fit being a 3rd order polynomial of the calculations close to the optimal distance. Table S1: All Experimental papers we could find that explicitly report the site occupancies. Table S2: All theoretical studies we could find who explicitly report their 24d:96h ratio. We use the crystal structure sites reported by Buschmann et al. as our framework.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a fast evaluation procedure to generate and energetically order all crystallographically predicted structures for crystals with partially occupied sites. 2. The strongest evidence is a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set and 19 of the 20 lowest energy structures having the 8:48 ratio. 3. The future path is extending this method to other ion conductors and addressing entropic and geometry relaxation effects.

    *Executive Summary*:
    "Solid-state electrolytes, specifically cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), are promising materials for high-energy-density lithium-ion batteries because they offer improved safety, longer cycle lives, and potentially reduced production costs compared to liquid electrolytes. However, experimental and theoretical efforts have been unable to identify the ground state configuration of c-LLZO, leading to a lack of consensus on its Li site occupancy and resulting in disagreement about the ground state in the literature. This study addresses the problem by developing a workflow to produce all possible structures of a c-LLZO unit cell and rank them energetically. The workflow begins by imposing a minimal Li-Li distance cutoff of 1.7 Å, which eliminates physically impossible configurations with overlapping atoms. This geometric constraint reduces the configuration space and limits the physically allowable 24d:96h ratios. The configuration space is further reduced by removing symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH) to perform fast approximate similarity searches. LSH reduces the complexity of symmetry checks from O(N^2) to O(N), allowing the processing of over 100 million structures. The remaining ~2 × 10^6 unique structures are then energetically ordered by fitting a multiple linear regression model to DFT energies. The training data came from 1235 single-point DFT calculations performed with the ONETEP code using the PBE functional. The MLR model achieved a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. Key results include: all structures occur within 5.8 eV of the lowest; 19 of the 20 lowest energy structures have an 8:48 ratio; the average energy for all structures is 1.47 eV higher than the ground state; and the 8:48 ratio dominates the lowest-energy structures. Geometry relaxation of 20 structures was tested and showed that movement from crystallographic sites is preferable to attain lower energies but movement to another site is not necessary. The workflow also highlights that many published literature structures are not reflective of a real system. The method could be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals. A database of all generated structures is made freely accessible to improve reproducibility. This research provides a complete, systematically ranked population of crystallographically predicted structures for c-LLZO, replacing arbitrary starting points with a full ranked population."

summary.title: Self-assembling materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces in cellular activities
summary.authors: Noriyuki Uchida; Takahiro Muraoka
summary.executive_summary: The cellular bio-interface is the primary theater of adhesion, signal transduction, and substance transportation, orchestrated by supramolecular assemblies like the extracellular matrix (ECM) and phospholipid bilayers. This feature article reviews recent developments in bioinspired supramolecular materials that mimic these dynamic bio-interfaces. The authors showcase how self-assembling peptide fibres (such as RADA16 and its derivatives A8G and A16G) form stiffness-controlled scaffolds for neuronal migration. Specifically, introducing glycine residues tunes conformational flexibility: while A8G forms bundled nanofibres and a robust hydrogel, A16G forms curved fibres with lower stiffness, enabling the injection of A16G-tagged N-cadherin (A16G-Ncad) to significantly enhance neuroblast migration into injured neonatal neocortex in vivo. For protein-mediated growth factor delivery, the authors introduce the Jigsaw-shaped Hydrophobic surface (JigSAP) peptide, which incorporates and slowly releases proteins; JigSAP-tagged VEGF promotes angiogenesis in a stroke model. They also describe redox-active gel-forming peptides that kinetically control stimulus-responsive transitions through methionine oxidation. To achieve stable blood carriers, metal-coordinated phospholipid nanosheets (bicelles) are designed: Chol-MBP binds Cu2+ ions to crosslink and stabilize DPPC membranes against dilution. Finally, the photoresponsive AzoMEx molecular machine undergoes photoisomerization to trigger endocytosis-like membrane deformation, facilitating the encapsulation and in vivo delivery of M13 phages to the spleen, liver, kidney, heart, lung, and brain. Key quantitative results include EGFP-JigSAP incorporation at 93 mol% compared to 3 mol% for untagged EGFP, a storage modulus of 1.1 x 10 4 Pa, and viral counts of [25.6 ± 13.2] x 10 9 virions/mg in the spleen. Collectively, these advances provide a bottom-up toolkit for constructing biomimetic interfaces for regenerative medicine and drug delivery.

Collectively, these advances provide a bottom-up toolkit for constructing biomimetic interfaces for regenerative medicine and drug delivery.

Research Context
The bio-interface is the field of contact between molecules, cells, and tissues. Interactions at bio-interfaces regulate adhesion, signaling, and substance transportation. Extracellular matrix (ECM) and phospholipid bilayers are principal bio-interfaces. ECM regulates cell migration and signals via ligands like cadherin. A gap exists in creating dynamic biomaterials that functionalize and control these interfaces. Existing liposomes and micelles are carriers but lack dynamic functionality. Stimuli-responsive lipid transformations regulate exocytosis and endocytosis. Need for materials with programmable stiffness, protein-loading, redox kinetics, and endocytosis-like machinery. Methods for delivering neuroblasts or growth factors are hindered by scaffold cell limits or protein-incompatibility. A molecular approach for synchronized membrane deformation and substance transport remains unexplored. Supramolecular chemistry offers a pathway to reconstruct these dynamic bio-interfaces.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can self-assembling supramolecular materials mimic bio-interface functions? The authors hypothesize peptides with repeating RADA form nanofibres via β-sheet bonding. Point mutations will tune hydrogel stiffness and morphology. JigSAP will incorporate and slowly release proteins beyond untagged protein limits. Cu2+ coordination will stabilize bicelles against dilution. AzoMEx photoisomerization will induce outside-in fission. They predict: A16G-Ncad will significantly boost neuroblast migration in vivo. A16G will form curved fibres with lower stiffness verified by TEM and MD simulations. JigSAP-tagged EGFP will reach 93 mol% incorporation versus 3 mol% untagged. AzoMEx will encapsulate M13 phages and preserve infectivity across five organs. These hypotheses are supported by experimental and in vivo data.

Methodological Details
The study uses self-assembling peptide fibres (RADA16, A8G, A16G) to construct hydrogels. A8G is a mutant of RADA16 with glycine replacing alanine. A16G has the terminal alanine of RADA16 replaced with glycine. The JigSAP peptide sequence is Ac-RIDARMRADIR-NH2. Peptides were assembled in aqueous media through β-sheet bonding and hydrophobic interaction. JigSAP concentration for circular dichroism (CD) was 1 wt%. CD analysis visualized a conformational change to β-sheet over 100 hours. JigSAP fibres have an average width of 3.2 nm and length of several µm. JigSAP hydrogel rigidity was 1.1 x 10 4 Pa. EGFP-JigSAP was incorporated at 93 mol%; non-tagged EGFP at 3 mol%. EGFP-5V incorporated at 66 mol%; EGFP-RADA16 at 55 mol%. Protein release: 21 mol% at 24h, increasing to 39 mol% at 168h. Non-tagged protein release stagnated at 5 and 8 mol%. VEGF-JigSAP was injected with 1.6 ng of VEGF-bound JigSAP. A16G-tagged N-cadherin was used to label neuroblasts. DPPC and Chol-MBP were mixed at a 5/1 ratio, 5.0 wt% total. Chol-MBP binds Cu2+ ions to crosslink the membrane. M13 phages were concentrated at 22.6 × 10 11 virions/mL. Nanosheets were diluted to 0.2 wt%. Mice received tail vein injections. Virion counts in spleen were [25.6 ± 13.2] x 10 9 virions/mg. The brain retained [0.2 ± 0.1] x 10 9 virions/mg. Confocal laser scanning microscopy (IV-CLSM) tracked blood circulation.

Procedures And Architectures
Peptides were designed with repeating amino acid motifs. Hydrogels formed via β-sheet hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic interaction. The JigSAP sequence incorporates a jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surface. Conformational transitions were analyzed using circular dichroism (CD) spectroscopy. Morphology was visualized via transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations modeled self-assembly and conformational change. Rheological analysis measured G' and G'' storage/loss moduli. Protein conjugation occurred at the C-terminus. Plaque assays quantified viral infectivity. Fluorescence intensity was tracked over 15 min. Tail vein injections were followed by IV-CLSM of the earlobe. M13 phages were encapsulated into AzoMEx-GVU liposomes.

Key Results
A16G-Ncad hydrogels significantly boosted neuroblast migration in vivo. A16G hydrogels had lower stiffness than RADA16, confirmed by TEM. JigSAP incorporated EGFP-JigSAP at 93 mol%; non-tagged was only 3 mol%. JigSAP released 21 mol% of EGFP-JigSAP at 24h, reaching 39 mol% at 168h. EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 release stagnated at 5 and 8 mol%. VEGF-JigSAP promoted angiogenesis in an ischaemic stroke model. DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets resisted dilution with Cu2+ crosslinking. Chol-MBP nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed in blood vessels. M13 phages were protected and retained infectivity in five organs. The spleen retained [25.6 ± 13.2] x 10 9 virions/mg. The brain retained [0.2 ± 0.1] x 10 9 virions/mg. M13 phages reached [18.3 ± 3.2] x 10 9 virions/mg in the liver. VEGF-bound JigSAP and JigSAP alone showed double-positive cell increases. A16G-Ncad hydrogel was visibly superior to A16G alone in vitro and in vivo. AzoMEx induced outside-in fission and M13 accumulation.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Point mutations tune hydrogel stiffness by altering peptide conformational flexibility. The Jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surface enables protein dimerization and nanofibre formation. Redox-active methionine oxidation controls stimulus-responsive kinetics. Metal-binding peptides crosslink membranes to stabilize bicelle morphology. Photoresponsive diazo cores trigger mechanical opening/closing for endocytosis-like fission. Fibrous selfassembly mimics both the structure and dynamic function of intrinsic scaffold cells. Supramolecular approaches offer a bottom-up toolkit for constructing biomimetic interfaces.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors note that the bio-interface materials field is still in its infancy. The number of scaffold cells to induce migration was limited. The paper reports only in vivo qualitative neuroblast distribution in injured cortex. Lipid bicelles are essentially unstable without crosslinking. No precise hydrogel stiffness values were reported in absolute units. In vivo phage display is presented as a potential application, not yet validated.

Claims
Fibrous self-assembly of A16G and N-cadherin mimics intrinsic neuro-regenerative scaffold cells. Migration was significantly higher in A16G-Ncad than A16G alone. A16G-Ncad hydrogel promoted neuroblast migration in vivo. A16G mimics both structure and dynamic function. Neuroblasts were seen sparsely in A16G alone and Ncad mixtures. Neuroblasts were sparsely observed in mixtures of A16G and Ncad. The strategy mimics both the structure and dynamic function. A16G-Ncad facilitates neuroblast migration into the injured neocortex.
JigSAP incorporates and slowly releases full-length growth factors. EGFP-JigSAP was incorporated at 93 mol% compared to 3 mol% untagged. Release was 21 mol% at 24h, reaching 39 mol% at 168h. JigSAP-tagged VEGF promoted angiogenesis in a stroke model. Non-tagged EGFP incorporated at only 3 mol%. EGFP-5V and EGFP-RADA16 release stagnated at 5 and 8 mol%. JigSAP demonstrates wide applicability to controlled sustained release. JigSAP-tagged VEGF promotes angiogenesis.
Metal-binding peptides stabilize lipid bicelles for prolonged blood circulation. Cu2+-mediated crosslinking improves the stability of DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets. Nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed in blood vessels. Nanosheets opposed the clogged aggregation of pure DPPC vesicles. Surfactant/phospholipid bicelles are essentially unstable. Spherical vesicles were aggregated and clogged in the earlobe. The approach enables prolonged circulation in the blood vessel. Metal-binding peptides stabilize the bicelle morphology.
AzoMEx triggers endocytosis-like outside-in fission for viral encapsulation and delivery. AzoMEx induces outside-in fission of GUVDOPC/AzoMEx liposomes. M13 phages accumulated in the deforming membrane area. M13 infectivity was retained across five organs after tail vein injection. Molecular approaches for synchronized deformation and transport remain unexplored. AzoMEx could be applied to phage display (not yet validated). Outside-in fission allows encapsulation of large biomacromolecules. Encapsulated phages can be delivered to multiple organs via blood administration.

Data And Code Availability
Materials and data availability are not specified.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Protein-tagging ablation showed dramatic differences in incorporation efficiency. A16G and A16G-Ncad ablation comparison showed higher migration. Metal-coordination ablation left bicelles essentially unstable. Oxidized forms of redox-active peptides remained dispersed in solution.

Ethical Considerations
Mouse studies followed tail vein injections and organ extraction. Institutional review was not cited.

Fig. 1 illustrates bio-interfaces regulating cellular functions. Fig. 2a shows peptide fibre morphology from A8G to A16G. Fig. 3a shows higher neuroblast migration in A16G-Ncad hydrogels. Fig. 3b shows sparse neuroblasts in A16G and Ncad mixtures. Fig. 4a and 4b model the JigSAP peptide and MD simulation. Fig. 4h compares 93 mol% vs 3 mol% EGFP incorporation. 1. The core contribution is a bottom-up biomimetic toolkit. 2. The strongest evidence is 93 mol% protein incorporation. 3. The future path is in vivo phage display and regenerative medicine.

summary.title: GUIDEMOL: a Python graphical user interface for molecular descriptors based on RDKit
summary.authors: Joao Aires (NOVA School of Science and Technology)
summary.executive_summary:
GUIDEMOL is a Python-based graphical user interface (GUI) software built on top of the open-source RDKit library, designed to process molecular structures and calculate molecular descriptors with minimal user intervention. Developed by Joao Aires at the NOVA School of Science and Technology, it leverages the tkinter package, the standard Python interface to the Tcl/Tk toolkit, to provide a minimalist, native look-and-feel interface suitable for scientists and students with no programming skills. judge_context:
Executive Summary
GUIDEMOL is a Python-based graphical user interface (GUI) software built on top of the open-source RDKit library, designed to process molecular structures and calculate molecular descriptors with minimal user intervention. Developed by Joao Aires at the NOVA School of Science and Technology, it leverages the tkinter package, the standard Python interface to the Tcl/Tk toolkit, to provide a minimalist, native look-and-feel interface suitable for scientists and students with no programming skills. The primary functional goal is to democratize access to well-established chemoinformatics tools used in QSPR/QSAR (quantitative structure-property/activity relationship) methodologies.

The application calculates RDKit descriptors, including 3D-specific descriptors like RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, and SMR_VSA, as well as electrostatic potential (EP) and voxel-based 3D grid representations of molecular structures. These 3D representations have recently gained attention for training deep learning neural networks and for use in 3D-QSAR and molecular similarity assessments. A command-line interface (CLI) is also provided specifically for grid calculations. The application supports 3D geometry generation via MMFF94 optimization, hydrogen addition, and metal removal. For the EP grid, it uses Gasteiger or MMFF partial charges. For voxels, it supports atomic number, partial charge, and Wildman-Crippen contributions to refractivity and logP. The GUI is built with buttons, checkbuttons, radiobuttons, entries, labels, and a scrollbar managed by a grid geometry manager. File and directory selection use tkinter.filedialog for native look-and-feel dialogs. A log file is created in the same directory for each molecule. A notable reproducibility observation concerns RDKit version 2022.9.5, yielding different results across runs or operating systems for the molecule COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br. The source code is released under a three-clause Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) license at https://github.com/jairesdesousa/guidemol.

Research Context
QSPR/QSAR methodology is used by scientists with varying levels of computer skills. Software for teaching is required as QSPR methodology permeates chemistry, biology, and materials science curricula. Existing open-source tools include the Chemistry Development Kit (CDK) Java library. CDK GUIs include PaDEL and the CDK Descriptor Calculator GUI. BlueDesc is a command-line tool converting MDL SDFile into ARFF and LIBSVM formats. ochem free web service coordinated thousands of descriptors. ChemDes integrates 3679 molecular descriptors and 59 molecular fingerprints. Proprietary software includes MOE, VolSurf+, CORINA Symphony, ChemAxon Calculator Plugins, and alvaDesc. The Python open-source RDKit software has implemented a wide range of chemoinformatics tools. Mordred is a Python package designed to calculate molecular descriptors via RDKit wrappers. The tkinter package is the standard Python interface to the Tcl/Tk GUI toolkit. Shi and Borchardt wrote JRgui to calculate Joback and Reid group contribution descriptors. 3D voxel grid representations have gained attention for training deep learning neural networks. Electrostatic potentials have long been used to establish relationships with molecular properties. Direct 3D representations can be used for pre-aligned structures or convolutional neural networks. A minimalist GUI is needed for routine chemoinformatics tasks and well-established descriptors.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study seeks to provide an easy-to-use GUI for non-programmers to calculate molecular descriptors. The central hypothesis is that a tkinter GUI enables access for non-programmers while preserving RDKit functionality. The research predicts that 3D grid representations can be processed by complex artificial intelligence algorithms. The study aims to provide both a GUI and a command-line interface for grid representations. The expected outcome is that the source code can be extended or used as a template for other chemoinformatics tasks.

Methodological Details
The software is implemented in Python using the tkinter and RDKit libraries. RDKit version 2022.9.5 is the underlying cheminformatics engine. The study implements seven 3D descriptors in the rdMolDescriptors module. The descriptors include PEOE_VSA and SMR_VSA. The GUI includes buttons, checkbuttons, radiobuttons, entries, labels, and a scrollbar. The grid geometry manager controls the tkinter widgets. Native look-and-feel file/directory dialogs use the tkinter.filedialog module. The 3D grid uses cubes with electrostatic potential at each cube c. The electrostatic potential formula sums partial charges q_i over distances r_ic. Atoms within 1 Å of the cube center contribute their partial charge. The cutoff distance is user-defined for atoms further than 1 Å. Voxelisation uses an atomic property and a user-defined 3D grid. The voxel formula uses an exponential decay with parameter σ. Implemented properties are atomic number, Gasteiger or MMFF partial charge. Atomic contributions to molecular refractivity and logP use Wildman-Crippen. Hydrogen addition uses AddHs with addCoords=True to preserve coordinates.

Procedures And Architectures
3D molecular models are generated with MMFFOptimizeMolecule. MMFF optimization uses mmffVariant='MMFF94' and maxIters=5000. Preprocessing options include metal removal via MetalDisconnector. Largest fragment selection uses LargestFragmentChooser with preferOrganic=True. Neutralization uses the Uncharger class. Hydrogen atoms are added via Chem.AddHs(). The GUI provides options to include or not specific descriptors. 3D grid coordinates and size are user-defined. EP grids use Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges. Voxel grids use an atomic property of atom i. The final value VoxG_c sums the property across atoms. Descriptors are saved to a csv output file. The output contains molecule name and molecule ID. The CLI uses a positional argument scheme with multiple flags. The CLI example calculates an EP grid with Gasteiger charges.

Key Results
The GUI supports seven 3D descriptors: RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, SMR_VSA. A notable reproducibility issue was observed with RDKit version 2022.9.5. Different values were obtained for GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM descriptors. Reproducibility issues occurred across different runs or operating systems. The reproducing example is the molecule COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br. The 3D grids can be specified by the user in the GUI. A CLI also enables calculation of EP and voxel grids. The source code was released under a three-clause BSD license. The software facilitates access by scientists or students. No programming skills are required to use the software.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
GUIDEMOL democratizes access to well-established RDKit and 3D-descriptor tools. The GUI simplifies routine tasks for chemists and students. By reducing programming barriers, it supports QSPR/QSAR education. 3D grid representations enable deep learning with large data sets. Electrostatic potentials connect atomic charges to properties. Voxel representations map atomic properties into 3D space. The CLI enables automation for grid calculations. The BSD license permits commercial and non-commercial use.

Contradictions And Limitations
A non-determinism issue affects certain RDKit descriptors across runs. Reproducibility of GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM is affected. The issue appears tied to the RDKit version or OS. The paper notes potential bugs and limitations to be fixed. The study lacks a formal performance/accuracy benchmark. No large dataset test is reported; only functionality and one reproducibility case. No formal error analysis is presented. No sensitivity analysis of the sigma or cutoff parameters. No quantitative validation beyond the reproducible example molecule. No report on actual user study or pilot data.

Claims
GUIDEMOL provides an easy GUI for non-programmers to calculate molecular descriptors. The interface is for scientists with varying levels of computer skills. The GUI requires no programming skills. It is an easy access point for RDKit tools. The GUI uses standard tkinter for native look-and-feel. Some RDKit descriptors are non-deterministic, yielding inconsistent values. Reproducibility issues occur across different operating systems. The software democratizes chemoinformatics but requires awareness of reproducibility.
GUIDEMOL supports both a GUI and a CLI for 3D grid representations. A CLI is provided for the calculation of grid representations. The CLI uses a positional argument scheme with flags. The example command calculates an EP grid with Gasteiger charges. The CLI's ability to calculate non-grid descriptors is not stated. No comparative benchmark between GUI and CLI. The dual interface offers both ease-of-use and automation options.
The source code is released under a three-clause BSD license. The code is released under a three-clause BSD license. It allows commercial and non-commercial use. The license enables extension and use as a template. No explicit report on third-party commercial applications. The open license supports reuse and extension.

Data And Code Availability
The source code is publicly available on GitHub. The URL is cited twice as the source of the code. The repository includes the three-clause BSD license. No formal dataset description is provided.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The preprocessing options act as a setup configuration. Metal removal uses the MetalDisconnector class. Largest fragment selection preserves organic matter. Neutralization uses the Uncharger class. Hydrogen addition is an optional preprocessing step. No formal sensitivity or ablation study is reported. The grid sigma and cutoff are user-defined parameters.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the GUI built with tkinter widgets. The CLI flags and example command are detailed in text. No formal tables or figures with quantitative data.

Three Takeaways
1. GUIDEMOL democratizes access to RDKit descriptors and 3D grids via a minimalist tkinter GUI for non-programmers. 2. The strongest evidence is the non-determinism reproducible with RDKit version 2022.9.5. 3. The future path involves the CLI for automation, extending the GUI template, and fixing bugs.

summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang, Tianzuo Li, Jiyeon Lee, Dahye Lim, Lianjie Xu, Yajie Liu, Jongcheol Seo, Wen-Bin Zhang
summary.executive_summary: The paper reports the first single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), consisting of two mechanically interlocked polypeptide rings that fold synergistically into a compact and integrated structure—a configuration extremely rare in nature. The design was achieved by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement, while synthesis was accomplished through a series of programmed streamlined post-translational processing events in cells without additional in vitro reactions. The target P-2 molecule contains few exogenous motifs and was thoroughly characterized by combined techniques, including LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to the linear control, cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability and exhibits enhanced stability against thermal or chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction. These results suggest that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability, representing an entirely new horizon in protein science. The researchers exploited the original protein fold itself as the entangling template rather than requiring an exogenous motif. By virtually splitting the wild-type DHFR between α-helix-C and β-sheet-5 (residues 88 and 89), they identified a cleavage that generated two highly intertwined segments (GLN +0.726), which then produced a catenane topology with a GLN of +1.120. Synthesis utilized two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs and a tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease recognition sequence for proof of topology. A linear control (l-DHFR) with extra amino acids at the termini was compared. SDS-PAGE showed l-DHFR at a molecular weight of approximately 22 kDa and cat-DHFR at less than 20 kDa, with the latter exhibiting faster mobility. Size exclusion chromatography (SEC) showed cat-DHFR eluting as a broader peak at a slightly larger retention volume. Far-UV CD spectra showed reduced ellipticity at ~200 nm and 210–230 nm, suggesting loosening of the secondary structure, yet the near-UV CD showed the overall folded state was intact. Activity assays revealed cat-DHFR has lower activity (~5 U/mg) than l-DHFR (~14 U/mg). Kinetics showed cat-DHFR has a Km approximately 5-fold higher than l-DHFR, and a kcat of about 38% that of l-DHFR; catalytic efficiency was reduced by an order of magnitude. Binding affinities increased substantially: KD for DHF ~173-fold larger, NADPH ~14-fold larger, and product THF ~3.6-fold larger. Under 5% DMSO, cat-DHFR retained 87% activity compared to 74% for l-DHFR, indicating enhanced solvent tolerance. Topology was inferred through protease cleavage and IMS-MS/CID, as no crystal structure could be obtained. Linker optimization showed a shortest-linker yield of ~1/5 the longest (~12 mg/L) with ~33% monocyclic side products.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The authors present a robotic platform designed to automate the collection of electrochemical reaction rate data, specifically for carbon dioxide electroreduction (CO2RR) to carbon monoxide (CO) at immobilized metal tetrapyrroles (CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc). Traditional mechanistic analysis in electrocatalysis relies on linearizing simple rate equations (Tafel and reactant order dependence), which fails to capture complex phenomena like surface coverage effects, mixed rate control, and side reactions—all of which are expected given the strong potential dependence of electrolyte/interphase behavior. This work introduces a single-cell robot that sequentially tests up to ten electrochemical cells, allowing for unique electrode, electrolyte, and gas-phase composition in each. The robot operates in a common-reservoir configuration with online CO/H2 quantification via gas chromatography. The authors use the platform to observe non-ideal CO2 and bicarbonate order dependences that shift with applied potential, contrasting with the single-reported complex kinetics at CoPc in literature. They interpret these via bicarbonate poisoning and potential-dependent mixed control, noting that COPc and CoTPP share a mechanism while FePc differs. The data robustness was established by comparing automated CoPc rates to literature, finding rates up to ten times lower but with preserved kinetic trends. Limitations include the undivided cell design, lack of membrane (causing 60% CO/H2 Faradaic efficiency closure due to oxygen crossover), and the use of Pt anodes potentially introducing HER. Data availability is noted as xlsx; code is not explicitly mentioned as a public repository.

Research Context
Mechanistic analysis in electrocatalysis traditionally relies on linearizing rate data based on voltage and concentration dependences. Linearization yields incomplete results for complex phenomena like surface coverage or mixed control. Cohesive kinetic analysis involves quantitative model fitting over wide reaction conditions but requires heavy data. Cohesive analyses highlight complex phenomena like competitive electrolyte adsorption and mixed control for CO2RR to CO on cobalt phthalocyanine. Many electrocatalytic reactions likely follow complex, non-linearizable mechanisms due to voltage-dependent equilibrium constant changes. A barrier to cohesive analysis is the months of intensive, menial experimentation and risk of human error. Automation is typically tailored for high-throughput screening rather than kinetic analysis.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can a robotic platform automate electrochemical kinetic analysis by accommodating unique electrode, electrolyte, and gas compositions per experiment? Is the CO2RR mechanism at CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc amenable to standard Tafel and reactant order analyses? Does non-ideal reaction behavior prevail across these catalysts? Are the observed kinetic behaviors explained by bicarbonate poisoning and potential-dependent mixed control? Do CoPc and CoTPP share a mechanism similar to previous reports, whereas FePc involves a species later in the catalytic cycle?

Methodological Details
Three catalysts were tested: cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc). CoPc was drop-casted at a loading of 5.98 x 10^{-11} mol/cm^2. CoTPP and FePc were drop-casted at loadings of 5.11 x 10^{-10} and 8.04 x 10^{-10} mol/cm^2 respectively. Electrolytes were made from 0.5 mol/L Na2CO3 and 1 mol/L NaClO4 stock solutions. Stock solutions were bubbled overnight with CO2 and stored. Electrolyte solutions were prepared to an overall 1 mol/L ionic strength. Data were collected in batches of ten electrolyses with the same electrolyte composition. The reference electrode was a leak-free Ag/AgCl calibrated daily against a saturated calomel electrode.

Procedures And Architectures
The robot uses a single cell body housing reference and counter electrodes with a line of ten cell pan pairs. The cell body moves horizontally to each cell pan and vertically to open and close onto the working electrode. Electrolyte was pumped through the electrolyte in port after opening. A common reservoir was used so the reservoir could be freshly bubbled with CO2. Gas was flowed through the gas in tubing; a gas chromatograph provided online CO and H2 detection. Cell body was rinsed after each set of ten electrolyses with milliQ water. Data were uploaded to an SQL database accessed by a python script. Python script outputted average current, partial CO current, and partial H2 current to Excel.

Key Results
CO2 order dependences were non-linear and/or changed with applied voltage. CoPc and CoTPP showed apparent bicarbonate dependence most negative at less reductive potentials and positive at more reductive. FePc showed greater bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials. The apparent order in CO2 for CoTPP was slightly below one and decreased at more reductive potentials. For FePc, the apparent CO2 order was more attenuated at less reductive potentials, and curves intersected. The automated CoPc rates were up to ten times lower than literature precedents. Faradaic efficiency for CO was typically under 30% for the new CoPc data. The newly measured COPc rates were well-correlated with previous work.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
CoPc and CoTPP share a mechanism akin to a previously proposed model. The mechanism for FePc likely involves a species later in the catalytic cycle as the MARI. Differences in how potential influences fluxes to and from poisoning species explain the trends. Opposing kinetic observations in literature might be reconciled by differences in operating conditions. Mechanisms that only qualitatively, but not quantitatively, fit the experimental data.

Contradictions And Limitations
The setup lacked a membrane between anode and cathode. Average CO/H2 Faradaic efficiency closure was c.a. 60% due to oxygen crossover. The use of a Pt counter electrode introduced potential for adventitious HER. A Pt anode might cause metal crossover to copper CO2RR cathodes. Acknowledge that flow configuration can have unexpected influence over measured kinetics.

Claims
Automation enables a more time-and labor-efficient workflow for collecting wide-ranging kinetic data. The user queues up to ten electrolyses for a single effort spent in lab. Automation accelerates and standardizes such workflows. The robot cannot automate kinetic analysis of reactions with <100% Faradaic efficiency. With further engineering, extensions may improve throughput and data reliability.

Data And Code Availability
Experimental data are available as xlsx files.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Newly measured CoPc rates were well-correlated with that of previous work. The new data preserve previously reported kinetic trends in CO production.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A shows the overall robot design with the cell body and cell pan pairs. Figure 1B shows the single-cell assembly and electrolyte configurations. Figure 2A-C show the three voltage-dependent bicarbonate inhibition trends. Figure 2D and 2E illustrate the poisoning and mixed control models. Figure 2F and 2G illustrate on-cycle poisoning models. Figure 3A-C show the CO2 order dependences. Figure 3D and 3E illustrate the saturation and mixed control models. Figure S5 shows the Faradaic efficiency closure. Figure S7 and S8 show the comparative CoPc rates. Figure S9 shows aggregated rates and Figure S10 shows selectivities.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first robotic system to automate reaction rate data collection by sequentially testing unique electrode/electrolyte conditions per experiment. 2. The strongest evidence is the detection of CO2 and bicarbonate order dependences that shift with applied voltage, non-interpretable via linearization. 3. The future path involves incorporating a membrane, alternative gas/electrolyte flows, and software to automatically enumerate mechanisms.

summary.executive_summary:
The paper reports the first direct real-space imaging of a π-hole—a π-electron-deficient cavity—in a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). Historically, π-holes were predicted theoretically but only observed indirectly through interpretation of data. The authors address this by imaging the π-hole in the 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) molecule, while confirming its absence in anthracene (An). Using a CO-functionalized tip, KPFM resolves the local contact potential difference (LCPD) across the molecules with atomic resolution, revealing a characteristic bow-tie pattern in FCl-An that matches theoretical electrostatic potential maps. The experiment was supported by total energy density functional theory (DFT) and SAPT0 calculations, and the supramolecular assembly was imaged by nc-AFM on an atomically clean Au(111) surface. The study further relates the π-hole to physical properties, specifically showing that the π-hole increases the ionization potential, weakens induced electrostatic interactions, and leads to a larger adsorption height for FCl-An compared to An, which was quantitatively resolved via specific-site force-distance spectroscopy.


The research bridges submolecular charge distribution to chemical properties, showing that the π-hole dictates adsorption height (330 vs 360 pm above Au(111)) and suppresses charge induction. The KPFM signal is shown to be highly dependent on tip-sample distance and requires specific height choice near Δf minima to avoid tip relaxation artifacts. The study concludes that scanning microscopy can now probe internal submolecular charge distributions that govern physical-chemical and mutual interactions of molecules. The results are presented as a coherent picture of electronic structure governing assembly and adsorption physics.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
The paper reports the first direct real-space imaging of a π-hole—a π-electron-deficient cavity—in a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). Historically, π-holes were predicted theoretically but only observed indirectly through interpretation of data. The authors address this by imaging the π-hole in the 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) molecule, while confirming its absence in anthracene (An). Using a CO-functionalized tip, KPFM resolves the local contact potential difference (LCPD) across the molecules with atomic resolution, revealing a characteristic bow-tie pattern in FCl-An that matches theoretical electrostatic potential maps. The experiment was supported by total energy density functional theory (DFT) and SAPT0 calculations, and the supramolecular assembly was imaged by nc-AFM on an atomically clean Au(111) surface. The study further relates the π-hole to physical properties, specifically showing that the π-hole increases the ionization potential, weakens induced electrostatic interactions, and leads to a larger adsorption height for FCl-An compared to An, which was quantitatively resolved via specific-site force-distance spectroscopy.


The research bridges submolecular charge distribution to chemical properties, showing that the π-hole dictates adsorption height (330 vs 360 pm above Au(111)) and suppresses charge induction. The KPFM signal is shown to be highly dependent on tip-sample distance and requires specific height choice near Δf minima to avoid tip relaxation artifacts. The study concludes that scanning microscopy can now probe internal submolecular charge distributions that govern physical-chemical and mutual interactions of molecules. The results are presented as a coherent picture of electronic structure governing assembly and adsorption physics.

Research Context
Submolecular charge distribution determines the physical-chemical and mutual interaction properties of molecules. The π-hole—a π-electron-deficient cavity in halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbons—was predicted theoretically. The existence of π-holes was predicted theoretically, but the direct experimental observation is still missing. The concept of π-hole has been developed exclusively on a theoretical basis using quantum calculations. Experimentally, π-hole existence has only been proven indirectly based on measured data interpretation. No direct experimental observation clearly proving the π-hole has been lacking so far. Scanning probe microscopy (SPM) with a functionalized probe is the most appropriate tool for direct visualization. Prior SPM enabled spatial resolution of chemical, spin structure, and sigma-hole charge.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the π-hole can be directly resolved in real space on a single molecule. The study aims to experimentally confirm the π-hole in FCl-An and its absence in An. KPFM is hypothesized to be an ideal imaging tool for the real space observation of the π-hole system. It is hypothesized that π-hole presence significantly affects adsorption height on metallic substrates. The predicted outcome is that the π-hole increases ionization potential and suppresses charge induction, resulting in a larger adsorption height.

Methodological Details
The experiments were conducted at 4.2 K using a commercial STM/nc-AFM microscope. The microscope was a Createc GmbH commercial STM/nc-AFM. Pt/Ir tips were sharpened by focused ion beam (FIB) and cleaned by gentle indentation of ~1 nm. The nc-AFM used a qPlus sensor with resonant frequency ≈ 30 kHz and stiffness ≈ 1800 N/m. Oscillation amplitude was 200 pm for nc-AFM. The Au(111) substrate was prepared by Ar+ sputtering (1 keV) and annealing at ~800 K. The STM topography was acquired in constant current mode with bias voltage. Images were captured in constant height mode. STM images were acquired at a base temperature of 4.8 K. FCl-An and An molecules were sublimated in UHV at room temperature. The molecular deposition lasted 15 s from two Knudsen cells. WSxM software was used for image processing. The surface supercell represented isolated molecules was a 6×6 unit cell. The supramolecular surface cell was a √39×√39 surface cell of Au(111). The surface cell was stretched by 1.20%, compressed by 1.06%, and angle reduced to 56.3° to match optimal unit cells. The Au(111) slab consisted of 4 atomic layers. The PBE version of the GGA functional was used for exchange-correlation. The surface Brillouin zone was represented by only one k-point (Γ). For free-standing molecules, PBE0 with tight basis was used. Van der Waals correction used the Tkatchenko-Scheffler method with Hirshfeld partitioning. The force tolerance for full optimization was 2 meV/Å. KPFM simulated images used the Probe Particle model adapted to a CO-terminated tip. The CO lateral spring constant was 0.25 N/m. DFT maps of electrostatic potential and electrical polarizability derived from 0.1 eV/Å external field were used. The CO tip termination was assumed to have a dz2-like quadrupole of -0.2 e/Å2. Molecular orbitals and potentials were calculated for MP2/cc-pVTZ geometries. Cluster calculations for SAPT0 used a single molecule and a 38-gold-atom layer. Gold layer was fixed; the molecule was fully relaxed. Au was optimized with PBE0 and Grimme's D3 dispersion correction and def2-TZVPP basis set. SAPT0 was done in cc-pVDZ (cc-pwCVDZ-PP for Au) basis set. SAPT0 used the PSI4 program. All calculations were carried out by the ORCA quantum chemistry program.

Procedures And Architectures
LCPD maps were obtained by fitting a parabolic expression to frequency shift vs bias spectroscopies. The spectra were collected at a 64 x 80 pixel rectangular grid of size 3 nm x 5 nm. The CO-functionalized tip was used for both anthracene and chlorinated molecules. Each data point was acquired in approximately 3 seconds. Each parabola contained 600 points. The parabolic fit form was Δf(V) = a × (V - LCPD)^2 + Δf*.:  The bias range was -150 to 400 mV for either molecule or tip. The acquisition height was chosen in the attractive regime. The tip-sample height was chosen close to the Δf minima to ensure the absence of tip relaxation. Δf* images showed an absence of submolecular resolution at the Δf(V) maximum. The PP model was adapted to a CO-terminated tip. The CO lateral spring constant was 0.25 N/m. The PP model used Pauli repulsion from DFT-calculated surface electron densities. Simulated KPFM maps were generated from DFT-calculated maps of electrostatic potential and electrical polarizability. The CO tip termination assumed a dz2-like charge quadrupole of -0.2 e/Å2. The cluster model represented one layer made of 38 gold atoms with (111) orientation.

Key Results
The KPFM LCPD maps revealed a characteristic bow-tie pattern in the central part of the FCl-An molecule. This internal LCPD variation matched the electrostatic potential of a free-standing FCl-An molecule. The bow-tie pattern was attributed to heterogeneous charge distribution due to fluorine and chlorine electronegativity. The presence of the π-hole was absent in the anthracene molecule. Submolecular contrast first emerged on FCl-An molecules independently of their adsorption site. The difference between the minima of two Δf-z curves was 30 pm, related to the adsorption height difference. The relative height of the molecules above the Au(111) surface was 330 pm for An and 360 pm for FCl-An. These heights matched DFT-calculated molecular assembly adsorption heights of 325 and 330 pm. The adsorption height of FCl-An was 30 pm higher than An due to the π-hole. More significant induced electron density was found in the An-metallic substrate interface compared to the FCl-An/Au(111) interface. The HOMO orbital of An was found close to the Fermi level, facilitating charge induction. The π-hole in FCl-An increased the ionization potential, suppressing charge density induction. The induction energy was larger for An than for the FCl-An molecule. The attractive interaction dominated the dispersion energy in all three molecule cases. SAPT0 energy decomposition gave very similar results to the DFT slab calculation of adsorption energies. SAPT0 and DFT calculations were performed on both a cluster model and a slab model. SAPT0 adsorption energy for the FCl-An molecule was smaller than for An. The adsorption energy trend was larger for An than for the FCl-An molecule in terms of the induction energy term.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The π-hole is a π-electron-deficient cavity that reverses the quadrupole moment to positive. The electrostatic interaction governs the nature of non-covalent bonds, being attractive or repulsive. The presence of a positive π-hole strongly affects non-covalent intermolecular interactions. The π-hole allows close approach of rings in heterodimers, increasing dispersion interaction and stabilizing heterodimers. The KPFM contrast is highly dependent on the tip-sample distance; submolecular contrast appears as distance decreases. Near the Δf minima, the electrostatic contribution is maximized and tip relaxation is absent. The π-hole increases the ionization potential of the molecule. A larger adsorption height of FCl-An arises from weakened induced electrostatic interactions. Scanning microscopy can probe internal charge distributions that govern physical and chemical properties. The π-hole is a π-electron-deficient cavity in halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbons.

Contradictions And Limitations
AFM images show a topographic effect where FCl-An appears brighter, not proving a π-hole. Therefore AFM images apparently do not provide any direct experimental evidence of π-hole. Tip relaxations at short distances cause a noticeable deviation in the LCPD signal from parabolic shape. At far tip-sample distance KPFM images do not exhibit intramolecular features. The π-hole is only theoretically developed, and direct experimental observation is missing. The KPFM contrast is highly dependent on tip-sample distance, necessitating specific height choices. The data showed no significant parabolic distortion within the bias range of (-150, 400) mV.

Claims
Kelvin probe force microscopy directly visualizes the π-hole on a single molecule for the first time. The experimental KPFM images reproduced the predicted bow-tie pattern of the LCPD signal. The bow-tie pattern matches the theoretical electrostatic potential for a free-standing FCl-An molecule. Theoretical KPFM simulations reproduce the experimental LCPD contrast with atomic resolution. The π-hole is present in FCl-An but absent in anthracene. The LCPD maps were acquired with a CO-functionalized tip. AFM images show FCl-An brighter than An due to topography, not π-hole. KPFM contrast disappears at far tip-sample distances, showing it is not a robust universal feature. Tip relaxations at short distances distort the KPFM signal. Real-space imaging of submolecular charge distributions becomes possible. Scanning microscopy can probe internal charge distributions that govern physical and chemical properties.
The π-hole increases the ionization potential and weakens the electrostatic bonding to a metallic surface, resulting in a larger adsorption height. The π-hole increases the ionization potential of the molecule. This results in larger adsorption height of the molecule. An had a smaller adsorption height of 330 pm while FCl-An had 360 pm above Au(111). More induced charge density was found at the An-metal interface than the FCl-An/metal interface. The induction energy was larger for An than for FCl-An molecule. DFT and SAPT0 calculations give very similar results of adsorption energies. The presence of chlorine atoms does not influence the adsorption height. The induced charge density is a consequence of attractive electrostatic interaction. π-hole presence modulates adsorption physics on metals. This weakens induced electrostatic interactions.

Data And Code Availability
The theoretical methods were implemented in the FHI-AIMS code. The PP-AFM code was used to simulate KPFM images. The ORCA quantum chemistry program was used for all calculations. The PSI4 program was used for SAPT0 calculations. The WSxM software was used for image processing. No repository link is provided in the text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Δf* images showed an absence of submolecular resolution, justifying the chosen height. Tip relaxations cause KPFM signal deviations, requiring height close to Δf minima. KPFM contrast is highly dependent on tip-sample distance. The SAPT0 energy decomposition on a cluster model gave very similar results to the slab model. For individual free-standing molecules, the hybrid PBE0 functional was used. The light basis and no k-grid were enough for Au(111) supercells. SAPT0 and DFT gave very similar adsorption energies of molecules on Au(111). All forces except those corresponding to a constraint were under 2 meV/Å.

Ethical Considerations
No ethical issues or animal research are mentioned.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the electronic distribution of PAH and the π-hole formation by substituting hydrogens with electronegative substituents. Figure 2 shows the molecular self-assembly and its resolved chemical structure. Figure 2b displays nc-AFM images distinguishing two species. Figure 2c shows the rhombic periodic structure with one An and two FCl-An molecules per unit cell. Figure 2d shows attractive electrostatic interactions and sigmahole. Figure S2 shows that deposition of An alone yields no self-organized structures. Figure 3a shows the electrostatic potential calculated for a free-standing FCl-An molecule. Figure 3c and 3f show simulated KPFM images matching experimental evidence. Figure S4 shows KPFM contrast dependence on tip-sample distance. Figure S5 shows absence of submolecular resolution in Δf* images. Figure S6 shows submolecular contrast first emerging on FCl-An molecules. Figure 4a shows Δf-z spectroscopy over the central benzene unit. Figure 4b and 4c represent calculated induced electron densities. Figure S7 and S8 show molecular orbital hybridization. Table S2 presents adsorption energies from DFT, SAPT0, and dispersion interactions. Table S3 presents the SAPT0 energy decomposition for all three molecules. Fig. S1 displays selected occupied orbitals of An and FCl-An with different shapes.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first real-space visualization of a π-hole on a single molecule using Kelvin probe force microscopy. 2. The strongest evidence is the characteristic bow-tie LCPD pattern matching the theoretical electrostatic potential of a free-standing FCl-An molecule. 3. The future path involves using scanning microscopy to probe internal charge distributions that govern physical and chemical properties.

summary.title: Machine learning force field ranking of candidate solid electrolyte interphase structures in Li-ion batteries
summary.authors: James M Stevenson; Garvit Agarwal; Leif D Jacobson
summary.field_subfield: Computational Materials Science / Machine Learning for Batteries
summary.executive_summary:
The Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) formed in lithium-ion batteries is a vital but poorly understood class of materials, combining organic and inorganic components and protecting electrode materials from unwanted side reactions.

During discharge, the anode must be unstable with respect to the cathode but stable with respect to the electrolyte, requiring the formation of a complex passivating SEI layer that separates metallic lithium from the organic electrolyte. However, key questions about SEIs—such as whether they are amorphous or crystalline and how Li+ moves through them—remain unanswered, limiting the development of next-generation batteries.

Existing pure density functionals work well for metallic systems but tend to badly underestimate reaction barriers, and hybrid functionals like wB97X yield improved barrier heights but struggle with metals and have very poor computational scaling for periodic systems, leaving SEI simulation out of reach. Machine learning force fields (MLFFs) promise to allow atomistic simulation with the accuracy and wide applicability of DFT but with the fast sampling of classical force fields.

In this work, they use a combination of classical sampling and a novel machine learning model to produce the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy. They describe a model and sampling procedure that describes the interaction of these materials and thus permits the ranking of candidate SEI structures. Multitask learning lets them train MLFFs to both pure and hybrid DFT labels simultaneously. They also integrate general organic chemistry data (SPICE) to shape the latent space via multitask training, observing no increase in PBE-head validation RMSE and only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE, implying the greatly increased scope of the data did not impose a heavy cost on model capacity.

The SEI simulator produced the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy. The authors chose wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD as the reference level of theory for non-periodic systems and PBE-D3 in a plane wave basis for periodic systems, with GFN1-xTB charge labels found most suitable for SEI training sets. They used enhanced reaction sampling using Artificial Force Induced Reactions (AFIR) and Nudged Elastic Band (NEB) on the QRNN potential energy surface. Each system started with 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6- in a 1 M solution with 7416 total atoms. The model was trained with a batch size of 64 and a learning rate of 2e-3, with only 1% of the data selected uniformly at random as the validation set.

After annealing at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps each, the QRNN models gave stable dynamics despite the extreme conditions. Each set of candidates was ranked by the mean potential energy over an MD trajectory of 20 ps at 300 K and 1 atm. Because each set of candidates has the same number of atoms of each element, the system energies are directly comparable. They validated the model against the best available calculations for surface reaction energy barriers, as experimental values like density, diffusivity, viscosity, or elastic modulus do not exist for any SEI composition. Figure 4 shows P-F and Li-O bonds associated with more stable structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable ones.

This work is claimed as the most complex redox reactive system simulated using an MLFF or any method of comparable accuracy. While validated against DFT barriers, the model's scope is still small compared to what is required, and future work will include the application of other model architectures, including Nequip and MACE. The SEI candidate structures and energies, along with plotting scripts, are publicly available via a Figshare link.

    The Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) formed in lithium-ion batteries is a vital but poorly understood class of materials, combining organic and inorganic components and protecting electrode materials from side reactions. During discharge, the anode must be unstable with respect to the cathode but stable with respect to the electrolyte, requiring the formation of a complex passivating SEI layer that separates lithium from the organic electrolyte. However, key questions about SEIs—such as whether they are amorphous or crystalline and how Li+ moves through them—remain unanswered, limiting battery development. Existing pure density functionals work for metals but badly underestimate reaction barriers, and hybrid functionals like wB97X yield improved barrier heights but struggle with metals and scale poorly for periodic systems, leaving SEI simulation out of reach.

    Machine learning force fields (MLFFs) promise atomistic simulation with DFT accuracy and classical force field speeds, but traditional force fields with fixed functional forms struggle with complex SEI systems. This work uses a QRNN model to rank candidate SEI structures by predicted energy, describing the interaction of these materials and thus permitting the ranking of SEI structures. They use multitask learning to train the MLFF to both pure and hybrid DFT labels simultaneously. They also integrate general organic chemistry data (SPICE) to shape the latent space via multitask training, observing no increase in PBE-head validation RMSE and only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE, implying unused latent capacity.

    The model used wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD as the reference for non-periodic systems and PBE-D3 for periodic systems, with GFN1-xTB labels being found most suitable for SEI training. They used enhanced reaction sampling (AFIR, NEB) on the QRNN surface to generate diverse chemistries. The SEI Simulator was used to create initial candidate structures with 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6- in a 1 M solution with 7416 total atoms. The model was trained with a batch size of 64 and a learning rate of 2e-3. Validation used only 1% of the data.

    After annealing at 400 K and 1000 atm, candidates were ranked by mean potential energy over 20 ps at 300 K and 1 atm. The model validated against surface reaction energy barriers, since experimental values (density, diffusivity, viscosity, elastic modulus) do not exist for any SEI composition. Figure 4 shows that P-F and Li-O bonds favor more stable structures, while C-O and Li-F bonds favor less stable ones. This work is claimed as the most complex redox-reactive system simulated using an MLFF or method of comparable accuracy. While validated against DFT barriers, the model's scope is still small compared to what is required, and future work will test other architectures like Nequip and MACE. The SEI candidate structures and energies are publicly released via a Figshare link.

Histological analysis revealed smaller, abnormally shaped nuclei and reduced actin filament amounts in the gut. No significant effect was seen with 100 ppm of a commercial mixture, compared to the 250,000 ppm applied treatment. The authors conclude that A. iva phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes may be useful for managing economically important insect pests while reducing pesticide risks.
