judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study uses Attenuated Total Reflectance (ATR) Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy to monitor molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells activated with CpG DNA and lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The central research question is whether CpG ODN-mediated immune activation leads to global molecular changes detectable by FTIR. The study finds that both CpG and LPS treatments increase total nucleic acid concentration early post-activation, with DNA synthesis following RNA synthesis. An RNA-specific peak (915 cm -1) identifies the early activation state, rising significantly within minutes. Total protein concentration rises rapidly, leveling off two hours post-activation. Both activated groups increase fatty acids, triglycerides, and cholesterol, suggesting a shared de novo lipogenesis pathway. The paper reports that Principal Component Analysis (PCA) with PC-1 explaining 83% of variation validated the spectral data. For CpG, the RNA-specific peak increased significantly from the first minutes (p < 0.001***) and was maintained until 2 hours (p < 0.1*). LPS showed increased total RNA up to 2 hours. The study concludes that FTIR spectroscopy can independently monitor activation dynamics, providing an aerial view of metabolic shifts not readily accessible by 'omics' techniques due to complex sample preparation. The study reports the use of replicate n=5 in data analysis.

Research Context
While innate immune responses to bacterial DNA containing CpG motifs improve survival, it remains unknown if this activation triggers global molecular changes detectable by FTIR spectroscopy. Prior studies establish that CpG DNA triggers macrophage proliferation and pro-inflammatory cytokine production. Synthetic CpG oligodeoxynucleotides (ODN) mimic this response and serve as potential immune adjuvants. LPS is a primary gram-negative bacterial cell wall constituent that stimulates macrophages through the TLR4 pathway. The recognition of LPS shares high homology with TLR-9 signaling carried out by CpG DNA. Both CpG and LPS require MyD88 as the adaptor protein and activate NF-kB and AP-1 transcription factors. Trending omics techniques provide precise quantitative data but require complex sample preparation that may alter chemical ratios. Bulk FTIR provides a broad view of relative metabolite amounts not readily accessible by other techniques.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether CpG ODN-mediated immune activation leads to detectable global molecular changes via FTIR. The hypothesis is that CpG and LPS will induce detectable shifts in nucleic acids, lipids, and proteins during activation. The authors predicted that the RNA-specific peak would mark the earliest activation period. The hypothesis predicts a time-dependent transition from RNA to DNA synthesis post-CpG treatment. It is expected that LPS will inhibit DNA synthesis and induce cell cycle arrest. The study predicts a shared synthesis pathway for fatty acids, triglycerides, and cholesterol between both treatments.

Methodological Details
The study used murine macrophage-like RAW 264.7 cells cultured at 37 °C with 5% CO 2 in DMEM. Cells were supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and 2 mM L-glutamine. Sub-culturing was performed in 1/10 ratio upon reaching confluency, generally every 2-3 days. Cells were harvested, spun at 1000 rpm 208 g for 10 min, and resuspended at 2x10 6 /mL. The control group was treated with 0.9% phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). CpG DNA was delivered as 1 µM K3 ODN, endotoxin-free, from Integrated DNA Technologies. LPS was delivered as 0.5 µg/ml from Sigma. Four different time points were used: 10 min, 30 min, 2 h, and 6 h. Samples were spun at 1000 rpm and washed with 15 mL of sterile PBS before analysis. The spectrometer was a Perkin-Elmer Spectrum One with a Diamond-ZnSe ATR unit. Cell samples of 1 µl were dried with mild N 2 flux for 5 min. Interferograms were collected with a 128 scan number and 2 cm -1 spectral resolution. The ATR surface was cleaned using a water-ethanol-water sequence and air-dried. Data analysis used five independent replicates (n=5).

Procedures And Architectures
ATR-FTIR spectra were recorded in the 4000-650 cm -1 region at 25°C. Air background was measured and subtracted automatically by the Spectrum One software. The PBS spectrum was recorded as a sample and subtracted manually. The spectrum of PBS was subtracted manually. The second derivative spectrum was used for side-peak band assignment. Concentration studies were carried out by integrating the curves under the peaks. Conformational alteration studies used bandwidth measurements at the 75% height of the peaks. PCA was performed on the spectra imported directly into Unscrambler 11.0 in the 3000-650 cm -1 region. Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests were used for normality testing in GraphPad Prism 8.3.

Key Results
PCA Principal Component 1 gave a variability of 83% and identified the vast source of variation. PCA Principal Component 2 had a variability of 11%. The 1750-850 cm -1 region had numerous peaks with high variation among samples. CpG DNA induced a significant increase in nucleic acid content (1238 cm -1) from 10 min until 6 h (p < 0.1*). CpG DNA stimulation significantly increased the ribose vibration peak at 915 cm -1 from the first minutes (p < 0.001***). The 915 cm -1 increase was maintained until 2 h after stimulation (p < 0.1*). LPS showed increased total RNA up to 2 h post-stimulation. There was a significant increase in CpG DNA treated protein content (amide I band) from 10 min until 2 h (p < 0.001***). LPS-induced protein concentration increased and then reduced starting from the 2 h time point. The ester C=O stretching peak near 1741 cm -1 increased significantly from the first minutes. LPS elevated triglyceride and cholesterol concentration after 10 min. A significant increase in the 1400 cm -1 fatty acid side chain COO- peak was observed.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The RNA-specific peak at 915 cm -1 can define the activation state within the first minutes. The initial period until 2 h was the extensive RNA synthesis phase followed by DNA synthesis from 6 h. LPS induced cell cycle arrest and inhibited DNA synthesis, explaining no nucleic acid changes after 6 h. CpG induced immune activation was short-lived and suppressed after 3 h of treatment. Protein reduction may involve histone release into the medium or vesicle-mediated secretion. Lipogenesis links fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis through a shared Acetoacetyl-CoA metabolite. CpG activation triggers lipogenesis to modulate Endoplasmic Reticulum and Golgi secretory activity. FTIR allows monitoring of molecular changes that are not readily accessible by omics techniques due to sample preparation issues. This study first demonstrates FTIR as an independent modality to monitor macrophage activation with CpG DNA and LPS.

Contradictions And Limitations
The absorbance of IR light by water superimposes other signals, a limitation overcome by ATR. Omics techniques provide precise quantitative data on specific molecules, unlike bulk FTIR analysis. The study lacks direct measurement of DNA synthesis beyond a 6 h inference from nucleic acid content. A key detail missing is the specific random seed or train/test split (not applicable to this experimental data). The study does not report a specific power analysis or sample size calculation beyond n=5 replicates. The exact composition of the water-ethanol-water cleaning sequence is not detailed. The exact identity of the 1238, 1110, and 1085 cm -1 peaks relies on literature comparison.

Claims
FTIR spectroscopy can independently monitor the global molecular activation dynamics of murine macrophages stimulated by CpG DNA and LPS. The study first demonstrates the use of FTIR as an independent modality. PCA validated the spectral data with PC-1 explaining 83% of variation. CpG DNA induced a significant increase in the RNA-specific peak at 915 cm -1 (p < 0.001***). Both activated groups showed a significant increase in triglyceride and cholesterol (1741 cm -1). Omics techniques provide precise quantitative data on specific molecules rather than bulk analysis. Water absorbance superimposes other signals, limiting pure infrared spectroscopy. This establishes FTIR as a rapid, non-invasive, and high-throughput tool for cellular metabolomics. It allows monitoring of metabolite shifts not accessible by techniques requiring complex sample preparation.

Data And Code Availability
The study reports the FTIR spectroscopy protocol is available online.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Data analysis used five independent replicates (n=5). The Spectrum One software performed automatic air background subtraction. The PBS spectrum was subtracted manually from cell samples. Data was smoothed using a 13-point Savitzky-Golay filter and baseline-corrected. Normality was tested with Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests in GraphPad Prism 8.3.

Ethical Considerations
Murine macrophage-like RAW 264.7 cells were cultured in DMEM with fetal bovine serum.

Key Figures Tables
Figure A1 presents a comprehensive spectrum of resting control RAW 264.7 cells. Table A1 shows peak assignments based on literature. Table A2 shows measurements of area integration regarding peaks of interest. Figure 1A shows PCA scores with PC-1 variability at 83% and PC-2 at 11%. Figure 2A shows the nucleic acid-phosphate vibration peaks at 1238 cm -1 and 1085 cm -1. Figure 2B shows bar diagrams of peak integration values. Figure 3A and 3B show the amide I and amide II peaks. Figure 3C shows integration of the amide I band. Figure 4D and 4E show the ester C=O stretching peak near 1741 cm -1. Figure 4B and 4C show the fatty acid side chain COO- peak at 1400 cm -1. Table 1 summarizes the treatment conditions, reagents, and concentration values.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is establishing FTIR spectroscopy as an independent modality to monitor murine macrophage activation dynamics with CpG DNA and LPS. 2. The strongest evidence is the significant increase in the RNA-specific 915 cm -1 peak from the first minutes (p < 0.001***). 3. The future path involves studying the mechanisms of CpG DNA induced protein loss and the importance of the lipogenesis pathway in cancer cells.

summary.title: The Foster method: Rapid and non-invasive detection of clinically significant American Foulbrood disease levels using eDNA sampling and a dual-target qPCR assay, with its potential for other hive pathogens
summary.authors: John F Mackay (dnature diagnostics & research Ltd); Rebecca E Hewett (dnature diagnostics & research Ltd); Noa T Smith (dnature diagnostics & research Ltd); Tammy L Waters (dnature diagnostics & research Ltd); John S Scandrett (Scandrett Rural Ltd)
summary.executive_summary: The Foster method is a rapid, non-invasive environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling and dual-target qPCR assay developed to detect clinically significant American Foulbrood (AFB) in honeybees. Diagnosis currently relies on subjective, time-consuming visual symptoms and invasive "roping" field tests that require dismantling hives. The Foster method replaces this with entrance-swabbing, which eliminates hive disruption. The assay targets two Paenibacillus larvae genes: the single-copy ftsZ for quantification and the multi-copy 16S for sensitivity, alongside a TaqMan® internal control to ensure DNA quality. Standards were generated from 10^6 to 2 copies per µL and used to convert cycle threshold (Cq) values to spores per 10 bees or swab sample. Across three cohorts of quarantine hives in New Zealand (5 regions, 2018-2020), nurse bee and entrance swabs were compared. A 10-bee sample and entrance swabs were evaluated. DNA was extracted using a 3 mL lysis buffer with zirconia beads on a Mini Beadbeater 16, followed by 65°C incubation and centrifugation. Spore counts from the first cohort (45 hives, nurse bees, whole-baseboard, entrance swabs) and the second (23 hives, 4 with clinical signs) were compared. The third cohort tested pooled swabs in groups of 8 and 12. Key findings: the AFBduo assay reliably detected down to 4 copies per 10 µL with ftsZ at 94% and 16S at 96% efficiency. The 16S marker amplified 3-5 cycles earlier but its copy number varied among isolates, so only the single-copy ftsZ was used for quantification. Bee DNA extracted at OD260/280 between 1.8 and 1.9 showed no inhibitors. Entry-swab P. larvae levels were similar to whole-baseboard swabs, showing hive dismantling was unnecessary to detect higher clinical levels. Hive 11 lacked visual signs but had high spores, then showed clinical signs two weeks later, demonstrating pre-clinical detection. A spore threshold of 565,000 or more yielded a 95% probability of clinical signs (p=0.00). High spores in bees but low on new (<2 weeks) hiveware in hives 11 and 12 indicated pre-infection state. The method could detect Nosema ceranae, but further work is needed to refine thresholds and assess pathogen accumulation. It is amenable to composite testing and provides clinically significant information. The method offers a rapid, non-invasive way to screen hives and inform biosecurity. Overall, it provides a scalable, cost-effective tool for beekeeper-led and inspector-led screening.

Executive Summary
The Foster method is a rapid, non-invasive environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling and dual-target qPCR assay developed to detect clinically significant American Foulbrood (AFB) in honeybees. Diagnosis currently relies on subjective, time-consuming visual symptoms and invasive "roping" field tests that require dismantling hives. Hive 11 lacked visual signs but had high spores, then showed clinical signs two weeks later, demonstrating pre-clinical detection. A spore threshold of 565,000 or more yielded a 95% probability of clinical signs (p=0.00). High spores in bees but low on new (<2 weeks) hiveware in hives 11 and 12 indicated pre-infection state. The method could detect Nosema ceranae, but further work is needed to refine thresholds and assess pathogen accumulation. It is amenable to composite testing and provides clinically significant information. The method offers a rapid, non-invasive way to screen hives and inform biosecurity. Overall, it provides a scalable, cost-effective tool for beekeeper-led and inspector-led screening.

Research Context
Diagnosis is centred on the beekeeper's skill in recognising clinical symptoms—a highly subjective and timeconsuming activity. Previous testing methods have relied on sampling that necessitates dismantling the hive and/or requires multiple visits to retrieve passive samples. Confirmation of AFB in beehive materials has been traditionally performed by culture, using selective media, and induced germination of spores. Confirmation by culture is a variable process and may take up to a week for results. PCR and qPCR have been demonstrated as effective tools, but most applications have not used the quantitative data generated; rather using the tool for rapid confirmation of culture isolates. The quantification aspect is important as low levels of AFB are often not clinically relevant and such hives may never develop clinical symptoms. In New Zealand, hive numbers have more than doubled since 2013. The increase in hive numbers and newer beekeepers less skilled in identifying clinical signs led to an increase in reported infected hives. Clinical signs can vary based on the AFB genotype present, with ERIC II strains exhibiting reduced clinical symptoms. Spores are extremely hardy and resistant to heat, caustic, and other chemical treatments with the ability to remain infectious for over 30 years. Only a few spores are required to cause an infection and yet a single infected larvae can generate many millions of spores. Most molecular publications to date have relied on the sole use of the 16S gene due to its high sensitivity as a multicopy target. Sensitivity can be at the expense of specificity, as evidenced by initial design and subsequent redesign of primers to improve specificity. Sensitivity can be compromised by deletions of target sequences or sequence polymorphisms. Hydrolysis probe ("TaqMan®") qPCR assays permit quantification of each target by selected fluorescent wavelengths. Internal controls may improve the sensitivity of previous studies whereby the presence of inhibitors possibly prevented the amplification of P. larvae targets. The ability to detect relevant levels of P. larvae from a single sample taken from the entrance would permit far more rapid sampling of hives and allow infected hives to be dealt with more quickly. Low levels may be due to the hygienic behaviour of bees to reduce overt infections.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central RQ was whether entry swabs could reliably detect clinically significant AFB levels without dismantling the hive. The central hypothesis was that the ability to detect relevant levels of P. larvae from a single sample taken from the entrance of a hive would permit far more rapid sampling of hives and allow infected hives to be dealt with more quickly. The study predicted that entrance swab P. larvae levels would differentiate clinical from non-clinical hives and allow detection of pre-clinical infections. The predicted outcome was that dismantling the hive to swab the whole baseboard was not required to detect the higher levels of P. larvae in clinically infected colonies. The secondary RQ was whether the entrance swabbing method could be applied to other bee pathogens. The prediction was that the same DNA sample could be used to test for Nosema ceranae. It was hypothesized that pooling eluates could reduce time and costs for screening. The study aimed to find a spore quantity threshold predicting clinical status. The null hypothesis was that entrance swabs would not capture relevant levels of P. larvae for diagnosis. The expected result was that nurse bee samples would contain higher levels of P. larvae than entrance swabs. The hypothesis that entry swabbing is non-invasive was tested against whole-baseboard swabbing. The prediction was that entry-swabbing would allow one-time sampling instead of repeated visits. The study hypothesized that the FtsZ gene was adequate for spore quantification. The secondary hypothesis was that the 16S gene would serve as a multi-copy sensitivity target. The prediction was that an internal control would ensure DNA quality for accurate Cq measurement. The prediction was that the method would allow rapid sampling of hives. The prediction was that Hive 11, showing no visual signs, would have high spores. The study hypothesized that high spore levels in new hives were due to an infected parent colony.

Methodological Details
The study evaluated P. larvae levels across three cohorts of hives sampled across five quarantine apiaries around New Zealand (East Coast, Wellington, Wairarapa and South Canterbury regions). Multiple hives were sampled two-monthly from late 2018 to early 2020. Samples included nurse bees, swabs from the hive entrance and swabs from over the entire baseboard. Subsequent samples comprised comparisons between bees and solely the hive entrance. Bees were collected from the brood frames using 50 mL sterile containers and frozen to euthanise the bees. Genomic DNA extraction from each sample containing 10 bees was performed using the Bee Pathogen DNA/RNA Extraction Kit. DNA extraction involved adding 3 mL DXL lysis buffer to 10 bees in a 5 mL tube with a mixture of 0.5 mm (~2.4 g) and 2.3 mm zirconia silica (~1 g) beadbeating beads. Bees were homogenised in a Mini Beadbeater 16 instrument for 3 minutes. Tubes were incubated at 65°C for 10 minutes with manual inversion every 3 minutes. 1 mL of the homogenate was transferred to a 2 mL microcentrifuge tube and centrifuged at 15,000 x g for 5 minutes. 500 µL of supernatant was transferred to a tube containing 450 µL AD buffer. Swabs were placed in tubes with 0.5mm zirconia silica beads (~0.8g) and 2.3 mm zirconia silica beads (0.3g). For pooled applications, individual swabs were added to 500 µL DXL buffer in a separate 2 mL microcentrifuge tube and vortexed for 10 seconds. Up to twelve swabs were pooled, with 60 µL of each swab eluate added to a beadbeating tube. A synthetic 153 bp standard was resuspended in TE buffer, pH8, quantified in nanograms per µL. Quantification standards were generated from 10^6 copies per µL down to 2 copies per µL. For all dilutions, the diluent was a pooled DNA sample extracted from bees free of P. larvae. The standard curve was used to convert the Cq's resulting from bee and swab samples to spore levels. Spore levels were computed as Spores per swab or 10 bees = 10 (Cq ftzZ-39/-3.48) x 50. Two clinical hives with skewed lower spore numbers were imputed using regression analysis. A binary logistic regression model was performed in Minitab to identify the relationship between spore numbers and clinical disease likelihood. Analysis of variance confirmed the correlation, illustrated in Supplementary figure 4. Statistical analysis was performed after imputing data points resulting in a total of 26 data points with paired clinical data. A p-value of <0.05 was considered significant.

Procedures And Architectures
The dual-target qPCR assay was the AFBduo assay (Hall et al., 2021) which targets the single-copy ftsZ and multi-copy 16S genes. The assay is a hydrolysis probe ("TaqMan®") qPCR assay. The assay incorporates an internal control for confirmation of suitable quality DNA. A synthetic standard incorporated both amplicon sequences. The standard was resuspended in TE buffer, pH8, quantified in nanograms per µL. Quantification standards were generated from 10^6 copies per µL down to 2 copies per µL.     The "Foster method" is a rapid, non-invasive environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling and dual-target qPCR assay developed to detect clinically significant American Foulbrood (AFB) in honeybees. Diagnosis currently relies on subjective, time-consuming visual symptoms and invasive "roping" field tests that require dismantling hives. The Foster method replaces this with entrance-swabbing, which eliminates hive disruption. The assay targets two *Paenibacillus larvae* genes: the single-copy ftsZ for quantification and the multi-copy 16S for sensitivity, alongside a TaqMan® internal control to ensure DNA quality. Standards were generated from 10^6 to 2 copies per µL and used to convert cycle threshold (Cq) values to spores per 10 bees or swab sample. Across three cohorts of quarantine hives in New Zealand (5 regions, 2018-2020), nurse bee and entrance swabs were compared. A 10-bee sample and entrance swabs were evaluated. DNA was extracted using a 3 mL lysis buffer with zirconia beads on a Mini Beadbeater 16, followed by 65°C incubation and centrifugation. Spore counts from the first cohort (45 hives, nurse bees, whole baseboard, entrance swabs) and the second (23 hives, 4 with clinical signs) were compared. The third cohort tested pooled swabs in groups of 8 and 12. Key findings: the AFBduo assay reliably detected down to 4 copies per 10 µL with ftsZ at 94% and 16S at 96% efficiency. The 16S marker amplified 3-5 cycles earlier but its copy number varied among isolates, so only the single-copy ftsZ was used for quantification. Bee DNA extracted at OD260/280 between 1.8 and 1.9 showed no inhibitors. Entry-swab P. larvae levels were similar to whole-baseboard swabs, showing hive dismantling was unnecessary to detect higher clinical levels. Hive 11 lacked visual signs but had high spores, then showed clinical signs two weeks later, demonstrating pre-clinical detection. A spore threshold of 565,000 or more yielded a 95% probability of clinical signs (p=0.00). High spores in bees but low on new (<2 weeks) hiveware in hives 11 and 12 indicated pre-infection state. The method could detect Nosema ceranae, but further work is needed to refine thresholds and assess accumulation. It is amenable to composite testing and provides clinically significant information.

summary.title: SPOT-Contact-Single: Improving Single-Sequence-Based Prediction of Protein Contact Map using a Transformer Language Model
summary.authors: Jaspreet Singh; Thomas Litfin; Jaswinder Singh; Kuldip Paliwal; Yaoqi Zhou
summary.executive_summary:
SPOT-Contact-Single is a novel protein contact-map predictor that leverages the pretrained attention maps from the ESM-1b Transformer-34 language model as an input feature to improve prediction for proteins without known evolutionary homologs. Traditional contact-map predictors, such as CCMpred, EVFold, and TrRosetta, rely on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and homology-based profile information, which are unavailable for many isolated proteins. SSCpred was a baseline single-sequence predictor using one-hot encoding and SPIDER3-Single, but it was less effective for homology-rich proteins. To address this, the authors used ESM-1b attention maps, which were extracted from all twenty attention heads of the last layer and every layer, then symmetrized and corrected. The model is an ensemble of six ResNet12 architectures—the Duta et al. (2020) improved version—trained on different feature combinations (one-hot, SPOT-1D-Single, ESM-1b attention). 

Training used the ProteinNet benchmark: 34691 proteins for training, 88 for validation, after removing redundant hits at an e-value <0.1 with HHblits and sequences with a length more than 500 residues. Testing was on SPOT-2018 (669 proteins, e-value <0.1 separation) and the Neff1-2018 set (46 proteins with Neff=1). CASP14-FM provided 15 free-modelling targets. On the validation set, the ensemble improved F1 by 4% over the second-best model. One-hot alone yielded an F1-score of 0.15 and an MCC of 0.14; adding SPOT-1D-Single improved the F1-score by 22.90%. The ESM-1b last layer alone achieved 0.51 F1, 0.50 MCC, 0.56 precision, and 0.95 AUC—a 242% and 178% improvement over the one-hot baseline. Concatenating all features added a further 2.92%. On CASP14-FM, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved 0.2061 F1 and 0.1925 MCC. On Neff=1 (5YKZ_A), it achieved 0.388 F1, outperforming TrRosetta (0.235), ESM-1b (0.252), and SPOT-Contact (0.215). Compared to TrRosetta, it was 22 times faster on CPU (116 seconds vs 1926 seconds) and 42 times slower on GPU. The method is limited to proteins with fewer than 1024 amino acids but is suitable for large-scale screening. The work is based on ProteinNet and does not provide a bibliography.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
SPOT-Contact-Single is a novel protein contact-map predictor that leverages the pretrained attention maps from the ESM-1b Transformer-34 language model as an input feature to improve prediction for proteins without known evolutionary homologs. Traditional contact-map predictors, such as CCMpred, EVFold, and TrRosetta, rely on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and homology-based profile information, which are unavailable for many isolated proteins. SSCpred was a baseline single-sequence predictor using one-hot encoding and SPIDER3-Single, but it was less effective for homology-rich proteins. To address this, the authors used ESM-1b attention maps, which were extracted from all twenty attention heads of the last layer and every layer, then symmetrized and corrected. The model is an ensemble of six ResNet12 architectures—the Duta et al. (2020) improved version—trained on different feature combinations (one-hot, SPOT-1D-Single, ESM-1b attention). 

Training used the ProteinNet benchmark: 34691 proteins for training, 88 for validation, after removing redundant hits at an e-value <0.1 with HHblits and sequences with a length more than 500 residues. Testing was on SPOT-2018 (669 proteins, e-value <0.1 separation) and the Neff1-2018 set (46 proteins with Neff=1). CASP14-FM provided 15 free-modelling targets. On the validation set, the ensemble improved F1 by 4% over the second-best model. One-hot alone yielded an F1-score of 0.15 and an MCC of 0.14; adding SPOT-1D-Single improved the F1-score by 22.90%. The ESM-1b last layer alone achieved 0.51 F1, 0.50 MCC, 0.56 precision, and 0.95 AUC—a 242% and 178% improvement over the one-hot baseline. Concatenating all features added a further 2.92%. On CASP14-FM, SPOT-Contact-Single achieved 0.2061 F1 and 0.1925 MCC. On Neff=1 (5YKZ_A), it achieved 0.388 F1, outperforming TrRosetta (0.235), ESM-1b (0.252), and SPOT-Contact (0.215). Compared to TrRosetta, it was 22 times faster on CPU (116 seconds vs 1926 seconds) and 42 times slower on GPU. The method is limited to proteins with fewer than 1024 amino acids but is suitable for large-scale screening. The work is based on ProteinNet and does not provide a bibliography.

Research Context
Homology-based profile information is a common trait of MSA-based methods. Many proteins have very few or no homologs to generate profile information. Generating evolutionary profiles is computationally intensive for many proteins. SSCpred uses one-hot encoding and SPIDER3-Single features. Features inspired by Natural Language Processing language models are now used.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can ESM-1b attention maps improve single-sequence-based contact prediction? Unsupervised features combined with one-hot and SPOT-1D-Single outperform SSCpred. An ensemble of models adds to this improvement.

Methodological Details
The training set used the ProteinNet benchmark. The dataset used high-resolution crystal structures. The 95% identity cut-off used the MMseqs2 tool. Redundant hits were removed at an e-value cut-off of less than 0.1. The training set originally had 39120 proteins. Proteins with a length more than 500 were removed. Final training and validation sets were 34691 and 88 proteins. SPOT-2018 was used as a stringent test set. SPOT-2018 and Neff1-2018 were used for testing. Neff=1 was used to identify isolated proteins. Neff was calculated against a February 2020 dataset. CASP14-FM provided 15 free-modelling targets.

Procedures And Architectures
The model used a 12-block ResNet architecture. This was the maximum depth that could be trained on the available GPU. The ResNet version by Duta et al. (2020) was adopted. It was shown to be better than vanilla and pre-act ResNet. Convolutional layers had a channel size of 64. The kernel size of the convolution was 3. Six models with different input features were trained. Direct models used Binary Cross-Entropy loss. Distogram models used Cross-Entropy loss. The learning rate was 0.001 for the Adam optimizer. The batch size of 1 was used during training. All models used early stopping of 3.

Key Results
The one-hot baseline F1-score was 0.15. The one-hot baseline MCC was 0.14. Adding SPOT-1D-Single improved the F1-score by 22.90%. ESM-1b last layer achieved a 242% and 178% improvement. Concatenating all features added 2.92% in F1-score. The ensemble had 4% improvement over the second-best individual model. SPOT-Contact-Single was 45% higher at 0.32. SPOT-Contact-Single had a 15% improvement over SSCpred. The method was 22 times faster than TrRosetta on CPU. TrRosetta was 42 times slower than SPOT-Contact-Single on GPU.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The method predicts contact-maps without using evolutionary information. Sequence profile generation takes significantly longer than the proposed method. Advanced architectural models such as Transformer may yield further improvements. The method is suitable for genomic scale prediction.

Contradictions And Limitations
It cannot predict contact-maps for proteins with more than 1024 amino acids. The single-sequence method is not yet as competitive as evolution-based methods. Single-sequence methods provide less information for the neural network. A random seed was not reported in the training setup.

Claims
SPOT-Contact-Single significantly improves on the single-sequence-based SSCpred benchmark. The method achieved a 15% improvement over SSCpred. The ensemble F1-score was 0.2061 on CASP14-FM. The long-range precision saw the most improvement over SSCpred. SSCpred performs adequately for proteins with few homologs. SSCpred is also a single-sequence-based contact-map predictor. SPOT-Contact-Single can be used as a screening tool. The method outperforms profile-based predictors without homologs.
SPOT-Contact-Single outperforms TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact without homologs. The F1-score was 45% higher at 0.32 on Neff1-2018. TrRosetta achieved only 0.235 and ESM-1b achieved 0.252. SPOT-Contact achieved only 0.215 on 5YKZ_A. SPOT-1D-Single is not competitive with evolution-based methods. Evolution-based methods provide co-mutation information. The method provides an alternative for isolated proteins. The improvement is largest on the low Neff set.
The method is significantly faster than profile-based methods. It was 22 times faster than TrRosetta on CPU. TrRosetta was 42 times slower on GPU. The prediction finished in 116 seconds on CPU. TrRosetta required 1926 seconds on GPU. TrRosetta was the baseline profile-based method. The method is suitable for large-scale prediction. Genomic-scale prediction is enabled by faster inference.

Data And Code Availability
TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact programs are available online. The ESM-1b program is available online from GitHub. The SSCpred web-server is available online from the university.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Six models were trained with different input features. Feature combinations are described in Table 1. The direct contact-map prediction performed slightly better. The validation ensemble had 4% improvement over second-best.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 depicts convolutional layers with channel size 64. Table 1 lists the six feature combinations. Table 2 shows the one-hot F1-score of 0.15. Table 3 compares direct and distance prediction strategies. Table 4 shows the ensemble validation results. Table 5 shows F1-score of 45% higher at 0.32. Table 6 reports a 15% improvement over SSCpred. Figure 2 shows precision for top predictions. Figure 3 shows F1-score vs Neff values. Figure 4 displays native and predicted contact-maps.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is using ESM-1b attention as a single-sequence feature. 2. The strongest evidence is the 15% F1 improvement over SSCpred on CASP14-FM. 3. The future path is using more advanced models such as Transformer or Performer.

summary.executive_summary: This paper describes EcoEvoApps, an open-source R package and interactive website designed to integrate theoretical models with empirical insights in ecology and evolutionary biology (EEB). While the synergy between empiricism and theory is recognized (Jeltsch 2013, Shou 2015, Laubmeier 2020, Servedio 2020), such integration remains limited. One major barrier is that the mathematical language of models may seem foreign to those from empirical backgrounds (Fawcett 2012), leading to worse student evaluations of quantitative courses (Uttl 2013). Most advances in quantitative biology focus on statistical models or programming, rather than the pedagogy of theoretical models (Lehman 2020, Grainger 2022). EcoEvoApps offers 11 interactive apps built with R and deployed on RStudio's shinyapps.io servers, providing a freely available platform for simulating fundamental EEB models. The apps were chosen by surveying undergraduate ecology syllabi and textbooks (Gotelli 2008, Begon and Townsend 2020). Nine core apps are localized in English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. The software includes functions with the prefix run_, which take parameter values, initial population sizes, and time steps to return population size dataframes, plus plot_ functions that return ggplot2 objects. The package also provides model-specific vignettes like predator-prey-interactions and a vignette for custom deployment. Example apps include Lotka-Volterra, Island Biogeography, and a predator-prey model illustrating the paradox of enrichment (Rosenzweig 1971), which explores effects of carrying capacity K on stability (Fig. 2). To evaluate the apps, the authors surveyed 51 students in an upper-division UCLA Ecology course who used the apps for Island Biogeography and Lotka-Volterra competition. Students completed ~15-minute video lectures and a guided exploration worksheet. On a scale of 1-7, 40/51 students reported the apps were moderately to very helpful (Fig. 3A). Students reported better understanding of carrying capacity and coexistence (Fig. 3B). Similar surveys at MU showed substantial gains in student confidence, especially among those expressing higher interest in related topics (Fig. S2.1). The UCLA IRB #20-002179 and MU IRB #2031063 reviewed the studies as exempt. EcoEvoApps is entirely open-source and written in R, leveraging R as a common programming language (Gentleman 2004, Lai 2019). Future work will incorporate evolutionary biology and population genetics. By enabling accessible simulation-based learning, the project aims to democratize theoretical insights that otherwise require years of quantitative training.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper describes EcoEvoApps, an open-source R package and interactive website designed to integrate theoretical models with empirical insights in ecology and evolutionary biology (EEB). While the synergy between empiricism and theory is recognized (Jeltsch 2013, Shou 2015, Laubmeier 2020, Servedio 2020), such integration remains limited. One major barrier is that the mathematical language of models may seem foreign to those from empirical backgrounds (Fawcett 2012), leading to worse student evaluations of quantitative courses (Uttl 2013). Most advances in quantitative biology focus on statistical models or programming, rather than the pedagogy of theoretical models (Lehman 2020, Grainger 2022). EcoEvoApps offers 11 interactive apps built with R and deployed on RStudio's shinyapps.io servers, providing a freely available platform for simulating fundamental EEB models. The apps were chosen by surveying undergraduate ecology syllabi and textbooks (Gotelli 2008, Begon and Townsend 2020). Nine core apps are localized in English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. The software includes functions with the prefix run_, which take parameter values, initial population sizes, and time steps to return population size dataframes, plus plot_ functions that return ggplot2 objects. The package also provides model-specific vignettes like predator-prey-interactions and a vignette for custom deployment. Example apps include Lotka-Volterra, Island Biogeography, and a predator-prey model illustrating the paradox of enrichment (Rosenzweig 1971), which explores effects of carrying capacity K on stability (Fig. 2). To evaluate the apps, the authors surveyed 51 students in an upper-division UCLA Ecology course who used the apps for Island Biogeography and Lotka-Volterra competition. Students completed ~15-minute video lectures and a guided exploration worksheet. On a scale of 1-7, 40/51 students reported the apps were moderately to very helpful (Fig. 3A). Students reported better understanding of carrying capacity and coexistence (Fig. 3B). Similar surveys at MU showed substantial gains in student confidence, especially among those expressing higher interest in related topics (Fig. S2.1). The UCLA IRB #20-002179 and MU IRB #2031063 reviewed the studies as exempt. EcoEvoApps is entirely open-source and written in R, leveraging R as a common programming language (Gentleman 2004, Lai 2019). Future work will incorporate evolutionary biology and population genetics. By enabling accessible simulation-based learning, the project aims to democratize theoretical insights that otherwise require years of quantitative training.

Research Context
Integrating theory with insights from observations and experiments is a fundamental driver of progress across the life sciences Mathematical models enable generalization across systems and help clarifiy the role and consequences of biological factors Clarifying the role and consequences of different biological factors Promoting a deeper conceptual understanding and highlighting important areas for further study Synergy between empiricism and theory can yield fruitful insights for EEB Applications in biological forecasts and at the interface of science and society Barriers to integration: mathematical language may seem foreign and equations cited less often Equation-heavy papers tend to be cited less often by empiricists Instructors of quantitative courses tend to receive worse student evaluations than those who de-emphasize them Calls for quantitative training focus on statistics or programming, not theoretical model pedagogy Interactive tools help users independently explore model structure and outcomes

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can an interactive platform of EEB models facilitate communication, collaboration, and learning of theoretical insights? Hypothesis: interactive tools increase student interest and understanding of quantitative concepts Hypothesis: EcoEvoApps apps are useful tools for teaching mathematical models in classroom settings Predicted outcome: students report the apps are moderately to very helpful for learning the models

Methodological Details
The package includes 11 interactive apps Models chosen by surveying undergraduate ecology syllabi and textbooks References used for model selection: Gotelli 2008 and Begon and Townsend 2020 A core set of nine apps available in five languages Apps freely available online on RStudio's shinyapps.io servers Apps can be launched locally from users' personal computers from the R console Functions for deployment use the prefix shiny_ Classroom study surveyed 51 students who used the shiny apps Apps used for Island Biogeography and Lotka-Volterra competition Learning activity in an upper-division Ecology course at UCLA Short video lectures (~15 minutes) and a worksheet Guided exploration through a worksheet available in Supplement S3 Students rated on a scale of 1-7 UCLA IRB #20-002179 and MU IRB #2031063 reviewed the studies Institutional review boards determined the studies constitute exempt studies

Procedures And Architectures
The EcoEvoApps open-source R package and website facilitate deployment Website address https://ecoevoapps.gitlab.io Simulations run using functions with the prefix run_ run_predprey_model requires parameter values, initial population sizes, and time steps The run_ function returns a dataframe of population sizes Plotting functions prefixed plot_ return ggplot2 objects predator-prey dynamics app includes a tab with the Lotka-Volterra model Apps include logistic growth in the prey and type II functional response Outputs in Fig. 1 generated via specific ecoevoapps code The app is available at https://ecoevoapps.shinyapps.io/predator_prey_dynamics/ Can be deployed from the R command line with shiny_predprey() Predator-prey app tabs: Lotka-Volterra, logistic growth, and type II response

Key Results
An overwhelming majority of 40/51 students reported the apps were helpful Students reported response of 6 or 7, Fig. 3A Students reported better understanding of carrying capacity and coexistence Similar results reported for students at the University of Missouri Using interactive apps led to substantial gains in student confidence Gains were largest among students expressing higher interest in related topics Confidence gains reported in Fig. S2.1 The predator-prey dynamics app illustrates the paradox of enrichment Paradox of enrichment visualized by altering the prey carrying capacity K Low K values of 200 result in dampened oscillations High K values of 500 result in unstable oscillations that limit persistence Unstable oscillations arise when isocline intersects to the left of the hump

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Simulation-based learning may not provide all the same insights as analytical solutions EcoEvoApps is entirely open-source and written in R R is among the most commonly used programming languages in EEB The package builds tools for easier access to theoretical insights A key distinguishing feature is that ecoevoapps is open-source and in R

Contradictions And Limitations
Simulation-based learning may not provide all the same insights as analytical solutions This describes the first release of EcoEvoApps, with 11 interactive apps integration remains relatively limited Building on preliminary evidence that apps are useful for teaching

Claims
EcoEvoApps facilitates learning insights from classic models by exploring parameter-driven dynamics. The app visualizes the paradox of enrichment The predator-prey model is explored via the MacArthur-Rosenzweig model tab Students explore effects of prey carrying capacity K on stability Low values of prey carrying capacity K = 200 result in dampened oscillations High values of prey carrying capacity K = 500 result in unstable oscillations Unstable oscillations arise to the left of the hump in the prey isocline Simulation-based learning may not provide all the same insights as analytical solutions Tools give everyone easier access to theoretical insights Accessible models take years of quantitative training to grasp
EcoEvoApps improves student understanding and confidence in mathematical models. 40/51 students reported the apps were moderately to very helpful Students reported response of 6 or 7 on a helpfulness scale Students reported better understanding of carrying capacity and coexistence Interactive apps led to substantial gains in student confidence Confidence gains largest among students expressing higher interest in related topics Confidence gains reported in Fig. S2.1 MU survey reported similar results with similar results (Supplement S2) The apps were moderately to very helpful for learning models as whole Apps serve as a bridge to help users become familiar with coding

Data And Code Availability
The EcoEvoApps R package ecoevoapps is entirely open-source and in R The ecoevoapps package can be installed from GitLab Web address ecoevoapps.gitlab.io The apps are freely available online

Ethical Considerations
The UCLA IRB #20-002179 and MU IRB #2031063 reviewed the studies Review boards determined the studies constitute "exempt" studies UCLA IRB #20-002179 MU IRB Project #2031063, Review #276104

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the predator-prey dynamics app tabs Figure 2 shows screenshots of the predator-prey dynamics app Figure 3A shows the percentage of helpful students Figure 3B shows understanding of carrying capacity and coexistence Figure S2.1 shows confidence gains at MU

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is an open-source R package with 11 interactive EEB apps 2. The strongest evidence is that 40/51 students found the apps moderately to very helpful 3. The future path will incorporate evolutionary biology and population genetics models

summary.title: CCN2 activates ERK-signaling via integrin av and enhances the interaction of ERK and DUSP6 in lymphatic endothelial cells
summary.authors: Shiho Hashiguchi (Fukuoka University); Tomoko Tanaka (Fukuoka University); Ryosuke Mano (Fukuoka University); Seiji Kondo (Fukuoka University); Shohta Kodama (Fukuoka University)
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental molecular biology; lymphangiogenesis; integrin signaling
summary.executive_summary: CCN2, also known as connective tissue growth factor (CTGF), is a modular and matricellular protein well-known as an angiogenic factor. However, its role in lymphangiogenesis and intracellular signaling in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) has remained unclear. In this study, primary cultured LECs were investigated to elucidate CCN2 signaling and its effects on lymphangiogenesis. CCN2 was found to dose-dependently upregulate lymphatic vessel endothelial markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) up to 100 ng/mL, with expression levels dramatically decreasing at 200 ng/mL. CCN2 further increased the expression levels of lymphangiogenic factors Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 (Vegfr3) but did not affect Kdr (Vegfr2) expression. In a phospho-receptor tyrosine kinase array, VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylation were unchanged by CCN2, while EGFR and EphB4 phosphorylation were increased, and ErbB4 and PDGFRa phosphorylation were decreased (p<0.001). Although VEGFRs are upstream of ERK, CCN2-mediated ERK phosphorylation was significantly increased (p<0.001) while total ERK protein was unchanged. Itgav, Itga9, and Itgb1 were predominantly expressed in LECs and were increased by CCN2 stimulation. Integrin av knockdown partially decreased CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040), suggesting CCN2 increases phospho-ERK via integrin av. However, integrin a9 knockdown slightly increased phospho-ERK, and integrin b1 suppression increased phospho-ERK without CCN2 stimulation. Treatment with 10, 50, and 100 ng/mL of CCN2 for 24 h slightly suppressed LEC growth, but no changes were observed at 48 or 72 h, indicating a weak growth inhibitory effect. Phospho-ERK was increased transiently and non-persistently, followed by a decrease at 8 h. DUSP6 was predominant in LECs, and immunoprecipitation showed CCN2 enhanced ERK and DUSP6 binding. DUSP6 siRNA increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001 for 15 m, p=0.04 for 24 h, p=0.004 for 48 h), indicating DUSP6 functions as a negative modulator of ERKsignaling. In an in vivo Matrigel plug assay, exogenous CCN2 increased Podoplanin-positive vessels, CD31 cavities, and b3-Tubulin nerves. Phosphorylated ERK and DUSP6 were increased in Podoplanin-positive cells in the CCN2 gel compared to control (p<0.05). The authors conclude that CCN2 activates ERK signaling via integrin av and promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo, and that DUSP6 suppresses excessive CCN2-induced ERK phosphorylation. Integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6-mediated lymphangiogenesis may be therapeutic targets of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).

judge_context:
Executive Summary
CCN2, also known as connective tissue growth factor (CTGF), is a modular and matricellular protein well-known as an angiogenic factor. However, its role in lymphangiogenesis and intracellular signaling in lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) has remained unclear. In this study, primary cultured LECs were investigated to elucidate CCN2 signaling and its effects on lymphangiogenesis. CCN2 was found to dose-dependently upregulate lymphatic vessel endothelial markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) up to 100 ng/mL, with expression levels dramatically decreasing at 200 ng/mL. CCN2 further increased the expression levels of lymphangiogenic factors Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 (Vegfr3) but did not affect Kdr (Vegfr2) expression. In a phospho-receptor tyrosine kinase array, VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylation were unchanged by CCN2, while EGFR and EphB4 phosphorylation were increased, and ErbB4 and PDGFRa phosphorylation were decreased (p<0.001). Although VEGFRs are upstream of ERK, CCN2-mediated ERK phosphorylation was significantly increased (p<0.001) while total ERK protein was unchanged. Itgav, Itga9, and Itgb1 were predominantly expressed in LECs and were increased by CCN2 stimulation. Integrin av knockdown partially decreased CCN2-induced phospho-ERK (p=0.0040), suggesting CCN2 increases phospho-ERK via integrin av. However, integrin a9 knockdown slightly increased phospho-ERK, and integrin b1 suppression increased phospho-ERK without CCN2 stimulation. Treatment with 10, 50, and 100 ng/mL of CCN2 for 24 h slightly suppressed LEC growth, but no changes were observed at 48 or 72 h, indicating a weak growth inhibitory effect. Phospho-ERK was increased transiently and non-persistently, followed by a decrease at 8 h. DUSP6 was predominant in LECs, and immunoprecipitation showed CCN2 enhanced ERK and DUSP6 binding. DUSP6 siRNA increased phospho-ERK (p<0.001 for 15 m, p=0.04 for 24 h, p=0.004 for 48 h), indicating DUSP6 functions as a negative modulator of ERKsignaling. In an in vivo Matrigel plug assay, exogenous CCN2 increased Podoplanin-positive vessels, CD31 cavities, and b3-Tubulin nerves. Phosphorylated ERK and DUSP6 were increased in Podoplanin-positive cells in the CCN2 gel compared to control (p<0.05). The authors conclude that CCN2 activates ERK signaling via integrin av and promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo, and that DUSP6 suppresses excessive CCN2-induced ERK phosphorylation. Integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6-mediated lymphangiogenesis may be therapeutic targets of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).

Research Context
CCN2 is a modular and matricellular protein well-known as an angiogenic factor. Previous studies showed CTGF enhanced lymphangiogenesis in renal and liver fibrosis models. CCN2 signaling in LECs in lymphangiogenic signaling has not been elucidated. Integrins are cell surface adhesion receptors for extracellular matrix proteins. Conformation change of the extracellular domain triggers activation of intracellular signaling pathways. VEGF-C-VEGFR-3 signaling is also crucial for the development of lymphatic vessels. Abnormal proliferation of lymphatic endothelial cells causes lymphangiomas and Kaposi sarcoma.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study investigated downstream signaling of CCN2 in primary cultured LECs. The study examined the gene expression levels of LEC markers and lymphangiogenic factors. The study investigated whether CCN2-mediated effects on ERK may involve integrin interaction. The study investigated whether CCN2 enhances the binding between ERK and DUSP6. The study hypothesized that CCN2 increases phospho-ERK via integrin av in LECs. The study predicted DUSP6 functions as a negative modulator of ERKsignaling in LECs.

Methodological Details
Primary cultured LECs were derived from the C57BL/6 mouse. LECs were cultured on 0.1% gelatin-coated culture dishes at 37C. LECs were cultured using the EGM2-Endothelial cell growth medium-2 bullet kit. Cells up to 6 passages were used for in vitro experiments. LECs were plated at 2 × 10 4 cells per well. LECs were stimulated with CCN2 doses 0, 12.5, 25, 50, 100 or 200 ng/mL for 3 h. Quantitative RT-PCR primers were listed in Table S1. siRNAs were designed using siDirect ver.2. 1.5 × 10 5 LECs were transfected with 25 pmol of target siRNA. The phospho-RTK array treated cells with 100 ng/mL of recombinant rat CTGF. 450 µL of growth factor reduced Matrigel was injected. The Matrigel injection had n=4 CCN2 group and n=3 control. Mice were used at 9 weeks of age. Most experiments were performed more than three times.

Procedures And Architectures
LECs were stimulated with CCN2 doses up to 200 ng/mL for 3 h. Cell proliferation was assessed by crystal violet staining method. Cell proliferation absorbance at 590 nm was measured. Sense and complementary strand RNAs having a two-mer overhang were synthesized. 1.5 × 10 5 LECs were transfected using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX. Protein samples weighing 5-20 µg were separated by SDS-PAGE. Primary antibodies were incubated at 4˚C overnight. 200 µg of total protein was incubated for the phospho-RTK array. 200 µg of total protein was incubated for immunoprecipitation. Protein A magnetic beads were used for protein purification. The Matrigel mixture was subcutaneously injected on the back. Matrigel plugs were embedded in paraffin and sectioned 4 µm thick. Morphology was observed using a fluorescence microscope and confocal microscope. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism software version 8.

Key Results
Lyve1, Podoplanin, and Prox1 were increased by CCN2 in a dose-dependent manner up to 100 ng/mL. At 200 ng/mL, their expression levels dramatically decreased compared with levels at 100 ng/mL. CCN2 increased Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 but did not affect Kdr expression. VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylations were unchanged by CCN2. RTKs EGFR and EphB4 phosphorylations were increased by CCN2. RTKs ErbB4 and PDGFRa phosphorylations were decreased compared with controls. Phospho-p38, JNK, AKT, NFkB, and Smad were unchanged in response to CCN2. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased in response to CCN2. Total ERK protein levels were not affected by CCN2 treatment. Itgav, Itga9, and Itgb1 were predominantly expressed in LECs. Itgav, Itga9, and Itgb1 expression were increased by CCN2 stimulation. Integrin av knockdown partially decreased CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. Integrin a9 knockdown caused a slight increase of CCN2induced phospho-ERK. Integrin b1 suppression increased phospho-ERK without CCN2 stimulation. CCN2 for 24 h suppressed growth at 50 and 100 ng/mL (p = 0.003 and 0.02). Dusp6 was predominant but Dusp16 was undetected in LECs. ERK and DUSP6 interaction was enhanced by CCN2. DUSP6 siRNA increased phospho-ERK at 15 min (p<0.001). Blood vessels were detected in the CCN2 group but not in the control group. Podoplanin-positive vessels were increased in CCN2-supplemented gels. CD31 cavities and b3-Tubulin peripheral nerves were increased in CCN2 plugs. Total ERK was similarly expressed in both the control gel and the CCN2 gel. Phospho-ERK was barely present in the control gel. DUSP6 was rarely detected in the control gel. Phospho-ERK and DUSP6 were significantly increased (p < 0.05) in the CCN2 gel.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
CCN2 activates ERK-signaling via integrin av in LECs. VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 were not activated by CCN2 in LECs. Integrins play key roles in endothelial cell migration and survival. DUSP6 functions as a negative modulator of ERKsignaling in LECs. CCN2-signaling is associated with disease progression and lymph node metastasis. Integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6-mediated lymphangiogenesis may be therapeutic targets of OSCC.

Contradictions And Limitations
No changes in proliferation were observed at 48 and 72 h. Phospho-ERK was increased transiently and non-persistently. VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 were not activated by CCN2 in LECs. Integrin b1 suppression increased phospho-ERK without CCN2 stimulation. Integrin a5 mRNA was not investigated because interaction was not reported. The relationship between FOXC1, FOXC2 and DUSP6 has not yet been analyzed. In vitro proliferation and in vivo Matrigel assays may not be comparable.

Claims
CCN2 activates ERK signaling via integrin av in LECs. Itgav, Itga9, and Itgb1 were predominantly expressed in LECs. Integrin av knockdown partially decreased CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased in response to CCN2. Integrin a9 knockdown caused a slight increase of CCN2induced phospho-ERK. Integrin b1 suppression increased phospho-ERK without CCN2 stimulation. Integrin av is critical for mediating ERK activation in LECs.
CCN2 enhances the binding between ERK and DUSP6. ERK and DUSP6 co-precipitated and interaction was enhanced by CCN2. DUSP6 siRNA increased phospho-ERK at 15 min. DUSP6 was predominant but DUSP16 was undetected. DUSP6 suppresses excessive CCN2-induced ERK phosphorylation.
CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo. Podoplanin-positive vessels were increased in CCN2-supplemented gels. CD31 cavities and b3-Tubulin nerves were increased in CCN2 plugs. Phosphorylated ERK and DUSP6 were significantly increased (p < 0.05) in the CCN2 gel. There was a discrepancy between in vitro proliferation and in vivo assays. CCN2 functions as a lymphangiogenic factor.

Ethical Considerations
Experiments were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Fukuoka University.

Key Figures Tables
Lymphatic marker expression was increased by CCN2 up to 100 ng/mL in Fig 1A. CCN2 increased Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 expression but did not affect Kdr in Fig 1B. VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylations were unchanged by CCN2 in Fig S1. p38, JNK, AKT, NFkB, and Smad were unchanged in response to CCN2 in Fig S2A-C. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased in response to CCN2 in Fig 2A, 2B. Total ERK protein levels were not affected by CCN2 treatment in Fig 2C. Itgav, Itga9, and Itgb1 were predominantly expressed in LECs in Fig 3A. Integrin av knockdown partially decreased phospho-ERK in Fig 3B. Integrin a9 knockdown caused a slight increase of CCN2induced phospho-ERK in Fig 3C. Integrin b1 suppression increased phospho-ERK without CCN2 stimulation in Fig 3D. Integrins b2 and b3 were unchanged by integrin b1 suppression in Fig S3. CCN2 treatment for 24 h suppressed LEC growth in Fig 4A. Phospho-ERK was transiently increased and followed by a decrease in Fig 4B. Dusp6 was predominant but Dusp16 was undetected in LECs in Fig 5A. ERK and DUSP6 co-precipitated and interaction was enhanced by CCN2 in Fig 5B. DUSP6 siRNA transfection was analyzed in Fig 5C. DUSP6 siRNA increased phospho-ERK at 15 min, 24 h, and 48 h in Fig 5D. Blood vessels were detected in the CCN2 group only in Fig 6A. Podoplanin-positive vessels and tubular structures were detected in Figs 6B, 6C. CD31-positive cavities and b3-Tubulin peripheral nerves were increased in Fig S4. Phosphorylated ERK was barely present in the control gel in Fig 7A, 7C. DUSP6 was rarely detected in the control gel in Fig 7B. qPCR primers were listed in Table S1. siRNA sequences were listed in Table S2. Primary antibodies were listed in Table S3.

Three Takeaways
1. CCN2 activates ERK signaling via integrin av. 2. CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo Matrigel assays. 3. Integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6-mediated lymphangiogenesis may be therapeutic targets of OSCC.

summary.title: Tumor PD-L1 selectively suppresses type I interferon in myeloid cells to suppress CTL recruitment to promote lung metastasis
summary.authors: John D Klement, Priscilla S Redd, Chunwan Lu, Alyssa D Merting, Dakota B Poschel, Dafeng Yang, Gang Zhou, David H Munn, Kebin Liu
summary.type_of_paper: Primary Research / In Vivo and In Vitro Study
summary.executive_summary: This study elucidates the mechanism by which tumor cell PD-L1 (tPD-L1) drives immune suppression and lung metastasis through an intermediate cell population. The authors challenge the prevailing paradigm that tPD-L1 primarily protects tumor cells from cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) lysis by demonstrating that, in vitro, tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage to tumor cells when alone with cognate CTLs. Instead, the authors show that tPD-L1 functions in vivo to promote lung metastasis independently of primary tumor growth. By utilizing mouse triple-negative breast cancer (4T1) and mismatch repair proficient colorectal cancer (CT26) cell lines, and a tumor-specific CTL line (2/20), they established that loss of tPD-L1 reduces lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner while having no effect on primary tumor size. They show that tPD-L1 engages myeloid-expressed PD-1 (mPD-1) to antagonize type I interferon (IFN-I) and STAT1 signaling, thereby repressing the expression of the CTL-recruiting chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10. The authors support this mechanism with single-cell RNA sequencing of human and mouse lungs, showing that human patient response to PD-1 blockade correlates with IFN-I response in myeloid cells. Collectively, the data supports a tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis that controls CTL tumor infiltration in lung metastasis.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study elucidates the mechanism by which tumor cell PD-L1 (tPD-L1) drives immune suppression and lung metastasis through an intermediate cell population. The authors challenge the prevailing paradigm that tPD-L1 primarily protects tumor cells from cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) lysis by demonstrating that, in vitro, tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage to tumor cells when alone with cognate CTLs. Instead, the authors show that tPD-L1 functions in vivo to promote lung metastasis independently of primary tumor growth. By utilizing mouse triple-negative breast cancer (4T1) and mismatch repair proficient colorectal cancer (CT26) cell lines, and a tumor-specific CTL line (2/20), they established that loss of tPD-L1 reduces lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner while having no effect on primary tumor size. They show that tPD-L1 engages myeloid-expressed PD-1 (mPD-1) to antagonize type I interferon (IFN-I) and STAT1 signaling, thereby repressing the expression of the CTL-recruiting chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10. The authors support this mechanism with single-cell RNA sequencing of human and mouse lungs, showing that human patient response to PD-1 blockade correlates with IFN-I response in myeloid cells. Collectively, the data supports a tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis that controls CTL tumor infiltration in lung metastasis.

Research Context
The prevailing paradigm is that tPD-L1 directly shields tumor cells from CTL lysis. However, this paradigm is challenged by emerging data suggesting CTL response may be site-specific. The durable benefit of PD-1/L1 blockade arises from coordinated suppression of metastases. It is unknown how tPD-L1 differentially drives metastasis versus primary tumor growth. There is emerging data on non-T cell PD-1 expression in myeloid and dendritic cells. How non-T cell PD-1 connects tPD-L1 to CTL suppression is incompletely understood.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Does tPD-L1 directly protect tumor cells from CTL-mediated killing? Hypothesis: tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage when an antigen-specific CTL meets a cognate tumor cell. Does tPD-L1 promote primary tumor growth? Does tPD-L1 promote lung metastasis? Does tPD-L1 function by promoting DTC colonization or metastasis growth? Hypothesis: tPD-L1 drives metastasis by suppressing CTL killing, not by seeding or extravasation.

Methodological Details
The study used 4T1 triple-negative breast cancer and CT26 mismatch repair proficient colorectal cancer lines. The choice of these lines mimics clinically advanced cancers with minimal ICB response. PD-L1 was genetically deleted using the lentiCRISPRv2 system to create PD-L1 knockout lines. The 2/20 tumor-specific CTL line recognizes the H2-L d-restricted AH1 gp70 epitope. BALB/c mice were used for the in vivo metastasis model. Lungs were harvested, inflated with India ink, and quantified one day post-injection. For single-cell RNA sequencing, leukocytes were positively selected using CD45 magnetic nanobeads. Cells were loaded at 2-3 x 10 3 targeted cells per Chromium Chip B. Bulk RNA sequencing of 4T1.WT and 4T1.PDL1-KO lungs was performed after 7 days. scRNA-seq of lungs was performed after 14 days. Cell viability was assured to be ≥ 80%. Reads mapped at 30-39K reads/cell with 1600 median genes per cell. High-quality cells were defined as 200 < feature count < 4000 with < 10% mitochondrial reads. The dataset included a human cohort of metastatic basal cell carcinoma patients. Survival data from BMS038 was accessed from the authors' processed files.

Procedures And Architectures
CRISPR lentivirus was produced using HEK293FT cells co-transinfected with three plasmids and Lipofectamine 2000. Tumor cells were selected with puromycin and sorted for marker-negative cells by FACS. Orthotopic tumors were established by injection at the right second mammary gland. Subcutaneous tumors were established by injection at the right flank. Metastasis models involved lateral tail vein injection. Antibody-mediated depletion of CD8+ T cells used 200 µg anti-CD8α i.v. every other day. Flow cytometry used FACSCalibur with CellQuestPro or LSRFortessa; analysis via FlowJo v10.6.0. Bulk RNA-seq utilized Novogene sequencing, STARv2.5 alignment, HTSeqv0.6.1 quantification, and DESeq2 normalization. scRNA-seq libraries used Chromium Single Cell 3' Reagent Kit v3 and Illumina NextSeq 500. Cells were clustered using the first 50 principal components and annotated via SingleR. Myeloid and T cell clusters were reclustered based on the top 20 principal components. TransferData transferred macrophage PHATE labels from a published human lung tumor-resident dataset. The tPD-L1 loss gene signature required ≥ 2-fold increase with padj < 0.05 by DESeq2. SHP-2 activation signature used the SHP-2 inhibitor SHP099. The patient dataset used the R survival and survminer packages. Pseudo-alignment was done with kallisto using default settings.

Key Results
In vitro, PD-L1 KO tumor cells showed no survival advantage against cognate CTLs. No difference in primary tumor growth was observed between WT and PD-L1 KO 4T1 or CT26. Loss of tPD-L1 increased CD3+ cell infiltration in the lung, but not in the primary tumor. No difference in initial tumor cell gp70 level in the lungs after 24 hours. PD-L1-deficient and competent 4T1 metastasized equally in RAGII-KO mice. Ablation of MHC class I antigen presentation or anti-CD8 antibody drove metastasis by suppressing CTL killing. Single-cell RNA sequencing showed ~7500 cells were captured on the Chromium Chip B. No change in bulk lung myeloid cell composition was detected by flow cytometry. Enhanced antigen presentation machinery was detected in macrophages. Pdcd1lg2 (PD-L2) was identified as an IFN-stimulated myeloid cell marker. Myeloid cell surface PD-1 was enhanced following tPD-L1 loss. RAW264.7 PD-1 loss increased sensitivity to poly(I:C) by BST2 expression. RAW PD-1 engagement suppressed autocrine and paracrine type I interferon release. Myeloid cell depletion by clodronate liposomes diminished tPD-L1 function in promoting lung tumor growth. Myeloid PHATE analysis showed differentiation restriction released after PD-1 blockade. Patient response to PD-1 blockade correlated with IFN-I response in myeloid cells.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
tPD-L1 functions indirectly by engaging myeloid PD-1 rather than CTL PD-1. The tPD-L1/mPD-1 axis creates an immunosuppressive, immunologically cold niche. The tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis controls CTL tumor infiltration. The PD-1/L1 axis functions as a negative feedback circuit for type I interferon. Interferon alpha's low response rate may be due to compensatory PD-1/L1 upregulation. Low response rates might explain the low efficacy of interferon alpha therapies. IFN alpha induced long-term, metastasis-free remission in a significant fraction of patients.

Contradictions And Limitations
A limitation is the exclusive analysis of lung metastases. Lung metastases may have a uniquely inflamed microenvironment in barrier tissue. The choice of lines mimicked clinically advanced disease with minimal ICB response. Contradictory findings exist for PD-L1 contribution to checkpoint blockade efficacy. tPD-L1 may be sufficient but not necessary for PD-1 blockade response in primary tumors. Recent publications highlighted the importance of DC-expressed PD-L1 controlling T cell function.

Claims
Tumor PD-L1 does not directly protect tumor cells from CTL-mediated cytotoxicity in the absence of other microenvironmental factors. tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage to tumor cells alone with CTLs. 2/20 CTLs do not need to differentiate from a naïve state. 2/20 cells exert antigen-specific cytotoxicity within minutes. Loss of PD-L1 renders cell lines unable to engage CTL-expressed PD-1. The cell lines show no expression of PD-L2. PD-L1 blockade was thought to function by blocking PD-1/L1 engagement. The direct-protection paradigm is a simplification of a more complex indirect mechanism. The protective role must depend on an intermediate factor only present in the metastasis.
Tumor PD-L1 promotes lung metastasis by suppressing CTL-mediated clearance through myeloid cell recruitment rather than primary tumor growth or seeding. Loss of tPD-L1 significantly decreases lung metastasis. No difference was observed in primary tumor growth. PD-L1 does not enhance DTC colonization in the lung. 4T1 metastasized equally in RAGII-KO mice. tPD-L1 drove metastasis by suppressing killing by CTLs. The durable survival benefit arises from coordinated suppression of metastases. Robust PD-L1 expression has been shown to promote both micro-and macro-metastatic growth. PD-L1 function is uncoupled at the metastatic site. The mechanism operates by enforc[ing] an immunologically cold microenvironment.
Myeloid cell PD-1 (mPD-1) bridges tumor PD-L1 to CTL recruitment by antagonizing type I interferon signaling. Myeloid cell surface PD-1 was enhanced following tPD-L1 loss. tPD-L1 engagement with mPD-1 creates an immunosuppressive niche. RAW surface PD-1 was upregulated in a cell-contact and IFNAR-dependent manner. RAW PD-1 loss increased sensitivity to poly(I:C). Disruption of RAW PD-1 or 4T1 PD-L1 expression enhanced IFNβ production. Myeloid cell depletion diminished tPD-L1 function in promoting tumor growth. The tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis controls CTL tumor infiltration. No change in bulk lung myeloid cell composition was observed. The PD-1/L1 axis functions as a negative feedback circuit for type I interferon signaling. IFN alpha therapies may fail due to compensatory PD-1/L1 upregulation. IFN alpha could be combined with TLR and STING agonists.
Human patients with metastatic basal cell carcinoma show an IFN-I-dependent response to PD-1 blockade, consistent with the mouse mPD-1 mechanism. Patient response to PD-1 blockade correlates with IFN-I response in myeloid cells. Myeloid cell PHATE analysis showed differentiation restriction released after PD-1 blockade. Enhanced interferon signaling, antigen presentation, and CTL-recruiting chemokine expression followed blockade. Mouse myeloid cell cluster identities were transferred to human lung myeloid cell scRNAseq. Human lung tumor-resident macrophages were used to develop cluster-identifying signatures. There is transcriptional heterogeneity between mouse and human myeloid cells. Human clinical response can be linked back to the mouse-derived mechanistic pathway. The mechanism supports the efficacy of ICB in the neoadjuvant and adjuvant setting.

Data And Code Availability
The patient dataset was accessed from authors' processed files on GitHub. The pseudo-aligned counts were generated following author's scripts. The PRJEB23709 dataset was accessed from EMBL and pseudo-aligned with kallisto.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study used multiple mouse cell lines and multiple metastasis models. The effect of myeloid depletion was verified by clodronate liposome depletion. The anti-CD8 antibody depletion and MHC ablation corroborated the CTL-suppression mechanism. Single-cell data were validated by flow cytometry and bulk RNA-seq. The human dataset was validated by PHATE and Seurat pipeline.

Ethical Considerations
The cell lines were tested bi-monthly for mycoplasma and were mycoplasma-free.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the in vitro CTL:tumor interaction and no survival advantage. Figure 2A and 2E show no difference in primary tumor growth. Figure 2F and 3D show that PD-L1 drove metastasis by suppressing CTL killing. Figure 3A shows increased CD3+ infiltration after tPD-L1 loss. Figure 3B shows no difference in initial tumor cell gp70 level. Figure 3C shows equal metastasis in RAGII-KO mice. Figure 4A shows single-cell RNA sequencing of 4T1 WT and PDL1-KO lungs. Figure 5G-I and S5D-F show PD-L2 as a marker for IFN-stimulated myeloid cells. Figure 6A-B shows enhanced myeloid cell surface PD-1 following tPD-L1 loss. Figure 6D-F show RAW cells with decreased pSTAT1 levels following engagement. Figure 6H-I show RAW PD-1 loss leading to increased poly(I:C) sensitivity. Figure 7A-C show myeloid differentiation restriction released after PD-1 blockade.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: tPD-L1 drives lung metastasis via an intermediate myeloid PD-1/IFN-I/Cxcl9/10 axis, rather than direct CTL protection. 2. The strongest evidence: Loss of tPD-L1 reduces lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner without altering primary tumor size. 3. The future path: PD-1/L1 functions as a negative feedback circuit that may explain interferon therapy failures.

summary.executive_summary: Extracellular glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), such as heparan sulfate (HS), are essential regulatory components of the extracellular matrix that bind growth factors and establish signaling gradients but are difficult to isolate and structurally characterize. This study describes the development of a hydrogel-supported stem cell microarray platform integrating glycosaminoglycan-protein conjugates to analyze how well-defined GAG structures influence growth factor signaling in murine embryonic stem cells (ESCs). By conjugating GAG polysaccharides to adhesion proteins and embedding them within a polyacrylamide hydrogel network, the authors created stable, ECM-mimetic microenvironments capable of binding and activating fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2). The array allows for high-throughput, multiplexed assessment of both growth factor binding and signaling activity in response to specific GAG structures. To establish a baseline for signaling and isolate glycan-specific effects, the study utilized mutant Ext1 -/- ESCs, which lack cell surface HS and cannot engage HS-dependent growth factors like FGF2. The hydrogels were prepared by depositing a thin poly(acrylamide) layer on glass and loading gelatin in its dehydrated form, with heparin (12 kDa) added at concentrations from 50 to 750 µg/mL. To retain heparin within the hydrogel, the authors employed NHS-activated crosslinking to gelatin at low levels (approximately 15% per chain), which was validated to enhance binding capacity 5-to 10-fold over physisorption. Characterization using FGF2, the heparin-binding protein HABP, and a CS-specific antibody (CS56) confirmed that NHS-crosslinking preserved the protein-binding specificity of the conjugated GAGs, including heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate (CS), and hyaluronic acid (HA), and that FGF2 binds most strongly to fully sulfated heparin. Cell seeding was optimized at 40,000 cells/cm², producing consistent monolayers that retained Oct4 expression without differentiating. Signaling was assayed by stimulating the array with 0.5 ng/mL FGF2 and quantifying phosphorylated-Erk1/2 (pErk1/2) relative to total Erk1/2 using a microarray scanner. FGF2 stimulation induced a heparin dose-responsive increase in Erk1/2 phosphorylation, with immobilized heparin showing slightly lower activity than soluble heparin (5 µg/mL) as a positive control, likely due to limited accessibility. The platform enables direct, rapid profiling of extracellular GAG activity on live embryonic stem cells and could accelerate the development of functional glycomaterials for cell-based regenerative therapies.

Executive Summary
Extracellular glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), such as heparan sulfate (HS), are essential regulatory components of the extracellular matrix that bind growth factors and establish signaling gradients but are difficult to isolate and structurally characterize. This study describes the development of a hydrogel-supported stem cell microarray platform integrating glycosaminoglycan-protein conjugates to analyze how well-defined GAG structures influence growth factor signaling in murine embryonic stem cells (ESCs).
