The hydrogels were prepared by depositing a thin poly(acrylamide) layer on glass and loading gelatin in its dehydrated form, with heparin (12 kDa) added at concentrations from 50 to 750 µg/mL. To retain heparin within the hydrogel, the authors employed NHS-activated crosslinking to gelatin at low levels (approximately 15% per chain), which was validated to enhance binding capacity 5-to 10-fold over physisorption. Characterization using FGF2, the heparin-binding protein HABP, and a CS-specific antibody (CS56) confirmed that NHS-crosslinking preserved the protein-binding specificity of the conjugated GAGs, including heparan sulfate, chondroitin sulfate (CS), and hyaluronic acid (HA), and that FGF2 binds most strongly to fully sulfated heparin. Cell seeding was optimized at 40,000 cells/cm², producing consistent monolayers that retained Oct4 expression without differentiating. Signaling was assayed by stimulating the array with 0.5 ng/mL FGF2 and quantifying phosphorylated-Erk1/2 (pErk1/2) relative to total Erk1/2 using a microarray scanner. FGF2 stimulation induced a heparin dose-responsive increase in Erk1/2 phosphorylation, with immobilized heparin showing slightly lower activity than soluble heparin (5 µg/mL) as a positive control, likely due to limited accessibility. The platform enables direct, rapid profiling of extracellular GAG activity on live embryonic stem cells and could accelerate the development of functional glycomaterials for cell-based regenerative therapies.

Research Context
Extracellular glycans, such as glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), provide an essential regulatory component during the tissue development and maintenance. However, their structural complexity and compositional heterogeneity make establishing structure-function relationships for this class of glycans difficult. Extracellular glycans, which also provide important biological functions in the ECM but are difficult to access in pure form synthetically or through isolation, have been comparatively less explored as components for biomaterials. Extracellular heparan sulfate (HS) polysaccharides, which belong to the family of glycosaminoglycans, are essential regulators of growth factor signaling and are being pursued as biologically active components of hydrogels for stem cell culture and tissue engineering. HS polysaccharides comprise chains of alternating N-acetylglucosamine and glucuronic acid residues that undergo sequential enzymatic modifications to introduce N-sulfation and to partially epimerize GlcA into iduronic acid (IdoA). Recent advances in chemical and chemoenzymatic HS oligosaccharide synthesis as well as genetic engineering of HS biosynthetic pathways have produced increasingly large numbers of chemically well-defined HS structures available for examination in the context of biomaterial design. Earlier work by Linhardt and co-workers evaluated the effects of HS structures on cellular responses, while Turnbull and co-workers observed MAPK activation in cells grown on arrays of oligosaccharides derived by partial heparin digestion.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The present study describes the integration of glycosaminoglycan-protein conjugates into a hydrogel-supported stem cell microarray platform to analyze the activity of extracellular glycans in growth factor signaling. Such platforms can enable rapid development and optimization of functional glycomaterials for stem cell-based regenerative therapies. The selectivity of FGF2 binding and activity in these cellular microenvironments was defined by the chemical composition of the HS polysaccharides. We present a method for the generation of hydrogel-based GAG microarrays for analysis of growth factor-mediated signaling in murine embryonic stem cells (ESCs). We hypothesized that arraying HS-protein conjugates on polyacrylamide hydrogels would generate stable ECM-mimetic microenvironments with the capacity to bind FGF2 and influence ESC signaling. The core hypothesis was that the selectivity of FGF2 binding and activity in these microenvironments would be defined by the chemical composition of the HS polysaccharides.

Methodological Details
For our cell model, we chose murine ESCs lacking the expression of Exostosin 1 (Ext1), which is a glycosyl transferase responsible for the assembly of HS chains. The Ext1 -/-ESCs lack cell surface HS structures and are unable to engage a range of HS-dependent growth factors, including FGF2. These mutant ESCs are ideally suited to isolate the effects of the arrayed GAGs on FGF2 signaling from those of endogenous HS structures. After screening several common surface passivation strategies for array construction, we found that a thin poly(acrylamide) hydrogel deposited on glass and spotted with a solution of gelatin (500 µg/mL) in PBS best supported ESC growth in well-separated colonies over 6 days. The gelatin, a commonly used substrate for murine ESC culture, was loaded into the hydrogel in its dehydrated form, which allowed the protein to enter and become entrapped within the crosslinked polymer network. To test whether GAG polysaccharides may similarly be arrayed and retained, we spotted the dry acrylamide substrates with gelatin solutions (500 µg/mL) in PBS buffer supplemented with increasing concentrations of heparin (12 kDa) as a model HS glycan. We also included conditions where the heparin was crosslinked via its carboxylic acid groups activated in the form of N-hydroxysuccinimide (NHS) esters to the solvent-exposed lysine residues in gelatin. The heparin was activated by treatment with NHS in HEPES buffer (100 mM, pH = 7.4) in the presence of the coupling reagent, 1-ethyl-3-(3-dimethylaminopropyl)carbodiimide (EDC), at 4°C for 18 hours. The activated heparin was then purified by size exclusion on a PD10 column to remove small molecule reagents and byproducts. We targeted low levels of crosslinking to promote the retention of the GAG in the hydrogel network without compromising its growth factor-binding ability. The quantitative crosslinking target was low levels of approximately 15% carboxylic acid crosslinks per chain. We arrayed a panel of chondroitin sulfate, dermatan sulfate, and hyaluronic acid GAGs as well as heparin polysaccharides chemically treated to selectively remove their 6-O-, 2-O-, and N-sulfates. The N-desulfated heparin was capped as acetamides (NAc-Hep) to better represent native HS structures. The array was then probed with FGF2, a CS-specific antibody (CS56), and the hyaluronic acid binding protein (HABP) to assess the preservation of the protein-binding specificities.

Procedures And Architectures
To establish whether the array format is suitable for directly assessing changes in stem cell signaling, we chose to examine the activation of the MAPK pathway in response to stimulation with exogenous FGF2. The requirement for HS in the formation of a signaling complex between FGF2 and its receptor, FGFR, and the well-characterized changes in the phosphorylation status of downstream kinases, such as Erk1/2, were well-established. For the on-array FGF2 signaling assay, Ext1 -/-ESCs (40,000 cells/cm²) were seeded on spots printed with gelatin (500 µg/mL) with or without NHS-crosslinked heparin (500 µg/mL) and grown for 48 hours. The cells were then placed in a fresh serum-free media containing FGF2 (0.5 ng/mL) and stimulated for 15 min at 37 °C. The cells were fixed, permeabilized, and immunoassayed for MAPK activity using antibodies against Erk1/2 proteins and their phosphorylated forms (pErk1/2). Fluorescence from the arrayed cells was detected using a microarray scanner and validated via fluorescence microscopy. The ratios of fluorescent signals corresponding to the phosphorylated-ERK1/2 (pERK, green) and total ERK1/2 (ERK, red) proteins were used to quantify the signaling response. We used soluble heparin (s-Hep, 5 µg/mL) as a positive control and benchmark in our assay. We performed fluorescent microscopy imaging and ImageJ analysis to confirm the co-localization of the pERK and ERK signals and to validate our quantification scheme. The remaining bound cells were cultured for additional 24 hours in the absence of serum.

Key Results
Both immobilization strategies resulted in a dose-dependent FGF2 binding, with the NHS-crosslinked heparin providing ~5-to 10-fold higher signal. After an initial decrease in binding activity during the first 18 hours, the heparin arrays remained stable with ~40% of FGF2 binding activity retained after 48 hours. Using the NHS-crosslinking strategy, we arrayed a panel of CS, DS, and HA GAGs, where FGF2 bound most strongly to the fully sulfated heparin. Removal of 6-O-, 2-O-, and N-sulfates resulted in progressive loss of FGF2 binding activity, consistent with the requirements of 2-O- and N-sulfation for FGF2 binding to HS. While ERK1/2 protein levels were similar across all conditions, only Ext1 -/-ESCs stimulated with FGF2 in the presence of immobilized or soluble heparin showed a significant increase in Erk1/2 phosphorylation. FGF2 stimulation of Ext1 -/-ESCs grown on gelatin spots containing increasing amounts of immobilized heparin (i-Hep, 0-500 µg/mL) showed a heparin dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation. CS56 and HABP proteins exhibited high specificity for CS and HA, respectively. Seeding the stem cells too sparsely (20,000 cells/cm²) resulted in slow growth and irregular colony formation. Too high seeding density (100,000 cells/cm²) led to rapid proliferation resulting in spot overgrowth and cell detachment. The intermediary seeding density (40,000 cells/cm²) produced consistent monolayers of Ext1 -/-ESCs that retained high levels of Oct4 expression and showed no obvious signs of differentiation.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The crosslinking facilitated the retention of the polysaccharides on the array during cell culture without altering the protein-binding specificity of the polysaccharides. The immobilized GAG structures were able to facilitate FGF-mediated activation of signaling events in live embryonic stem cells, which could be detected and quantified using immunofluorescence. We observed somewhat lower levels of MAPK activity on the arrayed heparin compared to its soluble form. This may be due to a more limited accessibility of the immobilized heparin to only a subset of FGFRs localized to the point of cell contact with the array. The array offers a convenient platform to systematically analyze biological activities of extracellular GAGs in stem cell signaling. This platform could accelerate the development of new bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based therapeutic applications by capitalizing on the rapidly expanding repertoire of synthetic and recombinant glycosaminoglycan structures.

Contradictions And Limitations
We observed somewhat lower levels of MAPK activity on the arrayed heparin compared to its soluble form. After an initial decrease in binding activity during the first 18 hours, the heparin arrays remained stable. The intermediary seeding density produced consistent monolayers, but the seeding density was a key optimization step. We used soluble heparin as a positive control and benchmark, and the arrayed activity was slightly lower than the soluble benchmark. The crosslinking was targeted to low levels of approximately 15% carboxylic acid crosslinks per chain to balance retention with binding. The paper does not specify the exact number of repeats or the exact polymer molecular weight of the acrylamide. The paper does not report the random seed or training/test splits, which are not applicable to this experimental assay but would be relevant for machine-learning-based downstream analysis. The exact concentrations of the PBS buffer components or the exact molecular weight of the gelatin protein are not reported. There is no demographic information provided as the model system is murine ESCs. The number of independent biological replicates and the exact significance test used are not reported.

Claims
NHS-activated crosslinking stabilizes GAG polysaccharides on hydrogel arrays and preserves their protein-binding specificities without compromising binding capacity. The NHScrosslinked heparin provided ~5-to 10-fold higher signal than physisorption. FGF2 binding to heparin showed the greatest preference for fully sulfated heparin. Removal of 6-O-, 2-O-, and N-sulfates resulted in progressive loss of activity. CS56 and HABP proteins exhibited high specificity for CS and HA. The crosslinking facilitated the retention of the polysaccharides on the array during cell culture without altering the protein-binding specificity of the polysaccharides. After an initial decrease in binding activity during the first 18 hours, the heparin arrays remained stable. The heparin arrays remained stable with ~40% of FGF2 binding activity being retained after 48 hours. This allows the array to serve as a reliable platform for systematically analyzing biological activities of extracellular GAGs in stem cell signaling.
The Ext1 -/- mutant ESC line isolates the effect of the engineered glycan microenvironment on FGF2 signaling from endogenous cell surface HS. Ext1 -/-ESCs lack cell surface HS structures and are unable to engage a range of HS-dependent GFs, including FGF2. These mutant ECS are ideally suited to isolate the effects of the arrayed GAGs on FGF2 signaling from those of endogenous HS structures. The cells were fixed and immunoassayed for MAPK activity using antibodies against Erk1/2 proteins and their phosphorylated forms. We observed somewhat lower levels of MAPK activity on the arrayed heparin compared to its soluble form. The platform enables direct, rapid profiling of extracellular GAG activity on growth factor signaling in live embryonic stem cells.

Data And Code Availability
No public data repository or code availability is reported in the paper.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Seeding density was tested at 20,000 cells/cm², 40,000 cells/cm², and 100,000 cells/cm², with 40,000 cells/cm² producing the optimized monolayers. Heparin immobilization was compared across physisorption and NHS-activated crosslinking. The crosslinking level was kept at ~15% carboxylic acid crosslinks per chain.

Ethical Considerations
No statement regarding ethical approval or IRB review is reported in the paper.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 depicts the cellular microarray approach to interrogate ECM-mediated cell signaling, including the structural pattern of GAGs. Figure 2 shows the generation and characterization of the hydrogel GAG arrays, including FGF2 binding and retention, and GAG selectivity. Figure 3 displays the optimized seeding conditions and colony growth. Figure 4 shows the FGF2 stimulation and ERK1/2 phosphorylation activity across heparin conditions.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a hydrogel-supported stem cell microarray platform for the direct, rapid, and multiplexed profiling of extracellular glycosaminoglycan activity on growth factor signaling in live embryonic stem cells. 2. The strongest evidence is that FGF2-induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation is heparin dose-responsive and selectively increases only in Ext1 -/-ESCs in the presence of immobilized or soluble heparin, with fully sulfated heparin showing the strongest binding. 3. The future path is to accelerate the development of new bioactive glycomaterials for stem cell-based therapeutic applications by systematically analyzing the biological activities of the rapidly expanding repertoire of synthetic and recombinant GAG structures.

summary.title: Robust Brain State Decoding using Bidirectional Long Short Term Memory Networks in functional MRI
summary.authors: Anant Mittal (University of Maryland); Priya Aggarwal (Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology); Luiz Pessoa (University of Maryland); Anubha Gupta (Indraprastha Institute of Information Technology)
summary.executive_summary:
This paper investigates decoding brain states from functional MRI (fMRI) data using a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) network. Decoding brain states of cognitive processes is valuable for Brain-computer interface (BCI) applications. fMRI is useful for determining cognitive or perceptual states, such as motor functions or attention shifts. However, the blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) response is not synchronized with stimuli presentation due to time-lag, typically necessitating time-point adjustment based on estimated delay. The paper notes that while conventional LSTMs encode past context, they do not encode future context, which is crucial for BOLD dynamics.

The authors propose a Bi-LSTM framework that captures information from both past and future time-instances, allowing for brain state prediction at every time-instance without time-delay adjustment. The framework was evaluated on Human Connectome Project (HCP) working memory data, where participants performed a "2-back" vs. "0-back" task. The dataset included N=400 participants from the N=1200 HCP data release. Data were preprocessed with field-map distortion correction and motion regression (6 translation parameters) via 3dDeconvolve with "ortvec" and "polort" options. Cortical data was parcellated into 360 cortical regions of interest (ROIs), yielding a 405 time-points sequence structured as a 360 by 405 2D-tensor. The brain states totaled S=9.

The Bi-LSTM was built with two hidden layers, 256 hidden activations each, and S=9 neurons; forward and backward activations were merged via vector concatenation (bi-LSTM-c), element-wise addition (bi-LSTM-a), or averaging (bi-LSTM-µ). The model was implemented in Keras on a GeForce GTX 980 GPU with batch 32, ADAM optimizer, learning rate 0.001, 100 epochs, no early stopping, and dropout 0.3. Imbalanced classes were handled via Sklearn's "compute_class_weight" routine. The model was compared to a unidirectional LSTM and a three-layer feed-forward Neural Network (ff-NN).

Experimental results showed that the Bi-LSTM-c achieved 0.84 ± 0.02 accuracy, while the unidirectional LSTM achieved 0.66 ± 0.18, an 18% improvement. The highest misclassification was in the "Others" class, and the model confused "body" and "tools" stimuli. The authors conclude that the Bi-LSTM works without hard-coded delay adjustment and that immediate future samples offer useful information. They acknowledge fixed window length and residual class imbalance as limitations. The bibliography is omitted, rendering citation analysis unavailable.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates decoding brain states from functional MRI (fMRI) data using a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) network. Decoding brain states of cognitive processes is valuable for Brain-computer interface (BCI) applications. fMRI is useful for determining cognitive or perceptual states, such as motor functions or attention shifts. However, the blood oxygen level dependent (BOLD) response is not synchronized with stimuli presentation due to time-lag, typically necessitating time-point adjustment based on estimated delay. The paper notes that while conventional LSTMs encode past context, they do not encode future context, which is crucial for BOLD dynamics.

The authors propose a Bi-LSTM framework that captures information from both past and future time-instances, allowing for brain state prediction at every time-instance without time-delay adjustment. The framework was evaluated on Human Connectome Project (HCP) working memory data, where participants performed a "2-back" vs. "0-back" task. The dataset included N=400 participants from the N=1200 HCP data release. Data were preprocessed with field-map distortion correction and motion regression (6 translation parameters) via 3dDeconvolve with "ortvec" and "polort" options. Cortical data was parcellated into 360 cortical regions of interest (ROIs), yielding a 405 time-points sequence structured as a 360 by 405 2D-tensor. The brain states totaled S=9.

The Bi-LSTM was built with two hidden layers, 256 hidden activations each, and S=9 neurons; forward and backward activations were merged via vector concatenation (bi-LSTM-c), element-wise addition (bi-LSTM-a), or averaging (bi-LSTM-µ). The model was implemented in Keras on a GeForce GTX 980 GPU with batch 32, ADAM optimizer, learning rate 0.001, 100 epochs, no early stopping, and dropout 0.3. Imbalanced classes were handled via Sklearn's "compute_class_weight" routine. The model was compared to a unidirectional LSTM and a three-layer feed-forward Neural Network (ff-NN).

Experimental results showed that the Bi-LSTM-c achieved 0.84 ± 0.02 accuracy, while the unidirectional LSTM achieved 0.66 ± 0.18, an 18% improvement. The highest misclassification was in the "Others" class, and the model confused "body" and "tools" stimuli. The authors conclude that the Bi-LSTM works without hard-coded delay adjustment and that immediate future samples offer useful information. They acknowledge fixed window length and residual class imbalance as limitations. The bibliography is omitted, rendering citation analysis unavailable.

Research Context
Decoding brain states is valued for Brain-computer interface (BCI) applications. fMRI is helpful in determining person's cognitive or perceptual state. Previous decoding methods used massive univariate analysis. Multivariate analysis integrates information across the spatial domain. Recent advances in time-sensitive machine learning models are attracting attention. LSTMs have shown to perform better than conventional decoding models. BOLD response is not considered to be synchronized with stimuli. BOLD latency usually requires time-point adjustment. The temporal context from future is also important for BOLD dynamics. Conventional LSTM models do not encode future context. Bidirectional LSTM acquires past and future time-instances. This allows explicit modeling of BOLD dynamics without delay adjustment.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central RQ is whether Bi-LSTM decodes brain states better than unidirectional LSTM. The central hypothesis is that explicit future context improves accuracy. The predicted outcome is Bi-LSTM will be more robust and require no delay adjustment. The hypothesis is validated by comparing accuracy on a standard dataset. A secondary prediction is the Bi-LSTM will handle temporal dependencies without adjustment. The paper predicts Bi-LSTM will perform better than its unidirectional counterpart. Accuracy will drop on the 'Others' class due to class distribution. The Bi-LSTM architecture will use past and future hidden activations.

Methodological Details
The study used task fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP). They randomly selected N=400 participants from the N=1200 data release. The data used a working memory task with 2-back vs. 0-back conditions. A control condition was a 0-back task. The task combined category representation with four stimuli. Each participant had data from two runs. Within each run there were 8 task blocks and 4 fixation blocks. Each task block lasted 27.5 seconds with fixation blocks of 15 seconds. Each scan was a 405 time-points long sequence of fMRI volumes. Preprocessing included field-map, functional-structural, and intensity normalization. Motion variables (6 translation parameters) were regressed out. They used 3dDeconvolve with the 'ortvec' option. Low-frequency signals were regressed via 3dDeconvolve with 'polort'. They used cortical data parcellated into 360 cortical regions of interest (ROIs). The cortical parcellation was developed by reference [7]. The region-averaged time-series was the input feature vector. No stimuli-brain-state synchronization was performed to adjust for delay. Fixation blocks were labeled 'others', yielding S=9 brain states.

Procedures And Architectures
The architecture was based on the specifications in reference [12]. Input activations pass through two hidden bi-LSTM layers. Each LSTM cell had 256 hidden activations. A fully-connected layer with S=9 neurons predicted the brain states. They employed inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation. Data from 400 participants was divided into 10 parts. 9 folds kept 360 subjects for development, 1 fold kept 40 subjects unseen. The development set was split into 80-20:training-validation sets. Validation data was generated to tune hyperparameters and prevent over-fitting. Training data was windowed to small overlapping sizes. Window size was w=40 with an overlap of 10 points. The model was implemented in Keras. Training used a GeForce GTX 980 GPU. Batch size was 32 with an ADAM optimizer and LR of 0.001. The model trained for 100 epochs with no early stopping. A dropout of 0.3 was applied in LSTM layers. Imbalanced weights were computed via Sklearn's 'compute_class_weight'. The model compared the bi-LSTM with a unidirectional LSTM and ff-NN.

Key Results
The unidirectional LSTM model overall accuracy was 0.66 ± 0.18. The bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM-c) accuracy was 0.84 ± 0.02. This is an 18% better performance than the unidirectional counterpart. Misclassification was highest for both models in the 'Others' class. The model confused 'body' and 'tools' stimuli.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Bi-LSTM works well without any hard-coded delay adjustment. Immediate future samples carry useful information for BOLD. This shows future context is available and decodable. Future work may involve tuning the window-size and overlap. The cortical regions for body/tools should be studied.

Contradictions And Limitations
Class imbalance still requires more sophisticated handling. The model sometimes confuses body and tools. The authors worked with a fixed window length. The random seed is omitted from the report. The exact number of iterations per epoch is omitted. The precise split for the validation set is omitted.

Claims
The Bi-LSTM decodes brain states 18% better than the unidirectional LSTM on working memory data. The unidirectional LSTM accuracy was 0.66 ± 0.18. The Bi-LSTM accuracy was 0.84 ± 0.02. The Bi-LSTM is 18% better than the unidirectional LSTM. Misclassification was highest for both in the Others class. The model confused body and tools. Temporal context from the future is useful. Bi-LSTMs are superior for decoding dynamic fMRI data.
The Bi-LSTM decodes brain states without the need for hard-coded BOLD time-delay adjustment. The Bi-LSTM works well without hard-coded delay adjustment. No stimuli-state synchronization was performed for delay. Past and future instances allow explicit delay-free BOLD modeling. Previous works required estimated BOLD delay adjustment. BOLD response is typically not synchronized with stimuli. Time-delay adjustment is not strictly necessary with Bi-LSTM. This improves the framework's robustness to latency.
Class imbalance negatively biases brain state prediction toward the 'Others' class. The Others class had many more time-instances. Compute_class_weight was used for imbalance. Misclassification was highest in the Others class. Class imbalance was majorly handled by weighting. More sophisticated imbalance handling is needed. Future work must refine class weighting.

Data And Code Availability
Data came from the Human Connectome Project (HCP). 400 participants were selected from a 1200-person release. Details are at [8], no direct link or code URL provided.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
They compared Bi-LSTM with unidirectional LSTM and ff-NN. The number of layers and units was kept same for comparison. Activation merging types include concatenation, addition, and averaging. A three-layer feed-forward Neural Network (ff-NN) was an ablation. A dropout of 0.3 was used for over-fitting. Inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation was employed. No early stopping was performed.

Ethical Considerations
No ethics statement or IRB approval is reported in the text.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 is a schematic illustration of Bidirectional LSTM. Figure 2 shows mean normalized confusion matrices. S = 9 brain states were decoded.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: Bi-LSTM decodes brain states without hard-coded delay adjustment. 2. The strongest evidence: Bi-LSTM accuracy was 0.84 ± 0.02 vs. 0.66 ± 0.18. 3. The future path: future work may involve tuning the window-size and overlap.

summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a phylogenomic reassessment of the thermophilic, spore-forming genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus, all members of the family Bacillaceae. The study is motivated by the limitations of 16S rRNA gene sequencing in differentiating closely related genera and species, instead advocating for a combination of Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI), Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI), and core-gene phylogenetics to establish taxonomical thresholds. Using whole-genome sequences from 113 genomes available on the RefSeq database, the study identifies 662 orthologous core genes and constructs a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree along with ANI and AAI dendrograms produced via UPGMA clustering. The analysis reveals that the genomes split into two main clades: clade I, which includes all Geobacillus and all Parageobacillus along with some Anoxybacillus species; and clade II, containing the majority of Anoxybacillus species. Clade I is subdivided into three clades: one containing Geobacillus, one containing Parageobacillus, and a third clade that the authors propose should be elevated to a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. Specifically, the authors recommend placing Anoxybacillus tepidamans and a single genomospecies from clade I-c into this new genus. The mean ANI and AAI values suggest the new genus is somewhat more closely related to Parageobacillus than to the other genera. Additionally, the study identifies six CDS unique to clade I-c. The results reveal a taxonomy problem: some Anoxybacillus species, notably A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus, showed inconsistent positioning among the trees and could not be clearly resolved into any existing or the proposed genus. The authors conclude that a broad phylogenetic framework considering closely related species together is essential for constructing a phylogeny and assigning genomic affinities, noting that single-genus assessments can produce incongruent taxonomies. The authors propose numerous taxonomic reassignments, including several Geobacillus strains, reflecting a broader taxonomic revision.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a phylogenomic reassessment of the thermophilic, spore-forming genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus, all members of the family Bacillaceae. The study is motivated by the limitations of 16S rRNA gene sequencing in differentiating closely related genera and species, instead advocating for a combination of Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI), Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI), and core-gene phylogenetics to establish taxonomical thresholds. Using whole-genome sequences from 113 genomes available on the RefSeq database, the study identifies 662 orthologous core genes and constructs a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic tree along with ANI and AAI dendrograms produced via UPGMA clustering. The analysis reveals that the genomes split into two main clades: clade I, which includes all Geobacillus and all Parageobacillus along with some Anoxybacillus species; and clade II, containing the majority of Anoxybacillus species. Clade I is subdivided into three clades: one containing Geobacillus, one containing Parageobacillus, and a third clade that the authors propose should be elevated to a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov. Specifically, the authors recommend placing Anoxybacillus tepidamans and a single genomospecies from clade I-c into this new genus. The mean ANI and AAI values suggest the new genus is somewhat more closely related to Parageobacillus than to the other genera. Additionally, the study identifies six CDS unique to clade I-c. The results reveal a taxonomy problem: some Anoxybacillus species, notably A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus, showed inconsistent positioning among the trees and could not be clearly resolved into any existing or the proposed genus. The authors conclude that a broad phylogenetic framework considering closely related species together is essential for constructing a phylogeny and assigning genomic affinities, noting that single-genus assessments can produce incongruent taxonomies. The authors propose numerous taxonomic reassignments, including several Geobacillus strains, reflecting a broader taxonomic revision.

Research Context
16S rRNA gene sequencing has limited resolution for distinguishing closely related genera and species. DNA-DNA hybridization was once the standard but is less high-resolution than ANI. Average nucleotide identity provides a higher resolution for bacterial genomes. Bioinformatic ANI alone is insufficient; core-gene alignment views vertical phylogeny better. The genera are moderate thermophiles and spore-formers from geothermal and compost sources. ANI measures genome similarity via BLAST and AAI preserves remote homologous protein similarity.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study tests how closely related thermophilic genera group in a broad phylogeny. Taxonomic affiliation should be verified using ANI and multilocus phylogenetic analysis. ANI and AAI are recommended for distant genomes as amino acid similarity is better conserved. Core-gene alignment should provide a better view of vertical phylogenetic relationships. The hypothesis is that combined analysis reveals hidden delimitation problems.

Methodological Details
A total of 113 genomes were selected for phylogenomic metrics including ANI, AAI, and core genes. The dataset used 32 Anoxybacillus strains and seventy-three Geobacillus strains. One representative assembly was included per validly described Parageobacillus species. Additional thermophile genomes from Australia included 31 chromosome-level and 33 scaffold assemblies. The 113 genome assemblies were obtained from the RefSeq database. Chimeric, contaminated, or frameshifted assemblies with suppressed RefSeq status were excluded. The core genome was identified using EDGAR 2.0 software. Geobacillus thermodenitrificans NG80-2 served as the starting reference for core genome discovery. Bacillus subtilis spizizenii TU-B-10T was included in the core gene analysis as an outgroup. Five assemblies with low CDS numbers were excluded to preserve core gene count. One assembly was removed as an exact duplicate of another Anoxybacillus strain. The final core gene set consisted of 662 orthologous core genes.

Procedures And Architectures
Methods followed the reassessment of Geobacillus by Aliyu et al. [36]. A core gene set was identified and compared against all assemblies via BLAST. CDS were concatenated and aligned using MUSCLE. A maximum-likelihood tree was built using the FastTree software package. ANI and AAI similarity matrices were calculated using ani.rb and aai.rb scripts. Both Ruby scripts are publicly available in the enveomics package. Draft genomes were concatenated with 100 N bases introduced between contigs. Similarity values were clustered via the DendroUPGMA UPGMA web server. Trees were plotted using the Interactive Tree Of Life tool. Genes unique to clade I-c were found via relaxed BLASTn alignment. The filtering criteria were 30% identity, bitscore 10, and 1% overlap. CDS for alignment came from Anoxybacillus tepidamans PS2.

Key Results
A core gene set of 662 orthologous genes per genome was produced. The maximum-likelihood tree splits into three groups: the outgroup, clade I, and clade II. Clade I consists of eighty-seven genomes, and clade II consists of twenty-four Anoxybacillus. Clade I includes all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and some Anoxybacillus species. Anoxybacillus sp. EFIL, Geobacillus sp. MMMUD3, and Geobacillus sp. DSP4a have ANI of 97.99, 97.14, and 97.64 respectively. Anoxybacillus sp. CHMUD had the most distant ANI value with 95.03 and AAI of 95.81. Six CDS were found to be unique to clade I-c. The candidate new genus is somewhat more closely related to Parageobacillus. A. tepidamans and one genomospecies in clade I-c are placed in Quasigeobacillus. Two Anoxybacillus species, A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus, showed inconsistent positioning. The two species could not be clearly resolved into any of the three existing genera.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Problems in the delimitation of the genera would not be revealed if each were considered alone. It is essential to consider closely related species together for construction of a phylogeny. When this occurs in the absence of broader phylogenetic assessment, new strains' genus designation becomes incongruent. The candidate new genus content also suggests a closer affinity to Parageobacillus. The evidence supports the need for Parageobacillus to be merged again with Geobacillus.

Contradictions And Limitations
Two species of Anoxybacillus showed inconsistent positioning among the trees. These could not be clearly resolved into any of the three existing genera or the new genus. A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus affinities remain unresolved at this point. The structure of the three phylogenetic trees reaffirms the distinctiveness of the two species in clade I-c. An alternative approach may be to merge these two species with Parageobacillus.

Claims
The authors propose a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov., for clade I-c. A. tepidamans and one genomospecies in clade I-c are placed in Quasigeobacillus. The average ANI and AAI values separate the candidate new genus. The candidates show a closer affinity to Parageobacillus. The three phylogenetic trees reaffirm the distinctiveness of clade I-c. Two Anoxybacillus species showed inconsistent positioning among the trees. The affinities of A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus remain unresolved. An alternative approach may be to merge these two species with Parageobacillus. The candidate new genus is somewhat more closely related to Parageobacillus. If merged, evidence would support merging Parageobacillus again with Geobacillus.

Data And Code Availability
Genomes were obtained from the RefSeq database. Whole genome sequences of two Anoxybacillus, four Geobacillus and one Parageobacillus strains came from an Australian thermophile study. Both Ruby scripts are publicly available in the enveomics package. Data was sourced from the RefSeq database, with an Australian thermophile study providing additional genomes.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Five assemblies with low CDS numbers were excluded from the core gene analysis. One assembly was removed as it was an exact duplicate of another Anoxybacillus strain. Anomalous genome assemblies with suppressed RefSeq status were excluded. The 31 chromosome-level and 33 scaffold assemblies included were assessed together.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the core gene maximum likelihood tree splitting into three groups. Figure 2 shows the two-way ANI UPGMA dendrogram with 114 genomes. Figure 3 shows the two-way AAI UPGMA dendrogram with 114 genomes. Supplementary Table S1 lists the included genomes per strain and assembly. Supplementary Table S2 lists the assemblies removed during core gene discovery. Table 3 shows the two-way ANI and AAI values per pair. Table 4 shows the CDS names, descriptions, and products for the 6 unique genes. Table 5 shows the DNA sequences for each of the 6 CDS unique to clade I-c. Table 7 shows the best hit for each CDS unique to clade I-c.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution: A new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov., is proposed to house A. tepidamans and a single genomospecies. 2. The strongest evidence: Clade I-c contains six unique CDS and its candidates show a closer affinity to Parageobacillus. 3. The future path: Closely related genera must be considered together in a broad phylogenetic framework to avoid incongruent taxonomies.

summary.title: The structural basis for regulation of the glutathione transporter Ycf1 by regulatory domain phosphorylation
summary.authors: Nitesh Kumar Khandelwal (University of Arizona); Cinthia R Millan (University of Arizona); Samantha I Zangari (University of Arizona); Samantha Avila (University of California -San Francisco); Dewight Williams (Arizona State University); Tarjani M Thaker (University of Arizona); Thomas M Tomasiak (University of Arizona)
summary.executive_summary:
The Yeast Cadmium Factor 1 (Ycf1) is an ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter that serves as a critical protective agent in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. It responds to cell stress by sequestering heavy metals such as cadmium, mercury, or lead into vacuoles and transporting the tripeptide glutathione (GSSG), the cell's main non-protein thiol, into the same compartment to maintain redox balance. Because ABC transporters regulate crucial membrane functions like lipid homeostasis and detoxification, Ycf1 is recognized as an attractive bioremediation target. Like other members of the ABC family, Ycf1 is regulated by phosphorylation; approximately half of all human ABC transporters are phosphorylated, and Ycf1 is expected to be regulated by phosphorylation on its intrinsically disordered regulatory domain (R-domain), yet the regulatory mechanism is poorly understood. Previous structural models of human CFTR and Ycf1 showed a mostly disordered R-domain without assigned sequence for the phosphorylation sites, limiting the understanding of R-domain interactions.

In this study, the authors used cryo-EM to determine two inward-facing conformations of endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1: IFwide and IFnarrow. The structures were resolved to 3.4Å and 4.0Å resolution, respectively, and the E1435Q NBD2 Walker B mutant was used to trap these conformations. The structures reveal that the R-domain (residues 901-935) is partially helical (residues 920-929) and is phosphorylated at three positions: S908, T911, and S914, which are confirmed by mass spectrometry and phosphostaining. These phosphorylation sites make extensive contacts with the NBD1 perimeter and the lasso domain through electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions, which stabilize the R-domain/NBD1 interface and are related by rigid body movements between the two states. Importantly, these interactions are nearly constant between the two structures, meaning the regulatory effect is driven by changes in the R-domain conformation rather than by the creation or loss of binding sites. Biochemical assays show that dephosphorylation substantially reduces ATPase activity and increases protease accessibility, indicating that R-domain phosphorylation is required for maximal ATPase activity and that the phosphorylated state is more ordered.

The findings provide a more complete model than previous ABCC structures, which resolved only small R-domain fragments, do not resolve phosphorylation sites, and do not assign sequence. The ordered R-domain position challenges the prevailing model that CFTR activation depends on the release of the R-domain. Instead, the results support a stimulatory R-domain architecture where R-domain phosphorylation drives association with the periphery of NBD1. The R-domain interactions are likened to a transmission 'clutch' that only engages a motor but does not perform work itself. Finally, the structures rationalize how mutations distal from phosphorylation sites contribute to dysfunction and that the binding site of lumacaftor, a clinically used corrector, resides near the R-domain binding site on the NBD1 perimeter.

Research Context
ABC transporters are regulated by phosphorylation; Ycf1 is expected to be regulated by phosphorylation on its R-domain, yet the regulatory mechanism is poorly understood. Previous structural models of human CFTR and Ycf1 showed a mostly disordered R-domain without assigned sequence for the phosphorylation sites. The lack of R-domain sequence assignment prohibits insights into the precise interacting regions. Previous cryo-EM models did not capture an ordered R-domain state with assigned sequence. Earlier structures showed a R-domain that was mostly disordered, limiting understanding of interactions. Cryo-EM of human CFTR and Ycf1 revealed a mostly disordered R-domain without assigned sequence. To date, no structure of an intact R-domain with the NBDs has been determined in any state.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how R-domain phosphorylation regulates the structural state and ATPase activity of Ycf1. It was hypothesized that R-domain phosphorylation induces a change from an unbound/disordered to a bound/ordered R-domain state. The study predicted that phosphorylation would stabilize an ordered R-domain that engages NBD1 and the lasso motif. The authors predicted that phosphorylation is required for maximal ATPase activity. Nonlinear regression analysis was used to generate kinetic parameters for at least three technical replicates. The substrate-stimulated ATPase activity was measured in the presence of oxidized glutathione (GSSG). The concentration of ATP in GSSG experiments was held constant at 1 mM. The basal ATPase activity in the absence of GSSG was subtracted before fitting.

The E1435Q dataset was processed in RELION (3.0 and 3.1) and cisTEM. Drift correction was performed using MotionCor2. The contrast transfer function (CTF) was estimated using CTFFIND4.1. Particle picking used a reconstruction of WT Ycf1 as a reference. Manual particle picking was performed on a subset of micrographs. An initial model was built using the SWISS-MODEL server with 6jb1 as a template. Manual model building was performed in COOT. Iterative real-space refinement and analysis were performed in Phenix. Secondary structure restraints were used extensively, and model building was guided by evolutionary couplings. Modrefiner was used in the early stages of refinement. Isolde was used to optimize model-to-map fit and improve geometry. Molprobity was used through Phenix and as a web service.

It responds to cell stress by sequestering heavy metals such as cadmium, mercury, or lead into vacuoles and transporting the tripeptide glutathione (GSSG), the cell's main non-protein thiol, into the same compartment to maintain redox balance. Because ABC transporters regulate crucial membrane functions like lipid homeostasis and detoxification, Ycf1 is recognized as an attractive bioremediation target. Like other members of the ABC family, Ycf1 is regulated by phosphorylation; approximately half of all human ABC transporters are phosphorylated, and Ycf1 is expected to be regulated by phosphorylation on its intrinsically disordered regulatory domain (R-domain). However, the regulatory mechanism is poorly understood, and previous structural models of human CFTR and Ycf1 showed a mostly disordered R-domain without assigned sequence for the phosphorylation sites, limiting the understanding of R-domain interactions.

    In this study, the authors used cryo-EM to determine two inward-facing conformations of endogenously phosphorylated Ycf1: IFwide and IFnarrow. The structures were resolved to 3.4Å and 4.0Å, respectively, and the E1435Q NBD2 Walker B mutant was used to trap these conformations. The structures reveal that the R-domain (residues 901-935) is partially helical (residues 920-929) and is phosphorylated at three positions: S908, T911, and S914, which are confirmed by mass spectrometry and phosphostaining. These phosphorylation sites make extensive contacts with the NBD1 perimeter and the lasso domain through electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions, which stabilize the R-domain/NBD1 interface and are related by rigid body movements between the two states. Importantly, these interactions are nearly constant between the two structures, meaning the regulatory effect is driven by changes in the R-domain conformation rather than by the creation or loss of binding sites. Biochemical assays show that dephosphorylation substantially reduces ATPase activity and increases protease accessibility, indicating that R-domain phosphorylation is required for maximal ATPase activity and that the phosphorylated state is more ordered.

The ordered R-domain position challenges the prevailing model that CFTR activation depends on the release of the R-domain. Instead, the results support a stimulatory R-domain architecture where R-domain phosphorylation drives association with the periphery of NBD1. The R-domain interactions are likened to a transmission 'clutch' that only engages a motor but does not perform work itself. Finally, the structures rationalize how mutations distal from phosphorylation sites contribute to dysfunction and that the binding site of lumacaftor, a clinically used corrector, resides near the R-domain binding site on the NBD1 perimeter."

summary.executive_summary:
This study investigates the impact of plant growth regulator (PGR) seed treatment and nitrogen (N) fertilization on the germination, structural dry matter yield, and physiological composition of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. The research was motivated by the need to improve forage production under climatic stress and degraded pasture conditions. Using a 2 x 4 factorial completely randomized design, the authors compared two commercial seed types (coated and conventional) across four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL.kg⁻¹) and, in a second experiment, across four N fertilization methods (no fertilization, soil, foliar, and soil + foliar). The PGR formulation consisted of auxin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹), cytokinin (0.09 mg.L⁻¹), and gibberellin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹). Germination was measured under a 12h photoperiod at 28ºC in a Mangelsdorf germination chamber, and plant growth was monitored in a greenhouse. 

Regression analysis of the PGR response revealed a quadratic effect, with the 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ treatment promoting greater germination. Root dry mass peaked at 12.8 mL.kg⁻¹. Leaf and pseudostem dry mass showed a significant interaction between seed type and PGR level: coated seeds performed best at lower PGR levels (8.85-9.57 mL.kg⁻¹), while conventional seeds required higher levels (15.5-18.1 mL.kg⁻¹). Soil N-fertilization consistently yielded higher dry mass for all structures regardless of PGR, but the combination of PGR and soil fertilization maximized results. The use of PGR alone increased chlorophyll a, linked to enhanced photophosphorylation and ATP synthesis. However, PGR had no significant effect on chlorophyll b, carotenoids, or the chlorophyll a/b ratio. Nitrogen supplied via foliar spray increased all chlorophyll fractions. The study concludes that exogenous PGR is a key tool for pasture establishment, with lower PGR levels recommended for coated seeds, and soil nitrogen application as the superior fertilization strategy for structural development and photosynthetic capacity.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the impact of plant growth regulator (PGR) seed treatment and nitrogen (N) fertilization on the germination, structural dry matter yield, and physiological composition of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. The research was motivated by the need to improve forage production under climatic stress and degraded pasture conditions. Using a 2 x 4 factorial completely randomized design, the authors compared two commercial seed types (coated and conventional) across four PGR levels (0, 8, 16, 24 mL.kg⁻¹) and, in a second experiment, across four N fertilization methods (no fertilization, soil, foliar, and soil + foliar). The PGR formulation consisted of auxin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹), cytokinin (0.09 mg.L⁻¹), and gibberellin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹). Germination was measured under a 12h photoperiod at 28ºC in a Mangelsdorf germination chamber, and plant growth was monitored in a greenhouse. 

Regression analysis of the PGR response revealed a quadratic effect, with the 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ treatment promoting greater germination. Root dry mass peaked at 12.8 mL.kg⁻¹. Leaf and pseudostem dry mass showed a significant interaction between seed type and PGR level: coated seeds performed best at lower PGR levels (8.85-9.57 mL.kg⁻¹), while conventional seeds required higher levels (15.5-18.1 mL.kg⁻¹). Soil N-fertilization consistently yielded higher dry mass for all structures regardless of PGR, but the combination of PGR and soil fertilization maximized results. The use of PGR alone increased chlorophyll a, linked to enhanced photophosphorylation and ATP synthesis. However, PGR had no significant effect on chlorophyll b, carotenoids, or the chlorophyll a/b ratio. Nitrogen supplied via foliar spray increased all chlorophyll fractions. The study concludes that exogenous PGR is a key tool for pasture establishment, with lower PGR levels recommended for coated seeds, and soil nitrogen application as the superior fertilization strategy for structural development and photosynthetic capacity.

Research Context
Shortening the soil preparation and planting window reduces the time to recover degraded pastures. Adverse climatic factors limit the duration for recovering degraded pastures. Greater seed efficiency in germination and speed of emergence is necessary. Management practices are essential to improve herbage production using favorable climatic conditions. Plant growth promoters act on effects similar to phytohormones. Phytohormones (auxins, gibberellins and cytokinins) regulate plant homeostasis. PGRs can potentiate plant performance in stress-prone environments. High levels of active principle per area are an uneconomical pasture management tool. Low concentrations of gibberellin of 5-10 g.ha -1 positively affect forage yield. Nitrogen expands the plant lifecycle and increases growth rates. Nitrogen is indispensable in amino acids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Soil nitrogen fertilization on degraded pasture increases water use efficiency.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to evaluate the effect of PGR and nitrogen fertilization on Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. Growth is assessed through germinative characteristics, dry matter yield, and physiological composition. The central hypothesis is that exogenous hormones increase the development of plant tissues. The authors predict higher germination and mass production with plant growth regulators. The hypothesis is that soil fertilization maximizes photosynthetic processes and growth rates. The authors predict a quadratic relationship between growth regulator levels and germination. The hypothesis is that coated seeds will show greater performance than conventional seeds. The authors predict an interaction between PGR and nitrogen fertilization on dry mass production.

Methodological Details
Experiments took place between June and September 2017 in Itapetinga-BA. The study used the Forage and Pasture Research Center and LAFIEP. Germination occurred in a Mangelsdorf germination chamber under a 12h photoperiod. Germination temperature was maintained at 28ºC. Each pot received eight liters or 12 kg of dry soil. Soil was collected at 0-20 cm depth, disintegrated, and sieved. A 2 x 4 factorial scheme was used in a completely randomized design. Two commercial seed types were compared: coated and conventional. PGR levels were 0, 8, 16, and 24 mL.kg⁻¹ of seed. PGR consisted of auxin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹), cytokinin (0.09 mg.L⁻¹), and gibberellin (0.05 mg.L⁻¹). Twenty-five seeds were used per replicate with four replicates per treatment. Thirty-two cells per replicate were used for initial growth assessments. Sterilized coconut residue was used to maintain constant humidity. Eight treatments with four plants per replicate totaling 32 experimental units were used. Standardization cut adopted an average residue height of 15 cm. Fertilization rates were 75 kg.ha -1 N and 3 L.ha -1 foliar. The foliar fertilizer composition is listed in Table 1.

Procedures And Architectures
Seed imbibition occurred for approximately two hours before wrapping in moist filter paper. Growth and development were evaluated in a greenhouse after seed treatment. Area productivity was estimated using 12 kg of dry soil. Daily germination counts were performed for 14 days to calculate GSI. Whole-plant yield was determined at the end of the experimental period. Roots, stems, and leaves were desiccated to find fresh and dry mass. The third fully expanded leaf was collected at 10 a.m. for pigment analysis. An aliquot of 200 mg fresh mass was prepared with 5 mL dimethyl sulfoxide. Pipments were quantified using absorption spectrophotometry at three wavelengths. Data were analyzed using the MIXED procedure of SAS with P ≤ 0.05. Tukey test compared means with significance at P ≤ 0.05. Single-degree-of-freedom contrast statements analyzed PGR linear and quadratic effects. The maximum point was estimated from a regression equation.

Key Results
PGR interaction was non-significant for germination and germination speed index. A quadratic effect of growth regulator levels existed regardless of seed type. The 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ treatment promoted greater germination. Coated seeds had higher germination and GSI than conventional seeds. Root dry mass production was not affected by seed type. The 12.8 mL.kg⁻¹ treatment resulted in higher root dry mass. An interaction existed between seed type and PGR for leaf and pseudostem mass. Coated seeds had higher mass at lower PGR levels (8.85-9.57 mL.kg⁻¹). Conventional seeds required higher PGR for leaf and pseudostem mass (15.5-18.1 mL.kg⁻¹). Leaf and pseudostem mass did not differ between seed types at high PGR. PGR and nitrogen fertilization interacted significantly for leaf, stem, shoot, and root mass. Soil fertilization yielded higher yields regardless of PGR levels. PGR reduced mass when combined with multiple fertilization but not in isolation. PGR increased root mass only when combined with multiple fertilization. No PGR interaction existed for chlorophyll a, b, total, carotenoids, and a/b ratio. PGR significantly affected only chlorophyll a. Nitrogen methods influenced chlorophyll a, b, and carotenoids. Coated seeds showed higher germination but lower mass efficiency at high PGR.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Hormones change balance and biosynthesis, increasing auxin, cytokinin, and gibberellin. Gibberellin increases germinative gene expression and overcomes mechanical barriers. Gibberellin reduces abscisic acid to promote germination. Seed coating protects against damage and provides nutrients to the embryo. Auxin in the PGR formulation increases rhizogenesis through cell multiplication. PIN proteins enable intracellular auxin transport. Conventional seeds required higher PGR due to reduced hormone use efficiency. Soil nitrogen drives photosynthesis by stimulating root-absorbed amino acids and proteins. Chlorophyll a drives the photophosphorylation and ATP synthesis processes. Auxins may indirectly influence chloroplast movement via homeostasis disorder. PGR acts as plant herbicides by blocking photosynthetic electron flux. Foliar nitrogen promotes cytokinin synthesis and delays senescence.

Contradictions And Limitations
The paper reports a quadratic PGR-germination relationship but lacks a regression table. PGR levels optimized for mass (15.5-18.1 mL.kg⁻¹) contrast with germination optima. Nitrogen effect on chlorophyll was foliar-only, leaving soil effect unclear. No full bibliography is provided, rendering citations unverifiable. The interaction between auxins and cytokinins is described but not experimentally disentangled. The study assumes 15 cm standardization, which might introduce cutting artifact.

Claims
Plant growth regulators (PGR) increase germination and structural mass but are optimized at low to intermediate levels. The 10.3 mL.kg⁻¹ treatment promoted greater germination. The 12.8 mL.kg⁻¹ treatment resulted in higher root mass. Lower levels (8.85-9.57 mL.kg⁻¹) optimized structural mass for coated seeds. Coated seeds showed greater performance only at lower regulator levels. Conventional seeds required significantly higher levels to respond. PGR should be applied carefully, with coated seeds using lower doses. Higher concentrations are uneconomical and may reduce forage mass.
Soil nitrogen fertilization drives mass production and chlorophyll, but foliar application is required for increased chlorophyll.  Soil fertilization yielded higher dry mass regardless of PGR. Foliar nitrogen increased production of all chlorophyll fractions. PGR had no significant effect on chlorophyll b, total, carotenoids, or ratio. The PGR and N interaction was significant for mass but not chlorophyll. Soil fertilization is the superior strategy for structural growth.
The interaction between seed type and growth regulator dictates structural efficiency. An interaction existed between seed type and regulator on leaf mass. Coated seeds had higher germination and GSI. No interaction existed for germination or germination speed index. Root mass was not affected by seed type. Pure seeds with higher embryo quality are more efficient.

Data And Code Availability
No data or code repository was disclosed in the text. The study utilized the MIXED procedure of SAS but reports no seed version. The source material is restricted to the provided text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
No random seeds were reported. PGR levels were fixed across treatments. The quadratic effect was estimated by regression.

Ethical Considerations
No statement regarding animal or human ethics is provided. No ethical approval numbers are cited.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 reports the composition of the foliar spray. Table 2 reports germination and GSI by seed type. Table 3 reports root dry mass production. Table 4 reports leaf and pseudostem mass. Table 5 reports the interaction of PGR and fertilization on mass. Table 6 reports chlorophyll and carotenoid content. Figure 1 illustrates the greenhouse environment.

Three Takeaways
1. PGR increases germination and tissue formation but optimized at low/intermediate levels. 2. Soil N-fertilization is superior for structural mass and chlorophyll. 3. Lower PGR levels and coated seeds offer higher efficiency for pasture establishment.

summary.title: Impact of Chronic Total Occlusion Lesion Length on Six-month Angiographic and 2-year Clinical Outcomes
summary.authors: Jihun Ahn; Byounggeol Choi; Yeon Choi; Jae Kyeong Byun; Ahmed Mashaly; Kareem Abdelshafi; Yoonjee Park; Young Jang; Woohyeun Kim; Eunjin Park; Jin Oh Na; Cheol Ung Choi; Eungju Kim; Chang Gyu Park; Hongseog Seo; Dongjoo Oh; Jinsu Byeon; Sangho Park; Hyeyon Yu; Seung-Woon W Rha
summary.field_subfield: Cardiovascular Medicine; Interventional Cardiology; Chronic Total Occlusion (CTO)
summary.executive_summary: This prospective observational study investigated whether the length of a chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion affects six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes in patients successfully treated with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) using drug-eluting stents (DES). The researchers enrolled 235 consecutive CTO patients who underwent successful PCI with DES between November 2004 and October 2010 at the Cardiovascular Center of Korea University Guro Hospital. Patients were divided into a long CTO group (angiographic lesion length ≥30mm, n=159) and a short CTO group (angiographic lesion length <30mm, n=76). The study aimed to address the knowledge gap concerning whether CTO lesion length significantly impacts outcomes in the DES era. The primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis at 6-12 months; secondary angiographic endpoints included in-stent restenosis (ISR), mean diameter stenosis (DS), minimal luminal diameter (MLD), and late loss (LL). The primary clinical endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), a composite of total death, recurrent myocardial infarction (MI), and revascularization (PCI and CABG). The study reported similar baseline clinical characteristics between groups, except that prior PCI was more frequent in the long CTO group and bifurcation lesions more frequent in the short CTO group. Procedural and in-hospital complications were similar, except for more frequent intimal dissection in the long CTO group. At two years, the incidence of death (total, cardiac), MI, and MACE was similar between groups, but the long CTO group had significantly higher rates of repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p < 0.05) and target vessel revascularization (TVR) (16.3% vs. 6.5%, p < 0.05). Multivariate analysis identified long CTO as an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53-11.9, p = 0.006). At six months, angiographic outcomes, including ISR (33.3% vs. 26.6%), binary restenosis (19.1% vs. 8.8%), and late loss (0.65 ± 0.82 mm vs. 0.46 ± 0.56 mm), were statistically similar between groups. The authors concluded that while long CTO increases the risk of repeat PCI and TVR, the overall safety profile and major clinical outcomes remained similar to the short CTO group in the DES era. The study is limited by its single-center prospective design, non-randomized structure, small sample size, lack of routine follow-up angiography, and a relatively short two-year follow-up period, requiring a larger long-term study to reach a final conclusion.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This prospective observational study investigated whether the length of a chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion affects six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes in patients successfully treated with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) using drug-eluting stents (DES). The researchers enrolled 235 consecutive CTO patients who underwent successful PCI with DES between November 2004 and October 2010 at the Cardiovascular Center of Korea University Guro Hospital. Patients were divided into a long CTO group (angiographic lesion length ≥30mm, n=159) and a short CTO group (angiographic lesion length <30mm, n=76). The study aimed to address the knowledge gap concerning whether CTO lesion length significantly impacts outcomes in the DES era. The primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis at 6-12 months; secondary angiographic endpoints included in-stent restenosis (ISR), mean diameter stenosis (DS), minimal luminal diameter (MLD), and late loss (LL). The primary clinical endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), a composite of total death, recurrent myocardial infarction (MI), and revascularization (PCI and CABG). The study reported similar baseline clinical characteristics between groups, except that prior PCI was more frequent in the long CTO group and bifurcation lesions more frequent in the short CTO group. Procedural and in-hospital complications were similar, except for more frequent intimal dissection in the long CTO group. At two years, the incidence of death (total, cardiac), MI, and MACE was similar between groups, but the long CTO group had significantly higher rates of repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p < 0.05) and target vessel revascularization (TVR) (16.3% vs. 6.5%, p < 0.05). Multivariate analysis identified long CTO as an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53-11.9, p = 0.006). At six months, angiographic outcomes, including ISR (33.3% vs. 26.6%), binary restenosis (19.1% vs. 8.8%), and late loss (0.65 ± 0.82 mm vs. 0.46 ± 0.56 mm), were statistically similar between groups. The authors concluded that while long CTO increases the risk of repeat PCI and TVR, the overall safety profile and major clinical outcomes remained similar to the short CTO group in the DES era. The study is limited by its single-center prospective design, non-randomized structure, small sample size, lack of routine follow-up angiography, and a relatively short two-year follow-up period, requiring a larger long-term study to reach a final conclusion.

Research Context
Successful CTO PCI is linked to improved clinical outcomes compared with failed CTO PCI. It is unclear whether long and short CTO lesions differ in outcomes during the drug-eluting stent (DES) era. Drug-eluting stents and newer devices have reduced restenosis and adverse events. Long coronary artery lesions remain a worse prognostic factor after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Procedural success rate for CTO patients is lower than non-CTO patients. There are no definite answers about CTO PCI outcomes according to lesion length. Longer coronary artery disease is a major predictor of MACE and restenosis after DES.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to determine if CTO lesion length impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes. Researchers hypothesized that adverse clinical outcomes would be more frequent in the long CTO group. The predicted reason was that the long CTO group has worse clinical risk factors such as prior MI. The hypothesis was that newer-generation DES was dominant in the short CTO group. The authors expected higher mortality and angiographic adverse outcomes in long CTO patients. They anticipated that long CTO guide wire passage into false channels would be more frequent.

Methodological Details
The study enrolled 235 consecutive CTO patients from Korea University Guro Hospital. Enrolled patients underwent successful PCI with DES from November 2004 to October 2010. The long CTO group had angiographic lesion lengths of 30mm or more (n=159). The short CTO group had angiographic lesion lengths less than 30mm (n=76). CTO was defined as complete coronary obstruction with TIMI flow grade 0. CTO required an estimated duration of 3 months or more. Duration was determined from the interval since the last episode of angina. De novo lesions were included; in-stent restenosis (ISR) lesions were excluded. Loading doses were 300–600mg clopidogrel and 200–300mg aspirin. Maintenance therapy was aspirin 100mg and clopidogrel 75mg daily. Cilostazol usage depended on physician discretion at 200mg post-loading then 100mg twice daily. Guidewires were used and atheroablative devices were not utilized. Success was defined as <30% diameter stenosis and TIMI grade 2 or higher. Quantitative coronary angiographic parameters were measured at three time points. Primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis at 6–12 months. Secondary angiographic endpoints included ISR, mean diameter stenosis, minimal luminal diameter, and late loss. MACE included cardiac death, recurrent myocardial infarction, and revascularization. Cardiac death was assumed unless non-cardiac death was confirmed. MACE was divided into target lesion revascularization (TLR-MACE) and target vessel revascularization (TVR-MACE). Q-wave MI was defined by new pathological Q-waves in two contiguous leads. Continuous variables used Student's t-test; categorical used χ2 or Fisher's exact test. Data were expressed as mean ± standard deviations. The logistic regression model adjusted for sex, age, hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered significant. Statistical analysis used SPSS version 20.

Procedures And Architectures
PCI was performed with current guidelines using standard techniques. DES was used and the type was decided by the operator. Various guidewires were used to cross the CTO lesion. Simple pre-dilation with balloon was mostly performed. Adjustive balloon dilatation achieved optimal outcome when needed. Quantitative coronary angiographic (QCA) parameters were measured at baseline, immediate post-PCI, and six months. Follow-up at two years was via interview, record review, and telephone contact.

Key Results
The long CTO group included 159 patients and the short CTO group 76 patients. Prior PCI was more frequent in the long CTO group. Bifurcation lesion was more frequent in the short CTO group. Intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. Total death incidence was 3.1% vs 5.2% with a p-value of 0.43. Cardiac death incidence was 1.2% vs 2.6% with a p-value of 0.45. Myocardial infarction incidence was 1.8% vs 2.6% with a p-value of 0.71. Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) incidence was 21.3% vs 13.1% with a p-value of 0.13. Repeat PCI incidence was 18.8% vs 7.8% with a p-value less than 0.05. Target vessel revascularization (TVR) was 16.3% vs 6.5% with a p-value less than 0.05. Long CTO was an independent predictor for repeat PCI with an OR of 4.26 and 95% CI of 1.53–11.9. For TVR, long CTO had an OR of 4.23 with a 95% CI of 1.52–11.8. The data for angiographic follow-up at 6–12 months were obtained for 99 of 159 long CTO patients. In the long CTO group, 45 of 76 short CTO patients (59%) were followed for angiography. In-stent restenosis (ISR) was 33.3% vs 26.6% with a p-value of 0.42. Binary restenosis was 19.1% vs 8.8% with a p-value of 0.12. Late loss was 0.65 ± 0.82 mm vs 0.46 ± 0.56 mm with a p-value of 0.13. The short CTO group vessel diameter was 3.11 ± 0.43 mm vs 2.92 ± 0.42 mm with a p-value less than 0.05.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The long and short CTO groups showed similar angiographic outcomes at six months. The long CTO group had worse clinical risk factors like history of prior MI and PCI. Newer-generation DES was dominant in the short CTO group. Paclitaxel-eluting stents were frequently used in the long CTO group. Procedural complications were similar between the two groups except for dissection. The long CTO group guide wire passage into false channels would be more frequent. In-hospital outcomes were not different between the two groups, supporting procedural safety and efficacy. Newer-generation DES is associated with superior cardiovascular outcomes. The long CTO group had a higher incidence of TVR and repeat PCI, but this did not translate into mortality. Less myocardial viability and previously developed collateral channels may play roles. These factors could lessen the harmful physiologic effect of restenosis in the target vessel. The short CTO group binary restenosis rate of 9.1% was similar to Hoye A et al. Vessel size differences did not affect the angiographic and clinical outcomes significantly.

Contradictions And Limitations
This was a non-randomized, single-center prospective registry, not a randomized study. Baseline clinical, lesion, and procedural characteristics were slightly different between groups. Newer-generation DES was frequent in the short CTO group, while first-generation stents were frequent in the long CTO group. Strict statistical adjustment could not account for unmeasured confounders or analytical bias. Follow-up coronary angiography was not routinely performed in all patients. Follow-up angiography depended on ischemic symptoms or physician discretion. The sample size was relatively small, and the study lacked power to prove angiographic differences. The two-year follow-up period was not long enough to evaluate long-term safety and efficacy. The long CTO group guide wire passage into false channels was predicted to be more frequent.

Claims
Long CTO is an independent predictor for repeat PCI but not for mortality or MACE in the DES era. Repeat PCI was higher in the long CTO group (18.8% vs. 7.8%) with p < 0.05. Long CTO was an important independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26). TVR was higher in the long CTO group (16.3% vs. 6.5%) with p < 0.05. Cardiac death and MI incidence was not different between the two groups. The small sample size limited the ability to prove differences in angiographic events. Follow-up coronary angiography was not routinely performed. PCI in long CTO lesions with DES is similarly safe to short CTO lesions in the DES era. Higher TVR did not translate to mortality, possibly due to less myocardial viability and collateral channels.
The long CTO group had higher rates of intimal dissection and prior PCI, reflecting a more complex procedure. Intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. Prior PCI was more frequent in the long CTO group. Bifurcation lesion was more frequent in the short CTO group. In-hospital outcomes were not different between the two groups. The long CTO group had worse clinical risk factors. Procedural complications were similar between the two groups except dissection.

Data And Code Availability
No specific data or code sharing statement was provided in the text.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A logistic regression model was used to estimate risks with adjustment for multiple factors. The analysis was adjusted for sex, age, hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion.

Ethical Considerations
The study protocol was approved by the Korea University Guro Hospital institutional review board. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 demonstrates baseline clinical and angiographic characteristics. Table 2 shows procedural and in-hospital complications. Table 3 summarizes clinical outcomes for the two-year follow-up. Table 4 lists the predictors for repeat PCI and TVR. Table 5 details the six-month angiographic outcomes. The short CTO group vessel diameter was 3.11 ± 0.43 mm vs. 2.92 ± 0.42 mm.

Three Takeaways
1. Long CTO increases the risk of repeat PCI and TVR without increasing the risk of mortality or MACE. 2. The study is limited by its non-randomized design, small sample size, and non-routine follow-up angiography. 3. Further prospective, larger, and long-term studies are needed to confirm the long-term safety and efficacy profile.

summary.title: Synthesis, Biological Activity and Molecular Docking of New Tricyclic Series as αglucosidase Inhibitors
summary.authors: Hatem A Abuelizz (King Saud University); Azman N I Nor; Iwana (Universiti Teknologi MARA); Rohaya Ahmad (Universiti Teknologi MARA); Anouar El-Hassane (Prince Sattam bin Abdulaziz University); Mohamed Marzouk (Prince Sattam bin Abdulaziz University); Rashad Al-Salahi (King Saud University)
summary.executive_summary: This study synthesizes twenty-five new tricyclic fused pyrimidine derivatives—specifically 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones—to evaluate them as α-glucosidase inhibitors for type II diabetes management. α-Glucosidase inhibitors delay carbohydrate hydrolysis, reducing postprandial glucose; however, available sugar mimetics like acarbose cause gastrointestinal side effects. The researchers modified scaffolds accepted in medicinal chemistry (pyridine, triazole, pyrimidine) to create non-sugar mimetics with potential for reduced side effects. A synthetic route produced 1,2,4-triazole intermediate B, then [1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones 2a-l (45-83% yields), thione 3 (90%), and imidoyl chloride 5. Compounds 6a-d and 6h emerged as active inhibitors; IC 50 values for 6d and 6h were reported as lower than acarbose, with 6h achieving the highest inhibition at 104.07 µM. Molecular docking against α-glucosidase (PDB 3W37) using Autodock showed 6h binding at -10.56 kcal/mol with three hydrogen bonds to Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469. Trp329 was identified as directing the ligand. The study supports the hypothesis that nitrogen-bridged pyrimidine substitution drives activity and proposes a new lead scaffold that differs from carbasugars.
